title: Responsibility, Hope and Solidarity in a Time of Pandemic
intro:
Message of His Beatitude Patriarch DANIEL of the Romanian Orthodox Church on the occasion of the Sunday of Romanian Migrants (August 16, 2020).

The year 2020 was declared by the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church as the Homage Year of the pastoral care of parents and children and the Commemorative Year of Romanian Orthodox philanthropists throughout the Romanian Patriarchate. These two themes, one of homage and the other commemorative, highlight two coordinates of major importance in church life and activity.

The declaration of 2020 as the Homage Year of the pastoral care of parents and children aims at promoting the biblical and patristic guidelines concerning the pastoral care of parents and children and the Christian model of the family, as well as emphasizing the role of Christian pedagogy in contemporary society, stressing that, in the context of the many pastoral challenges, the Church has the responsibility to identify and apply solutions that can help the Christian family in general.

The Christian family has always held a central place in our Orthodox teaching, being the most precious intimate setting for cultivating conjugal, parental, filial and fraternal love. It is a blessing and an icon of God’s love for humanity, a sacred space of the work of the grace of the Most Holy Trinity, oriented toward life and eternal love. In the family, the relationship between children and parents is understood above all from the perspective of man’s relationship with God. Children are born not only for an earthly life, but are also born so that they may become, through Baptism, children of God by grace (cf. John 1, 12‑13) and attain eternal life in the Kingdom of love of the Most Holy Trinity.

The spiritual upbringing of children and young people, through the simultaneous cultivation of freedom and responsibility, is essential in human society. The Holy Gospel and the Tradition of the Church emphasize the importance of the connection between man’s spiritual life and his social activity, between prayer and action, between piety and generosity, between Liturgy and Philanthropy.

Today we live in a world in which materialistic individualism makes its presence felt more and more, and people seek passing material wealth more than the spiritual wealth of faith and of generosity or giving.

At the same time, we are going through an extremely difficult period with regard to health and the value of life, in which a multitude of people are tried by the new epidemic, which has spread globally, a period in which there is great need for prayer and brotherly help, for drawing near to God and for practical solidarity. This period shows us how fragile human life on earth is and, therefore, how great the need is to keep a permanent connection with God, the Source of earthly life and of eternal heavenly life. That is why it is necessary to transform this period of medical crisis into a period of strengthening in faith through prayer and of increasing our love for our neighbors through good deeds. Let us illumine our lives through prayer, through reading the holy writings, through confession and more frequent communion, and also through every good deed of helping the sick, the elderly and the poor.

Today, the Romanian Orthodox Church contributes systematically and substantially to alleviating people’s suffering, both through its liturgical, spiritual and pastoral work and through its social assistance and philanthropic work. Numerous categories of disadvantaged persons—sick people, children from poor families without means of support or whose parents are working in other countries, lonely elderly people abandoned by their families, women who are victims of human trafficking or victims of domestic violence, persons with disabilities, people addicted to drugs or other kinds of addictions, the unemployed, the poor and others—are supported through many social programs and projects carried out at the level of the Romanian Patriarchate. To these are added both the religious assistance provided by chaplains in military units, prisons, hospitals and social institutions, and the social and philanthropic activity of volunteers in the parishes.

On the occasion of the Sunday of Romanian Migrants, we congratulate all the hierarchs and servants of the Holy Altars of the Romanian Orthodox Church abroad for their pastoral and missionary work of preserving and cultivating the Orthodox Christian faith and Romanian spirituality and identity, as preachers of philanthropy in the community and merciful fathers of those in need. We express our gratitude and appreciation to all those who support the pastoral, educational and social-philanthropic activities of the Romanian Orthodox Church, as well as to all merciful and generous Romanian Orthodox faithful. We urge them to continue their generous and beneficial work with great zeal and joy, for the glory of the Most Holy Trinity and for the good of the Romanian people.

With great appreciation and fatherly blessing,

† Daniel
Patriarch of the Romanian Orthodox Church

title: A Letter About the AROLA Conference (September 2020) from Preoteasa Camelia Downie
intro:
January 11, 2016: an important day for our family. No uprooting from one’s ancestral land is easy, whether forced or chosen. Three small children who don’t speak English, though they understand it fairly well, a new school, a new church, a new home and not a single friend. Kind people welcomed us at the airport and at home with the traditional Greek-American pizza. A large apartment, but old and dark as a cave. I sigh for my new home in Bucharest. Whatever made me come here?! Luggage scattered all over the house and not a single friend to pour your heart out to. Then trouble with the immigration office and a letter of denial because I had not shown up for an interview I knew nothing about, for the simple reason that I never received the invitation, which went back to the sender unopened. The logic of the absurd.

Welcome to the contradictory America. We appeal, the decision is overturned and we start all over again. At last we go to the interview with the whole household, armed with all sorts of proof that we are a family with a history and a pedigree, and with photos from our beginnings in Jerusalem in 2001. The interview was a success and we were waiting for the green card. Instead of the green card, a new denial because of the “vaccine waver”. We had skipped a step in the procedure. I let out a long, heavy sigh, grumble at the doctor who had not advised me properly, and think how good it would have been to have someone to ask for advice, someone who had already traveled this road.

I feel more and more alone. Not a single soul in church to speak Romanian with. My Aromanians greet me with “cum eşti?” instead of “ce faci?” I make do with “cum eşti?”, which reminds me of the Romanian of my husband, Fr. John. “Mom, look, a little Romanian! Let’s take him home with us so we can hear some Romanian too,” Grigorie, our eldest son, tells me, cheerful and full of hope, on hearing Romanian spoken by Felicia-Teodora, the mother of David, the little Romanian. Felicia, one of our Romanians from across the Prut, from the Republic of Moldova, young, beautiful, cheerful and with her lovely Moldovan speech, tells me: “Săru-mâna, doamna prioteasă. We’ve also moved here recently…”

But I think about how this scene would have gone if one or two big-hearted ladies from AROLA had said to me in our sweet ancestral tongue, “Welcome, sister in Christ!”, and had also given me an address where I could ease my longing for home with a warm mămăliguță, which my Muntenian soul craves. I go with the children to Worcester, to a Polish store where I was told I could find products from the East, our East, not America’s. I stand in front of the refrigerated display case and two big tears roll down my cheeks. “Why are you crying, Mom?” “Because I’m homesick. I saw tobă and sausages and remembered my mother’s Christmas treats.”

September 20, 2020: the AROLA Congress. I rush to the office to open Zoom so I can answer “present” and not be late. One, two, three ladies appear one after another, our dear Romanian women in folk costume, with headscarves framing their cheerful, gentle faces. Again I remember my mother and my Romania. Yes, but now it is different! Even if two big tears roll down my cheek again, this time they are tears of joy and optimism: I am among my sisters, Romanian women, speaking in our sweet Romanian tongue. I rush to the closet and put on my own ia, a hundred years old.

Before the Congress, someone told me: “It’s no great loss if we’re no longer part of AROLA; they don’t do much anyway.” At the time I had no arguments to tell them they were wrong (I didn’t know much about AROLA’s work). But now I do: AROLA may not be doing much, but for me it has made a huge difference. I found a shoulder to cry on, women full of gentleness and optimistic smiles; I found what I had been missing for five years: I found Romania and the Romanian women my heart longed for. I found the sisterhood, dedication and friendship we rarely find among our American or Americanized friends. Not at the same level of self-sacrifice. A culture centered on the self, foreign to us Romanians, who care even about “the neighbor’s goat”, but at least we care.

And I know something else: these ladies put their heart and love into what they do, even if they “don’t do much”. But is it a small thing to bring joy to a single mother of two little ones, who writes in her note to our sisters, “Heartfelt thanks for giving us a happy Christmas”? Is it a small thing that a young student uses her AROLA scholarship to buy the dress she has been circling in front of the store window for 3 weeks, without daring to tell her mom either that she had been eyeing it or how much it cost? Or the encyclopedia, or the medical atlas “too expensive for Dad and Mom”? And what more can I say about the children of Fr. Nicolae of Valea Plopului? Nothing, except that those who think AROLA doesn’t do much should bow their heads and write a check for the coming Christmas or for the dress in the shop window.

Be warned: you haven’t seen anything yet. Our Romanian women have only just begun! Watch out and don’t stand in their way! They are the daughters of those who once said at Oituz, “They shall not pass,” and who prevailed. They are the daughters of mothers who knelt in prayer knowing their sons and husbands were at war.

With much love and longing for my Romania and my Romanian sisters,
Preoteasa Camelia Downie

title: ROYA Virtual Congress
intro:
Dear ROYA members,

The Romanian Orthodox Youth of America announces the 2020 Youth Congress, which will be held virtually on Zoom on November 14, 2.00 pm – 4.15 pm EST, and November 15, 4.00 pm – 6.30 pm EST. At this Congress we will hold the ELECTIONS for the new ROYA Board and vote on the amendments to the ROYA Bylaws. Our guest speaker will be Fr. Ieremia, the new Abbot of Saint Demetrios the New Monastery in Middletown, NY, on Sunday, November 15, at 6.45 pm.

This Congress is a chance to discuss the work of our organization. We will review the events we held last year, present our plans for the future and discuss some of the problems we face. Delegates will send a report on the youth activities in their parishes, which we will present to everyone.

You can register for the Congress with the following link: https://forms.gle/A1KyxAjjRwZZjjZm7.

This is also the link for Delegate registration.

We are accepting nominations for Board positions here: https://forms.gle/G1YqufHMg65BvNSt5.

You do NOT need to be a parish delegate to nominate someone for a position. The deadline is next Thursday, November 12, at 6:00 pm EST.

**The Congress is open to the young people of our Metropolia, but only delegates will have the right to vote.**

 Delegates, you will soon receive an email with information about the reports you will prepare.

See you soon!

 

In Christ,

The ROYA Board

title: An Ordination to the Diaconate in Philadelphia
intro:
On October 31 – November 1, 2020, His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan Nicolae, Primate of the Romanian Orthodox Archdiocese of the United States and Metropolitan of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas, visited Holy Trinity Parish in Philadelphia, PA. The program of the visit began with Hierarchical Vespers on Saturday evening, October 31, when His Eminence addressed a short homily to those present.

The next day, Sunday, November 1, starting at 10:00 am, the Hierarchical Divine Liturgy was celebrated, during which His Eminence ordained the theologian Petru Bogdan Manea, the church’s chanter, to the diaconate. Serving with His Eminence were Dean Fr. Daniel Ene, secretary of the Eparchial Council and parish priest of Holy Trinity Church in Victor (in the Rochester area), NY, and Fr. Emmanuel Pratsinakis, former parish priest of Saint Thomas Greek Orthodox Church in Cherry Hill, NJ, a close friend of the Philadelphia priests. Naturally, the clergy were completed by the two local priests: Fr. Timotei Avram and Fr. Nicolai Buga, the parish priest.

By receiving the grace of the diaconate, Mr. Petru Bogdan Manea has chosen to serve God and the Church. The very term deacon (in Greek, διάκονος) reminds us through its meaning in the original language (“the one who serves”) that the one who receives the diaconate takes on equally the service of God and the service of people. The diaconate brings to mind the tribe of Levi, which Moses chose to consecrate to religious worship (Ezekiel 44, 11-15). Even though the deacons first chosen by the Holy Apostles were tasked with organizing the Christian agape meals and serving at tables, in the New Testament the term διάκονος, which appears in Philippians 1, 1 and Romans 15, 8, refers to and focuses on the fulfillment of the spiritual duties of these church servants. Service now becomes a privilege, not a burden or a chore: the privilege of helping others to hear, to see and also to respond to the word of divine Truth in the sacramental life of the Church.

In instituting the priesthood and the diaconate, the Savior unites them and grounds them in His own “sending” and ministry: “As the Father has sent Me, I also send you.” The Lord Himself had said earlier that He was “sent,” for “I do not seek My own will but the will of the Father who sent Me” (John 5, 30). The early Church preserved and continued the tradition of diaconal ministry.

As it has come down to us, the rite of receiving the grace of diaconal ministry includes several moving moments, which our new deacon, Fr. Petru Bogdan, also went through. The first is the tonsuring as reader. This takes place in the nave before the beginning of the Divine Liturgy and includes first the ritual tonsure and then the bishop’s reading of the prayer for the tonsuring of a reader (“O Lord God Almighty, choose this Your servant…”), after which the candidate receives the proper vestment, the sticharion, but not before being tested in the reading of the Apostle.

To be made a subdeacon, he then kneels again before the bishop, who reads the prayer “O Lord our God, who through one and the same Holy Spirit…”. As a symbol of the service he wishes to take on in the Church, the future deacon then helps the bishop wash his hands, pouring the water three times and answering the threefold question “How many of you are faithful?” with the words: “We are all faithful”.

The second important moment, which takes place during the Divine Liturgy, is the ordination to the diaconate proper. After the singing of the Axion, the candidate for the diaconate is led to the middle of the church, where he makes three great prostrations. He is brought by the priests before the royal doors, where the bishop stands, and they say: “Command, Most Holy Master, him who is brought before you to be ordained deacon”. Entering the Holy Altar through the royal doors, the candidate is taken by the hands by the priests and deacons, and all of them circle the Holy Table three times, singing the same hymns as at a wedding (though not in the same order). This shows that ordination is nothing other than the marriage of the new servant to the Church of Christ, into whose service he now enters. At the first circling, for example, they sing “O holy martyrs…”, because he now enters the company of those who confessed Christ and served Him, preaching His word. Then the bishop comes to the royal doors and, facing the people, presents the new deacon with the orarion, the cuffs and the large veil, saying three times (in Romanian, Greek and Latin): “He is worthy!” Each time the people answer: “He is worthy!”

There are, of course, other memorable moments. One of them is when the new deacon receives Communion for the first time as a servant of the altar. He has the honor of receiving the Eucharist before all the other deacons serving that day. Then, toward the end, he says the litany: “Let us stand aright! Having partaken of the divine, holy, most pure, immortal, heavenly, life-giving and awesome Mysteries of Christ, let us worthily give thanks to the Lord!”

The Divine Liturgy concluded with a beautiful homily by His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae on the text of the Holy Gospel (Luke 16, 19-31): “The rich man in today’s Gospel did not end up in hell merely because he was rich, but because he did not know how to use his wealth. He considered it exclusively his own; he thought that what he had was his due and that it was not right to share it with others. He ignored others; he did not see sickness, he did not see suffering, he did not see poverty, and he lived a life of luxury. He behaved as though he were the master of this world, and around him he neither saw nor heard: he did not see the poverty and did not hear the cries of those asking for help. He did not know how to see in his wealth the gift of God. Poor Lazarus, whose name means the Lord is my help, both by his name and by the silence presented in the parable, endured with faith and with hope: with faith that this, his sickness and infirmity, was God’s trial for his life, and with hope that this patient endurance of sickness would be rewarded, which happened in the life beyond.”

The celebration ended with a dinner in honor of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, offered by the family of the newly ordained Deacon Petru Bogdan. The priests and faithful of Holy Trinity Parish in Philadelphia, PA congratulate Deacon Petru Bogdan Manea and wish him many years of fruitful ministry in the Church of Christ!

He is worthy! Axios! Dignus est!

Fr. Prof. Nicolai Buga

title: Pastoral Letter of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church for the First Sunday of the Nativity Fast, 2020
intro:
To the most venerable monastic orders, the most reverend clergy
and the most beloved faithful of the Romanian Patriarchate,

Grace, joy and peace from God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit,
and from us fatherly blessings!

 

Most Venerable and Most Reverend Fathers,
            Beloved brothers and sisters in the Lord,

Continuing the tradition begun in 2008, the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church proclaimed 2020 as the “Homage Year of the pastoral care of parents and children” and the “Commemorative Year of Romanian Orthodox philanthropists” in the Romanian Patriarchate.

The two themes, of homage and of commemoration, highlight two coordinates of major importance in the life and activity of the Church. On the one hand, honoring the pastoral care of parents and children aims at cultivating Christian life in the family and promoting Christian education in contemporary society.

On the other hand, commemorating Romanian Orthodox philanthropists aims at promoting Christian philanthropy today as an essential work in the activity of the Church, including by identifying the great philanthropists who, over time, have supported spiritually and materially the social-philanthropic activity of the Romanian Orthodox Church.

Right-believing Christians,

The family has always held a central place in Christian teaching and life, being the most precious intimate setting for cultivating conjugal, parental, filial and fraternal love. Both Holy Scripture and Holy Tradition bear witness that the family is a blessing and an icon of God’s love for humanity, a sacred space of the work of divine grace, oriented toward life and eternal love.

As a fundamental human institution, the family was created and blessed by God in Paradise: “… God blessed them, saying: «Be fruitful and multiply; fill the earth and subdue it!»” (Genesis 1, 27-28). The family was likewise blessed and honored by the Savior Jesus Christ through His presence at the wedding in Cana of Galilee (cf. John 2, 1-11), where He worked the miracle of turning water into wine, thus showing the holy value of the conjugal family for the life of the Church.

The family, blessed by God to cultivate mutual love and to give birth to children, is a source of holy life for every people and for all humanity. In the family, the relationship between parents and children is understood above all in the light of man’s relationship with God.

Children are not born only for an earthly life; they are born also so that they may become, through Baptism, sons of God by grace (John 1, 12-13) and may attain eternal life through faith and good works. This is why the family has often been called the “little church” or the “church at home” (ecclesia domestica), precisely because of its communal character and the atmosphere of holiness it must cultivate. In the family the child learns what parental love means, learns to speak, learns to pray, learns faith in God, and here too, in the family, he learns giving and generosity.

Saint John Chrysostom reminds us that to be a parent it is not enough to give birth to children; one must also give them an education. In this sense, Saint John urges “let us strive to teach our children virtue and to call down God’s blessing upon them, for this is the greatest wealth, which increases our riches every day. Nothing is equal to virtue, nothing is more powerful than it”[1].

Unfortunately, the changes and transformations of recent centuries have led to a weakening of the role and importance of the family in society. In today’s world, parents and children live in a secularized and spiritually confused reality; they face many challenges and crises, such as estrangement from traditional values, poverty, unemployment, alcohol, infidelity, divorce, uncertainty about tomorrow, instability and disorientation, mutual alienation, migration, personal conflicts, etc.

In this context, in which “models” foreign to Christian values are being promoted, we must firmly affirm the holiness of marriage, solidarity within the family and between families, and the dignity of motherhood, fatherhood, sonship and brotherhood, as gifts of God’s love that must be cultivated in a communion of love and shared responsibility.

Knowing the current challenges facing the Christian family, Orthodox priests are urged to help personally, and also to encourage the lay faithful to support materially and spiritually large families, single-parent families and families in difficult situations, including through activities of religious and moral formation for the children of the community.

In order to develop a sound education for a blessed life, the Church must first of all guide parents to devote more time to the education of their children, since children’s character is formed not only through words and advice but also through the life and example of their parents. Clement of Alexandria reminds us that “a happy marriage should be judged neither by wealth nor by beauty, but by the fulfillment of virtue”[2], that is, by the quality of the family’s spiritual life.

Parents are called to live the Christian life through prayer and good works, and also to cultivate love and generosity in the family, after the image of the merciful love of the Most Holy Trinity, so that the family may always be a source of love and joy for the children.

Equally, parents are called to protect life from conception and to teach their children to treasure health as a gift of God that must be defended and cultivated responsibly.

Beloved faithful,

In 2020, the Romanian Orthodox Church commemorates Romanian Orthodox philanthropists. Among the distinctive virtues of the Romanian people, the culture of giving, of self-giving or of kindness represents an important legacy of the values and norms that have shaped the spirituality and culture of the Romanian nation.

The fruitfulness of the Gospel of Christ’s humble and merciful love in the spirituality of the Romanian people has led to the manifestation of love for God and neighbor in concrete forms, expressed either individually and spontaneously or institutionally and systematically.

The Romanian Orthodox Church remembers with gratitude all those who have striven throughout history to develop the Christian culture of giving. Through such efforts, hierarchs, priests and deacons, monastics and laypeople have contributed in an exemplary way to organizing the social-philanthropic work of the Church among the Romanian people.

In particular, we recall the names of some devout and generous Romanian princes, such as Saint Neagoe Basarab (1512-1521), founder of the infirmary (home for the sick) at Bistrița Monastery, Saint Constantin Brâncoveanu (1688-1714), founder of the infirmary at Brâncoveni Monastery, and Prince Grigorie II Ghica, founder of the hospital of Saint Panteleimon Monastery near Bucharest (1757).

In Moldavia, Saint Voivode Stephen the Great built the infirmaries at Putna and Pătrăuți, Prince Constantin Racoviță Cehan took the initiative of founding the Saint Prophet Samuel hospital in Focşani and the Precista hospital in Roman, and Grigorie V founded the Galata hospice in Iași, all of these being in the care of monastic establishments.

Valuable philanthropic work was also carried out by the hierarchs of our Church.  In Wallachia the following stood out: Saint Metropolitan Anthim the Iberian (1708-1716), who in the Foundation Charter of Antim Monastery provided funds for the education of poor children, the burial of the poor, alms for the needy, lodging for strangers, etc.; Metropolitan Grigorie II, together with Prince Alexandru Ipsilanti, was the founder of the first institution for orphans in Wallachia; Saint Hierarch Callinicus, abbot of Cernica Monastery (1818-1850) and Bishop of Râmnic (1850-1868), called by the people “healer of the sick and benefactor of the poor”, founded the infirmary on the Saint George island at Cernica Monastery; Metropolitan Nifon Rusăilă (1850-1875) founded the Nifon Seminary in Bucharest, which offered many scholarships to poor and outstanding students (1875).

Moldavia saw rich charitable activity especially in the time of Metropolitan Anastasie Crimca, founder of the infirmary at Dragomirna (1602) and of a hospital in Suceava (1619), and in the time of Metropolitan Veniamin Costachi (1803-1808, 1812-1821, 1823-1842), who bequeathed all his possessions to be used for philanthropic purposes; also notable were Saint Metropolitan Iosif Naniescu the Merciful (1875-1902) and Bishop Ioanichie Hasan of Roman (1747-1769), founder of the infirmary next to the Precista Mare church in Roman.

The foremost philanthropist hierarch of Transylvania was Saint Metropolitan Andrei Șaguna (1864-1873), who constantly took care to help poor and diligent students. Likewise, Metropolitan Vasile Lăzărescu (1947-1962) contributed substantially to building the Metropolitan Cathedral in Timișoara, gave material aid to the Romanians of Bessarabia and Transnistria and supported financially the Romanians oppressed by the communist regime, while Metropolitan Primate Miron Cristea (1919-1925), the future Patriarch of Romania (1925-1939), initiated the founding of a Seminary for war orphans in Câmpulung-Muscel.

Together with the princes and hierarchs mentioned, many lay philanthropists have distinguished themselves over time through generous charitable deeds.

Among them are the spatharios Mihail Cantacuzino (1640-1716), founder of the Colțea Monastery and Colțea Hospital in Bucharest, Safta Brâncoveanu (1776-1857), founder of the Brâncovenesc Hospital in Bucharest, Gheorghe Boldescu the Clucer (1775-1845) of Ploiești, Theodor Balș (1790-1867) of Darabani, Moldavia, Anastasie Bașotă (1796-1869) of Botoșani, Emanuil Gojdu (1802-1870) of Oradea, Alexandru Mocioni (1841-1909) and Emanuil Ungurianu (1846-1929) of Timișoara, Vasile Stroescu (1845-1926) of Bessarabia, the Golescu Family, Hagi Pop (†1808) and Alexandru Lebu (1835-1918) of Sibiu, Vasile Adamachi (1817-1892) of Iași, Stroe Belloescu (1838-1912) of Câmpina, Iorgu Dumitrescu (1851-1934) of Răcari, Teodor Stănescu (1868-1915) of Bucharest, Anastase Simu (1854-1935) of Brăila, Elena Dalles (1849-1921) of Giurgiu, Dumitru Seceleanu (1857-1932) of Buzău, and others whose faces and work have been highlighted during the Commemorative Year of Romanian Orthodox philanthropists, both through the reports, documentaries and materials broadcast by TRINITAS Television and Radio or published in the religious daily Lumina, and through the various commemorative events organized by the dioceses.

In the twentieth century, in Romania, the institutional philanthropic activity of the Church was brutally interrupted for almost half a century with the installation of the communist regime (1946-1989), precisely at a time when the most popular theme was social assistance itself.

Under communist persecution, the Church was forced to exercise only its sacramental, liturgical and pastoral mission, without carrying out institutional social-philanthropic activities and without being allowed an active presence in society.

Only after 1989, when religious denominations received real freedom to organize and serve in Romanian society, did the Church’s old philanthropic tradition become current again. Today the Romanian Orthodox Church contributes systematically and substantially to relieving people’s suffering, both through its liturgical, spiritual and pastoral work and through its work of social assistance and philanthropy.

At present, the Romanian Orthodox Church has one hospital (102 beds, 2 operating rooms, an ICU, an analysis laboratory), 20 medical-social centers, 55 home care and assistance service centers, 3 neuromotor rehabilitation centers (outpatient), 3 palliative care centers, an ambulance service and 49 homes for the elderly.

Thus, the social-philanthropic work of the Church is inspired by the philanthropic, healing, sanctifying and saving work of our Lord Jesus Christ and at the same time has a profound pastoral dimension, expressing a faith working through generous love and contributing to the cultivation of communion with God and with our fellow human beings, that is, to the development of a culture of giving or generosity.

Beloved brothers and sisters in the Lord,

The Nativity Fast, which begins today, is first of all a time of spiritual preparation, of sanctification of our soul and body through Confession and Communion. It is also an opportunity to strengthen communion, mutual help and works of mercy, which are fruits of the right faith and concrete expressions of our humble love for God and for people.

We are going through an extremely difficult period with regard to the health and even the lives of ourselves and of those dear to us. Many Romanians are afflicted by the new epidemic. Therefore, there is great need for more prayer, solidarity and brotherly help.

That is why we must turn this time of medical crisis into a time of strengthening in faith, through prayer, and of growth in our love for our neighbors, through good works, so as to bear witness “worthily and righteously” to the Gospel of Christ’s love.

In this sense, we address the priests and faithful of our Holy Church with the fatherly exhortation to organize themselves, in parishes, monasteries, deaneries and diocesan centers, to come to the aid of those who are suffering and in need, poor families, families with many children, the elderly and people who are alone, without children or relatives, especially those living in rural areas.

Trusting that this year too you will show Christian generosity and respond with love to our fatherly call in this holy work of charity and help, we thank you for the generosity shown in previous years and remind you of the words of the Lord Jesus Christ: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5, 7).

In closing, we express our gratitude and appreciation to all who support the pastoral, educational and social-philanthropic activities of the Romanian Orthodox Church, as well as to all merciful and generous Romanian Orthodox Christians. We urge them to continue their generous and beneficial work with much zeal and joy, to the glory of the Most Holy Trinity and for the good of the Romanian people.

With great esteem, we embrace you in a fatherly way and share with you the apostolic blessing: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all!” (2 Corinthians 13, 13).

title: ROYA Virtual Congress, November 14-15, 2020
intro:
With the Lord’s help, last weekend ROYA held its Youth Congress. It was a blessing to have with us His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, His Grace Bishop Ioan Casian, and the new Abbot of Saint Demetrios the New Monastery in Middletown, NY, Fr. Ieremia.

The Congress was preceded on Friday evening by an Akathist dedicated to Saint Catherine, the patron saint of our organization, in which several young people took part, together with Dean Fr. Mircea Panciuk of Edmonton, Canada. At the end of the Akathist, Fr. Mircea spoke to the young people about the importance of youth activities, especially at this time when young people are caught up in many concerns. The presence of Christ in their lives at this time is of an importance that cannot be described.

The Congress officially opened on Saturday morning with words of encouragement and greeting from the two hierarchs, followed by the roll call: 38 parish delegates, besides other participants. Next came a presentation of the organization led by Pompiliu Gîrlonța. Bogdan Manga then presented the organization’s activities since the last Congress in 2019.

This was followed by a session in which the delegates discussed the changes to the organization’s Bylaws. The Board presented the amendments in detail and then answered the delegates’ questions. After certain changes were made, such as the provision that the majority of board members be of Romanian origin, the new ROYA Bylaws were adopted by majority vote.

After a short break came the parish reports, with a brief presentation by the board followed by discussion among the delegates about the activities carried out in the respective communities. The second day, Sunday, November 15, continued with the rest of the parish reports, followed by open discussion about the success of certain activities in communities through the involvement of the priest and of many young people.

The next item on the agenda was the presentation of the state of the ROYA organization. The Board described how the ideas proposed at the last Congress had been implemented, and then the challenges ROYA still faces: the distance between parishes, the lack of visibility and the restriction of activities because of the epidemic. Plans for the coming year were also discussed.

Then came the vote for the new ROYA board, which concluded with the following positions:

Pompiliu Gîrlonța, president

Andrei Mărginean, vice-president USA

Ștefan Geleriu, vice-president Canada

Bogdan Manga, secretary

Claudiu Dima, treasurer USA

Metropolitan Nicolae and Bishop Ioan Casian thanked the outgoing board and addressed a message of congratulations and encouragement to the new board, setting as a goal the participation of one young person from each parish at the Youth Congress two years from now. Rareș Răducu, the former president, expressed his gratitude to the board he had worked with over the past two years and presented the gift he will leave to our organization: an icon of the Holy Great Martyr Catherine, painted in Romania by a young woman, with the ROYA logo in the background.

After a short break, Fr. Ieremia of Saint Demetrios the New Monastery began his talk on the theme “He who is holy, let him be holy still”. A true mission cannot be sustained without a permanent inner fire. In this connection, he urged the ROYA members to pray for one another daily, because when two people maintain a spiritual relationship through mutual prayer, God is almost automatically moved toward them. This prayer can be practiced when we carry others in our hearts during the Divine Liturgy, and so he urged the young people to attend as many Liturgies as possible and to approach the Holy Mysteries often, especially in these troubled times. Father concluded his talk with two encouraging messages: the first from Archimandrite Melchisedec, Abbot of Putna Monastery, to perceive not outward appearances but the heart of each person; and the second from the Epistle of Saint Paul to the Ephesians, to cultivate a spirit of peace and love for one another!

We pray to God to help the next two years be full of spiritual enrichment for all the young people of ROYA! Glory to God for all things!

 

Pompiliu Gîrlonța

title: Orthodox Hierarchs in Chicago Prayed for Patriarch Irinej of Serbia
intro:
On Tuesday, November 24, 2020, at the invitation of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas, the Orthodox hierarchs in Chicago celebrated a memorial service for Patriarch Irinej of Serbia at SS. Constantine and Helen Romanian Orthodox Cathedral in Chicago. Present were: His Eminence Metropolitan Nathaniel and Vicar Bishop-elect Timothy of the Greek Orthodox Metropolis of Chicago, His Grace Longin of the Serbian Orthodox Diocese of New Gracanica-Midwest, His Eminence Peter of the Diocese of Chicago and Mid-America (ROCOR), His Eminence Archbishop Paul of the Diocese of the Midwest (OCA), and the host, His Eminence Nicolae.

His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae and His Grace Bishop Longin together served the memorial service for the ever-memorable Patriarch Irinej of the Serbian Orthodox Church. At the close of the service, His Eminence Nicolae recalled the luminous figure of Patriarch Irinej and assured His Grace Longin of the prayers of the clergy and faithful of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas for the repose of his soul.

At the dinner that followed, the hierarchs discussed the pastoral challenges facing parishes during this time of pandemic, expressing the hope that, with God’s help, this crisis will soon be overcome. They expressed the wish that the joy of meeting again would continue on other occasions in the near future.

title: Te Deum for the National Day of Romania in Chicago
intro:
On Tuesday evening, December 1, 2020, the clergy and faithful of Ss. Constantine and Helen Romanian Orthodox Cathedral in Chicago prayed together at the Te Deum service for the National Day of Romania. His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, assisted by the priests of the Cathedral, offered prayers of thanksgiving to God for all the gifts and blessings poured out upon the sons and daughters of the Romanian people throughout the world, as well as for the sacrifice of those who brought about the Great Union of December 1, 1918.

In his address, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae recalled the stages of this process: on March 27, 1918, in Chișinău, Sfatul Țării decided by a majority vote on the Union of Bessarabia with Romania. On November 28, 1918, in the Synodal Hall of the Metropolitan Palace in Cernăuți, the General Congress of Bukovina was held, which decided on “the unconditional and everlasting Union of Bukovina, within its old borders up to the Ceremuș, the Colacin and the Dniester, with the Kingdom of Romania”. Greater Romania was completed through the proclamation of the Union of Transylvania with Romania on December 1, 1918, in Alba Iulia. Among the 1,228 official delegates of the National Constituent Assembly there were also many servants of the Church. Servants of the Church were also elected to the Great Council of the Romanian Nation and to the Governing Council, and the Romanian Orthodox Bishop of Caransebeș, Miron Cristea, the future Metropolitan Primate (1919) and later Patriarch of Greater Romania (1925), and the Greek Catholic Bishop of Gherla, Iuliu Hossu, were elected to the four-member delegation that presented the Act of Union to King Ferdinand.

His Eminence Nicolae then recalled with emotion his participation in the celebration of the Centenary of this event on December 1, 2018, in Alba Iulia. The Centenary celebration followed the events connected with the consecration of the People’s Salvation Cathedral in Bucharest on November 25, 2020, and the Cathedral’s first patronal feast, Saint Andrew the Apostle, on November 30, 2018. The Divine Liturgy at the Reunification Cathedral in Alba Iulia was followed by the Te Deum service and the remembrance of the moments of December 1, 1918, in the Union Hall and on Horea’s Field (today’s Tricolor Square).

His Eminence went on to recall that the history of the making of Greater Romania at the beginning of the 20th century corresponds to the history of the church life of Romanians in America: the founding of the first Romanian Orthodox parishes in Canada (1902) and the USA (1904), the establishment of the first Romanian Orthodox Deanery in Ohio in 1913, and the establishment of the Romanian Orthodox Diocese of America in communion with the Romanian Patriarchate in April 1929. To the honoring of the makers of Greater Romania we should add the honoring of the first Romanian missionaries on American soil. And we should take upon ourselves the continuation of their mission for the faithful of our parishes in the USA and Canada, the descendants of the first immigrants or the new generation of immigrants after 1989.

After the Te Deum service, a group of parishioners led by Fr. Vasile Mureșan presented a program of carols and Romanian patriotic songs.

title: Carol Concert: “Prin colinde românești, diasporei dăruiești!”
intro:
With the blessing of His Eminence NICOLAE, Archbishop and Metropolitan of the Americas, and with the support and blessing of His Eminence TEOFAN, Metropolitan of Moldavia and Bukovina, and of His Eminence CALINIC, Archbishop of Suceava and Rădăuți, the “Saint John the New” Byzantine Choir of Suceava will give a carol concert on Sunday, December 20, 2020, starting at 3pm EDT. The concert is hosted by the “Ion Irimescu” Art Museum in Fălticeni and will be streamed LIVE on the Metropolia’s Facebook page and through the doxologia.ro portal.

The “Saint John the New” Byzantine Choir is made up of graduates and students of the “Metropolitan Dosoftei” Orthodox Theological Seminary in Suceava. It was founded in 2013 with the blessing of His Eminence PIMEN of blessed memory, Archbishop of Suceava and Rădăuți. The conductor and coordinator of the choir is Rev. Prof. Constantin Dan Magdalena, professor of Liturgics at the Theological Seminary in Suceava. Words cannot convey the spiritual joy we felt last year when some of these young people delighted us with the beauty of traditional Romanian carols.

The concert is part of the eparchial MISSION FUND program and aims to raise donations both for the new parishes (missions) of the Metropolia that are going through difficulties and for the pastoral work of the Romanian communities in Latin America, and especially for the restoration of the wooden church of Saints Constantine and Helen Parish in Caracas, Venezuela.

We invite you to fill your hearts with the grace of the Nativity of our Savior on Sunday, December 20, 2020, starting at 3pm EDT, through the Metropolia’s Facebook page: https://www.facebook.com/mitropolia.us.

title: Two Exceptional Cultural Events in January in New York
intro:
In the Romanian-American community of New York, it has long been a tradition to celebrate the birthday of the greatest Romanian poet and journalist, Mihai Eminescu, as well as to mark festively the day of the Union of the Romanian Principalities of 1859, both events taking place in January.

On Sunday, January 17, 2021, at Saints Peter and Paul Romanian Orthodox Church in Astoria, New York, the parish priest, Fr. Theodor Damian, officiated a special memorial service for Mihai Eminescu, Grigore Vieru, Metropolitan Antonie Plămădeală and George Alexe. After the service, the proceedings of the Mihai Eminescu Symposium took place, marking 171 years since the birth of the “Evening Star” of Romanian poetry.

The symposium was held under the aegis of important institutions from Romania and the United States: the Academy of Romanian Scientists (US branch), the Union of Professional Journalists of Romania, the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas, and the Romanian Institute of Orthodox Theology and Spirituality (New York).

Fr. Prof. Emeritus Dr. Theodor Damian opened the symposium by marking the anniversary and associating it with a Sunday memorial service of admiration, given that there is always something new, something that requires interpretation, in Eminescu’s multidimensional work. Appreciation was expressed for the members of the Romanian-American community of New York who take part every year in honoring the genius Eminescu. This year, 2021, although overshadowed by the pandemic that has engulfed the entire planet, did not prevent us from speaking with love and admiration about Eminescu. We say with pride that this year’s symposium is the 28th, a respected tradition worthy of appreciation.

At the opening, the whole audience sang the hymn adopted by our church about Saint Stephen the Great as well as the one dedicated to Bessarabia. The vocal artist Lia Lungu performed, with talent and deep Romanian feeling, songs on Eminescu’s verses from “Rugăciune” and “Codrule, codruțule”.

Choosing you as our Queen,

Lift us up, save us

From the wave that torments us:

Be a shield of strength

And a wall of salvation.

Your adored gaze,

Turn down upon us,

O most pure mother,

And ever-virgin, Mary!

(Rugăciune)

The symposium, on the theme “Eminescu between the Sacred and the Profane,” continued with the presentation of valuable papers by our colleagues. These were:

  1. “Dan Toma Dulciu: Surprises in Modern Eminescu Research” - Fr. Dr. THEODOR DAMIAN, writer, professor emeritus at Metropolitan College of New York, president of the American Branch of the Academy of Romanian Scientists and of the Romanian Institute of Orthodox Theology and Spirituality, New York.
  2. “Eminescu and Genesis” - Dr. NAPOLEON SĂVESCU, president of the “Dacia Revival” International Society and president of the Society of Romanian Physicians of New York. A video clip was shown about genesis and Eminescu’s knowledge of the stars.
  3. “Eminescu Prefiguring the Dialectic between the Sacred and the Profane through a Poetics of Harmony and Complementarity” - Prof. ȘTEFAN STOENESCU.
  4. “Eminescu and the Theory of Relativity” - Prof. VALENTINA CIAPRAZI.
  5. “New Dimensions in the Biography of the Great Romanian Poet” - M.N. RUSU, literary critic and historian, editor-in-chief of the magazine Lumină Lină.
  6. “Between the Terrestrial and the Astral: Love in Eminescu” - Prof. Dr. DORU TSAGANEA.

Next, images of remarkable paintings and sculptures by members of the “Spiritus” Art Gallery, led by the artist VIORICA COLPACCI, were shown on the screen.

The scholarly and artistic works presented at the symposium contributed to a better knowledge of Eminescu’s genius. Let us remember the words of George Călinescu in Istoria literaturii române: “Rarely does it happen that a poet is sealed by destiny to illustrate in himself the joys and sorrows of existence, and that is why for a long time Mihai Eminescu will remain without equal in our poetry.”

***

On the afternoon of January 24, 2021, one week after the Symposium on Mihai Eminescu, the 28th Symposium dedicated to the Union of the Romanian Principalities took place in the same hospitable church in Astoria, New York. Held under the same impressive patronage of the Academy of Romanian Scientists (US branch), the Union of Professional Journalists of Romania, the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas, and the Romanian Institute of Orthodox Theology and Spirituality (New York), the symposium highlighted the historical importance of the Union of the two Romanian Principalities under the scepter of the same ruler, Alexandru Ioan Cuza.

The symposium began with the singing of three hymns: “Deșteaptă-te române”, “Când era să moară Ștefan” and “Basarabie frumoasă”. In his opening remarks, Fr. Prof. Theodor Damian emphasized the important role of the symposium in keeping alive the love of our people and in uniting Romanians for the progress of the whole nation.

The authors and papers presented were as follows:

  1. NAPOLEON SĂVESCU - “The Union, Past and Present.”
  2. Prof. Dr. DORU TSAGANEA - “The Present-Day Significance of the Union of the Romanian Principalities.”
  3. Literary critic and historian, editor-in-chief of the magazine Lumină Lină- N.RUSU - “A Family of Unionists: Iulia and Constantin Aricescu and D. Ciocârdia-Matila.”
  4. Prof. VALENTINA CIAPRAZI - “Europe, For and Against the Union of the Romanian Principalities.”
  5. Prof. Dr. THEODOR DAMIAN - “Saint Callinicus of Cernica and the Union of the Principalities.”

The artist LIA LUNGU, with the talent and sensitivity that characterize her and for which we admire her, performed the song “De la Dunăre la mare”.

Eng. VIRGIL CIUCĂ recited his own poems about Eminescu and about the Union, and a video was shown on the screen in front of the participants with the musical performance, by the “Divina Armonie” Choir, of the verses of the poem “Aduceți Basarabia Acasă”. The music was composed by maestro Valentin Mandric, and the choir was conducted by Marius Firică. This true anthem premiered in the hall of the Romanian Athenaeum in Bucharest.

Bring Bessarabia home,

Ancestral land from the dowry of the Dacians;

Bring Bessarabia home…

With a past from the time of the Thracians.

Bring BESSARABIA home,

The Bessarabians are our brothers by blood;

Bring Bessarabia home,

For without HER a whole country weeps.

The moderator of the two symposia was Prof. Mariana Terra.

In the volume Eminescu - Viața, Zoe Dumitrescu-Bușulenga observes: …“Eminescu desired and achieved a fusion, unique of its kind, with Romanian time and space, taking upon himself the cross of a mission of overwhelming significance: to know and to represent the integral truth of a history and of a spirit.”

We subscribe to this with a deep bow of gratitude and the highest appreciation. And let us remember that Eminescu will exist as long as we and our descendants read and cherish him.

Prof. Mariana Terra

title: Moments of Blessing for the Romanians of Central and Western New York
intro:
The last days of January were an occasion of great joy and blessing for the Romanians living in central and western New York State. His Eminence Metropolitan NICOLAE visited the faithful of Holy Trinity Parish in Rochester, NY and of its daughter community dedicated to the Holy Three Hierarchs in Syracuse, NY.

Saturday, January 30, 2021, the day honoring the Holy Three Hierarchs, began with the Divine Liturgy celebrated by His Eminence Nicolae among the Romanian community of Syracuse, NY, who celebrated their patron saints at the Greek Cathedral of Saint Sophia, host of the Romanian mission for many years. Serving the Divine Liturgy with His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae were Dean Fr. Daniel Ene, spiritual father of the Romanians in this part of America for more than 19 years; Fr. David Smith, parish priest of Saint Sophia Greek Church in Syracuse; and Fr. Ștefan Drăgoi, parish priest of Saint Mary Church in Norfolk, VA. The responses at the Divine Liturgy were sung by Protopsaltis Leonard Milea of New Jersey and Constantin Claudiu Bărdăzău, chanter of the Rochester church.

In his homily, His Eminence Nicolae highlighted the example of the Holy Three Hierarchs and offered a message of encouragement, saying: “We are once again in difficult times with restrictions, but we must remember that precisely now we Christians must be the light of the world. Christians should be the ones with strong faith, the ones who show their hope that everything will be according to the will of God. We must find solutions, and fear is not one of them; that is why we need repentance and much prayer.”

Immediately after the Divine Liturgy came the fellowship meal organized by the Ladies Auxiliary of Syracuse, observing the measures and restrictions imposed by the state authorities.

In the afternoon of the same day, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, together with Dean Fr. Daniel Ene, prayed at the Romanian Church Cemetery in Rochester, where most of the Romanians of western New York who have departed to the Lord are laid to rest, many of them founders and benefactors of the church dedicated to the Holy Trinity and Saint Empress Theodora in Rochester/Victor, NY. In the Romanian Patriarchate, 2021 is “the Commemorative Year of those who have fallen asleep in the Lord; the liturgical and cultural value of cemeteries.” The cold and the snowstorm outside did not keep His Eminence from praying for the souls of the departed.

The 32nd Sunday after Pentecost, January 31, 2021, was an occasion of prayer and hierarchical service for the Romanian faithful of the Image City, Rochester, NY. His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae celebrated the Divine Liturgy together with the parish priest, Fr. Daniel Ene, eparchial secretary and Dean of New York, New England and the Eastern USA of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas, and with Fr. Ștefan Drăgoi, parish priest of Saint Mary Church in Norfolk, VA. A Memorial Service was also served for the departed founders and benefactors of the church, and for Metropolitan Bartolomeu of blessed memory, ten years after his passing to eternal life. His Eminence emphasized the sacred duty we have to commemorate the departed, and especially Archbishop and Metropolitan Bartolomeu, who labored in the pastoral work of our Metropolia between 1965 and 1976.

New York State has been, and still is, sorely tried by this pandemic, and its rules and restrictions on organizing public events have been among the strictest. Even so, the presence of the faithful was a great joy, even at only 25% of the church’s capacity and with masks mandatory.

At the end of the Divine Liturgy, as a sign of gratitude for all his care, Fr. Daniel Ene presented His Eminence with an icon of special significance for this year, which is also dedicated to the pastoral care of Romanians in the diaspora. The icon depicts “Our Lady of Guadalupe – Patroness of the Unborn,” a missionary icon of the Holy Virgin, also known as the “Icon of the Mother of God of Guadalupe,” venerated as protectress of the Americas. Having appeared miraculously on the cloak (tilma) of Juan Diego, an Aztec Indian converted to Christianity, in Guadalupe, Mexico, in 1531, the image of the Holy Virgin carrying the Savior Jesus Christ in her womb has become known and venerated not only by the people of Mexico but by the entire Christian world. One of the traditions connected with the Guadalupe icon is that pregnant women or mothers who have just given birth come to venerate it and present their infants to the Most Holy Virgin, offering them to the protection of the one who received and carried the Son of God in her womb.

The icon presented keeps this image of the Mother of God at its center, together with the images of Saints Constantine and Helen, patrons of our Metropolia, alongside Saint George the Pilgrim and Saint Raphael of Brooklyn, patrons of the Deanery of New York, New England and the Eastern USA.

The day ended with a fellowship meal organized in honor of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae in the church hall. It was the first time in more than a year that such an event could be held. Everything, however, was prepared in keeping with the safety measures required by state law.

These were moments of blessing for the Romanians of central and western New York, and they can only be images of hope that through brotherly love and prayer we will be able to come out of this pandemic as quickly as possible.

Reported by,

Dean Fr. Daniel Ene

Rochester/Victor NY

title: His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae Meets with the Priests and Teachers of the Parish Schools
intro:
On the evenings of February 9-10, 2021, the priests and Parish School teachers of the Romanian Orthodox Archdiocese of the United States of America had the opportunity to meet virtually with His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae and with Very Rev. Fr. Daniel Ene, president of the Education Commission, to discuss the current situation of the Parish Schools, as well as the organization of the Religion Olympiad and of the educational projects to be implemented in the Homage Year of the Pastoral Care of Romanians outside Romania.

We were pleased by the large turnout, with most parishes represented by both the priest and the Sunday School teachers. Because of the restrictions imposed by the pandemic, children’s educational activities were organized differently this year, according to the possibilities of each parish: in person with the children who continued to attend the Divine Liturgy on Sundays, online, or by phone. It was an open and constructive discussion in which both the difficulties each school faces and the achievements at the parish level were presented, along with the joy of being close to children and parents in these times that test our faith. The resources and ideas shared by the participants were gathered into a document that was later published on the Metropolia’s educational portal, in the hope that these ideas and resources will be useful to all those involved in the education of children.

The organization of a virtual Religion Olympiad was also discussed. This year the Religion Olympiad will be held using the Zoom platform and the educational app Kahoot! on Sunday, May 16, 2021, according to the following schedule: Group B (2-3pm EST), Group C: 3-4pm EST. The topics for the Olympiad are based on the curriculum for September 2020 – January 2021.

The year 2021 has been declared the Homage Year of the Pastoral Care of Romanians outside Romania. On this occasion, Very Rev. Fr. Daniel Ene presented an educational project proposed for implementation in the parishes of our Metropolia. The project “Biserica - familia românilor de pretutindeni”, running from March 1 - August 22, 2021, aims to help bring together the communities in Romania and those in the diaspora by raising awareness of the active role the Church plays in the life of the community and in sustaining the bonds between the faithful. The participants showed their enthusiasm for this project, which gives children the opportunity to express their creativity, to learn more about the lives of children in Romania and to strengthen their attachment to their families and their traditional values.

The meetings continued with an exchange of ideas about projects and activities to be organized during this Homage Year: spiritual conferences with priests from Romania and the diaspora, the celebration of the Sunday of Romanian Migrants (the first Sunday after the Dormition of the Mother of God), workshops with Archdeacon Adrian Sorin Mihalache, activities to integrate mixed families into Romanian family life and culture, and collections of representative images from parish life photographed by children and young people.

In closing, Preoteasa Claudia Aileni, president of AROLA, presented the organization’s current projects, which aim to support the educational activities of the Sunday Schools and of the Romanian community in the diaspora: Mother of the Year; Moşii de iarnă (March 6 – an activity organized to explain to children what the commemoration of the departed means); the “Dumitru Stăniloae” Scholarship for the financial support of young men who wish to become priests, with the second Sunday of Great Lent (March 28) dedicated to fundraising events; and a spiritual evening on the theme “Woman and the Salvation of the World”, presented by Very Rev. Fr. Theodor Damian (April 10).

The next meeting of the priests and teachers is scheduled for the week of March 8-13, 2021.

title: Pastoral Letter of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church for the Sunday of Orthodoxy in the Year of Our Lord 2021
intro:
To the most venerable monastic orders, the most reverend clergy and the beloved faithful of the Romanian Patriarchate, 

Grace, peace and joy from God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and from us, fatherly blessings! 

Most Venerable and Most Reverend Fathers, Most Venerable Mothers,
Beloved faithful, 

We give glory to God, worshiped in Trinity, because, despite all the trials and temptations that all of humanity has gone through and is still going through, He has made us worthy this year as well to walk the path of repentance, beginning “the journey of the virtues […] girding ourselves with the good struggle of the fast”1, so as “to behold the most honorable Passion of Christ God and the Holy Pascha, rejoicing spiritually”2.

Today’s Sunday, called the Sunday of Orthodoxy, the first stop on the spiritual journey of Great Lent, was instituted by Saint Methodius, Patriarch of Constantinople, following the local Synod of Constantinople of March 11, 843, which officially sanctioned the final proclamation of the veneration of the holy icons3.

This dogmatic proclamation, however, came after a long crisis spanning the eighth and ninth centuries. It took the form of a struggle against the icons and those who venerated them and is therefore called the iconoclast crisis or iconoclasm.

The turmoil caused by the iconoclast crisis unfolded over two periods, marked by many persecutions of the icons by the Byzantine emperors, but also by strong resistance from brilliant theologians and holy men, defenders and venerators of the holy icons.

The latter, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, revealed to all the theological, liturgical and catechetical value of the icon in the life of the Church and of the Christian who cultivates communion with God and with His saints.

In the first period of the war against the icons (730-787), we note among the defenders of Orthodoxy Saint Germanus I, Patriarch of Constantinople (715-730), and Saint John of Damascus (675-749).

The former gave the first Orthodox testimony against iconoclasm, affirming that the tradition of depicting the Lord Jesus Christ in icons stems from His visible theophany, that is, from His incarnation, His life in the flesh, His sufferings and His saving death4.

For his part, Saint John of Damascus succeeded in admirably summarizing the Orthodox teaching on icons in his three treatises on the holy images. In this regard he says: In former times God, who is without body or form, could in no way be depicted (in an icon). But now, since God has been seen in the flesh and has lived among men, I can depict what is seen of God. I do not venerate matter, but I venerate the Creator of matter, who became matter for my sake, who took upon Himself life in the flesh and who, through matter, worked my salvation5.

The first iconoclast period ended with the Seventh Ecumenical Council of Nicaea in 787, convened at the initiative of the Holy Empress Irene, at which the clear and unequivocal distinction was precisely expressed between the veneration or relative honor given to the icon and the worship due to God alone.

The second iconoclast period broke out under the secularizing reign of the iconoclast emperor Leo V the Armenian (813-820) and lasted until 843. But God once again raised up wonderful, holy men, such as Saint Theodore the Studite (759-826) and Saint Nicephorus the Confessor, Patriarch of Constantinople (806-828).

Saint Theodore the Studite justified the practice of painting the icon of the Lord Jesus Christ on the basis of the incarnation of the eternal Son of God. Thus the icon of Christ the Lord is not merely the image of the man Jesus of Nazareth, but the image of the one Hypostasis of the Son and Word of God, who became man for the salvation of mankind.

The second period of the iconoclast crisis ended in the time of the Holy Empress Theodora6 and Saint Methodius, Patriarch of Constantinople, with the restoration of the veneration of the holy icons at the local Synod convened in Constantinople in 843. The decisions of the Seventh Ecumenical Council of Nicaea of 787 were then reaffirmed, and iconoclasm was definitively condemned together with all the heresies up to that time.

Because the work of the Synod of 843 concluded on the Saturday before the first Sunday of Great Lent (March 11), the official document, called the Synodikon of Orthodoxy, was solemnly read on the following day, the first Sunday of the Fast. From then on it was decided that every year, beginning in 843, the Triumph or Victory of Orthodoxy would be celebrated throughout the Orthodox world on the first Sunday of Holy and Great Lent, called the Sunday of Orthodoxy.

Beloved spiritual sons and daughters,

The veneration of the holy icons, as established by the Holy Fathers at the Holy Councils, is an act of confessing the truth of the Incarnation of the eternal Son of God, an act of communion with God and with His saints, and also a call to a holy life and to deeds of merciful love in every  place and at all times.

In order to confess the Orthodox faith, we are bound to cleanse our minds, to free ourselves from the passions and to do what is good and right, to be renewed and enlightened by the virtues, heeding the words of the Holy Apostle James: “faith without works is dead” (James 2:17). In this way we advance toward the likeness of the Image of the Holy God, toward deification by grace, of which Saint Gregory of Nyssa says: “Each of us is the painter of his own life: the soul is the canvas, the virtues are the colors, and Christ is the model we must paint”7.

Through today’s feast, the Sunday of Orthodoxy, or of the Triumph of the True Faith, we too are called to be victorious, with the help of God’s grace, over the passions of greed, arrogance and pride within us, which are always lying in wait for us, putting in their place the virtues of humility and merciful love toward the people around us, so as to rediscover in them the image of the humble Christ.

Orthodox Christians,

The year 2021, proclaimed by the Holy Synod as the Homage Year of the pastoral care of Romanians outside Romania and the Commemorative Year of those who have fallen asleep in the Lord; the liturgical and cultural value of cemeteries, offers an occasion to show more intensely our love and longing for our Romanian brothers and sisters beyond the country’s borders, and also an opportunity to show care for those who have passed from this life.

In this context, we recall that 2021 marks 150 years since the First Festival of Romanians Everywhere, a missionary and cultural event held in 1871 at Putna Monastery, initiated by the poet Mihai Eminescu and attended by figures such as the writer Ioan Slavici and the historian Alexandru D. Xenopol.

A century and a half since this event will be marked this year as well at the foundation of the Holy Voivode Stephen the Great, on August 15, the feast of the Dormition of the Mother of God, in order to affirm and strengthen the unity of Romanians in the country and beyond its borders and to strengthen the bonds of brotherhood, the communion of love and the working together for the common good of the Romanian people.

At the same time, in order to cultivate gratitude and love toward those who have departed to the Lord, every Orthodox Christian has the moral duty to commemorate in private prayer, at the Divine Liturgy and at the other holy services those who are no longer among us, to honor their memory and remember their good deeds, and to tend and beautify their graves, as well as the monuments of the Romanian heroes.

Also, according to the tradition established by our Church, on the Sunday of Orthodoxy the collection for the Central Missionary Fund is begun, through which parish communities in the country and abroad facing difficulties are especially helped, and social-philanthropic and educational activities that preserve the spiritual and cultural identity of Romanian Orthodox Christians are supported.

Generosity, an openhanded openness toward those in need, is a luminous expression of the Christian life of a person, of a community and of an entire nation. Throughout history, the Romanian Orthodox Christian has learned that only by giving will he receive, which led him to give to those in need from the little he had, so that he too might be helped in times of hard trial.

Thus the kindness and generosity always shown by our forebears and parents became for our people a blessed occasion to grow spiritually in faith and good deeds, to keep a strong bond of brotherhood with the Romanians living among strangers, and to keep the name of good Christians, showing that love for God is beautifully interwoven with love for one’s neighbor.

We are confident and hopeful that this year too you will respond with Christian generosity to the call to help those in need, contributing to the continuation of the missionary and social-philanthropic work of the Church, for the benefit of Romanian Orthodox faithful everywhere.

Wishing you a blessed fast, with much spiritual growth and benefit, we embrace you with a holy blessing: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all!” (2 Corinthians 13:13).

President of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church
