title: The “Mihai Eminescu” Literary Circle of New York Pays Tribute to Academician Ioan-Iovitz Popescu, an Exceptional Romanian Personality
intro:
ONE MAN, ONE UNIVERSE

The “Mihai Eminescu” Literary Circle, based in Astoria, New York, founded and led by its president, Rev. Prof. Dr. Theodor Damian, is known and appreciated, especially through the “Lumină Lină” journal, both in the homeland and in several countries on different continents. Over more than two decades, the circle has been a welcoming host for many cultural events. Valuable books in the humanities and the sciences have been launched there, exhibitions of painting, sculpture and contemporary fashion have been presented, and complex views on life have been exchanged in fruitful dialogue with friends from the homeland.

In the past year, because of the pandemic that temporarily brought the planet to its knees, the circle reduced the number of its sessions but did not cancel them. Thus, at the suggestion of Prof. Dr. Victoria Plaveti, a friend of the members of the Romanian-American community in New York, the book “Din viața lui Iovițu” (published by the Romanian Academy Publishing House in 2020, in an exceptional graphic form) was launched on Sunday, March 14 of this year. Its author is the eminent academician Prof. Dr. Ioan-Iovitz Popescu, who was Victoria Plaveti’s professor and mentor during her student years and later during her doctoral preparation in Bucharest.

At “Saints Apostles Peter & Paul” Romanian Orthodox Church, after the service celebrated with grace by the parish priest, Fr. Theodor Damian, and after the memorial services for the departed, the circle’s session began under the auspices of several prestigious institutions: the Academy of Romanian Scientists (New York branch), the Union of Professional Journalists of Romania, the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas and the Romanian Institute of Orthodox Theology and Spirituality in New York.

Theodor Damian, president of the circle, thanked the participants and read the moving e-mail message received from the author of the book: “Distinguished Rev. Prof. Theodor Damian, My warmest thanks for the extraordinary event in my life sketched in this book. My soul and my thoughts will be with you there. I take with me as partakers of this joy all my friends and colleagues from the Romanian Academy and from Măgurele. With Brotherly Christian love, Iovițu”. Theodor Damian then addressed the connection between religion and science, offering explanations showing that the two can naturally coexist. Mr. Iovițu, being a physicist of world stature, has an important word to say on this much-debated subject. The academician is fully convinced that science does not eliminate the divine, but that the two are intertwined. This explains the ethereal presence of his wife, Denisa, the woman of his eternal love, in the dreams of Victoria Plaveti. Although Denisa died following a dubiously performed operation, her husband, Iovițu, firmly states: “the one who has departed never departs completely,” because deep love is stronger than death.

Victoria Plaveti thanked family and friends for their friendly gesture of taking part in the launch of the book by Mr. Iovițu, a world-renowned scientist in the field of nuclear physics. He was and is “the most beloved of physicists, inventor of the Etherons.” He belongs to the quartet of the world’s most valuable physicists: 1. Albert Einstein (1920), 2. Niels Bohr, Atomic Ether (1913), 3. Ernest Rutherford, 4. Ioan-Iovitz-Popescu (1982). Victoria spoke with deep respect and admiration about Ioan-Iovitz-Popescu, an authority in both physics and linguistics, a new aspect full of complex meanings. She also spoke with emotion about the outstanding qualities, as a person and as a friend, of her former university professor.

The book is a selection of e-mail messages between the author and his friends in Romania and in other countries where research in various fields was carried out. Two distinct strands, love and a passion for scientific research, are intertwined throughout its nearly 400 pages: on the one hand, Mr. Iovițu’s passionate, infinite love for his wife, Denisa, to whom the book is dedicated, and on the other, his scientific research, especially in physics, with remarkable national and international achievements. The academician is recognized and appreciated for his contribution to correlating physics with linguistics, an entirely new and, for that very reason, fascinating field. His whole life stands under the sign of Orthodoxy, in which he firmly believes, and, more than that, he demonstrates that the Divinity exists.

Here are a few appreciations of the distinguished Romanian academician:

Gabriel Altmann: “Iovitzu contacted me and we began to realize his 1001 ideas. He proposed, deduced, verified, made da Vinci-like figures (though mathematical ones) and never stopped. Something in his head drives him to develop new ideas, to combine, to propose, to put them to work in science. He is a scientist par excellence; he lives for research.”

Gabriel Altmann’s messenger: “… the giant physicist Ioan Iovitz Popescu, who should approve the arrival of Spring!”

After a long life of intense and passionate research, the conclusion the academician has reached seems simple in words but is astonishing in the depth beyond the Word: “As you can see, I am, after all, a boastful sinner, whose only excuse, perhaps, is that he wishes with all his soul to demonstrate with facts that Denisa and the Life Beyond EXIST:” And he has demonstrated it.

M.N. Rusu, editor-in-chief of the “Lumină Lină” journal, considers the book “almost a masterpiece.” Iovițu is regarded as “the last learned encyclopedist who moves on several levels.” The early and tragic death of his wife, Denisa, reminded him of the famous Sic cognito from the book by the great classic writer Bogdan Petriceicu Hasdeu, banned under communism. The theory of intramundane and extramundane communication is illustrated in the book of the love between Iovițu and Denisa. M.N. Rusu emphasized what he considers most important in the volume launched: “An astonishing book in its radiant content, with vast meanings. Reading the book page by page, I could not believe it was written by a contemporary atomic scientist and encyclopedist. The academician belongs to the illustrious line of Romanian encyclopedists, which opens with Dimitrie Cantemir, B.P. Hasdeu, Nicolae Iorga, Lucian Blaga and Mircea Eliade. For Denisa’s Romanian tragedy, the system and its satellites must be held guilty. I read carefully pages of mythology, both in Denisa’s letters to her husband and in her husband’s letters to Denisa’s icon, simply mythological. I thank Academician Ioan Iovitz Popescu for the book sent through Vicki Plaveti. Reading it gave me the chance to know the soul and mind of Mr. Iovițu, a great thinking scientist. The book presented today is a truly historic love story, in every possible respect, suggesting to me that Denisa’s death is like an ancient Greek tragedy.” The literary critic and historian M.N. Rusu then expressed his happiness at being a contemporary of this book and its author.

Prof. Valentina Ciaprazi pointed out the modesty of the book’s title compared with the complex ideas of the letters and, above all, with the harrowing episode of Denisa’s death. The book “is a love story between two scientists. The loss of a loved one is life’s hardest lesson. But the spirit does not perish. The greater the love, the greater the spirituality that follows.” The connection between science and religion was then discussed again.

Prof. Mariana Terra thanked Mrs. Victoria Plaveti for the joy of offering us a book so profound in its essential ideas about human existence: life here on earth and the continuation of life Beyond. She highlighted the passionate work of the professor and academician who, like his wife, was nominated for the Nobel Prize in physics. The author firmly believes in God and expresses this wonderful creed more than once: “Denisa is with the Lord, more alive and stronger than ever. The Lord took her with Him, but at the same time left her in close communion with me.”

Prof. Nicole Smith read moving passages from the book about Denisa’s death, which occurred at a hospital in Târgu Mureș after an unsuccessful heart operation in which a valve was replaced. Was this a criminal act by the surgeon, or incompetence? Iovițu is convinced that everything was planned with malice and that the doctor is guilty of killing, not of negligence. The pain of Denisa’s earthly loss is eased by the thought that sooner or later he, Iovițu, will meet the love of his life again, there, Above, with the Lord, where they will be happy once more.

We offer a word of warm thanks to Prof. Victoria Plaveti, a former student of academician Ioan-Iovitz-Popescu. More than that, she is an exemplary model in the honor she paid to a MAN, the mentor who helped her become what she is today, a professor appreciated by her students and by her Romanian and Romanian-American friends.

Photojournalist Alex Marmara captured moments of the circle session on film.

***

The book “Din viața lui Iovițu” introduces us to a fascinating universe of earthly and eternal life, capturing a profound aesthetic of the love between spouses and of the passion for scientific research. The fact that a prestigious academician in the exact sciences, in physics, believes in God and respects our age-old traditions is one more proof, among many similar ones, that man, this unique and astonishing being, can conquer scientific strongholds with a soul dedicated to the One on High.

A true patriot, Ioan-Iovițu Popescu confesses: “I am proud to be Romanian… I am proud of our language.”

We too, the members of the “Mihai Eminescu” Literary Circle, are proud to have among us, in the homeland and in the diaspora, illustrious people like academician Ioan-Iovitz Popescu. We launched his book with love and full appreciation in Astoria, New York, here in a “little Romania” across the Atlantic.

Prof. Iana Târnăvean

title: Pastoral Visit to St. Dimitrios the New Monastery, Middletown, NY
intro:
At the end of the third week of Great Lent, St. Dimitrios the New Monastery in Middletown, NY put on festive attire to receive its shepherd, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae. The faithful close to the monastery came together in exemplary fashion to adorn the monastery church and welcome the pilgrims. Our hierarch’s pastoral visit began on Saturday evening when, together with the clergy of the monastery, he served Great Vespers with Litiya. The next day, faithful who had come from afar to the monastery took part in the bringing out and veneration of the Holy Cross, and then in the Holy and Divine Liturgy.

His Eminence Nicolae also offered us a beautiful spiritual word, from which we present a few excerpts:

On this Sunday, which falls a few days before the calendar midpoint of the Fast of Holy Pascha, we venerate the Holy Cross. Today’s Synaxarion says that just as the tree of life was planted in the middle of Paradise, so the veneration of the Holy Cross is placed in the middle of the Fast. If Adam ate from the tree in the middle of Paradise and through not fasting lost Paradise, we, through fasting and self-restraint, can be made worthy to taste of the new tree of life, which is Jesus Christ. So let us fast, and then receive the Body and Blood of the Savior. The Fathers add another reason for this veneration of the Holy Cross in the middle of the Fast, namely to strengthen the faithful on the path of the Fast through a spiritual meditation on what the cross means in our life, what sacrifice means in our life.

The Holy Gospel according to Mark presents to us the words of the Savior: “Whoever desires to come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow Me” (Mark 8, 34). In these words we find first of all a call addressed to our freedom. From the outset we marvel, for God came down from His glory, took on our human form, allowed Himself to be crucified on the cross, and yet He does not force us to follow Him. God, who created man free, respects man’s freedom in this work of redemption as well.

If, then, we wish to be followers of Christ, we must fulfill the three stages He announces: “let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow Me.” We find it hard to understand this call to deny ourselves (in English you have heard: let him deny himself, that is, in Romanian, să ne negăm pe noi înșine). Why would God ask us to deny ourselves? This does not mean denying our gifts or our personality; it means setting aside whatever stands in the way of our encounter with God, precisely what belongs to our selfishness of wanting to be as we are. And in this selfishness we do not let God come into our life.

To better understand what it means to deny ourselves, we must look to Christ Himself, who emptied Himself, who “did not consider being equal to You, God the Father, a thing to be grasped, but, being God before the ages, appeared on earth and lived among men” (Liturgy of Saint Basil the Great). If God Himself came and emptied Himself and took on our form in order to save us, how could we regain “the image of God’s glory” except by imitating God Himself, Christ made man? We too must leave behind what is ours, the things we hold dear. We cannot hope to be saved, that is, to attain communion with God and let the light of the Godhead shine on our face, unless we imitate Christ Himself. And let us leave behind these things that belong to our selfishness, let us empty ourselves of what fills us, so as to let God come into our life.

“Take up his cross” – Saint Paul explains in two places what taking up the cross means: “And those who are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (Galatians 5, 24). And in the Epistle to the Romans: “I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service” (Romans 12, 1). This is what it means to take up our cross: to offer our body as a sacrifice that is sanctified and becomes our reasonable service. How fitting these words are now in the Fast, when we pray, fast and try to let the body too take part in a spiritual sacrifice. If we want to be followers of Christ, if we want to be Christians, we must pass through this crucifixion of the passions and desires, and we too will come to the resurrection, that is, to communion with God. I would urge you to spend the four remaining weeks of the fast with this question: what does it mean for me to be a Christian?

After the Divine Liturgy, a memorial service was served for the founders of the monastery. The faithful present then stayed for the fraternal agape meal that followed, rejoicing in the sunshine that bathed the monastery and in the abundant grace God poured out upon us on this feast day.

title: The First Divine Liturgy in Romanian and the First Visit of a Romanian Orthodox Priest to Colombia
intro:
From March 25 to April 9, with the blessing of His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan Nicolae, Fr. Daniel Ene, Eparchial Secretary and Dean of New York, New England and the Eastern USA, was in Colombia at the invitation of Her Excellency Mrs. Claudia Tușa, Chargé d’Affaires of Romania to the Republic of Colombia, with multiple accreditation to the Dominican Republic and Panama.

It was the first visit of a Romanian Orthodox priest to Colombia, and on this occasion several meetings took place with the Romanian community and with the Orthodox communities of the country.

On the evening of the Annunciation, Fr. Daniel took part in a meeting with prominent members of the Romanian community in Bogota. The meeting was organized by the Embassy of Romania in Colombia, and although attendance was restricted, all those invited were glad to see one another again after a long time and to welcome a Romanian Orthodox priest among them for the first time. Also present was Mrs. Daniela Popa, whose parents became monastics and served as Abbot of Cernica Monastery and Abbess of Pasărea Monastery, respectively.

The next day, a working meeting was held with Her Excellency Mrs. Claudia Tușa, Chargé d’Affaires of Romania in Bogota, and Consul Mihail Stănescu. As a token of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae’s appreciation and care for the Romanians living in Colombia and for the Embassy staff, the ambassador received from him the Commemorative Icon of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas for 2021, the Homage Year of the Pastoral Care of Romanians outside Romania in the Romanian Patriarchate. The icon depicts “Our Lady of Guadalupe – Patroness of the Unborn”, a missionary icon of the Holy Virgin, also known as the “Icon of the Mother of God of Guadalupe” and venerated as protectress of the Americas. The icon presented keeps this image of the Mother of God at its center, together with the images of the Holy Emperors Constantine and Helen, patrons of the Metropolia, alongside Saint George the Pilgrim and Saint Raphael of Brooklyn, patrons of the Deanery of New York, New England and the Eastern USA. This gift is meant to be a source of blessing and protection not only for the building but above all for all those who labor, now and in the future, at the Embassy in caring for the Romanian people living in these lands.

The ambassador described the situation of the Romanians in Colombia and the difficulties they face. Colombia does not have a large community, but the Embassy of Romania estimates that about 400 Romanians are settled in Colombia and around 250 in Panama and the Dominican Republic. Few as they are, some of them have been in Colombia for more than 40 years. The largest community is in the metropolitan area of Bogota, but there are also three Romanian honorary consulates, in Medellin, Cali and Barranquilla.

On Friday and Saturday, Fr. Daniel traveled to the city of Cali, where he prayed with a young Romanian, Constantin Cătălin Botezat, who had been robbed and shot, losing the sight of his right eye, and who spent more than a month in a hospital in Cali.

Sunday, March 28, 2021, was the blessed occasion of the first Divine Liturgy in Romanian, which Fr. Daniel celebrated at the Greek Cathedral of the Dormition of the Mother of God in Bogota. The Divine Liturgy was also attended by His Grace Timoteo Luis Antonio Torres Esquivel, Bishop of Assos, Vicar for Colombia and Venezuela of the Greek Orthodox Metropolis of Mexico, Central America, Colombia, Venezuela and the Caribbean Islands (Ecumenical Patriarchate). These were blessed hours for the Romanians living in the Colombian capital, who, for the first time in the decades they have lived in Colombia, heard liturgical prayer in Romanian.

“It was the most beautiful gift I could have received for Pascha,” said Mrs. Scripcariu Mani Monica, who has lived in Bogota for many years and runs a small Romanian restaurant. Right after the Divine Liturgy, the ambassador, Fr. Daniel, Bishop Timoteo and Fr. Mijail Hernando García, the parish priest of the Cathedral in Bogota, had lunch at another Romanian restaurant, “Mediterranea de Andrei”, owned by Mr. Andrei Farcaș, who emigrated to Colombia several decades ago.

Fr. Daniel spent the following week among the small Romanian community in the cities of Barranquilla and Cartagena. There he had the opportunity to meet Mr. Virgiliu Faur, a former Romanian career diplomat and former consul of Romania in Colombia, now residing in Barranquilla. Familiar with the realities of the Romanian Orthodox Church, being close to Sâmbăta de Sus Monastery, as well as with those of Colombia, Mr. Faur had several meetings with Fr. Daniel in which they discussed the possibility of a Romanian Orthodox community in Barranquilla, where there are many Antiochian Orthodox Christians and no Orthodox church.

Before returning to the United States, Fr. Daniel accompanied Ambassador Claudia Tușa to Cucuta, a city on the border with Venezuela, at the invitation of Bishop Timoteo. On this occasion they also visited the property the Greek Archdiocese received from the Catholic community of Cucuta, a former Catholic convent, which will soon become the first Orthodox Theological Seminary and the first Orthodox women’s monastery in South America. During this visit, the ambassador also wished to learn about the situation on the border with Venezuela, which is now the gateway for the largest wave of migration in the world. Nearly 5,000 Venezuelan citizens cross the border into Colombia every day because of hunger and the harsh living conditions in Venezuela. The city has become a vast field of camps for Venezuelan refugees. Mrs. Claudia Tușa and Fr. Daniel, together with Bishop Timoteo of Assos, also had several important meetings: first with the Secretary for Border Affairs of the Department of Norte de Santander, Victor Bautista (an article on the government’s official website describes this meeting - http://www.nortedesantander.gov.co/Noticias-Gobernaci%C3%B3n-Norte-de-Santander/ArticleID/18985/Impulsamos-el-desarrollo-de-oportunidades-para-la-juventud ) and at Cucuta City Hall with the mayor, Mr. Jairo Tomas Yanez Rodriguez. They discussed the humanitarian problems facing the city, shaken by what is currently the largest migrant crisis in the world, one that has far surpassed the Syrian migrant crisis.

On Thursday, April 8, the day before returning to New York, Fr. Daniel Ene performed the Service of the Blessing of Water at the Embassy of Romania in Bogota. Present were Fr. Mihail of the Greek Cathedral, Ambassador Claudia Tușa, Consul Mihail Stănescu and the Embassy staff.

Fr. Daniel’s visit to Venezuela, to the Romanian Church of the Holy Emperors Constantine and Helen in Caracas, had been scheduled for April 8-14, but it was postponed because the border with Venezuela was closed by order of the Venezuelan president. The visit has been rescheduled for after Holy Pascha.

Fr. Daniel Adrian Ene

title: The Romanian Community of Las Vegas Spiritually Enriched by the Pastoral Visit of His Eminence Metropolitan NICOLAE of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas
intro:
The Orthodox Christians of the Church of Saint George the Great Martyr and Saint Dimitrios the New joyfully welcomed the presence of our Hierarch for two days, April 17 and 18, during which the order of church services was harmoniously combined with the long-desired fellowship and closeness among people, considering the cold distancing we have all lived through. The visit had a twofold significance: the inauguration and blessing of the “Memory Lane” and the celebration of the patronal feast of the Romanian Orthodox Church in Las Vegas through the commemoration of Saint George the Great Martyr.

As is fitting, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae was greeted in the traditional way with bread and salt by the ROYA president, Oana Butunoi, together with the children of the community.

The “Memory Lane” project came into being at the initiative of the Honorary Consul General of Romania in Las Vegas, Mrs. Lia Roberts, and through the efforts of the parish priest, Rev. Fr. Mihai Bălan, and the Parish Council, whose president is Mr. Panta Stanciu. Its two architectural and landscaping elements are meant to keep alive the memory of loved ones who have passed to eternal life. Thus, on Saturday, April 17, after Vespers celebrated by His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, the “Memory Lane” project was blessed. It numbers 49 thuja trees (the tree of life), each with a commemorative plaque bearing the donor’s name. In front of the church, Mr. Panta Stanciu built a monument whose face holds red granite plates inscribed in gold with the names of those who purchased the 49 trees. At the top of the monument stands a wooden cross handmade by Mr. Costel Șoarece. The monument was donated to the church by Mrs. Lia Roberts, wishing to keep forever the memory of her mother, IRINA ZEITLER.

The blessing was preceded by His Eminence Nicolae’s constructive, educational and spiritual discussion with the ROYA youth, closely guided by Dr. Camelia Bratu, the organization’s vice president. This was followed by a meeting with the members of the Parish Council, during which His Eminence was presented with a plaque commemorating the date on which he blessed the cross, the ground and the cornerstone on which this holy place stands.

The Divine Liturgy of the 5th Sunday of Great Lent was celebrated by His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae together with the parish priest, Fr. Mihai, and Fr. Vasile. The Holy Church offers us as an example to follow Saint Mary of Egypt, who lived in debauchery for 17 years. Her burning desire to enter the church and kiss the Holy Cross was fulfilled only through her fervent prayer to the Lord, and she chose to live the years of her life in the desert in repentance and humility, 47 years in all, according to the account of her confessor, Saint Zosimas.

In his homily, His Eminence Nicolae explained the Gospel of the day, Mark 10, 32-45: If you wish to be first, be servants of all. Christ teaches us that in the Church it is important to serve one another, according to the words of the Holy Apostle Paul: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6,2). The Church is different from the world. In the Church we do not speak of domination and lordship, but of service. The bishop is the first servant. His ministry, together with that of the priests and deacons, is to guide the people on the way of salvation. Our ministry is about finding the way to salvation together. Christ has called some of us to ministry. This means that we are invested with the grace to preach the word of the Gospel and to serve the sacraments, so that we may be servants and guides toward salvation, following His personal example.

At the same time, Saint George the Great Martyr and Trophy-bearer was commemorated, the patron saint of the Romanian Orthodox Church in Las Vegas, whose feast is celebrated on April 23. After the homily, the parishioners received small icons representing “the Homage Year of the pastoral care of Romanians outside Romania,” and because April 15 was His Eminence Nicolae’s birthday, all the faithful sang him the traditional “Many Years!”

After the Divine Liturgy, the participants were invited to the church hall for a fellowship meal, enjoying the Lenten dishes lovingly prepared by Mrs. Flori Constantin, AROLA president, together with the ladies of the parish. After the prayer of blessing of the food, a short artistic program was presented, opened with the singing of the two national anthems, of the United States of America and of Romania. Amid applause and emotion, the children of the community recited poems and impressed everyone with their piano performances of famous arias. At this great event of our community we were also honored by the presence of the Nevada Secretary of State, the Honorable Barbara Cegavske.

Every visit of His Eminence to our parish is an occasion of joy, and so, on behalf of the faithful, we thank him for his care, his service, his prayer, his word and his blessing.

Fr. Mihai Bălan

April 19, 2021

Editor: Elena-Mihaela Gliga

title: May 30, 2021: Day of Romanians Everywhere
intro:
Christ is risen!

Under Law no. 101/2015, adopted at the request of many Romanians abroad, the Day of Romanians Everywhere is celebrated on the last Sunday of May. In 2021, this Sunday falls on May 30.

The Day of Romanians Everywhere is a special day with a strong spiritual significance, a day for reaffirming the traditions and the values of the faith and culture of the Romanian people.

Therefore, the Romanian Patriarchate addresses a message of unity and brotherhood, of communion and solidarity, to all Romanians everywhere.

This year, 2021, declared by the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church the Homage Year of the Pastoral Care of Romanians outside Romania, our word of appreciation and spiritual encouragement addressed to all Romanian Orthodox faithful living far from their homeland has a special significance.

The pastoral care and increased attention shown by the Romanian Patriarchate to Romanian Orthodox faithful abroad has taken concrete form over the last decade in the founding of numerous new parishes and dioceses, which meet the spiritual needs of Romanian Orthodox faithful around Romania’s present borders (Bessarabia, Northern Bukovina, Serbia, Bulgaria, Hungary), of Romanians in Western Europe, in America, in Australia and New Zealand, as well as in the Holy Land, Cyprus, Turkey, South Africa and Japan.

Through her hierarchs and priests, the Mother Church blesses and encourages her spiritual sons and daughters abroad and, at the same time, learns of the problems they face in their aspiration for a better future. That is why, in Romanian Orthodox churches everywhere, Romanians feel the joy of finding and living their ancestral faith again, take part in liturgical life, ease their burning longing for their loved ones and their native places, and reaffirm their deep ethnic identity. Through their participation in liturgical life, in cultural events and in the social-philanthropic activities organized by the parishes of the Romanian diaspora, the enduring values of the Orthodox faith and of Romanian culture are promoted, Romanian traditions are handed down and the Romanian language is cultivated, all of which contributes to preserving the cultural, ethnic and ecclesial identity of Romanian Orthodox faithful outside Romania.

The contribution of the Romanian Orthodox Church, together with the State authorities of Romania, to preserving and cultivating Romanian identity is also meant to support the social integration of Romanians in their host countries, without cultural assimilation and without loss of national identity. In this sense, a harmonious coexistence of Romanians everywhere with the citizens of the countries where they now live is fostered, especially now when, in some places in the world, the medical, moral, spiritual and economic crisis sometimes shows itself in social tensions that can degenerate into interethnic and interreligious conflicts.

On the occasion of the Day of Romanians Everywhere, with much brotherly and fatherly love, we urge all Romanians living outside Romania to stay constantly in touch with their loved ones who remain in the homeland, in order to preserve the unity of the family and Romanian communion.

 

With much appreciation and fatherly blessing,

 

† Daniel

Patriarch of the Romanian Orthodox Church

 

 

* Message of His Beatitude Patriarch Daniel of the Romanian Orthodox Church on the Day of Romanians Everywhere, May 30, 2021.

title: The Sunday of Parents and Children: An Occasion to Honor and Support the Christian Family
intro:
Christ is risen!

 

 Approved by decision no. 629 of March 12, 2009 of the Holy Synod of our Church, the Sunday of Parents and Children, the first Sunday after June 1 – International Children’s Day, is an occasion to reaffirm the primary role of the family in raising and educating children for life.

The family is the crown of God’s creation and the setting blessed by Him in which the human being, as a child, begins to understand the mystery of God’s fatherly love for all people. The Savior Jesus Christ, the incarnate Son of God, blessed the family at the wedding in Cana of Galilee, performing the “beginning of signs” (cf. John 2, 2-11), helped parents in distress (cf. Mark 5, 22-43; Luke 7, 11-17), blessed the children (cf. Luke 18, 16) and revealed to mankind the love of the heavenly Father for the whole world (cf. John 3, 16).

The family is “the church in the home”, as Saint John Chrysostom called it, in which conjugal, parental, filial and fraternal love is cultivated. With the help of the parents, the child begins to feel God’s love for him and to cultivate love for those around him. The love of children for their parents is shown above all in communicating with them. The Lord Jesus Christ was a child, growing up in obedience to God the Father in heaven, to His Mother, the Holy Virgin Mary, and to Righteous Joseph, His guardian. The Holy Gospel says that “Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men” (Luke 2, 52).

The character of children is formed above all through their parents’ love for them and through their parents’ way of life. That is why parents are called to live the true faith, to cultivate love in the family, and the freedom and dignity of the human person, created in the image of God. In this sense, Saint John Chrysostom said: “Teach your child not to value money, nor worldly glory, nor only this present life. If he has such thoughts, he will be a wise man”[1].

Children born in the family and baptized by the Church in the name of the Most Holy Trinity can become citizens of the eternal heavenly Kingdom if, in their earthly life, they have cultivated the spiritual gifts received at Holy Baptism, as shown by the families that have given the Church several saints, inscribed in the calendar.

In recent decades, amid many challenges to the Christian family, the Church has intensified its efforts to strengthen it. In the Romanian Patriarchate, several years have been dedicated to the family and to education. For example: 2011 – the Homage Year of Holy Baptism and Holy Matrimony; 2016 – the Homage Year of the religious education of Orthodox Christian youth; 2020 – the Homage Year of the pastoral care of parents and children. The year 2021 is especially dedicated to the pastoral care of Romanians outside Romania, parents and children often living among strangers. In this context, from December 21, 2020 to August 22, 2021, the Romanian Patriarchate is holding the National Catechetical Contest Biserica: familia românilor de pretutindeni, addressed to the children in parish catechetical groups in Romania and in the diaspora enrolled in the National Catechetical Program Hristos împărtășit copiilor. The aim of the contest is to create spiritual bonds between catechetical groups in Romania and those in the Romanian diaspora. The participating catechetical groups designed and carried out cultural and philanthropic mini-projects, aimed mainly at the family.

The current pandemic has directly affected families in Romania and in the diaspora, as well as the education of children. Recent studies highlight the usefulness but also the limits of online education: stress, mental fatigue, signs of depression, loss of motivation, and difficulties in thinking, concentrating and making decisions. A sound education for life includes direct experiences lived within a concrete community, beginning in the family and continuing in school, in the life of the Church and in society.

In the context of the increasingly pronounced secularization of today’s society, there is a need for reaffirming the primary role of the family in raising and educating children for life, as well as for spiritual and material support of disadvantaged families and families with many children. At the same time, in order to respond to the deep spiritual needs of the generations of children and young people in today’s society, cooperation between Church, Family and School is very much needed, so as to cultivate the particular vocations of children and young people.

We address to Romanian parents and children everywhere a fatherly message of great esteem, together with the call to preserve and cultivate the Orthodox Christian faith, along with the values of Romanian spirituality, in the family, in the church and in society, for the joy of all children and parents!

 

With high esteem and blessing,

 

 

 

† Daniel

Patriarch of the Romanian Orthodox Church

 

* Message of His Beatitude Patriarch Daniel, Patriarch of the Romanian Orthodox Church, on the occasion of the Sunday of Parents and Children (June 6, 2021).

[1] Saint John Chrysostom, Despre slava deșartă și despre creșterea copiilor, Editura Institutului Biblic și de Misiune al Bisericii Ortodoxe Române, Bucharest, 2001, p. 427.

title: His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae Meets with the Priests and Teachers of the Sunday Schools
intro:
On Saturday, June 5, 2021, when Romania celebrates Teacher’s Day, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae held another virtual meeting with the priests and Parish School teachers of the Romanian Orthodox Archdiocese of the United States of America.

Wishing to improve the educational work of the Sunday Schools, several coordinators of the educational platform Resurse Educaționale Deschise Religie were also invited to this meeting. Developed by a team of about 300 religion teachers from Romania, the platform contains an impressive amount of material, useful both for religion teachers in Romania and for priests, teachers and catechists in the diaspora.

In an atmosphere full of interest and enthusiasm, the guests from the RED-Religie Platform, coordinated by Preoteasa Ionița Timiş, a teacher at the “Gh. Lazăr” National Pedagogical College in Cluj-Napoca, presented some of the materials available on the platform, suited to each age group of the Sunday Schools. The platform gives teachers, students and parents access both to religion textbooks with direct links to the corresponding video materials and to teaching and review exercises, assessment worksheets and additional activities (riddles, stories, 3 Minutes of Religion, puzzle games, crosswords, WordWall, StoryJumper, etc.). The platform also offers resources that promote national identity through the section “Românii de pretutindeni”. Here one can find materials about the Romanian language, culture and spirituality, presenting occupations, customs, people, places and historical events in a way that appeals to children. Both the platform coordinators and the Education Commission of our Archdiocese expressed the wish for future collaboration in using the rich resources on the platform, adapted to the needs of the children and young people of the Archdiocese.

The meeting continued with discussions about preparing for the 2021-2022 school year, when it is hoped that every Sunday School will begin its activity in person, in keeping with the regulations of each state. The curriculum for the coming year was discussed, along with ways to improve educational work through closer integration of the lessons with the liturgical calendar. Very Rev. Fr. Daniel Ene, president of the Education Commission, then offered some reflections on the Religion Olympiad, held virtually this year. The status of the ongoing educational project “Biserica – Familia românilor de pretutindeni” was also discussed; the project ends on August 22, the Sunday of Romanian Migrants.

We were glad to have this meeting and, with God’s help, we hope that the coming school year will allow us to help our children and young people know and appreciate more deeply the Orthodox faith they have inherited.

The Education Commission of the Archdiocese

title: Message of His Beatitude Patriarch Daniel of the Romanian Orthodox Church on the Sunday of Romanian Migrants
intro:
Homage Blessing for All Romanians outside Romania

The Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church has proclaimed 2021 the Homage Year of the Pastoral Care of Romanians outside Romania and the Commemorative Year of Those Fallen Asleep in the Lord; the Liturgical and Cultural Value of Cemeteries. The two themes, the homage theme and the commemorative theme, highlight two of the essential dimensions of the pastoral and missionary work of our Church.

In the present context of global migration, the Romanian Orthodox Church is developing and intensifying its mission and pastoral responsibility toward Romanian Orthodox faithful outside Romania, whom it regards as its faithful children and an integral part of the Romanian Orthodox communion everywhere. To this end, through the shared responsibility of all the hierarchs of the Holy Synod, and especially of the Romanian Orthodox hierarchs who shepherd the clergy and faithful beyond the borders of Romania, the Romanian Orthodox Church carries out rich liturgical, pastoral, missionary, cultural and social-philanthropic work in the parishes, monasteries, cultural institutions and social-charitable institutions of the Romanian Orthodox communities in the countries neighboring Romania and in the Romanian diaspora.

Given the large number of Romanians outside Romania (currently estimated at nearly ten million: six million Romanians living in historical or traditional communities in the countries neighboring Romania and four million Romanians living in church communities in the diaspora), the Romanian Patriarchate supports the efforts of Romanian Orthodox faithful settled temporarily or permanently abroad to preserve their religious, ethnic, linguistic and cultural identity.

In recent years, the pastoral care and special esteem shown by the Romanian Patriarchate for the Romanian Orthodox communities beyond the country’s borders have taken concrete form in the establishment of numerous parishes and of new dioceses, to meet the many spiritual needs of the Romanian Orthodox faithful in Bessarabia (Republic of Moldova), Serbia, Bulgaria, Hungary, Central and Northern Europe, Western and Southern Europe, the Americas, Australia and New Zealand, as well as in the establishment of representations (Jerusalem and Brussels) and Romanian Orthodox communities (Mount Athos, Syria and Lebanon, Cyprus, Turkey, South Africa, Japan, Croatia, Slovenia, the United Arab Emirates/Dubai).

The participation of the Orthodox members of the Romanian communities outside Romania in liturgical life, as well as in the cultural events and social-philanthropic activities organized by the parishes in the countries neighboring Romania and in the Romanian diaspora, is a blessing and a special joy both for them and for the servants of the Holy Altars.

At the same time, Romanian migrants need to live in harmony with the citizens of their adopted countries, for the sake of social integration, but without the cultural assimilation of Romanians.

With much fatherly love, we urge Romanians living far from their homeland to stay in constant contact with their loved ones who remained at home. We also advise the Orthodox faithful in Romania and abroad to cherish the family, made up of husband, wife and children, because the family blessed by God is the most precious intimate space in which conjugal love is expressed, as well as parental, filial and brotherly love. We exhort all to raise the young generation in the spirit of love for God, for the Church and for the nation, and to cultivate in children and young people the essential Christian virtues: faith, hope and love for God and for their fellow human beings.

We also urge Romanian migrants in various parts of the world to honor properly, according to our Orthodox Christian tradition, those who have passed on to eternal life. Remembering in prayer those who have fallen asleep in the Lord is an act of living Orthodox faith and a witness of love for our neighbors.

In particular, we thank the servants of the Romanian Orthodox Holy Altars outside Romania for their work and faithfulness. We also urge them to intensify their pastoral and missionary work of preserving and cultivating the Orthodox Christian faith and Romanian spiritual and cultural values.

We pray to the most merciful God to bless all Romanians, in Romania and abroad, and to grant them health and help, peace and joy, for many and happy years!

 

With great appreciation and fatherly blessing,

  

† DANIEL

Patriarch of the Romanian Orthodox Church

title: Pastoral Letter of the Holy Synod for the First Sunday of the Nativity Fast 2021
intro:
The Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church has sent a pastoral letter to all the faithful of the Romanian Patriarchate for the first Sunday of the Nativity Fast 2021.
Pastoral Letter of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church for the First Sunday of the Nativity Fast of 2021, on the significance of the Homage Year of the Pastoral Care of Romanians outside Romania and of the Commemorative Year of Those Fallen Asleep in the Lord; the Liturgical and Cultural Value of Cemeteries, in the Romanian Patriarchate.
 
To the most venerable monastic order,
To the most reverend clergy
 
and to the most beloved faithful
of the Romanian Patriarchate, 
 
Grace, joy and peace
from God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit,
and from us fatherly blessings! 
 
Most Venerable and Most Reverend Fathers,
Beloved brothers and sisters in the Lord,
 
The year 2021 was declared by the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church “the Homage Year of the Pastoral Care of Romanians outside Romania” and “the Commemorative Year of Those Fallen Asleep in the Lord; the Liturgical and Cultural Value of Cemeteries”  in the Romanian Patriarchate. These two themes, the homage theme and the commemorative theme, highlight two essential dimensions that are priorities in the pastoral and missionary work of our Church.
 
The Romanian Orthodox Church is thus not indifferent to the unprecedented scale that the migration of Romanians to other countries has reached in recent years. In response to this phenomenon, our Church, through its hierarchs, priests and deacons, is currently carrying out sustained pastoral work beyond the borders of Romania. It blesses and spiritually helps Romanian Orthodox faithful everywhere, whom it regards as its faithful children and an integral part of the Romanian Orthodox communion.
 
On the other hand, the remembrance in the Church of those who have fallen asleep in the Lord is an act of Orthodox faith and a confession of love for our neighbors. The commemoration of the departed and the veneration of heroes help develop a culture of gratitude and of communion between generations.   Their everlasting remembrance from age to age means their eternal commemoration from generation to generation.
 
Right-believing Christians,
 
In the books of the Old Testament we find testimonies that God, the Creator and Provider of all creation, shows special care for those who are away from their country and their people: “You shall not oppress a stranger, nor afflict him, for you know the heart of a stranger, because you were strangers in the land of Egypt”    (Exodus 23, 9), and elsewhere we read: “The stranger who dwells among you shall be to you as one born among you, and you shall love him as yourself; for you were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God”   (Leviticus 19, 34).
 
God Himself led and strengthened the people of Israel on their long journey to the Promised Land, guiding them “through that great and terrible wilderness, in which were fiery serpents and scorpions and thirsty land where there was no water; bringing water out of the flinty rock and feeding the people in the wilderness with manna”      (Deuteronomy 8, 15-16).
 
In the New Testament, merciful love for strangers becomes a rule of Christian life from the time of the apostles: “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling” (1 Peter 4, 9). In the Gospel according to Matthew, chapter 25 shows that love for one’s neighbor is the ultimate criterion of the universal judgment, more precisely the essential criterion for receiving blessing and inheriting the Kingdom of Heaven, for the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, the Righteous Judge, says: “I was a stranger and you took Me in”  (Matthew 25, 35).
 
In the context of the social, economic and political changes of the last century, the number of Romanian Christians outside Romania has grown.
 
In view of this reality, the pastoral care of the Romanian Orthodox Church for Romanians beyond its borders has taken concrete form in the establishment of dioceses, which have organized numerous parishes and monasteries,      to meet the spiritual needs of the Romanian Orthodox faithful in the historical Romanian communities: the Republic of Moldova and Ukraine, Serbia, Bulgaria, Hungary, as well as in the diaspora: Central and Northern Europe, Western and Southern Europe, the Americas, Australia and New Zealand.
 
Where particular pastoral and missionary circumstances did not allow for the establishment of dioceses, representations and Romanian Orthodox communities were organized , such as those in the Holy Land, Mount Athos, the Middle East, Cyprus, Turkey, South Africa, Japan and elsewhere .
 
Today, as a result of sustained pastoral efforts, the Romanian Orthodox Church has, beyond the present borders of Romania, four archdioceses and nine dioceses.   These eparchies include 1,337 parishes and branch parishes, as well as 64 monastic settlements, served by 1,245 Romanian clergy.  
 
Through the Romanian Orthodox hierarchs and clergy abroad, the Romanian Orthodox Church strives to build, buy or rent places of worship wherever there are Romanian communities, thus giving every Romanian Orthodox Christian the opportunity to take part in the holy services in Romanian and to stay connected with the Mother Church.
 
In the Romanian Orthodox churches outside Romania, Romanians feel the joy of rediscovering and living the faith of their forefathers, take part in liturgical life, ease their longing for their loved ones and their native places, and reaffirm their deepest identity.
 
Through worship, as well as through the cultural events and social-philanthropic activities organized by Romanian parishes abroad, the enduring spiritual values of Orthodoxy and of the Romanian people are promoted, Romanian traditions are passed on, and the Romanian language is cultivated. In this way the Romanian Orthodox cultural, ethnic and ecclesial identity is preserved, which ensures social integration in the host countries without cultural assimilation and without loss of national identity.
 
For this reason, the Romanian Patriarchate consistently provides financial help to these Romanian communities as far as it is able, while also taking the necessary steps with the competent State institutions to support Romanians everywhere.
 
As a sign of its constant pastoral care for Romanians settled permanently or temporarily abroad, the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church decided that the first Sunday after the feast of the Dormition of the Mother of God be dedicated to Romanian migrants.
 
Therefore, both the Sunday of Romanian Migrants, and the Day of Romanians Everywhere, established by Law no. 101/2015 and celebrated on the last Sunday of May, are days of deep spiritual significance, reaffirming the traditions and values of the faith and culture of the Romanian people.
 
Beloved faithful,
 
The Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church also declared 2021 the Commemorative Year of Those Fallen Asleep in the Lord in order to highlight and promote the liturgical and cultural value of cemeteries. From the standpoint of our spiritual identity, the cemetery is the place where the graves of those who have fallen asleep in the Lord lie, awaiting “the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come”, as the Orthodox Creed says. Therefore, the cemetery is also a symbol of commemoration and of communion between generations.
 
To honor the memory of those who have fallen asleep in the Lord, the Orthodox Church keeps a rich order of services and commemorations (memorial services) that include prayers and petitions for the forgiveness of their sins and the repose and salvation of their souls.
 
In particular, the commemoration of heroes of all times and places, like the veneration of the dead in general, is an expression of steadfastness in faith and of continuity and unity in thought and feeling across generations. The veneration of heroes is the sign that we do not forget and that we treasure their sacrifice, and of the hope of their eternal communion with Christ the Lord, in the hope of the Resurrection and of eternal life.
 
Romanian Orthodox cemeteries, some listed in Romania’s national cultural heritage, others containing valuable funerary monuments dedicated to national figures, highlight an essential spiritual dimension: the gratitude shown to predecessors over time, as well as the capacity of a faithful people for commemoration and communion with past generations.  
 
The cemetery has a deep liturgical and cultural meaning in our Romanian Orthodox Christian tradition. Caring for the sacred place where the bodies of those who have fallen asleep in the Lord are buried is a duty and a responsibility of Christians, keeping alive the flame of remembrance of the departed from age to age, or from generation to generation.
 
This honoring of cemeteries is a true culture of the Romanian soul, which believes, feels and confesses that love born of faith is stronger than death. The great number of commemoration lists and memorial services for the departed, for those who have fallen asleep in the Lord and for the heroes of the nation is a powerful factor in cultivating awareness of our national identity, unity and continuity. The history of the Romanian Orthodox Church bears witness across the centuries to the care it has shown for the memory of our forebears.
 
At every Holy and Divine Liturgy we commemorate the hierarchs of the Church; the founders, donors and benefactors of the holy churches; the Romanian heroes, soldiers and fighters of all times and places who sacrificed themselves on the battlefields, in camps and in prisons, for the defense of the homeland and of the ancestral Orthodox faith, for the unification of the nation, and for the freedom, unity and dignity of the Romanian people; and all those who have fallen asleep in Christ the Lord, the Conqueror of death.
 
Beloved brothers and sisters in the Lord,
 
With the help of the merciful God, we are at the beginning of the Nativity Fast, also called the Christmas Fast.  This period is first of all a preparation, a sanctification of our soul and body through Confession and Communion, as well as through works of mercy. Christian works of mercy, seen as the fruits of “faith working through love” (Galatians 5, 6), strengthen brotherly communion.
 
This year, we have been called to cultivate more deeply our brotherly communion with the Romanians living around Romania’s borders and in the Romanian diaspora. In particular, we thank the servants of the Romanian Orthodox Holy Altars outside Romania for their work and their faithfulness to the Romanian people, and for their work of preserving and promoting the Orthodox Christian faith and Romanian spiritual and cultural values.
 
At the same time, we urge Romanians living in various parts of the world to honor the memory and the graves of those who have passed on to eternal life, because only prayer and gratitude keep a living relationship between souls, a spiritual communion stronger than the physical death of the body.
 
We are going through an extremely difficult time for health and for the value of life, when many people are afflicted by the new epidemic that has spread across the globe. In this period there is great need for prayer and brotherly help, for drawing closer to God and for practical solidarity among people.   
 
Therefore, this year too, we address the priests and lay faithful of our Holy Church with the fatherly exhortation to organize collections of food, clothing and medicine in parishes, monasteries, deaneries and diocesan centers. These will be distributed first of all within the community, to those who are suffering and in need, to disadvantaged families with many children, to the elderly and to people living alone without children or relatives, especially those living in rural areas.
 
Confident that this year too you will show Christian generosity and respond with love to our fatherly call in this holy work of charity and help, we thank you for the generosity you have shown in previous years and remind you of the words of the Lord Jesus Christ: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5, 7).
 
We pray to the most merciful God to bless all Romanians, at home and abroad, granting them health and salvation, protecting them from all evil and strengthening them in every good work, to the joy of our Church and of the Romanian people everywhere, and to number those who have fallen asleep in the Lord among the righteous and grant them rest in the light and love of the Most Holy Trinity.
 
With great appreciation, we embrace you as a father and impart to you the apostolic blessing: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all!  ” (2 Corinthians 13, 13).
 
† DANIEL

title: Far from Our Native Land, but with Romania in Our Souls!
intro:
That is how we celebrated Romania’s National Day on Sunday, December 5, 2021, at “Saint George and Saint Dimitrios the New” Romanian Orthodox Church in Las Vegas. United by language and by longing, we made it a memorable day with an artistic program dedicated to the Day of the Great Union of Romania of December 1, 1918.

It was a double celebration: with joy in his soul, the parish priest, Fr. Mihai Bălan, read the Holy Gospel from Luke, chapter 13, verse 11, which tells of the healing of the bent woman, who becomes a symbol of strong faith, light, prayer and hope. Preparing for the great feast of the Nativity of the Lord calls us to open our hearts and to cleanse ourselves through prayer, fasting, confession and Communion. Only then is the miracle of healing of the body, and above all of the soul, revealed! That is why Fr. Mihai urges us all not to be shy before the Sacrament of Confession, but to free our burdened souls.

We are in the Nativity Fast, and, as every year, the month of December brings with it more generosity and openness; we become more merciful and more attentive to those around us. And because on December 6 we celebrate Saint Nicholas, protector of children and defender of the Orthodox faith, the little ones present at the service and at the artistic program were not forgotten this year either and received gifts from Saint Nicholas.

After the Divine Liturgy, the whole Romanian community was directed to the church hall for the traditional meal, which of course included fish soup, lovingly prepared by Mrs. Floarea Constantin. It was heartening that young and old alike proudly wore the Romanian ie, resonated with the symbolism of the day and went home more fulfilled.

The artistic program was opened by Mrs. Lia Roberts, Honorary Consul General of Romania in Las Vegas, who introduced the ROYA choir for the singing of the two national anthems: of the United States of America and of Romania. Next came an instrumental performance by the Gliga family together with violinist Ivo Gradev. The ROYA children, Alex, Nicu, Dominic, Chris, Jonchris, Matthew and Alexis, presented a short poetry montage, followed by a musical performance by Sara Spiridon and Cornelia Lopez. We stepped into the Transylvanian land of the Miorița through the caval of Ion Petrică, the “Bădia” of Las Vegas. And the Ciuleandra dance ensemble (Ioana, Svetlana, Raluca, Ana, Elena, Ioana, Lisa) captured the full attention of the audience.

The members of the Parish Council, Fr. Mihai Bălan, president Panta Stanciu, vice president Lia Roberts, Oana Butunoi, Floarea Constantin, Alla Popova, Svetlana Chirica, Daniel Popescu, Camelia Bratu, Ileana Danciu and Cristian Gliga, thank all who took part and offer the traditional greeting: Many years, Romania! Many years, Romanians everywhere!

Fr. Mihai Bălan

December 6, 2021

Editor: Elena-Mihaela Gliga

title: New Decisions of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church
intro:
On Thursday, December 16, 2021, the working session of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church took place in the “Teoctist Patriarhul” Aula Magna of the Patriarchal Palace, chaired by His Beatitude Patriarch Daniel.

By secret ballot, the Holy Synod elected His Grace Nestor Hunedoreanul, Auxiliary Bishop of the Diocese of Deva and Hunedoara, to the office of Bishop of Deva and Hunedoara, succeeding the ever-memorable Bishop Gurie Georgiu, who passed away in October 2021. The enthronement of His Grace NESTOR, Bishop of Deva and Hunedoara, will take place on December 26, 2021.

At the same session, the following decisions were also made:

  • The declaration of 2023 in the Romanian Patriarchate as “the Homage Year of pastoral care for the elderly” and “the Commemorative Year of hymnographers and church chanters (psaltai)”;
  • The inclusion in the Church Calendar of Saint Diadochos the Hierarch, Bishop of Photiki, commemorated on March 29. The liturgical texts of his synaxarion, service and akathist, as well as his icon, were also approved;
  • The approval of the liturgical texts of the service and paraklesis of Saint Symeon the New Theologian (March 12);
  • The approval of the text of the akathist of Saint Justin the Martyr and Philosopher (June 1);
  • The approval of the request of the National Agency against Trafficking in Persons to publish a flyer on preventing human trafficking and distribute it through the parishes of the Romanian Orthodox Church.

The Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church commends the social and philanthropic work of the dioceses, parishes, monasteries and social centers.

 

Press Office of the Romanian Patriarchate

title: Young Carolers at SS. Constantine and Helen Cathedral in Chicago
intro:
On Thursday evening, December 23, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae welcomed young carolers at SS. Constantine and Helen Cathedral in Chicago. This year the young people prepared for caroling by learning old carols rediscovered in recent years and cherished by Romanian Orthodox Christians for their theological value and musical beauty. His Eminence Nicolae urged the young people to keep caroling for their families, friends and acquaintances and to bring them the joy of the proclamation of the Nativity of the Lord:

The joy of the Nativity of the Savior of the world is proclaimed to each of us in this season through the carol, through the ancient song that reminds us of the sacred history of the event and its meaning for us. The carol is the folk versification of what Holy Scripture reveals to us about the birth of the Child. Children and young people go caroling on Christmas Eve, bringing each of us the good news of the Incarnation of the Word, the news of God’s coming down to earth to save mankind. The carol therefore brings joy because it carries this good news. Each of us receives the carol, repeats it and passes it on to our loved ones, just like any caroler. We could say that we too travel together with the carol and, together with those who were present, become witnesses of the great event.

The carolers received sweets, fruit and small icons, and thanked their host for the welcome.

You can watch the recordings of the carols here.

title: What Was New at the “Mihai Eminescu” Symposium in New York
intro:
At this  beginning of a year still threatened by the global pandemic, the Romanian community of New York hosted  the “Mihai Eminescu” Symposium on January 16, 2022, as part of Romanian Culture Day, an event that has most honorably reached its 29th edition.  As in previous years, the event is under the patronage of the Academy of Romanian Scientists, USA Branch, the Union of Professional Journalists of Romania, the Romanian  Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas and, locally, the Romanian  Institute of Orthodox Theology and Spirituality, New York. His Eminence Dr. Nicolae Condrea, Metropolitan of the Americas, sent a beautiful message  of  greeting, which the event’s main organizer, Prof. Th. Damian, read at the opening of the Symposium. We were glad to admire the Order of “Saint John Jacob of Neamț, the New Chozebite”, which Prof. Damian recently received from His Beatitude Daniel, Patriarch of the Romanian Orthodox Church, on reaching the age of 70, and we join in wishing him health and strength for his work.

Soloist Lia Lungu sang with deep feeling the song Rugăciune on verses by Mihai Eminescu. The whole audience sang the academic hymn Gaudeamus igitur and Imnul lui Ștefan Vodă, which created the right atmosphere for the event. The New York symposium was inspired by the celebration at Putna Monastery, on August 15-16, 2021, of 150 years since the First Festival of Romanians Everywhere and the First Congress of Romanian Students Everywhere. Theodor Damian was present there together with a delegation of young Romanians from the Metropolia of the Americas. The original event had been organized on August 15-16, 1871 by the students of the “România Jună” Society, led by Mihai Eminescu and Ioan Slavici. Just as our New York friends could not imagine missing Alba Iulia on December 1, 2018, at the centennial of the Great Union, so the celebration at Putna dedicated to Romanians everywhere, and above all to Eminescu, could not take place without them. At Putna they were given albums of monastic art and other books, which were shown to the participants at the Symposium  in New York.

In the already considerable history of this Romanian academic event, one new element was the hybrid format, with participants from different corners of the Romanian world attending on Zoom alongside those present on site. Because a webinar was used, as is usual in academic life, we missed the gallery of participants and the active chat we have grown used to over the last two years of literary gatherings on Zoom. But we have no doubt that other technical formats will be used for other kinds of events, such as literary gatherings with book launches and lectures.

A second new feature  of this 29th edition was the venue chosen for the academic event. My memories go back to 2006, when I was first invited to and took part in this “Mihai Eminescu” Symposium  in  New York.  Over the years the event was hosted at Harvard University in January 2007, then for several editions by the Consulate General of Romania in New York, occasionally by the Romanian Cultural Institute in the city, and even at various Romanian restaurants. The moving surprise was to find that this time the Symposium was held in the sacred space of “Saints Peter and Paul” Church in Astoria, New York, where a memorial service has always (I insist that this has been without exception) been  celebrated with deep feeling for Mihai,  the absolute poetic genius  of our national culture. I recognized that the setting of the holy place gave the event a certain elevation, and so I found this choice truly blessed.

Mrs. Oana Leonte of California, attending the event on Zoom, mentioned that in the UNESCO year 2000, Eminescu was celebrated at the Romanian House in Hayward, near San Francisco. The show Trecut-au anii, performed by actor Ion Caramitru, was staged at a Catholic Cathedral. The actor even made a point of saying that “this is the first time Eminescu has been recited in a church.” I am not convinced that this is quite so, but what is certain is that in that year of UNESCO recognition the actor carried the Romanians’ “peerless poet” to several continents. And now, in January 2022, the Eminescu Symposium found its place in an Orthodox house of worship, that is, in a church of the faith of the poet and his family.

The moderator of the event, Prof. Nicole Smith, announced the general theme of the Symposium:  Eminescu and the Spiritual Unity of All Romanians in Light of the 150th Anniversary of the First Festival of Romanians Everywhere – Putna – 1871.

The honor  of opening the Symposium was reserved for the university professor and writer from Sibiu, that is, myself. The topic I researched was entitled The Dramatic Journalistic Destiny of the Transylvanian Nicolae Cristea and the Moldavian Mihai Eminescu, an entirely new text supported by 21 bibliographic notes, in which the ideas were enriched with illuminating quotations from the journalism of the two writers. Nicolae Cristea and Mihai Eminescu were brought together by the boldness of their dignified political stance, their responsible patriotic feeling and their professional martyrdom. Destiny had it that in the very same year, 1883,  both were expelled from the stage of Romanian journalism, even though Eminescu was later invited to contribute to “Fântâna Blanduziei”, and Nicolae Cristea was among the founders of the new Sibiu newspaper “Tribuna”, over which he watched with his journalistic experience until his death.

Marian Nencescu, literary critic and historian and associate researcher at the “C. Rădulescu-Motru” Institute of Philosophy of the Romanian Academy, Bucharest, developed the theme Eminescu’s Encyclopedism. Building on a varied culture accumulated at each stage of his intellectual growth, the poet-philosopher left in his manuscript notebooks the proof of his encyclopedism, which is also evident in his original poetry.

The paper by Ştefan Stoenescu, essayist, comparatist and translator from  Ithaca, New York, entitled Symbols and Echoes of Some of Eminescu’s Poetic Compositions That Shaped Romanian Spiritual Unity, is to be published in the pages of the journal “Lumină lină”.

Literary critic  M. N. Rusu,  editor-in-chief of the journal “Lumină Lină”, New York,  illustrated the idea of his paper, entitled Eminescu and the Military  Unity of the Romanian People, with the names of some of the founders of the modern army to whom the poet felt connected.

Dr. Doru Tsaganea, professor of mathematics at Metropolitan College of New York, presented in his well-grounded and captivating style the theme The Congress of Romanian Students at Putna Monastery in the Context of the European Political Situation of 1870-1871. The objectives formulated with great political finesse by Eminescu in his articles Să facem un Congres and Echilibru lay at the foundation of the student event of 150 years ago, when Putna was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, where a religious celebration was accepted, but not one with a  national subtext, which is what that celebration in fact was.

Mrs. Valentina Ciaprazi, writer and professor of French language and literature at  LaGuardia College, New York, addressed the theme Eminescu’s Spirituality, a Reflection of Authentic Romanian Spirituality. But the speaker’s thoughts turned toward the homeland and toward the young talents of today’s Moldavia. The professor, who left Botoșani,  follows their development not only with interest but also with concern about the wrong direction taken by the followers of the aesthetics of ugliness. In a sad world in which statues are torn down and artists are blamed, we feel with sorrow that culture itself is despised. Eminescu is still relevant today. For us he embodies Greater Romania itself. From his youth he proved to be responsible, and as a poet he did not shy away from rebuking Romanians for their faults, but he did so as a father. He identified himself with Decebalus and with Trajan, since for him Greater Romania existed long before it was achieved. His nationalist political activity was stifled, beginning with the first file of prohibition in June 1883. Posterity was no fairer, because it contested his verses of high national character and looked for xenophobic accents in them, as is insinuated, moreover, in various literatures of the world.

At the close of the session, Fr. Theodor Damian, writer, professor emeritus at Metropolitan College of New York, president of the American Branch of the Academy of Romanian Scientists and of the Romanian Institute of Orthodox Theology and Spirituality, New York, developed the theme Eminescu, the Romanian Diaspora and the Motherland. Its central idea was the truth that wherever Eminescu was, in Cernăuți or in Blaj, in Vienna or in Berlin, patriotic feeling always accompanied him. But then, as now, love of country was considered dangerous by some.  Eminescu showed his concern for the motherland both as a poet and as a journalist. He organized the first celebration of Romanians everywhere in the Austro-Hungarian Empire at Putna Monastery. Young people were called to take up the defense of national identity. At Putna a new Deșteaptă-te române came about, for young people from all the territories inhabited by the descendants of the Dacians were called there. The monastery chosen, a foundation of Stephen the Great, was itself a unifying symbol. Ciprian Porumbescu sang at Putna  to all of Dacia. The celebration then was both religious and national. Turning to history is an act of piety. Eminescu held that, if in the past a history was imposed on us, we must forge the future ourselves.

The Symposium concluded in a spirit of traditional continuity. Prof. Damian announced that exactly one week later a similar event would take place in New York, namely a symposium dedicated to the Union of the Romanian Principalities, a scholarly event that has likewise  reached its 29th edition.

The entire course of this New York Symposium brought the homeland into dialogue with its fellow Romanians across the Atlantic, proving that at the beginning of the 21st century authentic Romanian identity can flourish on any meridian of the world.

 

Anca Sîrghie
