title: Symposium Dedicated to the Union of the Romanian Principalities in New York
intro:
A blessed, frosty January day, lit by an almost unnaturally brilliant sun in the splendid blue vault of the sky. It was as if nature had strived to give this day a special aura, an atmosphere of joyful celebration. The faithful of “Saints Peter and Paul” Church in New York took part devoutly in the Divine Liturgy, and afterwards shared in a moment of  deep spiritual experience: the annual Symposium dedicated to one of the historical events of first importance that marked the destiny of our people, the Union of the Romanian Principalities.

Through the tireless efforts of Fr. Prof. Dr. Theodor Damian, surrounded by a devoted group of teachers, writers and journalists from the Romanian community of New York, the Symposium dedicated to the Union of January 24, 1859 has now, in January 2022, reached its 29th edition.

The Symposium was preceded by a short artistic moment, full of patriotic feeling, during which everyone present in the church sang two hymns dear to Romanians everywhere: Deșteaptă-te române and Basarabie frumoasă.

Before the holy altar, where the Symposium was held, framed by the Cross of the Savior Jesus, the icon of the Mother of God and the icons of so many other saints of Orthodoxy, the guests presented  their papers.

In his opening address, Fr. Theodor Damian made a point of emphasizing that in recent years, so troubled and so hard, festive occasions dedicated to the great events and the great personalities of Romanian history and culture have become increasingly rare, if not nonexistent, and more superficial and lacking in content and spiritual vibrancy, even in Romania, where not even Mihai Eminescu, the legendary figure of Romanian culture, is celebrated any longer as he should be. In New York, the community of “Saints Peter and Paul” Church, though not very large, is the only one that for 29 years has never forgotten to celebrate the illustrious forebears of the nation and the great events that marked its history, “making waves” here in America, far from the motherland, with wonderful echoes in Romania. Fr. Theodor Damian thanked the whole community and the church’s group of intellectuals, who, he said, are “the little leaven that leavens the whole lump”: literary critic M.N. Rusu, Prof. Dr. Doru Tsaganea, Prof. Valentina Ciaprazi, Prof. Ștefan Stoenescu, Dr. Flaviu Riţiu, Prof. Nicole Smith and photojournalist Alex Marmara.

As moderator of the symposium, Prof. Nicole Smith announced that the venerable Prof. Ștefan Stoenescu, who was to have presented the paper “The Union of the Principalities in Eminescu’s Formative  Consciousness”, had let it be known that he could not travel to New York but would send the paper for publication, and that literary critic and historian M. N. Rusu was ill.

Prof. Dr. Doru Tsaganea was invited to speak about “The Union of 1859 as an Important Moment in the Creation of the National and Sovereign Romanian State.” Thanking Fr. Damian for the opportunity to pay sincere homage to this great event in the country’s history, Prof. Tsaganea  recalled the year 1959, when Romania celebrated 100 years since the Union of the Romanian Principalities; although the country was in the depths of communism, the great celebration was lived by everyone in an atmosphere of joy and genuine patriotic enthusiasm that had nothing to do with the communism of those times. With strong  patriotic accents, the speaker praised Christianity and its values, in total opposition to communist ideology, which he considers an anti-Christian movement. Referring to the situation in today’s world, Prof. Tsaganea invited the audience to join the international movement to save Christianity and preserve national sovereignty. Giving examples from world history and from that of our nation, Prof. Tsaganea urged peaceful resistance, “without bloodshed”, to preserve the rights of freedom and democracy. Our duty, the speaker stressed, is to keep Romania in a Europe of homelands! Prof. Tsaganea’s fine address ended with strong and well-deserved applause.

Prof. Valentina Ciaprazi was invited in turn to present her view on “The Contribution of Napoleon III to the Union of the Romanian Principalities.” Taking a leap into the history of nineteenth-century Europe, she showed that under the Second Empire (Le Second Empire) of Emperor Napoleon III, France once again became one of the greatest powers in Europe, and that the emperor showed major interest in the two Romanian principalities, Moldavia and Wallachia. At the Vienna conference in 1855, France launched for the first time the idea that a Moldo-Wallachian union was needed, and three years later, in Paris in 1858, the importance of the Romanian nation in Europe was emphasized, as a “Latin nation par excellence”. The double election of Al. I. Cuza in Iași and then in Bucharest was considered a triumph by Napoleon III, who justified his interest in the Union of the Principalities by saying that it was a just and civilizing cause that had to be defended. That is why he would fight to establish Romania in Europe, to modernize it and to align it progressively with the other European countries. The great Romanian poet Vasile Alecsandri is said to have presented himself before Napoleon III, declaring: “The Romanian people bless you and acknowledge you as the Savior of Romania”.

Dr. Flaviu Rițiu, a longtime member of the church, spoke about the European geopolitical context at the time of the Union, highlighting the great electoral turmoil in Iași, where there were still many politicians who had not understood the importance of Cuza’s election, to the point of rigging the votes. There were also still many European countries that opposed the unification of the two countries and, after Cuza’s double election, contested the act of Union. Sharing his own memories of the great celebration of the Union of the Principalities in communist Romania in 1959, Mr. Rițiu stressed the need to maintain and cultivate the Christian religion as the religion of love.

At the close of the Symposium, Prof. Nicole Smith gave the floor to the parish priest, Prof. Dr. Theodor Damian, to present to the participants a great personality of the Romanian Orthodox Church, Archimandrite Melchisedec Ștefănescu, and his contribution to the achievement of the Union of the Principalities.

Showing that the Romanian Orthodox Church has always been beside and for the people, Fr. Theodor Damian stated that the Church was also directly involved in the act of Union at every level. Born in the Neamț region into a family of priests with a deep tradition in the Orthodox priesthood, Archimandrite Melchisedec studied in Piatra-Neamț, at the Socola Theological Seminary in Iaşi and in Kiev, later becoming a professor and bishop at Huși, Ismail and Roman. As a deputy in the ad-hoc Divan in Iași, he campaigned persistently for the idea of reuniting the two Romanian lands.

Elected Bishop of Roman in 1879, he soon became Minister of Religious Affairs of Romania. As a historian and full member of the Romanian Academy, he studied in depth the historical events of the past as well as those of the world in which he lived. He sacrificed his whole life to the high ideal of the Union, emphasizing the divine character of the idea of Unity. Through division, Archimandrite Melchisedec said, we become tools placed in the service of darkness. He was among the first to state firmly that the Romanians are not a small people, but a people that was forced to live in slavery and barbarism, and that God’s mercy has been and will always be upon it.

Fr. Theodor Damian concluded that, in a happy combination of Bible, history and politics, Archimandrite Melchisedec’s thought encouraged generations of Romanians to resist the humiliation of colonization, to vote for Unity, never again to be divided, and to fight for the salvation of their common homeland.

As a crowning moment of this fine celebration of the first and most important step toward the union of all Romanians in their common homeland, Romania, the participants in the symposium joined hands and, forming a circle suggesting the Romanian hora, sang the immortal song Hora Unirii on verses by Vasile Alecsandri.

“And let the Holy Sun see/ On a feast day/ Our brotherly hora/ On the Romanian plain,” says the poet, convinced that the whole universe, the Holy Sun, looked on with love and worked for the Union of the Romanian Nation.

 

Valentina Ciaprazi

January 24, 2022, New York

title: Pastoral Visit in Easley, South Carolina
intro:
On Saturday, January 22, and Sunday, January 23, 2022, the Romanian Orthodox parish of Saint Gregory the Theologian in Easley, SC put on festive garments. His Eminence Nicolae, Romanian Orthodox Metropolitan of the Americas, was among the faithful of the Greenville, SC area, and they celebrated Saint Gregory the Theologian, the patron of the parish. Those present on Saturday evening at the Akathist service learned about the life and ascetic struggles of Saint Anthony the Great, celebrated in the Orthodox Christian calendar every year on January 17.

On Sunday, January 23, the parishioners from the Greenville, SC area were joined by faithful from Columbia, SC and Atlanta, GA. Together they rejoiced in a Holy and Divine Hierarchical Liturgy dedicated to Saint Gregory the Theologian, the protector of the church in Easley, SC.

We give thanks to the Good God for gathering us in the house of prayer where, in the liturgical setting, each of us received a ray of the light (of the enlightenment) of the blind man of the Holy Gospel, as interpreted by His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae:

“To Saint Peter’s confession at Caesarea of Palestine, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God’ (Matthew 16, 16), Christ answers with the words: ‘Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but My Father who is in heaven’ (Matthew 16, 17). The same can be said of the confession of the blind man of Jericho. Hope and faith in the Messiah who can heal him had grown in his soul, and they now receive validation through this confession. Before the confession of the children at the Lord’s Entry into Jerusalem, ‘Hosanna to the Son of David,’ the blind man of Jericho recognizes Christ as the Messiah with the eyes of his soul and bears witness.”

We all then took in the homily about Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, great theologian, archbishop and poet. The saint left us over 45 orations, 400 poems and 245 letters. The Divine Liturgy was made unique by the presence of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, who at its end officiated the Great Blessing of Water together with parish priest Fr. David Hudson.

The joy was made complete when, young and old, we enjoyed the delicious dishes prepared both by members of the parish and by several faithful from Atlanta and Columbia, friends of our parish. Abundance and good cheer marked the beautiful Sunday we spent with spiritual benefit in the bosom of Christ.

Parish priest Fr. David Hudson and the Parish Council thank all those who labored to make the patronal feast a memorable one: from those who, to everyone’s joy, took pains to cook the appetizing dishes, to those who prepared the church for the event, making sure every detail was in place; from those who gave of themselves in singing, to those who made the effort to travel a long way to attend the Holy and Divine Liturgy.

May the Lord accept their sacrifice, and may Saint Gregory the Theologian intercede for them before Christ!

 

Reported by

Mihaela Livingston

title: The Story of 20 Years of Romanian Life in Western New York: A Day of Joy and Blessing at Holy Trinity Church in Rochester/Victor, NY
intro:
Sunday, February 13, 2022 was a blessed occasion for the community of the church dedicated to the Holy Trinity and to Saint Theodora the Empress (February 11) in Victor, NY, shepherded by Dean Fr. Daniel Ene, as His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan Nicolae visited the parish. It was a double celebration: the parish’s second patronal feast, of Saint Theodora, Empress of Byzantium, and the 20th anniversary of the beginnings of the church in this part of the world.

The program began with Matins and continued with the Hierarchical Divine Liturgy celebrated by His Eminence Nicolae, who was joined by the parish priest, Fr. Daniel Adrian Ene, and Fr. Ștefan Drăgoi of Saint Mary Parish in Norfolk, VA. The Divine Liturgy was followed by a memorial service for the departed founders of the church.

The faithful present at the holy services were able to venerate the holy relics kept in this church: relics of Saint Theodora, Empress of Byzantium, Saint John Maximovitch, the Holy Great Martyr Catherine, the holy and righteous Anna, mother of the Virgin Mary, and the Holy Martyr Ephraim the New, the slipper of Saint Gerasimos of Kefalonia, and a vestment of Saint Philothea of Curtea de Argeș.

In the homily that followed, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae spoke about the meaning of the 33rd Sunday after Pentecost, of the Publican and the Pharisee, bringing tears to the eyes of those present through the depth of his words. Humility and its role in the spiritual ascent was the main theme of his message. His Eminence also spoke about the period of the Triodion that we have just begun and about the life of Saint Theodora the Empress.

At the end of his homily, he congratulated the parish priest and all those who labor for this model parish on its achievements over these 20 years and, as a sign of recognition, presented a certificate of merit to mark the occasion, which reads: “NICOLAE, by the Grace of God, Metropolitan of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas, We give thanks to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, praying always for you, since we Heard of your father faith in Christ Jesus and of your love for all the Saints, according to the words of St. Paul (Col 1, 3-4), WE HAVE DEEMED WORTHY OF RECOGNIZING, the 20th ANNIVERSARY of HOLY TRINITY ROMANIAN ORTHODOX CHURCH, VICTOR NEW YORK and GRANTING this MERIT CERTIFICATE, as a testimony for ages to come, praying the Almighty God to reward all clergy and faithful of this parish with complete health and good progress in all things. February 13, 2022”

On the same occasion, he awarded Elena and Ioan Bocîrnea the American Metropolitan Cross for laity, the highest distinction given to lay people in our Metropolia, for their sacrifice, dedication and love for Christ and for the Church in Rochester, NY, over these 20 years.

At the end, the parish priest, Fr. Daniel Ene, thanked His Eminence Nicolae for celebrating the Liturgy and for all the fatherly care he has shown the parish and its priest over these 20 years, sharing memories of the first founding meeting of the church in Rochester, NY, held on January 26, 2002, and stressing that this celebration is only the beginning of a story of more than 20 years of Romanian life in western New York State. Two more anniversary events will follow: on June 12, 2022, we will celebrate the main patronal feast of the Holy Trinity, and on October 9, 2022, we will also mark Fr. Daniel’s 20 years in the priesthood. Fr. Daniel then presented a painted icon of Saint George the Pilgrim, patron of the Romanian parishes on the East Coast of the USA, whose pilgrimage with his holy relics had just concluded in the parishes of our Metropolia in the USA with the blessing of His Beatitude Patriarch Daniel and His Eminence Metropolitan Teofan of Moldavia and Bukovina.

The day of joy and blessing ended in the church’s social hall, which proved too small for the number of people at the festive meal held in honor of the day and of the guest, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae. The food and everyone’s joy were crowned by a short piano concert given by Dr. Mihai Dascălu and young Elena Coman.

Glory to God for all things!

Fr. Daniel Ene, Parish Priest

~~~

History of Holy Trinity Church in Rochester/Victor, NY

In building churches and monasteries, Christians have put something of their own souls into them, showing their love for the right faith. The story of the purchase, furnishing and upkeep of the church dedicated to the Holy Trinity, Saint Andrew the Apostle and Saint Theodora the Empress of Byzantium in Victor, New York, belongs to this same tradition.

Efforts to establish the first church of the Romanian community in central and western New York State began more than 20 years ago through the dedication of the Romanian faithful of Rochester, who wanted a house of worship more than anything else. The first meeting took place on December 1, 2001, Romania’s National Day, and as a result of this meeting the church’s certificate of incorporation (ID #23-7055260) was signed on December 21, 2001, and filed with the Monroe County clerk for registration. On January 26, 2002, the 143rd anniversary of the Union of the Romanian Principalities, with the blessing of His Eminence Iosif, locum tenens of the Romanian Orthodox Archdiocese in America and Canada, the first general founding assembly of the church was held, with Fr. Timotei Sas present, at Holy Spirit Greek Orthodox Church on South Ave, Rochester, NY. On this occasion the first parish council of what was then Holy Trinity Mission was elected. A series of community meetings followed in preparation for another significant moment in the history of our church, the arrival of a permanent priest, and on March 8, 2002, through the kindness of the secretary, Fr. Nicholas Apostola, the parish received its charter as part of the Romanian Orthodox Archdiocese in America and Canada.

The long-awaited day of a permanent priest came with the ordination to the priesthood of Deacon Daniel Adrian Ene and his installation as parish priest by His Eminence Archbishop Nicolae on October 12, 2002, in the beautiful Holy Spirit church of the Greek community on South Ave, Rochester, NY. It can be said without doubt that this day was historic, because from that moment the community began to grow and become stronger. In this early period, from October to December 2002, the Divine Liturgy was celebrated in the chapel of Holy Spirit Church and then, as the number of faithful grew, in the chapel of Annunciation Greek Church on East Ave., Rochester. None of this would have been possible, however, without the love and blessing of His Eminence Nicholas of Detroit, Metropolitan of the Greek Orthodox Church, who supported the work of the Mission by allowing services in these holy churches. There were also difficulties, to name only a few: parking in spaces reserved for the Greek community, a limited schedule we could not always fit into, not being able to use the social hall for fellowship meals after the Divine Liturgy, and the church alarm going off deafeningly during the general assemblies of our Mission. All of them, however, strengthened the desire to find a place of our own for the community of Romanian Orthodox Christians.

The desire to have our own house of worship was there from the very first moment, and with the blessing and help of the good God, the church at 56 Andrews Street, Victor, NY, then owned by Willowbrook Christian Church, was found for sale. Although the purchase of the church was completed on July 30, 2003, the first Divine Liturgy in our community’s new church was already celebrated on Palm Sunday, followed, naturally, by the first Romanian Pascha in Rochester in a church of our own. The newly purchased church, however, had been built almost 100 years earlier, in 1901 to be precise, by St. John’s German Lutheran Church of Victor, NY. The first service in this church was held on October 23, 1901; the architect and builder was Theodore Norton.

Several years followed of beautifying the new building and adapting it to Orthodox worship. We mention a few of these works.

As early as September 2003, work began on converting the parish school space into an apartment for the parish priest, thanks to the labor and donations of many faithful. The church windows were painted by Mr. Costel Nacu at the beginning of 2004.

Also in 2004, the church bell was raised, and on April 9, 2005, the Holy Cross in the church garden was blessed. On April 9, 2006, the plaque honoring the church’s benefactors and supporters was installed, followed by extensive consolidation and remodeling work both inside and outside the church. On July 7, 2007, the church was paid off in full and the title deed was received. After this, the project of painting the church in the Byzantine style began, carried out by Vali and Ramona Isari. By the end of 2009 the church was fully painted.

On June 21, 2010, the property next to our church at 68 Andrews Street was purchased and paid for in cash; there is a plan to build a new Romanian center for western and northern New York State there, a project we hope will begin soon.

In the meantime, the social hall, together with the parish school and the kitchen, was completely remodeled at the beginning of 2011, and in August-September 2011 the carved iconostasis, together with all the church furniture, was brought from Romania. The woodwork was skillfully made by Mr. Constantin Tudorei of Grumăzeşti, Neamţ.

From a pastoral and missionary point of view, our church, through its parish priest, has also tried to help the Romanians in neighboring cities and support their spiritual growth. Every month Fr. Daniel Ene celebrates the Divine Liturgy for the Romanian community in Syracuse, NY, and every three months for the Romanians in Buffalo and Ithaca, NY.

The consecration of Holy Trinity Church in Victor, NY, took place on October 9, 2011, in the presence of His Eminence Archbishop Nicolae, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicholas of Detroit, His Grace Vicar Bishop Ioan Casian of Vicina, many priests from Orthodox parishes in the northeastern United States and from Romania, and the Romanian Orthodox faithful of the area.

Saint Basil the Great says that nothing is more proper to our nature than to be in communion with one another, to need one another and to love one another. He also says: “I call that the most perfect community of life from which private ownership of property has been removed, from which disagreement of opinion has been excluded, from which all disturbance, rivalry and quarreling have been driven out, and in which all things are held in common: God, salvation; in which the many are one and the one is not alone but in the many. Nothing can be compared with life in communion, says Saint Basil the Great. What can equal this life? What happiness resembles it? What is more perfect than this bond and union? What is more pleasant than the union of souls? The members of the community are equally masters of one another.”

title: New Decisions of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church
intro:
On Thursday, February 17, 2022, in the “Teoctist Patriarhul” Aula Magna of the Patriarchal Palace, under the chairmanship of His Beatitude Patriarch Daniel, the working session of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church took place.

During this session, the Holy Synod approved the canonization of the Venerable Teofana Basarab (the first known nun of Romanian descent), with the title: Saint Teofana  Basarab the Venerable, as well as her inclusion in the calendar of the Romanian Orthodox Church, with her feast day on October 28.

The Holy Synod decided that, for health reasons, His Grace Bishop Daniil Stoenescu be transferred from his ministry as Bishop of Dacia Felix to the position of Auxiliary Bishop of the Diocese of Deva and Hunedoara, with the title Densuşeanul, since his personal residence is within the territory of this diocese. The locum tenency of the Bishop of Dacia Felix will be held by His Beatitude Daniel, Patriarch of the Romanian Orthodox Church, who will be commemorated at the religious services celebrated in the places of worship of the Diocese of Dacia Felix as Locum Tenens of the Bishop of Dacia Felix.

The Holy Synod appreciated the results of the “Masa bucuriei” program, carried out by the Social-Philanthropic Department of the Patriarchal Administration during 2021 as well. The total value of the goods donated in that year was 3,140,866 lei. These goods benefited 222 social-philanthropic institutions of the Romanian Patriarchate, which provided assistance to 19,824 people, the number of beneficiaries continuing to grow.

The Holy Synod noted with joy the launch of the project Eco-initiatives in the parishes of the Romanian Orthodox Church in Romania and the Republic of Moldova, which aims to initiate environmental education and identify solutions for increasing ecological responsibility within the Romanian Orthodox Church both in Romania and in the Republic of Moldova.

Regarding the organization of the Population and Housing Census of Romania from February 1 to July 17, 2022, the Holy Synod approved that the diocesan centers in Romania and abroad pass on to the clergy the exhortation to encourage the faithful to fulfill this civic duty and to declare their religious affiliation correctly, especially through self-enumeration, between March 14 and May 15, 2022.

The Holy Synod especially appreciated the social-philanthropic activity of the dioceses, parishes, monasteries and social centers in 2021, a year marked by the pandemic, and urges the faithful of the Romanian Orthodox Church, at the beginning of the Homage Year dedicated to prayer (2022), to remain united around the moral imperative of helping those who suffer and of manifesting faith in the Lord Jesus Christ through prayer and deeds of Christian love.

title: Pastoral Letter of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church for the Sunday of Orthodoxy in the Year of Our Lord 2022
intro:
To the most venerable monastic order, to the most reverend clergy and to the most beloved faithful of the Romanian Patriarchate, 

Grace, joy and peace from God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and from us fatherly blessings!

Most Venerable and Most Reverend Fathers,
Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ the Lord,

The Seventh Ecumenical Council, convened by the Holy Empress Irene (752-803) in 787 and presided over by Saint Tarasios, Patriarch of Constantinople, building on the biblical and patristic tradition of the six Ecumenical Councils, established that, just as the Holy Cross is venerated, so too must the Holy Icons be venerated: “As the figure of the precious and life-giving Cross, so also the venerable and holy icons, whether in colors, mosaic or any other suitable material, should be set forth in the holy churches of God, on the sacred vessels and vestments, on walls and on wood, in houses and by the roadsides; namely, the icon of our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ, of our spotless Lady, the holy Theotokos, of the honorable angels and of all the saints and holy men”[1].

However, the victory of the Seventh Ecumenical Council did not mean the end of the struggle to defend the right faith. Heavy storm clouds gathered in the clear sky of Christianity when another iconoclast emperor (an opponent of icons), Leo the Armenian (813-820), ascended the throne of Byzantium. But this time too, God did not leave His Church without a strong defense.

The theological resistance in this new war was led by another great defender of Orthodoxy, Saint Theodore the Studite (759-826), who, a century after Saint John of Damascus († 749), raised his voice and set down in writing the renewed foundation for the veneration of icons, in simple words of great spiritual depth.

This is his argument: “We know that the Son of God, having truly become man, was like us in all things. And since man can be depicted, this means that Christ too can be depicted. The painted icon is for us a holy light, a saving remembrance for us who see Him being born, baptized, working miracles, crucified, buried, rising and ascending into heaven, not deceived into thinking these things are not so, our sight working together with the contemplation of the mind, and through both sustaining faith in the mystery of salvation”[2].

The final victory of the veneration of the Holy Icons was proclaimed by the Council of 843, convened by the Holy Empress Theodora, another Orthodox empress, who, together with Patriarch Methodios of Constantinople (843-847), on Saturday, March 11, 843, in the Church of Blachernae in Constantinople, reaffirmed the decisions of the Seventh Ecumenical Council, confirming them and establishing them as final decisions valid for the whole Church.

The next day, Sunday, at the end of the Divine Liturgy, the Synodikon of Orthodoxy was solemnly read from the solea of the Church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, in the hearing of the right-believing people, who were present in impressive numbers.

Thus, from that year, 843, the first Sunday of Great Lent has become, for the whole Orthodox world, the Sunday of Orthodoxy, a great and holy feast on which the victory of the right faith over all heresies and errors is celebrated. 

Right-believing Christians,

The Sunday of Orthodoxy, celebrated since 843 throughout Orthodox Christendom, reveals to us God’s unceasing care for the Orthodox Church.

When we honor, venerate and reverently kiss the Holy Icons, we meet Christ, the Mother of God and the Saints of God.

Saint Theodore the Studite states very clearly that the veneration of the icon of Christ is directed to the Person of Christ: “The icon of Christ is nothing other than Christ, except, of course, for the difference of substance, as has already been shown many times. Therefore its veneration is a veneration of Christ, since nothing of the material of the icon is venerated, but only Christ, Who is portrayed in it. And things that have one likeness also have one veneration”[3].

Therefore, we believe and confess, as the God-bearing Fathers believed and confessed, that in the holy churches, when we take part in the Divine Liturgy, we partake of sanctifying divine grace by listening to the Holy Gospel, through the prayers said before the Holy Icons, and most fully by partaking of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Holy Eucharist.

When we venerate the icon of Christ, the Lord Jesus Christ is before us, and when we partake of the Body and Blood of Christ, the Lord Jesus Christ comes to dwell within us, that is, He becomes the Life of our life (cf. John 6, 53-54).

Beloved faithful,

It has become a tradition in the Romanian Orthodox Church to hold a collection on the first Sunday of Great Lent in all parish and monastery churches to support the missionary work of the Church.

The Central Missionary Fund is intended for the missionary and social work of the Church and for supporting poor parishes in Romania and abroad. The establishment of the Central Missionary Fund was decided in the time of Patriarch Justinian Marina, of blessed memory, at the session of the Holy Synod of September 18, 1956, when it was decided that a collection would be held on the Sunday of Orthodoxy in all the parishes and monasteries of the Romanian Patriarchate.

Following the organization of the Romanian diaspora through the establishment of new eparchies, parishes and monasteries, the Holy Synod decided in 2011 that this collection should be extended to all the eparchies of the Romanian Patriarchate, both in Romania and abroad.

The basis for such collections is found in Holy Scripture, which tells us in the book of the Acts of the Apostles that “all who believed were together, and had all things in common, and sold their possessions and goods, and divided them among all, as anyone had need” (Acts 2, 44-45).

Saint Paul the Apostle, in turn, was concerned about the needs of the Christians in Jerusalem, who were in difficulty, and initiated “a certain contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem” (Romans 15, 26).

Our Romanian tradition of generosity is very rich in acts of charity and in care for the Church of Christ and for the right-believing people. The Romanian people are hardworking and generous, loving God and their neighbors.

From their work and savings, the Orthodox faithful have given generously for the building and upkeep of places of worship and for the support of all the Church’s activities.

Still fresh in recent memory is the solidarity shown by the Romanian Orthodox faithful at the beginning of the pandemic in 2020 and throughout it, when the Church supported hospitals with what they needed to get through a very difficult period.

Thus, churches, monasteries and cathedrals helped the hospitals. A true communion of Christian love was formed then between the physicians of bodies and the shepherds of souls, which helped us pass more easily through the great trial of the pandemic.

Therefore, we urge you this year as well to open your hearts and help those whom life has brought into hardship. So “let each one give as he purposes in his heart, not grudgingly or of necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9, 7), supporting with your gift the missionary and social-philanthropic work of our Holy Church in Romania and abroad.

Let us use the period of Great Lent as an occasion for humble prayer, sincere repentance and works of mercy, and let us go to confession more often and partake more often of the Holy Eucharist, in preparation for the great feast of Holy Pascha.

Assuring you of our fatherly love, we bless you with the apostolic blessing: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all!” (2 Corinthians 13, 13). Amen!

President of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church

title: Pan-Orthodox Vespers at the Romanian Parish in Western New York
intro:
The year 2022 marked 20 years since the founding of Holy Trinity Parish in Victor, NY. Among the events occasioned by this important moment in the life of the parish was hosting and organizing the festivities of the Sunday of Orthodoxy.

On this occasion, clergy representing the Orthodox churches of the area (Greek, Ukrainian, Macedonian, American – OCA, and Coptic Egyptian) took part in the Vespers service, raising prayers to God for peace and reciting the confession of faith together, affirming with one voice the faith of the apostles, the faith of the holy fathers, the right faith, the faith by which the whole universe has been established.

At the end of the service, the Very Rev. Abbot Ieremia Berbec spoke to the participants about ­“The Demands of Being a Christian According to Fr. Arsenie Papacioc”.

Dean Fr. Daniel Ene, the parish priest, then thanked all the priests and faithful for taking part and offered them gifts, among them an icon of Saint Empress Theodora of Byzantium, whose holy relics are kept for veneration in this church. To celebrate the restoration of the holy icons, Empress Theodora led a huge procession of icons through the streets of Constantinople on Sunday, March 11, 843, the first Sunday of Great Lent that year. Since then the Church has celebrated the restoration of the icons on the first Sunday of Great Lent, known as the Sunday of Orthodoxy.

The festivities concluded with a Lenten agape meal held in solidarity with the tragedy the Ukrainian people are going through, with the donations received going exclusively to support humanitarian efforts for those severely affected by the war.

 

Reported by

title: Sunday of Orthodoxy at the Maramureș-Style Church in Caracas, Venezuela
intro:
On the first Sunday of Great Lent we served the Holy and Divine Liturgy of Saint Basil the Great, Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, attended with love and devotion by a multitude of faithful, both Romanians and local Venezuelans. As it was the Sunday of Orthodoxy, in the homily I spoke about the importance of Orthodoxy and its tradition, as well as about other aspects found in the following paragraph:

“Orthodoxy, then, in its character as authentic Christian tradition, means right doctrine in accordance with the faith received from the Holy Fathers, and this is of the same importance as the preaching of the Gospel. Correct doctrine is one side of the coin, and the other is evangelization. Correct doctrine is the guarantee of a sound foundation for evangelization; evangelization is, at the same time, a natural and living continuation of correct doctrine. The spirit of evangelization is not an additional activity in the life of the Orthodox Church, and the desire to pass on the Truth and Tradition to others is not just another occupation of the Church, but the authentic sign that the Body of Christ (the Church) is alive, growing, abiding and dynamic. The absence of evangelization is not merely a partial defect in the life of the Church; rather, it points to the presence of a corrupted faith and the falsification of the truth.”

The faithful were urged to practice prayer with dedication and devotion, so that the love of God may warm all hearts and turn the evil intentions of some into good thoughts toward the Christian people.

At the end of the Divine Liturgy the procession with the icons took place, commemorating the triumph of Orthodoxy over the iconoclasts, with all the faithful singing the appointed troparia with great joy and enthusiasm.

During the service, prayers of thanksgiving were also offered, especially because our small community suffered no loss of life during this coronavirus pandemic, the church having always been close to those who suffer, both through prayer and through acts of charity.

Given the challenges Venezuela is facing, the love of our brothers and sisters, shown through prayer and almsgiving, has helped us continue on our difficult road and answer God’s call in our lives.

The Maramureș-style Orthodox church dedicated to the Holy Emperors Constantine and Helen in Caracas, the capital of Venezuela, was built in the 1990s and consecrated by Patriarch Teoctist in 1999. The church is under the jurisdiction of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas.

title: New Romanian Orthodox Parish Dedicated to All Saints in Los Angeles, California
intro:
By the will of the good God and through the care of His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan Nicolae of the Americas, the All Saints Romanian Orthodox Mission in the Californian metropolis of Los Angeles now has a suitable place for church services and a community space.

All Saints Romanian Orthodox Church is taking shape north of Los Angeles, California, at the request of Orthodox faithful full of sacrificial love and through the work of Rev. Fr. Iustinian Deac. The parish was registered in accordance with its bylaws and regulations in Sacramento on July 24, 2020. It is the only Romanian Orthodox mission registered in the state of California during a period that was troubled for the whole world because of pandemic restrictions.

In the midst of the pandemic, when churches were closing for fear of death, a tiny group of Christians was laying a new Romanian and spiritual foundation, with hopes for better things and a better future for the citizens of Romanian origin living in the Los Angeles metropolitan area.

As of April 3, 2022, we have settled north of Los Angeles in a new location, 11921 Saticoy St, North Hollywood, CA 91605, through the kindness of the family of Rev. Fr. Viorel Vasile Vișovan and Preoteasa Gabriela.

On the 4th Sunday of Lent, of Saint John Climacus, Very Rev. Fr. Adrian Daniel Ene, Metropolitan Secretary and Dean for the East Coast of the United States of America, visited the new Californian mission and celebrated the first Divine Liturgy at the new location together with the priest in charge of the mission, Rev. Fr. Iustinian Deac.

The singing at the chanters’ stand was led by Deacon Valentin Despoiu, whom we thank.

Glory to God for all things, and thanks to the faithful for their sacrificial love!

title: Online Conference “Saint Symeon the New Theologian, Our Contemporary”
intro:
With the blessing and participation of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, on Saturday, May 28, 2022, the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas organized on Zoom and Facebook the third conference dedicated to the “Homage Year of prayer in the life of the Church and of the Christian” and the “Commemorative Year of the holy hesychasts Symeon the New Theologian, Gregory Palamas and Paisius of Neamț”, with guest speaker Deacon Dr. Mihai Iulian Grobnicu of the Parcul Domeniilor Parish, Patriarchal Chapel.

After the opening prayer, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae gave a brief summary of the previous meetings, followed by Deacon Florin Ciprian Petre’s presentation of the rich activity and  elaborate theological studies of Deacon Dr. Mihai Iulian Grobnicu, crowned by his doctoral thesis on “Pnevmatologia Sfântului Simeon Noul Teolog. O analiză dogmatică actuală.” 

The guest speaker offered a detailed presentation of the life and theological work of Saint Symeon the New Theologian (11th century), explaining why he has devoted much of his time to studying this important figure of the Church. From the presentation we learned that Saint Symeon’s work contrasts with that of his predecessors and that he has been labeled an “innovator”, with teachings that step somewhat outside the conservative zone of theology, since he (Saint Symeon) based himself on a concrete, conscious experience of the presence of the Holy Spirit and of God in the life of every person. 

At the end of this detailed presentation, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae led the question-and-answer session toward an analogy between the theology of Saint Symeon the New Theologian and that of Saint John Climacus, and then that of Saint Sophrony Sakharov. His Eminence Nicolae concluded that “we must open the treasure chest of values found not only in Holy Scripture but also in all the spiritual jewels of the Holy Fathers.” The spiritual gathering ended with the closing prayer and the hierarch’s blessing. 

The ZOOM recording of the conference can be found here.

Reported by

Fr. Orlando Stelian Geonea

title: Message of His Beatitude Patriarch DANIEL of the Romanian Orthodox Church on the Sunday of Parents and Children (June 5, 2022)
intro:
The Sunday of Parents and Children: Common Prayer

and Cooperation for Communion and Salvation

 

Approved by decision no. 629 of March 12, 2009 of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church, the Sunday of Parents and Children, the first Sunday after June 1, International Children’s Day, is an occasion to reaffirm the primary role of the family in the spiritual growth of children and their formation for life.

In the family, the child begins to understand the mystery of God’s fatherly love for all people. Therefore, the education of a child means not only knowledge and preparation for material life, but also spiritual growth, or the cultivation of the goodness of the soul as its beauty in its relationship with God and with others. In this sense, parents are called to cultivate the practice of praying together, as a source of joy and lasting love in the family. Prayer is the foundation of human life and spiritual growth; it helps us face the hardships of life and foretaste, even in this world, the light and joy of the resurrection and of eternal life. Prayer is not only the work of the person who addresses God, but also the mysterious work of God’s grace in the soul of the one who is in communion with Him. Nothing can replace prayer, and no activity is more precious than it, because prayer gives us inspiration and strength to speak the good word and to do the good deed.

This year, the Sunday of Parents and Children coincides with the 7th Sunday after Pascha, on which the Gospel passage is read about the high-priestly prayer of our Savior Jesus Christ, spoken shortly before His Passion (John 17, 1-3). This prayer reveals God to us as the Father of an eternal Son, Who came into the world to give people eternal life. The great mystery, or ultimate aim, of the prayer of the Lord Jesus Christ is the unity of the Church. He prayed that all who believe in Him “may be one”, that is, may live in communion, just as the Father and the Son are one, that is, live in communion, in a mutual gift of love and holiness: “Holy Father, keep through Your name those whom You have given Me, that they may be one as We are” (John 17, 11). The high-priestly prayer also shows us that Christ’s joy is fulfilled when His disciples keep the right faith and the unity of the Church (cf. John 17, 13).

In an increasingly divided and secularized society, in order to respond to the deep spiritual needs of the generations of children and young people, the Church calls parents, educators, schoolteachers and professors to permanent cooperation, in a spirit of fraternal communion and practical solidarity, so that the education of children may become a major shared concern. In recent decades, amid many challenges to the Christian family, the Church has intensified its activities concerning the education of children and young people. The year 2022 is especially dedicated to highlighting the importance and role of prayer in the life of the Church and of the Christian. In this context, from November 15, 2021 to May 21, 2022, the Romanian Patriarchate organized the National Catechetical Competition Rugăciunea în viaţa mea, which aimed to cultivate people’s relationship of communion with God and with their neighbor through prayer. Parish catechetical groups of children and young people from Romania and from the diaspora took part in the competition, and the winners received their awards on May 21, 2022, on the historic patronal feast of the Patriarchal Cathedral, the Holy Great Emperors and Equals-to-the-Apostles Constantine and his mother Helen.

We address to Romanian parents and children a fatherly message of great esteem, together with the exhortation to keep and live the right faith, to practice prayer in the family, and to cultivate parental, filial and fraternal love, to the glory of the Most Holy Trinity and to the joy of all children and parents!

 

With high esteem and blessing,

 

† DANIEL

Patriarch of the Romanian Orthodox Church

title: Exchange Between Romanian Youth from the USA and ASCOR Iași Students
intro:
From July 28 to August 3, 2022, an exchange is taking place between young Romanians from the United States of America, members of ROYA (Romanian Orthodox Youth of the Americas), and young people from ASCOR Iași, together with their colleagues from ATOR and Students for Life in Iași.

After the ROYA members took part in the International Camp at Oașa Monastery (July 18-27, 2022), they set out, accompanied by the ASCOR Iași students, on a route through Transylvania, Neamț and Iași, with the last stop to be in Bukovina, at Putna Monastery.

The aim of this exchange is to cultivate friendships between young Romanians living in the United States and those in Romania, united as they are by the same faith, the same language, the same values and the same desire to get involved in society through volunteering.  The relationships between young people from Romania and those from the diaspora have been built over time, reaching a high point at the Anniversary Student Celebration and Congress at Putna Monastery on August 14-16, 2021. The ideal shared by the young people of ASCOR Iași, ROYA and the participants in the 2021 Putna Celebration is a continuation of the ideal of the generation of Mihai Eminescu, Ioan Slavici, Ciprian Porumbescu and other young people who understood the need for cultural unity, “in thought and in feeling”.

As part of this exchange, the ROYA youth extended an invitation to the students of ASCOR, ATOR and SPV Iași to visit the Romanian communities in the United States and to take part in a series of events organized across the ocean.

title: Prayer – the Presence and Work of the Holy Spirit in Man
intro:
The Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church proclaimed 2022 as the Homage Year of prayer in the life of the Church and of the Christian. Also, in the context of the 1,000th anniversary of the repose of Saint Symeon the New Theologian († 1022) and the 300th anniversary of the birth of Saint Paisius of Neamț († 1722), the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church proclaimed 2022 as the Commemorative Year of the Holy Hesychasts Symeon the New Theologian, Gregory Palamas and Paisius of Neamț.

Prayer is the foundation of man’s spiritual life and growth; it is saving and sanctifying, because it fills us with the presence of the All-Merciful God.

Holy Scripture is rich in countless exhortations to pray. In the Old Testament, in the book of Ecclesiasticus, the wise Jesus, son of Sirach, says of the man of prayer: “He will give his heart to rise early to the Lord who made him, and will make supplication before the Most High. He will open his mouth in prayer and will make supplication for his sins” (Ecclesiasticus 39, 6-7).

In the New Testament, we see the Lord Jesus Christ both taking part in the services in the synagogues (cf. Mark 1, 21) and praying in solitude (cf. Luke 5, 16). The Savior taught His disciples the Our Father prayer, the source of inspiration for all other prayers. In the Pauline epistles, numerous counsels and requests for the increase of prayer can be found. Thus, the Holy Apostle Paul urged the Christian community in Ephesus: “Pray also for me, that utterance may be given to me, that I may open my mouth boldly to make known the mystery of the gospel” (Ephesians 6, 19), while to the Christians in Thessalonica he wrote: “We give thanks to God always for you all, making mention of you in our prayers” (1 Thessalonians 1, 2).

Prayer, as the presence and work of the Holy Spirit in man, brings comfort, peace and joy; it unites us with the Most Holy Trinity, the source of joy and eternal life, as well as with the Church of Christ of all times and all places. Without prayer there is no Church and no Christian life. When we lose the joy and peace of the soul, it is a sure sign that we are no longer praying as we should or as much as we should.

The Orthodox Christian must pray as much as possible, because prayer helps us to face the hardships of life and to foretaste, already in this world, the strength and joy of the Resurrection and of eternal life. Prayer is the victory over man’s estrangement from God, from himself and from his neighbors; it is a source of communion and becomes the life of our life.

In the context of the restrictions caused by the worldwide pandemic situation of recent years, as well as the problems created as a result of the war in Ukraine, the need has been seen to emphasize the practice of prayer in the life of the Church and of the faithful and to intensify the doing of good deeds.

The faithful, as members of the mystical Body of Christ, are united with one another by grace, the suffering of one being borne by the whole ecclesial community, according to the apostolic exhortation: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6, 2), and according to the spiritual counsel: “pray for one another” (James 5, 16). In this sense, Fr. Prof. Dumitru Stăniloae says that prayer “can also be considered a means of transcending people from a life closed in selfishness and in the world to the life of communication in God, as His kingdom. Prayers indicate such a transcending, or a going out of man closed in selfishness, toward God in Trinity, the God of love, even when in prayers we ask for goods necessary for earthly life, as conditions of preparation for the kingdom of God”.[1]

Starting from the exhortation of the Holy Apostle Paul: “Pray without ceasing!” (1 Thessalonians 5, 17), under the guidance of the Holy Spirit and through the spiritual practice of the Holy Fathers, the prayer “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner”, called both “the prayer of the mind” and “the prayer of the heart”, has become the best path for the enlightenment of the soul and the sanctification of the Christian’s life.

Also, through the practice of unceasing prayer, hesychasm was born in the Church: the longing for stillness and watchfulness, or the state of peace and spiritual joy in contrast with the agitated world.[2]

Therefore, with much fatherly love, we urge all Romanians living far from their homeland to remain united through continuous prayer with God, the Creator of heaven and earth, and at the same time with their loved ones who have remained in Romania.

Romanian migrants in various parts of the world are called to cherish and cultivate prayer in the ecclesial community as well as in the family, prayer being the source of pure love for God, for loved ones and for one’s neighbors.

At the same time, we paternally urge the servants of the Holy Altars of the Romanian Orthodox Church outside Romania to increase prayer and to multiply their missionary and pastoral activities of preserving and cultivating the Orthodox Christian faith and Romanian spiritual and cultural values.

We pray to the All-Merciful God to bless all Romanians, in Romania and abroad, and to grant them peace and health, help and joy, for many and happy years!

With great appreciation and fatherly blessing,

† Daniel
Patriarch of the Romanian Orthodox Church

Notes

[1] Fr. Prof. Dr. Dumitru Stăniloae, Spiritualitate și comuniune în Liturghia ortodoxă, Ed. IBMBOR, Bucharest, 2004, p. 9.

[2] See: André Scrima, Despre isihasm, trans. by Maria-Cornelia Ică, Anca Manolescu, Toader Saulea and Sorana Corneanu, Bucharest, Ed. Humanitas, 2003, pp. 74-75.

title: 86th Anniversary of the Annunciation Cathedral, Olmsted Falls, Ohio
intro:
The year 2022 brought the Annunciation Cathedral in Olmsted Falls, Ohio 86 years blessed by the good God, years in which thousands of Romanians, some continuing and others beginning, have carried out the most important work of a person on this earth: the work of the salvation of the soul, which can never be conditioned by time and space. These 86 years of our Romanian church’s existence on American soil bring spiritual growth when we think of the countless offerings of prayer brought to the holy altar, which have comforted souls seeking salvation in the apostolic Orthodox faith inherited from our forefathers. In this way every Romanian has been able to become “a light to the Gentiles” of true life in Jesus Christ our God, awakening in others the curiosity and desire to follow the way of truth and life as well.

So that each of us might understand, in this time of weakening faith caused by the turmoil in the world, that our Savior Jesus Christ, together with all the saints and the Mother of God, is with us, this year’s anniversary was blessed with the great joy of having in our midst the Myrrh-Streaming Icon of the Mother of God from Hawaii (Iveron). As its caretaker, Deacon Nectarios, says: “The icon goes only where the Mother of God wishes.” The news of its coming to our church arrived in the message: “we can be there Saturday evening, if you are available,” and we understood at once that it could not have been better: Saturday evening, just as we were beginning the celebration of the church’s anniversary with Hierarchical Vespers, together with our Archbishop and Metropolitan, His Eminence Nicolae, who completes the joy of our parish at every anniversary and beyond.

The icon of the Mother of God gathered at our church about 600 faithful, Romanian, Greek, American, Russian, Ukrainian, Antiochian and Albanian, first to comfort them, and then for them to celebrate the 86 years of existence of the Church of her Son among the Romanians. Through her prayers and grace may she keep it pure and spotless for our children’s children, until the second coming of her Son! We thank the Mother of God for stopping at our church as well!

This wonderful icon is a copy of the Iveron Icon of the Mother of God from Mount Athos. It was received as a gift in 1997 by its present caretaker, Deacon Nectarios of Hawaii, and in 2007 the icon began to stream myrrh; in 2008 it was officially recognized as a wonderworking icon by the Synod of ROCOR. This year marks 15 years during which the icon has worked thousands of miracles, comforted millions of people and traveled throughout the Orthodox world, showing people tangibly the gift of God for the strengthening of their faith.

Our anniversary celebration continued the next day, Sunday, September 18, when His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, together with Very Rev. Fr. Ioan Gherman, celebrated the Hierarchical Divine Liturgy. In the homily of His Eminence Nicolae, on the Sunday after the Elevation of the Holy Cross, we were urged to cast off all weaknesses and sins and to follow Christ, the one true God, who is the Way, the Truth and the Life.

After the Divine Liturgy came the fellowship meal at the Crystal Party Center, where, besides the anniversary banquet, we enjoyed an artistic program of Romanian songs and poems by the Sunday school children, who reminded us of the “iarba verde de acasă.”

We thank first of all our Archbishop and Metropolitan, His Eminence Nicolae, for clothing this celebration with fatherly love; the Ladies Auxiliary for the delicious food of these two days of celebration; the Parish Council for the good organization; the Sunday school teachers together with our little ones; and all the members of our parish, because we are all one large family blessed by God and because each one contributes to the upkeep and care of this holy place. Glory to God for all things!

Your brother in Christ,

Fr. Petru Neaga, Parish Priest
Olmsted Falls, OH

intro:
A few years ago a new family joined our community (2016). It was the first family with more than 2 children, namely 4, three of whom were past their teenage years (at the time). Ever since then we began to think that our Orthodox young people need to socialize and form friendships with other Orthodox young people, and that the only way to help them (as we are a small church with an aging population) is to organize activities for young people to which we also invite other parishes.

Besides this, we unfortunately began to realize that Orthodoxy in America is very different from the one we know in Romania, Russia and Greece. Putting all these realities together, we concentrated everything into the YAR Mission and Vision:

Our YAR mission is to create the right environment and foundation for the Pan-Orthodox young adults, where they can rediscover the authentic Orthodox spirit, receive the right teachings, and revive the old ethnic traditions, build a sound fellowship, and support each other during these difficult times.

Our YAR vision: The future of the Orthodox Church is not about adapting to the times and being cool; it is about being authentic, living in truth and love, and becoming the temple of the Holy Spirit. Without the right teaching, inspiration, support, and communion with other Orthodox Christians our young adults will be confused, weak, and lost. This will impact the whole Orthodox Church in her assembly and jeopardize her future.

On September 17, 2022 we were able to launch the first edition of a retreat for young adults aged 18 to 35, the St. Siluoan Young Adults Retreat (YAR). At this launch the event enjoyed the participation of 28 young adults.

It was intense work, but it was rewarded. We added a special section for YAR to the church website (https://www.stmichaelorthodox.com/about-3), created a mission and vision for this program, a poster and a brochure, and began promoting it. Those who organize events of any kind know that the hardest part is not the organizing but the effective promotion that brings in participants. And above all we asked for the help of our patron, Saint Silouan, who sent us resources and young people in abundance.

Starting from the mission of St. Siluoan YAR, we tried to combine the spiritual aspects with relaxation and fun in a balanced way. The Divine Liturgy started our journey, and Fr. John, the YAR host, opened the day with a talk on the teaching of Saint Silouan, emphasizing love of enemies, including the enemies of the Church.

In the relaxation and fun category, we began with getting-to-know-you and energizing exercises, continued with 2 interesting workshops (How to Prepare Koliva and a Wood Carving Workshop with wood artist Dimitrios Klitsas) and ended with a campfire and a fireside chat. Although 12 hours had passed since the program began, our young people let themselves be drawn in by the hosts and joined in Greek and Romanian folk dances.

The high point of the event was the spiritual conversation on the theme Confession and the Spiritual Father in the Orthodox Church, led by Protosyngellos Ieremia (Berbec), Abbot of Saint Demetrios the New Monastery in Middletown, NY. Fr. Ieremia was a fitting choice for our young, intellectual and knowledge-hungry audience (Father holds a doctorate in Mathematics from the University of California, Berkeley).

The Abbot from Middletown reached the hearts of his audience through the simplicity and yet spiritual depth of a dialogue built like a pyramid around the Holy Fathers and contemporary Saints. The presentation, structured following mathematical logic, began by explaining the undeniable truth that we humans are selfish and that selfishness is so well camouflaged within us that we need another person to bring it to light. In the same direction, using the words of the Psalmist, the speaker said “that all men are liars” and that is why we cannot trust our own judgment, needing a second person who observes things from the outside much more clearly and objectively and who can help us on our spiritual journey. Father went further along the line of Saint Silouan and Saint Sophrony, explaining that Adam, through disobedience, cut the umbilical cord of the living bond with God and was cast out of Paradise. This bond can be restored only through repentance, and the surest path is obedience to the Church, experienced through obedience to one’s spiritual father in the sacrament of confession.

Protosyngellos Ieremia introduced the figure of Fr. Arsenie Papacioc (of the 55 participants in the spiritual conversation only 5 people, being Romanians, knew who Fr. Arsenie was) and the bond he had, as a disciple, with the Abba of Techirghiol. He explained that the bond of trust with one’s spiritual father, in which you hand over your heart to him completely and submit to obedience, is built over time. The conversation ended with a question-and-answer session. Vespers followed, at which Fr. Ieremia served together with Fr. John, and the singing was done by our protopsaltis together with other cantors taking part in the event.

The participants welcomed and appreciated the organization of such an event and, in response, also took part in the all-night vigil for the feast of Saint Silouan (September 23 – 24). After the service they were glad to enjoy tea and pies together, even though the hour was late.

Our immediate goal, to help young people build healthy friendships based on common interests and longing for God, was achieved. At the initiative of our protopsaltis, Loukas Mironidis, the young participants of different ethnicities have already settled the details and will go hiking in the Monadnock mountains in New Hampshire. Here we have included the registration link, in case there are readers who wish to join (https://forms.gle/99B3ompLRBvqySbK8).

And at the next all-night vigil, for Saint Porphyrios (December 1-2), we will again welcome the young people with hot tea and pies, Lenten ones this time. Their youth, enthusiasm and beauty have inspired us and have already put us to work organizing the second edition of the St. Siluoan Spring Young Adults Retreat at the end of May 2023.

But until then, so that we do not lose our practice and they do not lose interest, we have prepared a few more activities that we hope will engage them even more in the bond of fellowship that has begun, timidly but surely, to take shape.

We hope that our initiative and example will serve as inspiration for other parishes as well. And we are ready to offer support and “knowhow” to those who wish it.

 

With love in our Lord Jesus Christ,

Preoteasa Camelia Downie
