title: First Divine Liturgy in Romanian in the State of Utah
intro:
With the blessing of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, the Romanians of the Salt Lake City, Utah area took part in the first Divine Liturgy served in Romanian in the midst of their community.

Through the kindness of the Greek community, the Holy and Divine Liturgy was served at the Prophet Elias Greek Orthodox Church by Rev. Fr. Ștefan Drăgoi of the Saints Joachim and Anna Parish in Seattle, WA. In his homily, Fr. Ștefan spoke about the road that must be traveled from each person’s wish to have a Romanian parish to the uniting of the whole community in this common goal, supported and embraced by all. Prayer offered in one’s mother tongue not only eases the longing for the lands of one’s forebears but settles like a balm on the soul, comforting every heart that is weary and weighed down by daily cares, by too much work and too little rest, by the pain of loneliness and the lack of communion and fellowship.

About 35 people attended the Divine Liturgy. They thanked His Eminence for his missionary care and expressed the wish that this event be repeated, perhaps even becoming a regular activity. 

Fr. Ștefan Drăgoi

title: Addition to the Anniversary Album - His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan Nicolae, 20 Years of Episcopal Ministry in America
intro:
Vladika Nicolae – the friend of the Romanians in America

 

Every anniversary is a stop for remembrance, but also for hope in God’s mercy for the things to come.

I was glad to receive the written invitation of His Grace Ioan Casian, Romanian Orthodox Bishop of Canada, to write a few lines about the work and personality of His Eminence Archbishop Nicolae Condrea, Romanian Orthodox Metropolitan of the Americas, now at this anniversary hour, marking 20 years since His Eminence’s election, ordination and enthronement as spiritual shepherd of the Romanian Orthodox Christians living on the American Continent.

When I think how quickly two decades have passed since His Eminence began his work as a Romanian Orthodox Hierarch in lands far from the Homeland, one thought echoes in my mind: man stands under “the helm of time”, as the Moldavian scholar Miron Costin wrote more than 300 years ago.

It is a joy and a blessing from the Lord God to be called to the work of Chief Shepherd, but also a great responsibility for the salvation of the souls of the faithful entrusted to one’s care.

Born on April 15, 1967, in historic Tomis, the young Nicolae Condrea was inspired by the missionary zeal of the Holy Apostle Andrew – Protector of Romanians everywhere, which led him to the work of the episcopacy, understanding that the life of a Hierarch means first of all preaching the word of the Gospel in the World and serving one’s fellow human beings.

When I met Hierarch Nicolae, I saw a man of the Church, a seeker of truth, responsible, well prepared, eager to answer the call of the Church with a yes, and steadfast as an oak with green branches.

I said to myself then: behold, in the Garden of the Mother of God in Romania, another worthy, self-sacrificing and devout Hierarch has sprung up, who will bring forth much spiritual fruit in the Field of the Lord!

And indeed, I was right!

Because he proved to be a missionary servant, Vladika Nicolae received from the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church a special obedience: the organization and coordination of the Romanian Orthodox Church in the Americas - by no means an easy mission – this modern “Galilee of the Gentiles”, a religious and social space strewn with challenges of all kinds, where not just anyone can succeed.

Passing through times of trial, from then until today, with constant patience and with much wisdom and kindness, His Eminence has known how to steward with diplomatic skill, like the good steward of old, all the activities and the course of the Romanian Orthodox Church in America, so that, by the blessing of the Lord God and through the election of the Holy Synod, he was raised to the rank of Metropolitan of the Americas in 2016.

Today, the Metropolia of the Americas appears like a spring flower, tended and cherished.

For the Orthodox Romanians of the American diaspora it is like a spiritual mother who holds all her children close to her heart with great warmth and love, keeping alight the torch of love and remembrance for Romania!

This is also due to the care and dedication of Metropolitan Nicolae, who continues to carry his cross with self-denial, fulfilling with ardor the ordinance of the Lord God, strong in suffering and steadfast in the face of difficulties, not tempted by vainglory, his mind set on heavenly riches.

Now, in closing, I confess that I am honored to have had the opportunity to meet Metropolitan Nicolae Condrea, and I express my joy that the Romanians of the Americas are shepherded by a hardworking and missionary hierarch, as well suited as can be for such a mission!

May the Lord God grant him health as strong as diamond, a watchful mind for guarding the ancestral faith, and help in all his pastoral-missionary work, always pouring out blessing and goodness upon the clergy and the right-believing People!

 

Many good and healthy years!

 

† Calinic

Archbishop of Argeș and Muscel

title: Spiritual Camp at St. John Cassian Parish, San Antonio, Texas
intro:
From September 14 to 17, 2023, the SPIRITUAL CAMP “CREȘTINUL ÎN CONTEMPORANEITATE” took place at the Parish of St. John Cassian and St. Andrei Șaguna, Metropolitan of Transylvania, in San Antonio. On this spiritual ascent we were strengthened and encouraged by the spiritual workshops and lectures given by Rev. Archdeacon Prof. Sorin Mihalache of the Dumitru Stăniloae Faculty of Theology in Iași. The meetings took place over 4 days, full of information and exercises beneficial for spiritual growth and the cultivation of the virtues.

On the first day, Thursday, September 14 

- a review of some takeaways from last year’s meetings concerning the role of attention in the spiritual life according to the Philokalic authors (Theoliptos of Philadelphia, Isaac the Syrian, Hesychios the Sinaite);

- the components of attention were presented: selection, orientation and coherence of attention, as well as the obstacles most often encountered in exercising attention with regard to selection and orientation

- emphasis on the fact that attention cultivated and practiced in daily life allows for a well-ordered life, and that the habit of watching over oneself helps greatly in the practice of prayer.

- a brief inventory of the obstacles to attention in the everyday setting: noise, sensory overstimulation, cognitive overload (a great deal of unstructured and fragmented information), fatigue, an ever-growing amount of entertainment and multiple exposure to it, multitasking, and increasing social and professional obligations:

In the second part, several practical solutions for improving attention were mentioned:

- seeking out and arranging a quiet place for prayer, reading and meditation

- stretches of time in which to do one single small thing - the unit of time

- carrying out an activity at a calm pace

- practicing a 3-minute pause.

On the second day, Friday, September 15 

- how each person’s intention changes their perception of reality and, of course, their way of acting. Hence the importance of spiritual habits that always direct attention toward the edifying, beneficial aspects of daily experience. Aspects of this kind are found in Philokalic literature concerning the management of sensibility and the guarding of the senses;

- The spiritual life in fact presupposes this constant work of governing the movements of the soul and the activity of the senses, in order to keep the mind undisturbed by external things that would burden the soul and hinder the work of prayer, the relationship with one’s neighbors and service to them.

On the third day, Saturday, September 16 

- the workshop on Spiritual Intelligence took place. Considerations on Spiritual Intelligence were discussed from the perspective of the spiritual experience of the Philokalic authors.

- Spiritual Intelligence brings together the efforts of certain authors in the field of psychology to offer a structured understanding of what is specific to spirituality in relation to other human activities or experiences (solving logical problems, physical abilities, musical inclinations, etc.).

- In the workshop, attended by 23 people, three of the characteristics of Spiritual Intelligence were discussed, together with the way they are captured and valued in the Philokalia: openness to cultivating inner states and dispositions of a spiritual nature (prayer, stillness, contemplation, wonder), the habit of a metaphysical view of the surrounding reality (one that seeks to grasp the cause of things and their purpose, the meaning of existing realities, and the harmonies and beauties of the surrounding world), and the inclination to give spiritual meaning to life’s experiences. Each of these three characteristics of the spiritual life is also identified by the Philokalic authors as part of cultivating an inner Christian life, which is important to emphasize in the context of present-day life, marked by a pronounced culture of exteriority.

On the fourth day, Sunday, September 17 

- The theme of the lecture was COMPASSION: UNIVERSAL and INDISPENSABLE. The importance of cultivating compassion in the parent-child relationship, in the couple, in the extended family, with friends and neighbors, and at work. The following aspects were addressed:

- the important distinction between EMPATHY and COMPASSION, the latter containing, besides feeling and perceiving the other person’s state, the component of helping, the desire to come to their aid to relieve their suffering. (In this respect, from a neuropsychological point of view, compassion receives as its linguistic equivalent a word well known in Orthodox Christianity, namely mercy).

- The starting point was the text of the Sunday Gospel, from which to draw meanings related to Compassion.

- Christ Himself shows us the image of the supreme love full of compassion, and He also calls all of us to this living expression of compassion: Whoever desires to come after Me…

- Then, Christ’s words in the Gospel text show us that the living expression of compassion is possible only through the denial of the selfish self, which does not allow us to place the other at the center of our concerns. The counsel to deny ourselves highlights a point of major divergence between Christian spirituality, life in Christ, on the one hand, and the life of the world on the other. Often in society we encounter something diametrically opposed, since contemporary culture places great emphasis on PLEASURE, POWER and COMPETITION, each of which, and all of them together, negatively affect the expression of compassion toward people. From this point of view it was emphasized that self-denial means enduring lovingly, losing in favor of the other, continuing to love the one who does not thank you for it, bearing the burdens of others. Taking up the cross, indicated by Christ as the second step of the Christian life, also proves essential in expressing compassion. Being able to help others and serve them requires a pure gaze and a pure heart that do not stumble over the other’s shortcomings. For this reason, only the one who knows his own faults and tends to them (my sin is always before me) can show the strength to forget his own good in order to do good to another. Finally, and most emphatically, compassion is not a power of love that a person can offer another effortlessly and from his own psychological reserves. Compassion is God’s heavenly love for us, felt by those who have drawn near to Christ and who radiate God’s love toward their neighbors. That is why the last step in the effort to cultivate compassion is the concern to follow Christ, a work that crowns a person’s effort to grow in mercy toward his neighbors, enriched by the divine mercy he himself has received, a mercy that heals him and makes him capable of mercy toward another. 

On the other hand, it was emphasized that the experience of compassion has a significant impact on harmonious development, in terms of EXPRESSION, COMMUNICATION and SOCIAL CONNECTEDNESS, and also at the physiological level. Recent findings in neurophysiology show that practicing compassion is cardioprotective, has a beneficial impact on the immune response, regulates the inflammatory response, and tones the vagus nerve, thereby regulating the activity of the visceral organs. The experience of compassion also promotes well-being, offering satisfaction and the sense of a meaningful life, and it increases resilience, enhancing HEALTH in general.

Finally, it was emphasized that, living in the experience of God’s merciful love for man, every Christian ought to show the world endless love and mercy, offering help with great generosity, embracing the world, loving everyone, being full of compassion for each person, growing in diligence in doing good, and fulfilling all this with great joy, thus bearing witness to God’s merciful love for all people.    

The lecture concluded with the text of MATTHEW 5, 43-48: You have heard that it was said, “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.” But I say to you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who spitefully use you and persecute you, that you may be sons of your Father in heaven; for He makes His sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. For if you love those who love you, what reward have you? Do not even the tax collectors do the same? And if you greet your brethren only, what do you do more than others? Do not even the Gentiles do so? Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.

For all these things we give glory to God worshipped in Trinity, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and with the hope of bearing fruit we look forward to future meetings.

Fr. Valentin Ilieș

title: Lecture on Christian Meditation at the Resurrection of the Lord Parish, Sacramento, CA
intro:
On September 23, 2023, the Resurrection of the Lord Parish in Sacramento had an exceptional guest in the person of Archdeacon Prof. Sorin Mihalache of the Dumitru Stăniloae Faculty of Theology in Iași. Fr. Professor gave a lecture on the theme “Should I Get Lost in Thought or Rein My Thoughts In? On Christian Meditation, Mindfulness and Some Other Current Mental Practices in a Neuroscientific and Philokalic Evaluation.” Our faithful know Fr. Professor mostly from his extensive online activity: lectures, sermons and presentations on topics that often go beyond the sphere of theology, such as the exact sciences, mathematics,  physics and the neurosciences. The lecture addressed several aspects of cultivating the inner work, as it is valued in the experience of the holy authors of the Philokalia and in some recent research in the neurosciences.

The first point presented was that it is important to realize that the mind is the core of the human being. The content of our thinking and reflection is an intimate part of the person that most often remains unknown to those around us. In the spiritual life of the Orthodox Christian, watching over one’s thoughts is essential, since everything begins with a good or an evil thought. In daily life, however, constantly under the barrage of everyday responsibilities, information, advertising and entertainment, people find no respite to be alone with themselves and acquire the habit of examining their own thoughts. And this can have harmful consequences, since a repeated thought, good or evil, sanctified or passionate, ends up turning into a word and then into a deed. The conclusion of this first stage of the presentation was that it would be useful, following the Philokalic authors, to strive to understand that thoughts and reflection are the core of our being and that the spiritual life must also include the sanctification of this hidden part of us. Some scientific estimates suggest that a person has between 60,000 and 80,000 thoughts a day. Many of them are thought fragments, chained together in what is called the frenzy of thoughts, a continuous movement of the untrained mind that brings no benefit. How many of these thoughts are good? How many are dedicated to God? How many are sanctified by prayer? Such questions would help us acquire a certain watchfulness over our reflection, so that we can observe our thoughts carefully and confess them in the Sacrament of Confession, in the effort to cleanse the mind as well.

A second point presented at the lecture concerned the importance of thinking in our conduct and our deeds. Both the Philokalic authors and recent research in the neurosciences show that our inner state, the dispositions that accompany us throughout the day, are closely linked to the content of our thoughts. Thinking plays a part in depressive dispositions, but through its content it also matters for well-being. Our reflection can support us in doing good works, but it can also hinder us in the virtuous life. This is important because, as another observation notes, everything we consume (as cultural or life experiences), all our efforts to gain knowledge, and above all the striving of prayer, leave their imprint on the mind, increasing its light or its darkness. Living in the world and taking in portions of experience and cultural productions, of virtuous life or entertainment, a person trains the mind to desire more and more either the world or God, to follow either the saints and their virtues or the celebrities of consumer culture. In this respect, the principle expressed by the spiritual life, and confirmed today by neuroscientific research, indicates that repetition, the sustained work of the mind, becomes essential to its formation. This is how we understand the striving of the saints to set a guard over the senses, to guard their thoughts against evil thinking, and to place the mind again and again in a state of prayer. For this exercise, understood as a person’s ascetic effort to empty himself of worldly and useless things, prepares him to receive God.

A final important point of the presentation concerned some of the spiritual practices mentioned in the Philokalia that precede or strengthen watchfulness over one’s thoughts and the work of prayer. Without doubt, prayer and confession are the most effective ways to cleanse our inner reflection, as they strengthen the bond between man and God, that is, the work of God’s grace in man. According to some Philokalic observations, certain measures could help in this work. Among them was mentioned the act of bowing in worship, performed in moments of stillness and withdrawal from the noise of the world, for prayer and meditation. The verse Be still, and know that I am God! (Ps. 45, 10) indicates, in a way, that knowledge of God is possible if a person interrupts the worldly dynamic of his life. Another important measure that can support prayer is stillness, withdrawal from the noise of the world: “He who seeks to pray with power must shut the door (emphasis ours) and raise his mind from all that is vain or temporal, sitting in a quiet cell, in a secluded corner” (Saint John Climacus, The Ladder, Step 27, ch. 3, in the Philokalia, vol. IX). Another way to improve prayer, for the cleansing of the mind, is cultivating attention. In this regard, Philotheos of Sinai was quoted, who observes that we must unite prayer with attention, because attention purifies prayer, and prayer in turn purifies attention.

This is because, Philotheos says, attention “watching without ceasing, recognizes those who enter. And hindering their entry a little, it calls upon the Lord Jesus Christ for help to drive away the cunning enemies. And prayer hinders them by opposing them. And Jesus, being called upon, drives out the demons together with their fantasies” (Philotheos of Sinai, Chapters on Watchfulness, ch. 25, in the Romanian Philokalia, vol. IV). Finally, reading and meditation can help train our reflection, so that we seek more and more the content that increases our virtue and the light of edifying meanings, to replace the frenzy of fragmented and scattered thinking. Peter of Damascus and Isaac the Syrian urge us, in the texts included in the Philokalia, to value reading in stillness, because it is the source of pure prayer, and Isaac the Syrian observes that unceasing meditation on Scripture is the light of the soul.

Observations such as these underline the need for a person interested in the spiritual life to also take up careful work focused on his own thoughts, as an essential part of the path of purification and illumination, toward a life in communion with one’s neighbors and with God.

From the perspective of new scientific research, Fr. Archdeacon succeeds in shedding light on the teaching of the Philokalic fathers who, in their time, without contemporary technology at their disposal but with the light of the Holy Spirit, intuited what the neurosciences confirm today through experiments and instruments. This ability to move with ease in both directions, from the spiritual realm to the empirical realm of the exact sciences, and to demonstrate not contradictions but the difference in language between science and religion, makes Fr. Archdeacon, through his studies, a bridge between spiritual thought and the rigor of secular scientific research.

We thank the Good God for the wonderful opportunity to have Fr. Archdeacon Sorin Mihalache in our midst, exclaiming with gratitude the words of the Akathist of Thanksgiving: “We thank You for the people Your providence has placed in our path.”

 

Fr. Teodor Gîrlonța

title: 7 Years since the Elevation of His Eminence Nicolae to the Dignity of Metropolitan
intro:
His Beatitude Daniel, Patriarch of the Romanian Orthodox Church, officiated the ceremony elevating His Eminence Nicolae to the rank of Metropolitan. The event was attended by hierarchs of the Romanian Orthodox Church and representatives of the central authorities. 

In his homily entitled A Higher Dignity Means a Greater Responsibility, His Beatitude highlighted the importance of the episcopal ministry.

The solemnity of the service, far from being merely a formal ceremony in which the insignia of the new Metropolitan’s rank are presented, is in fact meant to highlight his role as teacher of the right faith, minister of the Holy Mysteries, chief shepherd of the clergy and faithful of his diocese and defender of church unity in the Metropolia entrusted to him, said the Patriarch of Romania.

His Beatitude also explained to the faithful present the meaning of the episcopal insignia.

For his part, His Eminence Nicolae showed the importance of establishing a Metropolia for the Romanians living on the American continent.

The elevation of the Archdiocese to the rank of Metropolia is the fulfillment of an older idea for a better organization of the Orthodox Romanians scattered not over one continent but over several, for the USA and Canada are not just two countries but, by their size, two continents, to which the South American one is added. Our Metropolia now offers the proper ecclesiastical administrative framework for the unity of all Orthodox Romanians by encompassing several dioceses, said His Eminence.

Representatives of the state and of the Archdiocese in the United States also spoke during the ceremony.

title: Pastoral Letter of the Holy Synod for the First Sunday of the Nativity Fast 2023
intro:
To the most venerable monastic orders, the most reverend clergy

and the most beloved faithful of the Romanian Patriarchate,

 

Grace, joy and peace from God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit,

and from us fatherly blessings!

 

 

Most Venerable and Most Reverend Fathers,

Beloved brothers and sisters in the Lord,

 

Following a beautiful practice established in 2008, the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church proclaimed the year 2023 in the Romanian Patriarchate as the Homage Year of the Pastoral Care of the Elderly and the Commemorative Year of Church Hymnographers and Cantors, thus urging us to reflect on the care the Church has for all generations, and therefore also for the elderly.

For the hierarchs, clergy and faithful of the Romanian Patriarchate, honoring the elderly is a moment of gratitude toward those who gave us birth, raised and educated us, toward those who sacrificed themselves so that we might be free in our country and in our ancestral faith. It is an occasion to remember also the holy families of the Old and New Testaments, as well as the holy families in the history of the Orthodox Church, who brought into the world the great saints of the Church, models for us today. Nor do we forget the elderly scholars who formed many generations of people of culture, offering our country light for the soul. Last but not least, we remember our parents and grandparents who, through their kindness, wisdom and love, left to the world as their legacy a new generation of people living on this earth.

If the year 2022 was dedicated to prayer and hesychasm, as a spiritual work of proclaiming the unceasing prayer of the mind and heart, in the commemorative year 2023 prayer is considered in relation to the beauty of church singing, psalmody itself becoming communal prayer in the liturgical life of the Church.

 

Orthodox Christians,

The traditional human community has always cared for the elderly, regarding them as a source of blessing and wisdom, and also of merciful love, through their participation in the education of children and young people.

Holy Scripture speaks to us of the respect the Jewish community showed to the elderly. In the Old Testament, respect for the elderly was made into a commandment that everyone had the duty to fulfill: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20, 12), or “You shall rise before the gray headed and honor the presence of an old man, and fear your God: I am the LORD” (Leviticus 19, 32).

Whoever did not respect his elderly parents was seen as a blasphemer: “Whoever forsakes his father is like a blasphemer, and whoever angers his mother is cursed by the Lord” (Ecclesiasticus 3, 16).

The New Testament shows us clearly that the wisdom of the elderly comes from their closeness to God through prayer and from the virtuous life they lead. Thus the Righteous Simeon was not only a learned man but also a man of constant prayer, enlightened by the Holy Spirit to recognize the Messiah in the Child Jesus: “this man was just and devout, waiting for the Consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him” (Luke 2, 25). The Righteous Simeon carried in his arms the incarnate Word of God and presented Him as “A light to bring revelation to the Gentiles, and the glory of Your people Israel” (Luke 2, 32). Thus we understand why, in the Christian Tradition, the Righteous Simeon becomes a model and protector of the elderly: he was learned, righteous, God-fearing, patient, full of faith and hope.

The bodily weakness of old age is covered by the strength of wisdom, the richness of knowledge, and the beauty of gentleness and goodness. In this sense, Saint John Chrysostom teaches: “Weakness of the body in no way harms the strength of faith. The bent gray head united with winged faith is an adornment of the Church. In it the Church rejoices especially”[1]. Old age must be understood above all as the age at which we draw near to the end of our earthly journey, when the Lord Jesus Christ leads us to the house of the heavenly Father (cf. John 14, 2).

Today, unfortunately, there are very many elderly people who live in great loneliness, isolated from the community, feeling somehow useless to it or, even more, traumatized by their own aging, and they even reach despair. Statistics, worldwide, show that the aging process is a very accelerated one, with 9.6% of the world’s population being elderly, that is, approximately 800 million people. In Romania, out of 19.2 million inhabitants, 3.7 million people are over the age of 65 (almost 20% of the country’s population), according to the report of the National Institute of Statistics.

In an individualistic secularized society, social policies are contradictory: on the one hand, a considerable effort of material investment and human resources is made to increase human longevity; on the other hand, the elderly are seen by the active population of a society as a burden.

In this context the Church is called to devise new and current pastoral forms and methods, drawing closer to the needs and expectations of the elderly.

A priority in the pastoral care of the elderly is their involvement in raising and educating children, especially with regard to prayer. Through their spiritual maturity, the elderly can help greatly in cultivating liturgical life and in preserving Christian values in our culture, for the good of society and of the family.

In some regions of the country, children call their grandparents bunul and buna, because they feel more strongly the kindness of soul of the elderly. It can be seen that grandparents also have a special fondness for their grandchildren and grandchildren for their grandparents, and therefore this fact should be used for the good upbringing of children.

Another priority that the Church must keep in mind in the pastoral care of the elderly is to consider old age a privilege, a time of spiritual growth and enrichment through prayer. Old age is not a burden, but a gift from God. Old age is a period of a person’s life when he has the chance to draw closer to God. The prayer of the elderly is the source of their wisdom, and also a blessing for the whole community.

Today, the Romanian Orthodox Church carries out extensive work in concrete support of the elderly. This work takes shape in social services and in social-philanthropic projects and programs dedicated to the elderly. Thus there are 27 day centers, 53 residential centers, 30 home care services and 21 home socio-medical care services. Besides these institutions dedicated specifically to the elderly, there are also 61 social assistance offices and 120 social canteens and home meal services whose beneficiaries are mostly elderly people.

At the same time, we note with joy that summer camps were organized throughout the Romanian Patriarchate, in which children and young people, through the coordinating priests, carried out intergenerational workshops and many activities between the elderly and the young, in which wisdom and life experience met in a harmonious and happy way with the enthusiasm, spontaneity and innocence of children, with both generations exchanging values.

Charitable organizations of the Filantropia Federation offer licensed residential, day center and home services to more than 1,000 elderly people daily. Hundreds of specialists in these social institutions of the Romanian Orthodox Church, providers accredited by the Ministry of Labor and Social Solidarity, offer specialized support to the elderly through licensed services, in compliance with the national legislation in force.

In the context of this Homage Year, on April 11, 2023, a Protocol of Cooperation in the Field of Social Inclusion and Social Assistance was signed between the Romanian Patriarchate and the Ministry of Labor and Social Solidarity, with the aim of intensifying cooperation in the social field, both with regard to long-term care and to the other social programs and projects aimed at all disadvantaged social categories.

Among the most important national campaigns, we mention: the “Sănătate pentru sate” campaign, through which Orthodox Christian doctors travel to rural areas and offer free consultations especially to the elderly, with more than 12,000 beneficiaries so far; the “Donează sânge, salvează o viață!” campaign, which in the 10 years since it began has resulted in the collection of more than 23,000 liters of blood, with the help of the volunteers of the Chapel of the National Cathedral; and, last but not least, the telemedicine program (screening and diagnosis) implemented by several organizations of the Filantropia Federation, which provides medical services to mostly elderly patients who do not have the physical or financial means to access specialist consultations.

 

Beloved faithful,

The Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church also proclaimed the year 2023 as the Commemorative Year of Church Hymnographers and Cantors, thus offering an occasion to commemorate those who labored, inspired by God, to compose church hymns and to sing them, for our advancement in the knowledge of God. The hymns contained in the liturgical books of our Church are the creations of hymnographers inspired by the Holy Spirit, and they help us understand the scriptural text, as part of Holy Tradition. The texts of the hymns sung in the services of the Orthodox Church deepen and explain the theological richness of the Word of God. Church music is the Gospel sung.

In this sense, Fr. Dumitru Stăniloae said of the hymnographic language that: “God is so great that only poetry can attempt to express Him”[2]. The theological and spiritual depth of the liturgical texts comes from their constantly drawing on the Holy Scriptures and on the writings of the Holy Fathers of the Church, who meditated long and deeply on the Word of God.

The theology expressed in church hymnography is among the richest in meaning and, at the same time, illuminating for the faithful of our Church; that is why it must be drawn upon more in today’s sermons and catecheses.

Hymnographers such as Saints Ephrem the Syrian, Romanos the Melodist, John of Damascus, Andrew of Crete, Cosmas of Maiuma, Theophanes the Confessor and Joseph the Hymnographer, Metrophanes of Smyrna, Stephen the Sabbaite, Kassiani and others are composers of church hymns of great beauty in form and of inspired theological depth.

Liturgical hymns have been sung on the territory of our country since the beginnings of Christianity, and the art of psaltic chant was taught by great teachers and hymnographers (composers) both in the princely schools, such as the Saint Sava school in Bucharest, and in the monastic schools, such as the schools at Putna and Cozia Monasteries.

We also remember with gratitude the psaltai or church cantors who were also composers or creators of national culture and language, such as: Filotei the Monk of Cozia, Eustatie the Protopsaltis of Putna, Filothei Sin Agăi Jipei, Hieromonk Macarie, Anton Pann, Ștefanache Popescu, Ioan Popescu-Pasărea and others.

 

Beloved brothers and sisters in the Lord,

With God’s help, we are at the beginning of the Nativity Fast, also known as the Christmas Fast. This period is, first of all, a preparation, a sanctification of our souls and bodies through Confession and Communion, and also an occasion for mutual help and almsgiving.

Deeds of Christian almsgiving, seen as fruits of the right faith, are the concrete expression of humble love for God and for people.

In the present context, marked by violence and much suffering, we need to increase our prayer for an end to the war and for the spiritual strengthening of those who suffer because of it. Today, when around us we see signs of physical and spiritual death: greed and violence, suffering and insecurity, poverty and indifference, let us pray to the Lord Jesus Christ to strengthen us in our work of helping the sick, the elderly, orphans, the poor, and those who mourn and are sorrowful.

Therefore, this year as well, we address the priests and lay faithful of our Holy Church with the fatherly exhortation to organize collections of food, clothing and medicine in parishes, monasteries, deaneries and diocesan centers. These will be distributed to those who are suffering and in need, to disadvantaged families with many children, to the elderly and to people living alone, without children or relatives, especially those who live in rural areas.

Trusting that this year too you will show Christian generosity and will respond with love to our fatherly call in this holy work of charity and help, we thank you for the generosity shown in previous years and remind you of the words of the Lord Jesus Christ: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5, 7).

We pray to the All-merciful God to bless all Romanians, at home and abroad, of all ages, granting them health and salvation, protecting them from all evil and strengthening them in every good work, to the joy of our Church and of the Romanian people everywhere.

With great joy, we embrace you in a fatherly way and share with you the apostolic blessing: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all!” (2 Corinthians 13, 13).

title: Romania’s National Day Celebrated at Saints Joachim and Anna Church in Seattle, USA
intro:
Saints Joachim and Anna Church in Seattle hosted a notable ceremony in honor of Romania’s National Day, coordinated by the parish priest, Fr. Ștefan Daniel Drăgoi. The event was an expression of unity and respect for Romanian tradition and identity.

In a solemn liturgical setting, those present took part in a Te Deum service, marked by Fr. Drăgoi’s words on the significance of the Great Union and of national values. During the service, a new gilded bronze reliquary was blessed, in which the holy relics of Saint John Maximovitch were placed.

Fr. Drăgoi then blessed a granite commemorative plaque placed in the church narthex, dedicated to the founders, living and departed. Parish priest Fr. Ștefan Drăgoi noted that just as the heroes of the Romanian nation defended the country, culture, freedom and dignity of the Romanian people, so the founders of the church are the heroes of this community, who sacrificed their own resources so that our Romanian Orthodox tradition and spirituality might endure in this distant and often desacralized land.

The festivities continued with a performance by the Datina ethno-folk ensemble, featuring theater, traditional Romanian songs and dances suited to the occasion. The atmosphere of joy and respect for Romanian traditions carried on at the festive meal, where participants had the opportunity to taste traditional fish dishes.

This initiative of the Seattle church brought the Romanian community together, highlighting the importance of preserving values and traditions beyond the country’s borders.

Fr. Ștefan Drăgoi

title: Hierarchal Visit of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae to South Carolina
intro:
On Saturday, January 27, and Sunday, January 28, the faithful of Saint Gregory the Theologian Parish in Easley, SC rejoiced in the hierarchal visit of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae on the occasion of the Church’s patronal feast. Saturday Vespers and the Sunday Divine Liturgy were a true source of spiritual joy and fraternal communion for the faithful of the parish.

Flowing, profound, of high intellectual caliber, with direct references to theological and historical sources, His Eminence Nicolae’s sermon was for all those present at the Divine Liturgy a blessing, an occasion for learning, an invitation to reflection and a true Christian exhortation.

The parable of the wedding of the king’s son, read on the 14th Sunday after Pentecost, is the equivalent of “the Kingdom of God to which we are all called.” We have all learned that the wedding spoken of in the Holy Gospel according to Matthew (22, 1-14) is the wedding of Christ, and He is the Bridegroom. The Kingdom of God is seen as a wedding to which we are all invited: “both bad and good!” The tares are separated from the good wheat at harvest time. At the coming judgment, people will be separated according to their deeds: those who sought Christ in the face of their neighbor and did works of mercy will be separated from those who refused Christ;

His Eminence Nicolae reminded us that the judgment is not arbitrary but is our own judgment. It will be about whether we sought Christ or refused Christ. Jesus will come at the end of the world. Christ Himself tells us: “And this gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a witness to all the nations, and then the end will come” (Matthew 24, 14). Thus, at the final judgment, no nation will have the excuse of not having heard of Christ.

The Kingdom of God is the Church. The time of the Church lies between the “already” and the “not yet”. The “already” refers to the coming of Christ on earth (a historical fact that took place more than 2000 years ago), while the “not yet” refers to the Kingdom of God, which is not yet fulfilled. The Kingdom is here, it is the Church, but this Kingdom will be fulfilled at the Second Coming of the Savior. It is up to us to believe and enter the Kingdom of God now. The Second Coming of the Savior does not depend on our faith. It is a historical, undeniable fact in which we are all called to take part. Knowing that it is a historical fact, we have only two options: to believe and seek Christ, or not to believe and refuse Christ. His Eminence Nicolae concluded: “If we desire a Christian ending to our life, painless, blameless and peaceful, and a good defense before the fearful judgment seat of Christ, then there is only one exhortation: ‘Enter the Kingdom of God in order to know Him, for He offers Himself to us! Do not refuse Him!’”

His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae also briefly recalled the life and work of Saint Gregory the Theologian, patron of the parish in Easley, SC. A defender of the right faith concerning the divinity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, an orator and poet, Saint Gregory is an example for every Christian and every servant of the holy altars.

Expanding on His Eminence Nicolae’s words, Fr. Bogdan Cojoleancă spoke further about the two times: “Already” and “Not yet”. While the first dates back 2000 years, the “not yet”, though perceived as distant, is shorter than we think. It is this “not yet” that we must take care of. It is our personal time, the time the Lord has appointed for each of us.

The Parish Council and the Ladies’ Auxiliary extend warm thanks to all who contributed to preparing this event: from the large attendance at Church to preparing and bringing delicious food to the agape meal, from the harmonious responses of the chanters to the special decoration of the Holy Church!

Recorded by

Mihaela Livingston

title: Pastoral Letter of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church for the Sunday of Orthodoxy in the Year of Our Lord 2024
intro:
Pastoral Letter of the Holy Synod
of the Romanian Orthodox Church
for the Sunday of Orthodoxy in the Year of Our Lord 2024

 

To the venerable monastic orders, the reverend clergy and the most beloved faithful of the Romanian Patriarchate, 

Grace, joy and peace from God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and from us fatherly blessings!

Venerable and Reverend Fathers,
Beloved brothers and sisters in the Lord,

Divine Scripture teaches us that our Holy Church is “His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all” (Ephesians 1, 23). The Church, having as its head the Savior Jesus Christ (Ephesians 1, 22), continues in the world, through the presence of the Holy Spirit, the saving work of Christ, preaching His word, imparting divine grace, and leading to the Kingdom of God all who believe, are baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity and follow Him.

But the Light of Christ, from the very beginnings of Christianity, has met with opposition, which over time took the form of heresies, schisms, persecutions and various disturbances coming from the enemies of the Church. There was no point of Christian teaching that was not attacked, denied or misinterpreted by the teachings of various heretics. The mystery of the Holy Trinity, the divinity and humanity of the Savior, the ever-virginity of the Mother of God, the Holy Sacraments, the Holy Icons, the Holy Cross: all were contested.

The struggle was great and hard, but each time there arose hierarchs and fathers strengthened and enlightened by the Holy Spirit who, during the Holy Ecumenical Councils, refuted the erroneous teachings and established the right faith.

Today, on the first Sunday of Holy and Great Lent, also called the Sunday of Orthodoxy, we remember the victory of the right faith over the iconoclast heresy, while also celebrating the victory of Orthodoxy over all heresies.

Although from the first Christian centuries the Holy Icons had a special place in the worship of the Church and were an important part of the religious life of the faithful, there were voices that rejected them and became fierce fighters against them, that is, iconoclasts.

The first Byzantine emperor to issue official acts against the veneration of icons was Leo III the Isaurian (717-741). Between 726 and 729 he promulgated several iconoclast decrees. It was a turbulent period for the Church, in which the defenders of the right faith suffered: some were tortured, others exiled, and others died as martyrs. Numerous icons, true treasures of the Orthodox Church, were also destroyed at that time.

One of those who rose up resolutely in defense of the Holy Icons was Saint John of Damascus, the great theologian and monk of the Monastery of Saint Sabbas in the Judean desert. Other fathers who defended the veneration of the Holy Icons with solid arguments were Saint Theodore the Studite, Saint Nikephoros the Confessor, Saint Gregory the Decapolite and others.

The disturbances caused by the iconoclasts continued, so that in 787 Empress Irene (†802), as regent, with the support of Patriarch Tarasios of Constantinople (784-806), convened the Seventh Ecumenical Council at Nicaea, in the province of Bithynia in Asia Minor. The Council, attended by some 350 bishops, decided that the veneration of icons is a practice pleasing to God. It also specified that icons may be painted and must be venerated, because they depict the faces of holy persons, and that veneration is addressed not to the material of the icon but to the person represented on it.

Peace, however, did not settle upon the Church even after the Seventh Ecumenical Council of 787. The opponents of icons continued the struggle. To put an end to the controversies, Empress Theodora of Byzantium (842-846), together with Patriarch Methodios, convened a Council in Constantinople in March 843. The Council established the Orthodox teaching on the veneration of icons on the basis of Holy Scripture and the writings of the Holy Fathers, and declared valid all the decisions of the seven Ecumenical Councils. Since the restoration of the veneration of icons took place on the eve of the first Sunday of Great Lent, this Sunday was named the Sunday of Orthodoxy.

Since then, every year, on the first Sunday of Great Lent, which is a first stop on the spiritual ascent toward the Resurrection, the Orthodox Church throughout the world recalls the victory over the iconoclasts and pays tribute to those who fought for the right faith.

The word “Orthodoxy” means “right belief” or “right glorification”. Orthodoxy means “to believe rightly” not in something, but in Someone, in the true God. Orthodoxy is the living bond of man with Christ, who leads us to God the Father, to eternal life, for Christ the Savior says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14, 6). In other words, faith in our Savior Jesus Christ is the true way that leads us to eternal life.

The Sunday of Orthodoxy is also a remembrance of the faith of our forebears, which is the faith of the Holy Apostles, the Holy Fathers and the martyrs, and of the way our forebears lived and defended the true faith. The Sunday of Orthodoxy is a moment of reflection and of awareness of the duties that fall to us as well: to preserve the treasure of faith inherited from our forebears and pass it on to future generations, so as to fulfill our duty toward God and toward those who came before us.

Orthodox Christians,

The foundation of the iconographic representation of our Lord Jesus Christ, of His Mother and of the saints is the Incarnation of the Second Person of the Holy Trinity, the Son of God.

Saint John the Evangelist says: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1, 14). And Saint John the Theologian also testifies: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life, the life was manifested, and we have seen, and bear witness, and declare to you that eternal life which was with the Father and was manifested to us” (1 John 1, 1-2).

Thus, the icon of our Savior Jesus Christ reminds us of the humility of the Son of God, who “made Himself of no reputation, taking the form of a bondservant, and coming in the likeness of men. And being found in appearance as a man, He humbled Himself and became obedient to the point of death, even the death of the cross” (Philippians 2, 7), in order to make us human beings sons of God by grace (cf. John 1, 12). The Savior humbled Himself and came down from heaven to earth in order to raise people from earth to heaven.

The icon is not an idol, as the persecutors of the Holy Icons wrongly claimed and as those who reject their veneration claim today. An idol is an invented god that does not exist in reality, a carved image that pagans worshipped, believing that it heard them and fulfilled their requests. The icon is an image of a real person, whether our Savior Jesus Christ, the Mother of God or the saints of God.

There is a spiritual bond between the icon and the person depicted on it, and we venerate not the material (the wood or the canvas) but the person painted, so that a mystical bond is established between the prototype and us. When an Orthodox Christian prays before the icons, he does not say “icon, help me!” but “Lord, have mercy on me!”, “Mother of God, or Most Pure Virgin, help me!”, “Holy Hierarch Nicholas, or Saint George, pray for us!”.

Icons set before us scenes from Holy Scripture or the faces of persons whose lives were pleasing to God and who were made worthy of the bliss of eternal life in the Kingdom of Heaven, reminding us that man is called to holiness.

Icons are windows to eternity, through which our soul, looking upon holy things, is lifted up and grows spiritually. It is hard to imagine an Orthodox Christian home or a church without a single icon. Such a space would be like a desert, a desolate place, without God.

The icon facilitates communication with the person depicted on it, to whom we direct our prayer. Before the icon, prayer is more intimate, humbler and more intense. The icon helps us gather our thoughts and focus our attention on prayer. The grace-filled presence of the person depicted on the icon becomes a teacher who reminds us that we are all called to become partakers of eternal bliss and that we too can attain the Kingdom of God through the works of faith.

The icon shows us that man can overcome sin and attain deification, with the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit and through a pure life.

Our beloved spiritual children,

The Romanian Orthodox Church, as “the spiritual mother of the Romanian people” (Mihai Eminescu), has always cared for her children, wherever they were, in the homeland or beyond its borders. Through various social and philanthropic assistance programs, soup kitchens have been built for people of modest means, and homes for the elderly, medical facilities for the sick, homes for children and more have been established. This charitable work has been possible through the contribution of every member of the Church, who gave generously from their little.

One of the Savior’s commandments is to be merciful: “Therefore be merciful, just as your Father also is merciful” (Luke 6, 36). Almsgiving is the expression of the virtue of goodness. The Orthodox Christian knows that when he is merciful he becomes like God, and “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9, 7).

Let us not forget our neighbor who is in need, the hungry, the naked, the thirsty, the sick, the one in prison, the stranger and the wanderer, the suffering, the sorrowful and the estranged, the one left on the streets without shelter, understanding that in each of these our brothers and sisters Christ our Savior Himself mystically suffers (cf. Matthew 25, 35-36).

To support the missionary, pastoral, social and philanthropic activities of the Romanian Orthodox Church, the Central Missionary Fund was established, into which the donations from every parish and monastery of the Romanian Orthodox Church are deposited. The Central Missionary Fund is an expression of the solidarity of Romanian Orthodox Christians and also a witness to the unity of our people.

Each year, the support of this fund benefits parish communities, churches, monasteries and social institutions in Romania and in the diaspora, which thus contribute, through their missionary, social, educational and charitable activities, to preserving our Romanian identity.

This year as well, therefore, we address the priests and faithful of our Holy Church with the call to take part in the collection for the Central Missionary Fund and to contribute, each according to their means and heart, out of love for God and for their neighbors, aware that by helping the Church of our people we help ourselves as an Orthodox people.

Hoping that our call will be heard and that you will respond with Christian generosity, we thank you for your generosity and pray to God to bless you with His rich gifts and to help you in your spiritual ascent toward the glorious feast of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ!

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all! (2 Corinthians 13, 13).

The text is signed by Patriarch Daniel together with all the members of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church.

title: Pastoral Visit to Sacramento, CA
intro:
On April 27 and 28, 2024, the faithful of the Resurrection of the Lord Parish in Sacramento, CA rejoiced in the presence in their midst of His Eminence Nicolae, Romanian Orthodox Metropolitan of the Americas. It has become a beautiful tradition for the faithful of our parish to receive hierarchal blessings each year on the bright feast of the Entry of the Lord into Jerusalem.

On Saturday, April 27, at midday, His Eminence arrived in Sacramento, where he was awaited by the parish priest, Fr. Teodor Girlonta. After lunch, His Eminence met  with the members of the Parish Council in the church’s new social hall. He was  informed of the recent administrative accomplishments, as well as of the problems that arose in carrying out the work on the social hall. On the faces of all those present one could see gratitude for all the blessings poured out by the Good God in answer to the prayers and sacrifice offered. Then the future plans for the church building were presented, at which point His Eminence proposed that the Parish Council consider, in the near future, the beautiful and moving moment that would crown all these efforts, namely the consecration of the church. The proposal was received with great joy and interest by all present. His Eminence Nicolae also answered all the questions put to him, explaining in detail the rite of the consecration of the church, its symbolism, and what such an event involves  from an organizational point of view.

Our hierarch then took part in Vespers together with parish priest Fr. Teodor and the faithful present. At the end of the service, Metropolitan Nicolae gave a homily explaining the significance of that day, Lazarus Saturday, and its context within Great Lent. He emphasized the direct way in which the Savior spoke, without parables, about the fact that He would be seized, mocked and crucified, and on the third day would rise from the dead. In Christ’s dialogue with Martha, the Savior reveals to her that “Your brother will rise again” (John 11, 23), for “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11, 25). This statement of the Savior is fulfilled shortly afterward, when Lazarus is raised from the tomb with his hands and feet bound. His Eminence Nicolae spoke of the power of the divine word, which, once spoken, does not return void. Saturday ended with a dinner of Lenten dishes prepared by the ladies of the parish.

On the second day of the pastoral visit, the feast of Palm Sunday, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae celebrated the Holy and Divine Liturgy together with parish priest Fr. Teodor Girlonta and Fr. Aurel Zmeu. At the end of the Divine Liturgy the willow branches were sprinkled with holy water and a memorial service was served for those who have fallen asleep in the Lord.

 In his homily, His Eminence Nicolae spoke about the importance of the feast of the Entry of the Lord into Jerusalem:

“The Jews who had come to meet Him together with their children, just as at the Feast of Tabernacles, began to wave palm branches and cry out: Hosanna! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord! The King of Israel! These are a few words from Psalm 117 used at the Feast of Tabernacles, but now with a unique meaning. Hosanna means save, as does the name Jesus, the Savior. Those who welcomed Christ with palm branches now recognize Him as the awaited Messiah, the Savior of the Jewish people. That this is so, and that there is no misunderstanding, we discover in the Holy Gospel according to Luke, chapter 19: hearing these words of welcome, the scribes and Pharisees said to the Savior: ‘Teacher, rebuke Your disciples.’ And the Savior answers them: ‘if these should keep silent, the stones would immediately cry out’ (Luke 19, 39-40)…

This week it is fitting for us to follow spiritually the Lord’s steps toward the crucifixion, to desire to defend Him before the judges, to show our steadfastness in the faith and not to deny Him. Let us too suffer together with Jesus the Man, who suffered for us and offered His life on the Cross as a ransom! With the assurance that He passed through death, conquering it as God, with the joy that the powers of hell have been shattered, with the faith that we too partake of the light of the Resurrection at every Divine Liturgy, and with the hope that if Christ is risen, we too shall rise!”

In closing, parish priest Fr. Teodor Girlonta thanked His Eminence for his rich homily and for serving together with them. He also thanked the Metropolitan for the effort  he makes every year to come to Sacramento for Palm Sunday, an effort that means a round-trip flight of about 8 hours between Chicago and Sacramento. Then the faithful were anointed and blessed by their hierarch. The feast day ended with a fraternal agape meal of Lenten and fish dishes lovingly prepared by the ladies of the parish.

The presence of our hierarch on this chosen day of holy feast made our church too small to hold everyone, a sign of the faithful’s appreciation and joy at every meeting with their Metropolitan. Glory to God for all things!

Fr. Teodor Girlonta

title: Consecration of the Parish Church of Saint Nicholas and the Holy Prophet Elijah the Tishbite in Surrey/Vancouver
intro:
On Sunday, June 9, 2024, in a solemn festive atmosphere, His Eminence Metropolitan Iosif, together with His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae and His Grace Bishop Ioan Casian, as well as the priests of the diocese’s parishes present at the congress, performed the consecration of the parish church, followed by the Divine Liturgy. After the Gospel reading, His Eminence Metropolitan Iosif delivered a rich homily. Also, at the appropriate moment, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae explained the meaning of the service of consecration of a church for the whole parish community and urged those present to sanctify and renew their lives in the Holy Spirit.

At the end of the service, His Grace Bishop Ioan Casian, as a sign of high appreciation for his fruitful and rich pastoral and missionary work, elevated Fr. Corneliu-Iulian Dragomir to the rank of Iconom Stavrofor, bestowing on him the belt and the epigonation. He also presented the parish priest, on behalf of the parish, with an icon of its patron saints, Saint Nicholas the Hierarch and the Holy Prophet Elijah the Tishbite. His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae awarded Fr. Corneliu-Iulian Dragomir the distinction of the American Metropolitan Cross, together with an icon of Saint Nicholas the Hierarch. His Grace Ioan Casian then presented Preoteasa Ligia Dragomir with a diploma of merit together with the festive medal of the Romanian Orthodox Diocese of Canada, prepared for this congress. The ruling hierarch awarded several diplomas of merit and medals to the founders and benefactors of the church, as well as to several clergy and laypeople of the diocese for their pastoral and missionary work as a whole. His Excellency Gabriel Rotaru, Consul General of Romania in Vancouver, also took part in the beautiful events of the Saint Nicholas and Holy Prophet Elijah the Tishbite Parish in Surrey/Vancouver, and received a medal from His Grace Bishop Ioan Casian as a sign of appreciation.

For his part, His Eminence Metropolitan Iosif presented His Grace Ioan Casian and the Romanian Orthodox Diocese of Canada, for their spiritual strengthening, with a fragment of the holy relics of Saint Callinicus of Cernica, a most precious gift from His Beatitude Patriarch Daniel of the Romanian Orthodox Church on the occasion of the 5th Congress of the Romanian Orthodox Diocese of Canada. His Eminence read the deed of donation that accompanied the holy relics and then awarded His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae the diocesan distinction of the Order Metropolitan Visarion Puiu, cross and encolpion, of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolis of Western and Southern Europe. The same distinction was also awarded to His Grace Bishop Ioan Casian. Fr. Corneliu-Iulian Dragomir in turn received a pectoral cross as a distinction from the Romanian Orthodox Metropolis of Western and Southern Europe.

His Grace Bishop Ioan Casian presented each of the two distinguished guests, His Eminence Metropolitan Iosif and His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, with an icon of the Savior Jesus Christ Pantocrator, together with the French-language album Jesus.L’enciclopedie.

At the end, all the faithful present at these beautiful events venerated in the Holy Altar, kissing the Holy Gospel, the Holy Cross and the Holy Table. All received small icons from the ruling hierarch and then enjoyed the festive agape meal prepared with love and skill by the members of the parish community together with Fr. Corneliu-Iulian Dragomir. 

Fr. Nicolae Codrea

title: Patronal Feast at Saints Joachim and Anna Romanian Orthodox Parish in Seattle, WA
intro:
Our parish has been under the protection of Saint John the Archbishop since its beginnings, when services were held in the chapel of the Russian Orthodox cathedral, the place where the Archbishop gave up his holy soul into the hands of the Lord while accompanying the wonderworking Kursk Icon of the Mother of God. After the purchase of our present church, Saint John protected the parish and its faithful through the many upheavals it faced, until God arranged for a parish priest to be found who would devote himself to this church.

By the mercy of God, with the blessing of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae and with the goodwill of the Russian Orthodox Metropolis of San Francisco, at the end of 2022 our parish received a fragment of the wonderworking relics of Saint John Maximovitch, which were placed in a beautiful bronze reliquary.

The solemn patronal feast service took place on Sunday, June 30, 2024, when Matins was served, followed by the Holy and Divine Liturgy, with a considerable number of faithful taking part. The festivities ended with a fellowship meal skillfully prepared by the ladies of our community.

Fr. Ștefan Drăgoi

title: Presentation of the Orthodox Communities in Latin America Under the Jurisdiction of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas
intro:
Following the sustained and constant efforts of the Orthodox faithful, Romanian and of other nationalities, and of Fr. Daniel Ene, who has made numerous pastoral visits to Latin America, new Missions of the Metropolia have been founded and parishes received in COLOMBIA, ECUADOR, MEXICO and CHILE:

  1. BARRANQUILLA, COLOMBIA

Saint John the Wallachian Romanian Orthodox Church / Mission

  1. QUITO, ECUADOR

Saint Joseph the New of Partoș Romanian Orthodox Church / Mission

  1. CANCUN / PLAYA DEL CARMEN, QUINTANA ROO, MEXICO

Saint Joseph the Confessor of Maramureș Romanian Orthodox Mission

title: Patriarch Daniel’s Message for the Sunday of Romanian Migrants Calls for Care for the Sick
intro:
On Friday, His Beatitude Patriarch Daniel issued a message for the Sunday of Romanian Migrants entitled “Health Is the Gift of God, and This Gift Must Be Guarded, Cared For and Sanctified”.

“The priestly ministry has always included the duty of the clergy to care for the sick, in fulfillment of the commandment the Lord Jesus Christ gave to His disciples when He sent them out to preach: ‘Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons. Freely you have received, freely give’ (Matthew 10, 8),” the Patriarch of Romania wrote.

The full text:

Health is the gift of God,
and this gift must be guarded, cared for and sanctified

Considering the need to intensify the care of those suffering in soul and body, the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church declared 2024 the Homage Year of the Pastoral Care of the Sick and the Commemorative Year of All the Holy Unmercenary Healers.

In the world we live in, people tend to withdraw more and more into their own individuality, focusing only on themselves and their own needs. The Church, however, prays for all humanity and especially for those who suffer, for the sick, the poor and orphans, according to the exhortation of our Savior Jesus Christ to love our neighbor: “Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these My brethren, you did it to Me” (Matthew 25, 40).

Since illness has become an integral part of life, suffering cannot be entirely removed, but it is our duty to care for our fellow human beings who suffer.

For this reason, the priestly ministry has always included the duty of the clergy to care for the sick, in fulfillment of the commandment the Lord Jesus Christ gave to His disciples when He sent them out to preach: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons. Freely you have received, freely give” (Matthew 10, 8).

In contemporary society, the pastoral care of the sick faces a number of difficulties for which we must find suitable solutions. Old age, which is of course not the same as illness, is nevertheless a period of life in which the frailty of the body exposes the elderly to physical suffering, and very often, especially in the absence of proper spiritual guidance, this leads the sick person to withdraw into isolation and to a worsening of his condition, failing to understand that bodily suffering is also a call to seek spiritual health. Unfortunately, the extensive use of technology in the care of the sick, positive in itself, has become a factor leading to their isolation.

On the other hand, daily life has become very complex, the pace of work has accelerated, and we no longer find time to visit the sick in the hospital or those who are alone and suffering at home. Besides proper medical care, the sick person also needs comparable spiritual comfort, which no medical treatment can replace. Emotional support, compassion, understanding and effective communication between the sick person, their family and the medical staff are the main conditions for furthering the healing of those who suffer.

Our Savior Jesus Christ, His Mother and the Holy Unmercenary Healers are the true healers of the sick, often inspiring the work of the physician who treats them.

Through the work of the Holy Spirit in the world, especially through the Holy Mysteries, the servants of the Church continue the mission on which Christ sent them, healing and easing the suffering of countless sick people.

We wish this Sunday, dedicated to Romanians living far from their homeland, to be for all a day of gratitude and love, of fulfillment and joy together with all their loved ones, a day on which we thank the clergy and faithful of the Diaspora for their steadfastness in Romanian identity values and for their sacrificial service.

With much fatherly love, we urge all Romanians living far from their homeland not to forget that health is a gift from God, but this gift must be guarded, cared for and sanctified. And if we have lost it, we must seek it with great faith and hope, praying to God, to the Mother of God and to the Holy Unmercenary Healers to heal our souls of sin and our bodies of illness.

 

With great appreciation and fatherly blessing,
† Daniel
Patriarch of the Romanian Orthodox Church

title: Patronal Feast of Saints Joachim and Anna Church in Seattle, WA: A Celebration Full of Grace and Communion
intro:
In an atmosphere of deep emotion, Saints Joachim and Anna Church in Seattle, WA celebrated its patronal feast with great solemnity on Sunday, September 8, 2024, bringing together an impressive number of faithful. The event was marked by a series of spiritual and festive activities that brought the community together in an atmosphere of communion and gratitude.

The festivities began on the eve of the feast with Vespers with Litiya. On this special occasion, the new liturgical vessels and vestments brought from Romania were blessed, adding a note of solemnity and ritual beauty to our celebration. The Divine Liturgy was celebrated with great solemnity by the parish priest, Fr. Ștefan Drăgoi, together with faithful who had traveled long distances from all over the state of Washington. During the Divine Liturgy special prayers were offered for the children beginning a new school year. This was a particularly moving and meaningful moment, an opportunity for all present to ask God’s blessing on the young students, in hope of a year full of success and accomplishment in their studies.

The service also included a memorial service for the reposed founders of the church, an occasion to remember those who contributed to building and developing this house of worship. The prayers for the repose of their souls were accompanied by a deep sense of gratitude and respect for their efforts and sacrifices.

After the service there was a special artistic program presented by the “Datina” ethno-folk ensemble. The program was greatly appreciated by all the participants, paying tribute to our national traditions and culture through a series of artistic moments full of energy and authenticity. To close the festive day, the community shared a bountiful fraternal agape meal, generously provided by the ladies of our parish. The common meal was an expression of solidarity and brotherly love, strengthening the bonds among the members and bringing warmth and conviviality to the event.

This feast was not only a commemoration of the church’s spiritual patrons but also a celebration of our community and our traditions, an occasion of joy and spiritual reflection. Saints Joachim and Anna Church remains a place of meeting and communion, continuing to enrich the lives of its faithful through prayer, dedication and culture.

We close with a word of gratitude and blessing for all who helped organize this event and for every member of the community who took part, making this year’s patronal feast a memorable moment full of grace.

Fr. Ștefan Drăgoi, Parish Priest
