title: The Paraklesis of the Mother of God Sung by the Young People of ROYA Chicago
intro:
The Orthodox young people of SS. Constantine and Helen Cathedral in Chicago have made a moving video in which they sing the Paraklesis of the Mother of God, thus bringing honor to the Theotokos. The recording captures the solemn and profound atmosphere of the moment, with the young people gathered around the icon of the Mother of God, offering prayers and hymns full of devotion.

Against the backdrop of icons and lit candles, their voices resound in a peaceful harmony, inviting viewers to join in prayer and contemplation. Every verse of the Paraklesis is rendered with clarity and devotion, reflecting the love and respect these young people have for the Orthodox faith and for the Mother of God.

The video, now available on the cathedral’s YouTube channel, was made to bring a fragment of the beauty of Orthodox prayer into the homes of all those who could not be physically present at the event. It also serves as a message of hope and trust, reminding everyone of the power of the intercession of the Mother of God in the lives of the faithful.

Through this initiative, the Orthodox young people not only keep the tradition alive but also share it with a wider community, showing how faith can also be expressed through modern means of communication.

title: Spiritual Camp in San Antonio, Texas
intro:
In the context of the “Homage Year of pastoral care and care for the sick” and the “Commemorative Year of all the Holy Unmercenary Healers” in the Romanian Patriarchate, and with the blessing of His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan Nicolae, the spiritual camp See, you have been made well. Sin no more took place at the Parish of Saint John Cassian and Saint Andrei Șaguna. This spiritual event took place over three days, September 13 – 15, 2024, under the guidance of Archdeacon Sorin Mihalache, supported by his wife, Georgiana Mihalache. The participants in this camp were the faithful of the parish, of all ages, who benefited from the spiritual and interdisciplinary experience of Archdeacon Sorin Mihalache and were helped to open themselves more to the wonderworking and therapeutic dynamic of spiritual life in the Orthodox Church.  

The camp opened on Friday, September 13, at 5.00 pm, with the service of Vespers on the eve of the Feast of the Elevation of the Holy Cross. After Vespers, starting at 6.30, the opening session of the workshop dedicated to Cultivating Attachment took place, attended by members of the Saint John Cassian parish community in San Antonio. The participants, Romanian and American, introduced themselves and expressed their expectations for the workshop. The meeting continued with a session presenting some of the most important points of Attachment Theory, as well as the relevance of these aspects to children’s development and to the shaping of their relationship with their parents.

On Saturday morning, starting at 9.00, Matins and the Divine Liturgy were celebrated in honor of the Feast of the Elevation of the Holy Cross, officiated by Fr. Valentin Ilieș. Starting at 11.30, the sessions of the workshop dedicated to Cultivating Attachment continued, joined by other participants from the community of Saint John Cassian Church. The workshop sessions focused on how attachment style and experiences can decisively influence the way a child communicates in the family with parents and peers, as well as the way the child grows up and perceives and responds, as an adult, to the needs of mutual help.

After lunch, the workshop for the faithful of Saint John Cassian Parish continued, addressing the four attachment styles and the behaviors that correspond to them. In the last part of the workshop, the sessions were dedicated to the secure attachment style, an occasion to highlight a number of clinical and neuropsychological observations that prove to converge with practices found in the Christian spiritual life. Christian love shown toward others, expressed both in the maternal bond and between spouses and siblings within the family, can be an excellent point of reference for emotional regulation and for shaping a healthy relationship among family members, provided that the exhortation of the spiritual life accompanies Christian love with the constant effort to cultivate the virtues and the generous self-giving of each person to the others.

An important point of the workshop concerned the role of the spiritual father in strengthening the believer’s hope in God’s help and loving work. Christian spirituality reveals, in essence, that human life unfolds under the auspices of God’s providential care, so that, in concrete terms, every believer is called to live this experience of divine love and help, as they are expressed and active in the Holy Mysteries of the Church, in the hymns of the Church, and in family and community relationships strengthened by Eucharistic Communion.

In the last part of the meeting, which ended at 7.00 pm, the participants asked questions and expressed their own conclusions about the experiences and interaction at the workshop. Their conclusions highlighted their intention to cultivate the two dimensions of behaviors that support secure attachment: “to grow in responsiveness toward those who most need our love” and, respectively, “to increase sincere openness toward the people from whom we ourselves expect more help”.  An essential role here, for personal growth in these two directions of attachment relationships, is played by the experience of the spiritual life, by prayer and confession, and by cultivating interpersonal relationships in the community of faith. Likewise, in order to cultivate secure attachment, it is important to relate properly to everyday happenings and events, looking above all for their spiritual meanings and lessons, with the effort to keep the commandments and cultivate the virtues in everyday life.

On Sunday morning the program of parish activities began with Matins, followed by the Divine Liturgy, served by Fr. Valentin Ilieș, Fr. Dan Suciu and Archdeacon Sorin Mihalache. The homily was given by Fr. Dan Suciu, who said:

As He usually does, Jesus invites us to heaven if we follow Him, step by step, here, in this life. For us Orthodox Christians, to follow Him means to live in Him and like Him. Life in Christ saves and is a continual discipleship. Disciples eventually become Apostles (those who are “sent”). The more disciples there are in the Church, the more apostles there are to preach His Good News to others. But one cannot follow the One Who offered His life on the cross unless one imitates Him. This means “self-denial”, the ultimate crucifixion. He never asks us to do anything He has not already done. Speaking of “self-giving”: the eternal Person of the Son of God, co-eternal and almighty, comes down into our human condition in order to redeem it. As Saint Paul tells us in Philippians: “He made Himself of no reputation, taking the form of a bondservant…” To deny ourselves means to shift the emphasis: from our body to our soul, from ourselves to others, from our will to God’s will, from our opinions to God’s commandments, from our ways to God’s ways, from this world to His Kingdom, from this life to the life to come! All of these are opportunities for eternal investment. He reminds us that by “taking up our cross” we ACCEPT difficulties and suffering as opportunities for our salvation rather than as tragedies. When we carry our cross with faith, it becomes a CROWN, the halo of the Saints as reflections of the halo of Christ, the Sun of Righteousness. When we carry our cross without faith, it becomes an inner “JOY”, a self-destructive struggle. Jesus does not ask us to take up our cross and go anywhere on our own: He reminds us that, by following Him, our own cross becomes an extension of His cross. We will carry our cross IN Him and WITH HIM.

At the end of the Divine Liturgy, Archdeacon Sorin Mihalache gave the lecture “Personal Development in the Mirror of the Transfiguration of the Lord”. The lecture explored some of the edifying meanings of the Gospel text presenting the Transfiguration of the Savior, a feast that falls 40 days before the Elevation of the Holy Cross. Starting from the text of the Gospel of Saint Matthew (17:1-9), four possible characteristics of man’s spiritual edification were highlighted, which can serve as points of evaluation or reference for a Christian perspective on personal development. They could be formulated concisely as criteria for evaluating an authentic spiritual life. First, they are symbolized in the ascent of the mountain, to the high place set apart, elements that suggest the search for high spiritual meanings joined with readiness for the transforming struggles of the spiritual life, and with the choice to keep these struggles hidden, in an inward form, far from the world’s approval. Second, as the Gospel text suggests in a symbolic reading, the authentic search for the spiritual meanings of life, ready for the effort of ascetic struggle and discreet at the same time, does not remain unrewarded: God reveals Himself to those who seek Him, as He did in history, and as the text also shows, first as light, then as the One Who speaks with the prophets (symbolically included in the presence of Moses and Elijah), as a bright cloud – as He was also present in the episode of the Exodus – as a voice that speaks (to the prophets) and, finally, in Jesus Christ (“This is My beloved Son! Hear Him!”). The text then shows that man’s spiritual edification is authentic only insofar as man encounters the divine infinite and has the strength to understand his own nothingness (a situation expressed symbolically in the fact that on hearing the Voice the disciples “fell on their faces to the ground”). Finally, the last stage of man’s spiritual edification, as it appears in Christian spirituality, is the very work of Christ accomplished for humanity, since He is the One Who “touches” the disciples and tells them “arise” and “do not be afraid”.

Through the mystical experience of God, through the Holy Mysteries, man can be strengthened by God’s touch, rising from a horizontal life spent under the dominion of the world and living illumined by hope in Him, capable of love, of kindness, of sacrifice, of tireless generosity toward others. Through meanings such as these, Christian spirituality offers people today the broadest project of personal development, one that focuses not only on skills or niche capabilities suited only to increasing professional performance, but also on the virtues and above all on self-giving and drawing near to Christ and, through Him, to all our fellow human beings, this being the way of sanctifying life for others and for God. In this way, the Christian answer on the subject of personal development consists in a life centered on Christ Transfigured, Crucified and Risen, and in following His Life, together with Him, the Way by which man can offer others His pure Love, and offer himself in a state of sacrifice, this being the work that perfects all human labors. 

Sunday’s program continued with a memorial service marking 40 days since the falling asleep in the Lord of one who remains in our hearts, the founder of Saint John Cassian Parish in San Antonio, Prof. Dr. Cornel Pașnicu. After the memorial service, all the faithful took part in the fellowship meal, during which Fr. Dan Suciu gave the catechesis On Life in Christ and on the witness we give to others by cultivating the virtues, as our dear brother and friend, Prof. Cornel Pașnicu, did. As part of these events, at the end of the catechesis, all those who were born or celebrated their name day in September were congratulated. Another event at the end of the day on Sunday was the meeting of all the young people of the parish school, who began preparing the folk dances to be performed at the Romanian festival on October 12, 2024.

We give glory to God for these days overflowing with grace and joy around the Sunday after the Elevation of the Holy Cross, and we thank all the participants and all who labored.

 

Fr. Valentin Ilieș

title: Lecture on the Valences of Suffering in Sacramento, CA
intro:
On Sunday, September 22, 2024, Resurrection of the Lord Parish in Antelope, CA welcomed as its guest, with the blessing of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, Archdeacon Adrian Sorin Mihalache, professor at the Faculty of Orthodox Theology in Iași. Father Archdeacon is known to our faithful from his previous visits to Sacramento and from the lectures he gave on those occasions. Likewise, the books he brought on those occasions, Ești ceea ce trăiești, The Relationship between theology philosophy and science: an eastern christian perspective, and his latest publication, Miracolul cunoașterii, have offered and continue to offer a good insight into the interests, understanding and knowledge Father Archdeacon has in many fields. Very interesting were the reflections that follow from presenting the results of various research in the field of neuroscience, in the light of the spiritual teachings and experiences recorded in patristic and philokalic literature. Neuroscience, with the many possibilities opened up by technology (equipment, digital techniques, computerized assessment) and with its potential for researching many aspects of the inner life and of the hidden mechanisms of human behaviors, states and attitudes, confirms, without explicitly seeking to do so, what the Holy Fathers experienced, described and understood centuries ago. Through the work of the Holy Spirit, through ascesis and deep self-examination, and through watchfulness over their most intimate inner states, they came to know the movements of the human soul and how a good inner life, enlightened by grace, helps toward a sound “knowledge of oneself”. The philokalic writings and the patericons are full of such examples.

The novelty that Father Archdeacon brings in his presentations lies in this power of understanding and accurate observation in identifying, in the research and experimental results of recent sciences in various fields such as cosmology or neuroscience, many of the lights of understanding brought to light through the spiritual labor of the saints, on the humble, well-trodden path of the experience of faith, the saints having as their aim not theoretical knowledge crowned with prizes and distinctions such as the Nobel Prize, but His very Life given to us, the source of eternal life.

The theme of the lecture chosen for the gathering was The Valences of Suffering, as an inventory drawn from Christian spirituality and neuroscience. In the first part of the gathering, the guest presented the current cultural context and the way people relate to suffering. Contemporary culture, marked by entertainment and marketing productions, as well as by services increasingly specialized in wellness, in cultivating a state of well-being, tends to isolate or reject the experience of suffering. At the same time, enjoying prosperity and entertainment, we are less and less prepared to accept suffering, which is also illustrated by the production and consumption of painkillers, which has become a habitual way of countering the experience of pain in its various forms. Finally, at the end of this first part, the guest emphasized that it is important, as persons created in the image of God, to reflect not only on suffering but also to observe how we react when we encounter it: how patient we are in experiencing suffering, or our own illness, or the pain of someone close to us, and above all how good we manage to remain throughout our trials.

In the second part of the presentation, the guest set out an extensive meditation starting from the episode of the healing of the sick man at the Pool of Bethesda (John 5, 1-16). The many sick people with their various sufferings can be an icon of the numerous bodily and spiritual sufferings of the world we live in. On the other hand, “waiting for the moving of the water” mentioned in the text comes close, in meaning, to the condition of the sick person who suffers (patient meaning in English not only a sick person but also the patience that every suffering patient must show), and of course to the waiting for complete healing, which is at the same time the sign of the vulnerability of man who, in all situations of suffering, cannot heal himself, but depends on, awaits and receives divine healing.

Another important aspect emphasized by the guest referred to the fact that the man who had been sick for 38 years, presented in the Gospel text, did not lose his patience and his hope in God that he would be healed, which is a powerful lesson of encouragement, a model of patient conduct in suffering fitting for a man of faith.

The guest then emphasized that the healing of the sick man at the Pool of Bethesda depends on the connection with other people. In this sense, the sufferer, finding that he “has no man” to put him into the pool, will in the end be healed by the God-Man Christ, Who is both the Pool and the One Who has the Living Water, the Healer of all.

The next part of the presentation raised another important conclusion regarding the Christian spiritual perspective on suffering: it can be caused by personal sin, by wrongdoing, by breaking the commandments, from which one can also glimpse the path of healing, which is intertwined with the path of amendment.

In the last part of his talk, the guest set out the complementary perspective on suffering, which rounds out and completes the spiritual understanding offered by Christ and which in many circumstances sheds light on everyday conditions and experiences concerning illness and the possibility of healing. In this last part, the presentation followed the Gospel text that presents The Healing of the Man Born Blind (John 9, 1-7). In connection with this passage, attention was drawn to the question of the disciples, who wanted to know the reason why the blind man had suffered from birth. Here one can glimpse the need we always feel as human beings to have an explanation, a reason for our own illness or suffering or that of our neighbor. But the wonderful meaning that completes the spiritual lessons of suffering in the life of the Orthodox Christian is revealed in the deep, meaningful answer that Christ the Lord gives the disciples, when He reveals that “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but that the works of God should be revealed in him” (v. 3). This wonderful meaning reveals that not all suffering and illness are a consequence of sins, and that in some situations there is a mysterious work of God that allows, beyond our understanding, even the righteous or innocent to suffer, and in this His work is revealed!

In connection with all these aspects, during the gathering some results of recent medical research were also cited, highlighting the importance of cultivating compassion, the beneficial impact of virtuous emotions such as altruism or generosity, and the beneficial effects of forgiveness and mutual help on health. All these findings, which bring to light both the role of doctors and the medical sciences and the therapeutic potential of the spiritual life, show that spiritual health is obtained in a state of solidarity among people and doctors, and that often someone’s suffering is the very reality that calls us to live together, in order to offer substantial help to the one who awaits our support. And of course, in all these situations, whether we wish to help someone or are suffering ourselves, prayer and liturgical life, in close connection with our fellow human beings and with God, are the essential dimensions of consolation, which bring light in the midst of trials and open the way to bodily and spiritual healing.

At the end of the lecture came a series of questions and discussions with the participants. The guest also briefly presented his latest book, published by Basilica Publishing House of the Romanian Patriarchate: Miracolul cunoașterii: Științele, Filosofia și Teologia în dialog despre tainele universului și ale vieții is an interdisciplinary approach to current themes in the field of fundamental research, cosmology and the life sciences, neuroscience and topics of cognitive psychology, in the openness they show toward certain philosophical examinations and their spiritual meanings, as these can be offered by Orthodox Christian theology. Its 530 pages present various miraculous, interesting and challenging aspects from the field of scientific knowledge and from the sphere of philosophical reflection, in an engaging manner meant to arouse interest and edifying reflection.

After the lecture ended, Father Archdeacon offered his books, with autographed dedications, to the faithful who wished to have them, after which we all took part in the fellowship meal, a moment of joy and communion prepared and offered on this occasion by the Ladies of our Parish.

We thank the Lord for His care and for these uplifting joys that spring from the encounter with the lights of the holy fathers and with the illuminating insights of our own day, as they are brought to light by the scientific world, to His Glory! We thank His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae for the hierarchical blessing that allowed and supported this event!

We also thank Archdeacon Adrian Sorin Mihalache for the effort of coming to us and for the spirit-filled words and wisdom he shared with those of us present at the gathering, and we pray that the Lord will watch over him on his journey through the Romanian communities of the USA.

Fr. Teodor Alin Gîrlonța

title: Heartfelt Meeting with Archdeacon Adrian Sorin Mihalache in Las Vegas
intro:
On October 9, 2024, “St. George and St. Demetrios the New” Church in Las Vegas put on festive garments as we rejoiced in the presence of Archdeacon Adrian Sorin Mihalache. The meeting was the third in the last three years, reason enough to say that it has become a tradition when this guest stops on the West Coast of the United States of America.

The lecture given by Father Archdeacon addressed aspects of the spiritual life amid the many challenges of our society. The presentation, which lasted 60 minutes, had four parts. The first part discussed the theme On Self-Care and Self-Denial in the Era of the Self-Care Industry. On this point, mention was first made of today’s concern with health care in people’s lives, explained on the one hand by excessive expenditure of energy at work, and on the other by the powerful advertising that presents the many services of this kind. In this regard, the guest emphasized that Christian spirituality proposes a temperate way of life, in which care for the body should not lead to neglect of the things of the soul. In this sense, self-denial, present in Christian life, appears as a way of strengthening the self, which is oriented toward fulfilling the commandments and following the words of God.

This is stated clearly in the words of Christ: “Whoever desires to come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow Me” (Mark 8) (the term used in the Gospel text is telos, which means will, intention and desire). Man, the guest emphasized, is the fruit of his own desires, which is why today we need to judge our desires carefully and reveal them to our spiritual father, since they exert a strong influence on the path of the spiritual life, depending on whether we are accustomed to choose only care for the body and the fulfillment of bodily wishes, or self-denial and struggle to fulfill the commandments. Another important aspect raised here concerned “taking up the cross” and “following Christ,” which is the core of self-denial. In everyday life, this conduct can be glimpsed in a humble, gentle way of interacting with others, in the habit of not imposing ourselves on those close to us over the small stakes of everyday life. The spiritual life, in Orthodox Christianity, is marked by the ease with which a person entrusts himself to the Lord’s care, becoming lovingly obedient to others (husband to wife, children to parents, brothers and sisters to one another, the young to the older, and all to their spiritual fathers, to the hierarchs and to the word of God).

In the second part of the talk, these aspects concerning the cutting off of one’s will were connected with willpower, under the title: Willpower and the Struggles of the Spiritual Life. Recent Neurophysiological Discoveries and Philokalic Observations on the Benefits and Challenges of Self-Control. Many passages of the Christian Philokalia reveal that willpower is cultivated in the ascetic struggles of the spiritual life. Some recent neurophysiological discoveries wonderfully confirm these philokalic observations, showing indirectly what benefits the practice of fasting and guarding the senses can have for increasing self-control, in the context of the current challenges raised by consumer society. On this second point of the presentation, the guest emphasized that the model of successful power in circulation today aims at the force with which some people impose themselves on others, lead them in an authoritarian way or control them excessively. The society we live in strongly promotes a culture of power, whether financial or economic, political or social, or arising from celebrity. Powerful, as cultural productions try to convince us, is the one who does not give in and who manages to impose himself in the end. The one who gives in, the voice of consumer culture seems to tell us, is weak rather than wise. Compared with this profile, the Christian spiritual life proposes an inverted hierarchy. Powerful is the one who can disregard himself, who sets aside his own interests and needs in order to fulfill those of others. Edifying here are the words of the Savior: “Whoever desires to become great among you, let him be your servant” (Matthew 20, 25-27)

It is interesting, the guest emphasized, that according to current findings in medicine and psychology, when we are willing to be flexible and to help others at the expense of our own interests, we are less stressed and healthier. Psychology notes that stress originates in our thoughts rather than in the situations or people around us. Often, when we see situations that trouble us or people who irritate us, it is mostly the mind that is involved in this perception. Stress is triggered by unexpected (unpredictable) events whose course we cannot control. In situations like these, the Christian, accustomed to entrusting himself to the Lord’s care, gains a very great power over everyday life and over history. He no longer tries to influence great things or events, against which he would have no chance of fighting, but entrusts himself to God’s care, thereby reducing an important part of the emotions and cares of this world. At the same time, medicine shows how stress proves to be an important disruptive factor for the immune system, as well as for the cardiovascular, digestive and hormonal systems, and even for the functioning of the nervous system. The conclusion of this second point of the lecture was that the life of faith is lived with great hope in the Lord, and thereby the virtuous person no longer aims at the stakes of this world, avoiding many of the silent confrontations that everyday life brings, and through this the balance of the soul is strengthened together with that of the body. In the end, this is also the profile of the Christian life which, following the Lord’s Prayer, the Our Father, settles into the conduct expressed by the phrase “Thy will be done,” in place of one’s own will.

Here the third point of the presentation came in, since whoever renounces his own will becomes calm and reaches gentleness more quickly. A golden chain links these: struggle, meaning the renunciation of one’s own will, brings rest, and rest brings gentleness. At this point the guest spoke about the third topic of the meeting: On Calm and Gentleness in Raising Children and in Family Life. Medical and Spiritual Costs and Benefits.

In this regard, the guest noted that being calm involves an important distinction, because the calm someone has when everything is in its place and pleasant is very different from the calm someone shows in the midst of trials (such as physical pain, frustration or injustice suffered). On the other hand, it was also emphasized that being calm, which is beneficial compared with nervous reactions, means less than being gentle. Gentleness, about which many philokalic authors have written wonderful pages, is a calm permeated with much goodness. Calm can be cold, arrogant, condescending and even contemptuous. Gentleness can never be malicious. In this regard, it is again Christ who gives us the teaching about gentleness, and if we are His, we must live with gentleness. He teaches us that His gentleness springs from His humility and gives rest to the soul!

Finally, the guest also addressed the theme Cognitive Flexibility. On the Benefits of Humility in Professional Life, in the Couple and in the Family. This proves especially useful in education and in teamwork. Cognitive flexibility could be described as the capacity to see the other’s perspective, and also to hold and accept ideals flexibly, to be resilient. Together with the strength to keep going and not abandon what we wish to achieve, however hard that road may be, it is important to be wise and able to adapt to the concrete conditions of life, so as to understand the needs of others as well, to try to help them, and to continue to struggle with oneself. And, above all, no matter how much we have managed to achieve of what we set out to do, our attention must remain turned toward God, Who with love and care accompanies us on the path of salvation. “See that no one renders evil for evil to anyone, but always pursue what is good both for yourselves and for all. Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, in everything give thanks; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you” (1 Thessalonians 5, 15-18)

At the end of the presentation, which despite its density did not run much beyond 60 minutes, the participants offered comments and asked questions about the relationship between fulfilling the wishes of others and abandoning one’s own spiritual work, and also about the ways we can deepen our spiritual life.

We thank Father Professor for this rich and beneficial word! We thank him for the effort he made and for the patience with which he amazes us every time. This year Father Archdeacon had a very busy schedule, with activities and lectures in Texas (San Antonio and Austin), in California (Hayward, San Jose and Sacramento), in Oregon (Portland), in Washington State (Seattle), and in Vancouver (three lectures, on different days, in three different locations). Nevertheless, Archdeacon Adrian Sorin Mihalache also made time for the faithful of our parish. We thank him, especially since his journey will continue to Los Angeles and then, for two more activities over 4 days, to Georgia (Atlanta), ending his American tour of nearly 7 weeks with a lecture in our community in New York.

We feel that he, with his labor, is an example for each of us, through the sacrifice he makes, traveling a great deal and staying away from his family and loved ones, and making the sacrifice of being with us. It is beautiful and heartening when you can leave all your own things behind and become a ready helper and supporter of your neighbor!

From this wonderful meeting we keep all these teachings, which tell us that cutting off one’s will is strengthening and brings peace, that kindness shown to others is healthy, and that the humility the Lord shows us is restful! We therefore keep these messages of encouragement, these luminous philokalic and theological insights that can orient our life on the right path when we sacrifice ourselves for the one beside us and give ourselves to serving God by serving our neighbor.

Finally, our thanks go to His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae for giving his fatherly blessing for this event, and to the faithful who worked to make our meeting with Archdeacon Adrian Sorin Mihalache possible, covering the expenses needed for its good organization! May the Lord accept all things to His glory and for our salvation!

Fr. Mihai Bălan

title: Akathist to Saints Tarachus, Probus and Andronicus and a Conference by Archdeacon Prof. Dr. Adrian Sorin Mihalache in Los Angeles
intro:
By the mercy of God and with the blessing of His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan Nicolae, Archbishop and Metropolitan of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas, on Thursday, October 10, 2024, Holy Trinity Church in Los Angeles, California marked 28 years since the relics of Saints Probus and Andronicus were brought to the church. These saints, commemorated on October 12 (together with Saint Tarachus), have become the protectors and intercessors before God of the worshipers and of all the faithful of our Church. The anniversary began at 5:00 pm with the Akathist served before the holy relics of Saints Probus and Andronicus. The service was celebrated by Very Rev. Archimandrite Nikodim Bibarț (Elevation of the Holy Cross Parish, Upland), Fr. Constantin Alecse, the parish priest, and Archdeacon Prof. Dr. Adrian Sorin Mihalache from Romania, a special guest invited to give a spiritual conference at our church.

During the fellowship meal, Mrs. Lucia Sava, Consul General of Romania in Los Angeles, briefly introduced herself to the community as the new Consul General and spoke to the faithful about the consular services offered to Romanians on the West Coast of America.

Thanking everyone present for taking part in both the service and the session of spiritual reflection, the parish priest, Fr. Constantin Alecse, welcomed on behalf of all the participants the presence of our distinguished guest, Archdeacon Prof. Dr. Sorin Adrian Mihalache, in our midst, and expressed gratitude for his accepting the invitation and for the personal sacrifices he made for our community by giving the conference on the theme “Inner Stillness and the Noise of the World”. The parish priest then gave a brief presentation of the biography of the evening’s guest, Fr. Prof. Dr. Deacon Sorin Adrian Mihalache. Our parish’s channel on www.rumble.com [https://rumble.com/c/SfantaTreime] holds a collection of video/audio recordings of some of the conferences Fr. Adrian Mihalache has given on several continents, as well as a few texts from his works.     

The speaker noted from the outset that a discussion about “the noise of the world” (of modern civilization!) is much needed today, along with spiritual measures for preserving, as far as possible, “inner stillness”. For each of the situations discussed, there are circumstances that keep us from noticing the dangers and influences hidden in noise. In the case of audible noise, our own adaptive mechanisms could deceive us. After spending a long time surrounded by noise, we might adapt so that we no longer notice it, through a process of desensitization; yet even without sensing its presence, we would keep suffering its harmful effects, both cognitively and on our health in general.

Attention and performance in various cognitive tasks could be affected by noise, even though we no longer perceive it as a disturbance. Sleep quality could decline and various health problems could appear, yet as long as we are adapted to this noisy environment, we will hardly make the connection between sound and quality of life. Drawing on several recent findings from medicine and brain science, and guided by certain Philokalic reflections, the speaker highlighted three kinds of interference that lead to a fragmented life: audible noise, sensory overstimulation and cognitive overload. Reading data from neuroscience side by side with observations gathered from the experience of hermits, we can glimpse how, in the ordinary setting of life, these forms of noise weaken attention and lucidity. Finally, with regard to these situations, the speaker mentioned several measures, recommended by the anchorites or arising from experimental findings, that could help us in our effort to cultivate stillness.

In the case of emotional interference, as well as informational noise, we should remember that the senses need protecting and information needs careful filtering, to relieve the mind, as the reverse of the cognitive overload mentioned earlier. In all this one can see how many obstacles to stillness are hidden in the ordinary course of life and daily activities. That is why suitable measures for cultivating stillness must address both the outward field of life and the inner space.

In the last part of the conference, the speaker stressed the Christian’s need to keep in mind the warnings of the saints who experienced the value of stillness. Because of the world’s interference, “the mind is darkened and becomes barren when it speaks worldly words, or receives them into its thoughts and converses with them, or when the body together with the mind busies itself in vain with things subject to the senses, or when the monk gives himself over to vanity” (quoted from Philotheus of Sinai, Trezvia minții și cerul inimii). The conduct of stillness recommended by the hesychast saints thus calls for a much more attentive, more vigilant stance in the setting of the world, in which vanities are set aside for “the gain and the beloved and sweet beauty of virtue” (Ibid., p. 176.).

In closing, the speaker mentioned that a work of his, published in 2021, is available to all who are interested: “Bruiajele lumii și fragmentarea lăuntrică” - On the noise of consumer society and the fragmentation of the human inner life. Philokalic notes and some recent findings from brain science. (Offprint from the Journal of the Saint Dionysius Exiguus Center for Theological Studies, Romanian Orthodox Diocese of Italy, Rome (2021).

An interesting short “Questions and Answers” session followed, in which, besides pertinent questions about the challenges facing society today, those taking part expressed their joy at attending a conference of such high scientific and theological caliber, and thanked Fr. Prof. Dr. Adrian Sorin Mihalache for the wonderful conference, extending to him an open invitation to return to our community to continue the spiritual work on the foundation he laid in our souls today.   

Reported by Antoanette Rastian
Director-coordinator of parish activities of
Holy Trinity Romanian American Orthodox Church, Los Angeles, California

title: Archdeacon Dr. Adrian Sorin Mihalache Among the Romanian Community of the Atlanta Area
intro:
From October 11 to 14, 2024, the Romanian Orthodox Christians of the Atlanta metropolitan area in the state of Georgia, USA, had among them a distinguished guest who, through his wisdom and the gift he has received from God, brings much knowledge and light to the spiritual life of the faithful as well as to their medical and behavioral well-being. Archdeacon Adrian Sorin Mihalache visited the community of the Atlanta area for the second time, this time with a personal and spiritual development workshop entitled “Cultivating Attachment” and a lecture entitled “On Calm and Gentleness in Raising Children and in Family Life: Medical and Spiritual Costs and Benefits”.

The workshop, held in the social hall of Saints Constantine and Helen Church in Lilburn, was intended mainly for parents. It was attended by faithful from the host community and from Saint Mary Church in Dacula. The sessions took place on Friday, over three hours, and on Saturday, over 10 hours. The meeting, organized as a program of structured learning experiences, consisted of a series of exercises and group discussions on tasks focused on the characteristics of attachment and the way it shows itself in the family. The types of attachment were presented, along with how they can be recognized and, above all, how the appropriate conduct and behavior of parents, who offer care, support and emotional regulation, decisively shapes the formation of children’s attachment from early childhood. In the second part of the workshop, the various effects that the attachment style children develop from their early experiences has on their later life were presented, both in interpersonal relationships and in family life when they themselves become parents.

In the last part of the workshop, through interactive exercises, the participants were able to take stock of the obstacles that stand in the way of cultivating attachment, also reviewing concrete ways of cultivating attachment in daily life. Attentive care, hugs and parents’ messages of validation or appreciation can in fact improve children’s experiences of attachment. On the other hand, honest communication, asking open questions more often and the habit of sharing our needs can improve interpersonal relationships and attachment in adults’ relationships with others. Throughout the workshop, and in the discussions on the various topics related to attachment, the guest emphasized the many points of convergence between the content of attachment theory and the way the human person is understood in Orthodox Christian anthropology. At the center of this convergence lies the human person’s need to be cared for from birth, and the significant impact of love and care not only on the whole process of a child’s growth and formation but also on an adult’s healthy way of living and relating, interpersonally and in the family. In this sense, the Christian life, at the heart of which God’s care, the help of the Mother of God and of the Saints, and the experience of communion are constantly affirmed, can be not only the expression of the human person’s vocation to be the object of divine love and of the love and care of others, but also the healthy setting in which this need for attachment is fulfilled, in the family and, in its fullness, in the communion of the Church, in the Holy Mysteries.

On Sunday, Archdeacon Dr. Sorin Adrian Mihalache served the Divine Liturgy with Fr. Nicolae Clempuș at Saint Mary Church, dedicated to the Protection of the Mother of God, in Dacula. In his homily, the Archdeacon highlighted four timely aspects of the Parable of the Sower (Luke, 8, 5-15). First, he highlighted the meaning of the first verse of this parable, which presents God as the Creator and Provider of the world and of history, the One Who placed in creation and in man seeds that bear fruit both as living forms and as meanings, fruits that nourish human understanding. Second, he stressed that Christ explains the parable to show that man needs more than the ability to receive God’s words with his ears. What is required is a certain receptiveness, with one’s whole being, to the message addressed to him, and an effort of living so as to bring one’s whole life into harmony with the words of God: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear!” (Luke 8, 8) and “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to the rest it is given in parables, that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand” (Luke 8, 10).

Third, he offered some insights into the features of today’s world and life that concern the society we live in, and into how timely is the picture offered by the three kinds of seed that bear no fruit: the person who sets the course of his life beside the beaten path of Tradition, the person overcome by temptations and trials (the rocky soil), and the person overcome by cares, pleasures and riches. Finally, he mentioned some of the meanings of the seed that fell on good soil, which symbolizes the good person, those who, “having heard the word with a noble and good heart, keep it and bear fruit with patience” (Luke 8, 15)

During a short break after the Divine Liturgy, refreshments prepared by the ladies of the Church Committee were served, and the faithful stayed for the lecture. The talk, which lasted 70 minutes, had three parts. To begin with, the guest emphasized how difficult it is for people today to experience calm in the context of present-day society. The pace of life, daily pressures and the continuous flow of information are real obstacles that make it hard to keep one’s balance emotionally and in the dynamics of personal and family life, as well as professionally. In this regard, the guest discussed the many scientific findings concerning some of the cultural characteristics of today’s society, such as sensory overstimulation, cognitive overload, multitasking work patterns and data smog (the unstructured cloud of information that reaches us every day through the digital connections at our fingertips). All these cultural shifts, which have grown ever more intense in recent decades, have significantly changed the setting of our lives, making it ever harder for people today to find a moment of rest.

In the second part, the guest pointed out an instructive distinction between the calm someone shows in the midst of trials (such as physical pain, frustration or injustice suffered) and the calm that accompanies the good moments of life. Of course, in the cultural context already mentioned, with its many challenges, calm becomes ever harder to attain and to keep. A discussion about calm also proves important if we consider its beneficial effect on health. The guest mentioned some recent scientific findings showing that calm, by considerably reducing stress, proves to be cardioprotective, improving cardiovascular parameters as well as the immune response. In addition, calm has many other benefits when it characterizes the way parents behave, emotionally, in relationships within the family, and in the formation of children and adolescents.

In the third part, the guest emphasized that Christian spirituality speaks much more about gentleness than about calm. Gentleness, about which many Philokalic authors have written wonderful pages, can be distinguished from calm by the fact that it is accompanied by great kindness. Unlike calm, which can also be distant, even contemptuous, gentleness also expresses kindness toward the other.

The texts of the Philokalia contain many observations about gentleness and its place in the spiritual profile of the ascetic. And, of course, at the heart of this teaching on gentleness we find the example of the life of Christ. If we live a life in Him, and if we are His, gentleness ought to characterize our life and the concrete way we behave. But it is essential that Christ shows that His gentleness springs from His humility and gives rest to the soul! “Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11, 28-29)

A session of interaction with the faithful followed, with questions and answers on what had been presented. At the end, the guest signed copies for those who wished to purchase the book Miracolul cunoașterii, and heard the impressions of all those present. Both the workshop and the lecture were received by the faithful with great enthusiasm and a desire to learn, and they bore very positive fruit in the life and spiritual growth of the community.

We owe thanks to His Eminence Nicolae, our Archbishop and Metropolitan, for blessing this visit and for his unceasing care for the spiritual state of our faithful. Many thanks to Deacon Dr. Adrian Sorin Mihalache, who, despite the fatigue of touring America in just a few weeks, made an extraordinary effort at the workshop and the lecture.

Last but not least, we must also thank our faithful, who took part in 10 hours of the workshop and 3 hours of the lecture and absorbed the advice, teachings and words of wisdom with which our guest delighted us. We hope to have such uplifting experiences more often.

Fr. Nicolae Clempuș,
Parish Priest

title: Together around the Living Christ at the Patronal Feast of the Transylvanian Saints at Holy Trinity Church, Philadelphia
intro:
Ecclesia, the church, a most beautiful gathering together around the Living Christ, in His Body and Blood, once again brought together souls devoted to the Lord Jesus Christ at Holy Trinity Church, where the vibrant community of Romanian faithful from Philadelphia and the surrounding area celebrated, over two days, October 26 and 27, 2024, the patronal feast of the Transylvanian Saints, confessors of the ancestral faith. His Eminence Nicolae, Romanian Orthodox Metropolitan of the Americas, also took part in the celebration.

On Saturday evening, in the gentle light of the vigil lamps and candles, the united voice of the faithful and of the choir, in prayer together with those of His Eminence Nicolae, of Fr. Mircea and Fr. Sabin, friends of Holy Trinity Parish, of the parish priest, Fr. Timotei, and of Deacon Bogdan, served the Holy Service of Vespers. His Eminence Nicolae offered his word in the sermon after the service, in which he also marked the feast of Saint Demetrius the Myrrh-streamer. The service was followed by a dinner prepared by the Ladies of the parish, where the clergy together with the council members were able to discuss the various projects concerning Holy Trinity Parish.

On Sunday, the second day, Metropolitan Nicolae celebrated the Hierarchical Divine Liturgy together with the parish priest, Fr. Timotei, and Deacon Bogdan. The faithful, in large numbers, awaited with love and spiritual longing the arrival of the distinguished guest, Metropolitan Nicolae. As on the previous day, the Hierarch was welcomed with bread and salt by a group of faithful dressed in folk costumes, a tradition of Holy Trinity Parish; this is a solemn moment that marks the beginning of a great feast of the Christian community, the bread being the symbol of life, which man offers to God, and the salt being considered, in folk sayings, “God’s manna”, both underlining the sacred character.

Amid the turmoil of worldly life around us, the sermon of His Eminence Nicolae turned our ears, the ears of the faithful, to the truth of the resurrection, the miracle Christ worked for the daughter of Jairus, and then went on to set before us in spirit the spiritual models and examples of humility of the Holy Transylvanian Confessors, as well as the miracles worked by Saint Demetrius the New, protector of Bucharest, also celebrated on this Sunday. His Eminence and the parish priest then anointed the foreheads of the faithful with holy oil.

The blessing then rested upon everyone at the common meal, where the most beautiful gathering together around the Living Christ, in His Body and Blood, just as at the Mystical Supper, was able to enjoy choice traditional dishes prepared by the community, while continuing to rejoice in the presence, counsel and blessings offered by His Eminence Nicolae.

Reported by a member of the Holy Trinity Parish Council,

Bogdan Astratinei

title: The Lecture and Workshop Tour of Archdeacon Sorin Mihalache in the USA and Canada, September 6 – October 15, 2024
intro:
Brief Notes on the Spiritual Life of Romanian Orthodox Christians in North America

It matters little how many times someone visits North America. It matters little, even, how much time one spends in the federation of states in this region. Writing an article about such an experience remains considerably difficult.

In everyday language we speak of the United States of America as a single entity. And so it is, since it is a republic. Yet this federal constitution brings together, in a region more than twice the area of all the states of the European Union, 50 states, some of them (Texas, for example) larger than France. The United States of America means 50 states with as many geographic, demographic and historical particularities, with their own legal and administrative specifics, and with cultural, economic and spiritual patterns that easily rival an entire continent of countries… With such size and diversity, the USA, with more than 330 million inhabitants, is an immense challenge for any visitor or explorer, for an expert seeking to assess various social aspects, or for the Christian missionary. And from there, of course, comes the difficult task of capturing in words, on a few written pages, the breadth and novelty of the American experience.

For the Fourth Time in North America

At the beginning of September I arrived in the United States of America for a 7-week program in several states of North America and in Canada. This is the fourth time in the past five years that I have come to the USA at the invitation of His Eminence Nicolae, Primate of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas. In all, this time there were 14 lectures and four workshops in these locations (structured learning experiences averaging 10 hours, intended for groups of 20 participants on average). The lecture topics varied, generally sharing an assessment of aspects related both to the ordinary practices of Christian spiritual life, in the family and in the community of faith, and to the various challenges arising from the recent coordinates of social and cultural life in postmodern society. Three of the workshops (in Austin, San Antonio and Atlanta) focused on cultivating attachment in couple and family relationships, and the other workshop had as its theme Cultivating Attention in the family, in professional work and in spiritual life. The challenge was somewhat greater because some of the discussions and interactions on the topics of the workshops and lectures in Texas, which were held in English, involved clarifying nuances.

Preparations with Blessings

From the outset, something important must be mentioned, something both essential and natural for a clergyman. For this journey I carefully followed all the proper steps: the itinerary was clarified with the organizers well in advance, the list of communities where these activities would take place was finalized, and most of the titles of the lectures and workshops were also set. All of this was presented to His Eminence Nicolae and His Eminence Archbishop Nathaniel to receive the blessing of the hierarchs. With great goodwill and a desire to support the activities of the parishes, His Eminence Nicolae sent his invitation to His Eminence Teofan, Metropolitan of Moldavia and Bukovina, and all the documents then went to the Romanian Patriarchate for the blessing of His Beatitude Patriarch Daniel. In the ordinary light of Orthodox Christian spiritual life, this path of preparing a visit is nothing other than the natural course for any activity carried out in Orthodox Christian communities abroad. The key word in all of this is the blessing of the hierarchs under whose jurisdiction these activities take place[1].

The American tour began in Texas, in the communities of Austin and San Antonio, and continued in California, in San Jose, Hayward and Sacramento. Next came Oregon, with the city of Portland, and Washington State, in the north of the West Coast, with several activities in Seattle. The journey and activities continued in the province of British Columbia in Canada, with three lectures in Vancouver, and then back down the West Coast to Las Vegas, Nevada. The stay on the West Coast ended with a lecture in Los Angeles, the largest city in California. The visit and activities in the Romanian communities of the USA concluded on the East Coast, in Atlanta, Georgia, and, as a last stop, in the parish community of Saint Nicholas Church in New York.

12,500 Kilometers on American Soil. That Is to Say, Very Little.

This route, which crossed only 7 of the 50 North American states and a single Canadian province, British Columbia, nevertheless added up to more than 30,000 kilometers, of which 12,500 were covered on American soil in 7 weeks. And although it does not represent even a fraction of the immense American space, it was a demanding effort and more than enough to glimpse the psycho-cultural, socio-demographic and economic diversity of this universe: the America of liberties and of license, the America of opportunities and challenges, of riches and disputes, the America of potential and paradoxes. The small effort made in these travels, in this short span of time, was for me an occasion to glimpse the immense missionary work that our Church and its clergy carry out here, traveling again and again across the vastness of Canada and the two Americas, an expanse hard to take in, which has no fitting comparison anywhere in Europe, an expanse that demands considerable effort.

Beyond the very great distances, America brings together many contrasts: prosperity and economic challenges, social and political disputes greatly inflamed by the approaching elections, cosmopolitanism, immigrants and multiple fractures within communities, advanced technologies, avant-gardism, the invasion of the homeless, exhibitionism, license and an immense thirst for spirituality, the emancipation and hyper-emancipation of young people from the authority of their parents, but also a true cult of family life, a remarkable attention to the spiritual culture of the human inner life, and an appetite for the communal experience of Orthodox Christianity in liturgical communion within the Church.

As a cultural constant in the midst of these challenging realities, where light and shadow intertwine, I was able to learn how Romanian Orthodox Christians live their lives and carry out their work and mission. Besides the pressing demands of a high-performing economy, those who live here have felt, and still feel, other pressures in daily life: the instability of the job market[2] and the serious situation of the housing market[3]. To these challenges one may add other traces left by the events of recent years or of even more recent times, those that have deeply marked the social and cultural life of North Americans: the CoVid-19 pandemic, social movements such as “me too” and “black lives matter”, or the attack on the Capitol almost 4 years ago. And, of course, this inventory cannot leave out the situations and events of the last two years and the last few weeks: the wars in Ukraine and Israel (there are many Russians and Ukrainians in the USA, and many Jews as well), and the presidential election campaign, with the two assassination attempts against one of the candidates for the highest office in the state.

A dense atmosphere, with a varied emotional coloring, covers a broad spectrum, from exuberance to worry. Beyond these internal challenges and problems, the American economy is challenged by the strong currents of the global economy and by the large number of immigrants who, ignoring all risks and consequences, cross the borders and try to settle in the USA. Here too we meet a wave of cultural challenges, noticeable especially to the attentive eye of a traveler from a conservative society, used to living in a world of traditional values. These are the expressions and practices belonging to emancipated diversities, sometimes surprising and at other times troubling, in the forms present in society and in public spaces, as they are discussed in schools and high schools, in universities, organizations and corporations.

The Condition of the Orthodox Christian in North America: Three Challenges

It is in this complex social and informational setting that the life and work of Romanians in the USA unfold and are tested day by day. This is also where the pulse of our Orthodox Christian communities is found, oases of Romanian identity, hospitality and friendship. As residents on American soil, Romanians must meet the demands of this developed society, which, for the sake of tomorrow’s security, call for excellent performance, a considerable workload and a high degree of professionalism almost everywhere in the service sector, in state or private companies, and in the financial or manufacturing sectors. In the USA, whoever works, works seriously, whether native-born or immigrant. This is the rule rather than the exception. On the other hand, based on my visits and activities on American soil over the past 5 years, I believe Romanian Orthodox Christians face at least three further important challenges, in addition to all the others.

The first of these stems from the very condition of being an Orthodox Christian, since the spiritual life implies a pure, honest and courageous witness given in this challenging setting. It means expressing, where appropriate, belonging to and faith in Christ the Truth. The organizational and societal culture of North America and the life of communities small and large form a context that is both organized and competitive, with clear rules and with well-defined and often pressing requirements and expectations. These are felt both professionally and in the wider social environment, in economic and financial life. At the same time, Orthodox Christianity and the spiritual life bind a person to the Cross and the Love of Christ, which are, above every other condition, his first and last vocation. Most of the time these do not meet harmoniously, and the Christian who wishes to keep the imprint of his spiritual life in his soul, his mind and his life is in a constant effort to fit his socio-cultural setting to the demands of the spiritual life. Through this, the one who struggles can gain vigilance and greater precision about the details that make the difference between a life deeply anchored in the life of the Church and a merely formal belonging.

On the other hand, Romanian Orthodox Christians are constantly challenged and called to make a considerable cultural effort to preserve their language and identity in North American cities that are most often cosmopolitan. In a multicultural context, the identity and ethos of their land of origin are often felt by Romanians here to be vital; closely bound up with them are the meaning of life and well-being, cultural comfort and the reference points for relating to other cultures and communities. That is why middle-aged families struggle hard, in a many-colored cultural environment, to save and strengthen the imprint of Romanian identity in the lives and character of their children, in the coming generations. Even if we think of everything only in relation to the presence of the many Orthodox Christian communities, such as those of the Greeks, Serbs, Ukrainians or Russians, the face of the new generation of young Orthodox Christians born to Romanian parents on American soil is considered the belt that keeps the bond of language and history, of ethos and genealogy, with the Romanian matrix.

This, however, requires sustained effort: Romanian language courses, courses in the history of Romania, Orthodox religion olympiads in the Romanian Orthodox parishes, cultural events, and days dedicated to the Romanian communities, organized periodically, weekly, monthly, yearly…

Finally, and at the same time, Romanian Orthodox Christians, cherishing their ancestors and taking responsibility for their extended family, keep up their relationship with their relatives in the homeland through another constant effort, despite the considerable distances that separate them from those at home. Thus, often accompanied by their children, they come again and again to Romania, 10-12,000 kilometers each year, to give their children the chance to meet their loved ones and the places dear to their hearts, spending weeks with their extended family and in monasteries. Their pilgrimage effort is considerably greater than the one we make when we leave our homes to visit the holy places or monasteries in Romania or in Greece.

Cultural and Social Challenges for the Life of Communities of Faith

Regarding all these major challenges, in the places where I held activities I met Romanian Christians, concerned for their life in the Orthodox Church of Christ, who bear admirable witness to the faith and to His Church. This is not only because they take part constantly, with openness and commitment, in the liturgies and services celebrated at the end of the work week, but also because they are involved in the projects carried out in the communities to which they belong: catechetical activities, Sunday school, efforts to build a place of worship or to fit out adjoining social spaces. And, of course, on this occasion I also met extraordinary priests who, with great responsibility and a considerable readiness for effort, with diligence and grace, take on the immense work of building up and edifying the communities to which they belong.

In their missionary work, priests face numerous difficulties. First of all, there is the considerable distance separating the homes of the faithful from the place of worship. In the USA all distances are, or if they are not, seem to be greater than any distance in Europe… This makes regular participation in parish life more difficult. Then there are the laws and regulations, the obligations and formalities one must fulfill in order to draw up and obtain the approvals needed to carry out a building project or to fit out a place of worship or a social space. All these structures, intended to host events or catechism lessons, whether full-fledged buildings or simple annexes, require considerable investments of time and resources, as well as close attention to compliance with financial, economic and administrative rules[4].

Besides these administrative problems, priests are called to provide pastoral care and spiritual guidance to the faithful, and here too there are many challenges. There are problems between spouses concerning the practices of the spiritual life, or others related to the upbringing of children, especially in mixed (Romanian-American) families. There are also economic or professional challenges faced by some of the faithful in the parishes, who are left without work for a time and must move to other towns or states to improve their chances of financial recovery. Finding a stable, well-paid job is a major challenge in the USA. All of this makes difficult the priest’s work, which is always directed toward gathering the community around the Church. To counter professional and economic challenges, housing problems or those concerning the choice of a good school for the children, problems that usually act centrifugally and break things apart, priests seek again and again to hold activities that increase the time families of the faithful spend interacting in the church, so as to draw ever tighter the ties between the families of the extended family. The various activities held at the end of the week, which themselves require considerable effort, can increase the participation and attachment of the faithful to the living pulse of the community of faith. In many places, however, participation is made considerably harder by the fact that, even for faithful living within the same community (as is the case in Seattle or New York), arriving at activities on time is difficult. For those who live farther away, traffic sometimes adds as much as two hours to the time needed to reach the event. (In this way an activity held on a Saturday morning, for example, takes up half the day, including travel to the church and back home, which discourages many from taking part.)

Yet the priests, helped by fervent faithful accustomed to taking part in the missionary and catechetical work of the Church, do not give up the effort and the struggle with the challenges of this society, so as to keep bringing to light the truth and the fulfillment of communal spiritual life. There is a great deal of diligence and a great deal of grace in this work. In fact, much grace brings much diligence.

Many Joys and the Signs of Diligent Work

In each of the communities I visited, I noticed the diligence and generosity of the priests and the efforts of the clergy to strengthen ever more the bond of the faithful with the Church and with the other members of the community.

In Austin, at Saint Mary Church, I was pleasantly surprised by the involvement and substantial help the faithful gave Fr. Gabriel in preparing the technical, economic, administrative, financial and banking file so that the building project for the new place of worship could receive approval from all the relevant offices of the Texas authorities. During the days I was there, the mayor of the town himself took part in the blessing of the site where construction of the new place of worship was to begin. Many faithful, eager to experience and gain as much as possible from the workshops and lectures, took part in all the activities occasioned by the Feast of the Nativity of the Mother of God and by the blessing of the new church’s building site, without missing the workshop and the lecture scheduled for those days[5].

In San Antonio, at Saint John Cassian Church, I noticed a growing interest in topics concerning the challenges of spiritual life in today’s society and in the workshop sessions, as well as the very friendly atmosphere of the meeting with the participants. I also noticed an excellent custom of community life, present in the Austin and Sacramento communities as well, a custom for which, in San Antonio, Fr. Valentin Ilieș and Preoteasa Cristina have labored for years: after every Sunday Liturgy, the faithful stay to commemorate the departed, to celebrate those who had birthdays during the week, to give them presents and to share a meal, spending hours together, grandparents and parents, adults and children. The gathering occasioned by the Divine Liturgy each Sunday usually ends around 5:00 p.m., which can make for a true Sunday spent in the extended family of the Church[6].

In the community of Sacramento, California, at the Resurrection of the Lord Church, I was able to see, this time completed, a spacious building for the community’s social activities, built through the involvement of the faithful under the coordination of Fr. Teodor Gîrlonța. The gathering that followed the lecture, with the dinner shared with the participants and the interaction there, showed how important it is to have such a generous space, offering comfort and inner peace, for lives and life stories to be woven together[7].

In Vancouver, at Saint Nicholas Parish in Surrey, I met again a wonderful priest, Fr. Cornel Dragomir, who, with great longing and love for the homeland, has created in front of the church a true Romanian memorial garden, with a bust of Mihai Eminescu and a signpost marking the distance to Iași (8921 km) and Timișoara (8894 km), places much farther away than the North Pole (2235 km)! In the generous churchyard and in the spaces for social activities, the community here holds many activities for children, teenagers and parents.

I found a special interest in the dialogue between medicine and Christian spirituality at Saint George Parish in New Westminster, BC, Canada. The lecture held there after Vespers had many special echoes, and at the dinner shared with the participants, Fr. Nicu Liuță, who already has studies, interests and practice in biology and in the field of medical services, showed great interest in the possibility of extending the visibility of this illuminating presence of Christian theology in the sphere of the sciences, medical care and psychotherapy.

On October 9, in Las Vegas, at Saint George and Saint Dimitrios the New Church, I had the joy of meeting again Fr. Mihail, who, with the help of some big-hearted ladies (vice president Camelia and Mrs. Liza), managed to facilitate a lecture dedicated to some key topics at the confluence of spiritual life and neuroscience: self-care, willpower, gentleness and cognitive flexibility. Although time was extremely limited, the lecture drew lively reactions, questions and discussion, proof that the topics proposed by the participants were closely connected to their concerns. The Las Vegas community, a true oasis of Romanian identity, is gathered around a remarkable place of worship that radiates peace, inner stillness and joy, just like the Christians I met there[8].

A special experience took place in the community of Holy Trinity Church in Los Angeles on Thursday, October 10, since two days later, on October 12, was the feast of Saints Probus and Andronicus, whose Holy Relics are kept in this church. For this reason Fr. Constantin Alecse scheduled the Akathist service for the evening of October 10, before the planned lecture. The service was celebrated together with Fr. Nikodim Bibarț in the presence of many faithful, among them Mrs. Lucia Sava, Consul General of Romania in Los Angeles. After the Akathist, attended by a considerable number of faithful, considering that the activity took place on a weekday, came a dinner and the lecture “Inner Stillness and the Noise of the World.” The questions and interaction with the faithful at the meeting revealed a real concern among those present for preserving, at home, at work and in life, an environment suited to the spiritual life, a real challenge if we consider that the famous and provocative Hollywood district, the main center of the American film and television industry, is a 16-minute drive from the place of our meeting[9].

A special joy was seeing again, after several years, the Romanian Orthodox Christian communities of Atlanta. I was impressed by the remarkable achievements of Fr. Nicolae Clempuș, who has completed the fitting out of generous spaces for catechetical activities for children and young people, and by the interest and intense concern of the parents in the parish for the education of their children. The workshop held for the community of Fr. Nicolae and Fr. George Acsente, as well as the lecture given for the Romanians of Atlanta, were an excellent occasion for reflection on the challenges raised today by the information society and the free circulation of symbolic capital in the digital universe, especially given that few things are suitable for young children and for those still growing and being formed. I had the joy of taking part, together with the two priests and their families, in a profitable and joyful gathering at the home of one of the wonderful families of this place: Șandor Doru and Mihael. Many other faithful from the two communities attended, and the interaction and dialogue, carried on with great energy and attention, were for me the sign of a living concern for the upbringing of children and for family life in the light of Orthodox Christian spiritual life.

I found a similar concern in the community of Saint Nicholas and Saint George Church in New York, where a lecture was organized on the role of attachment in the upbringing of children and teenagers and in family life. I was glad to find here again our welcoming host, Fr. Marius Dumitrescu, together with Florina, Petru and Danielle Radu and several other faithful. In the evening, far from noisy Manhattan, we were able to explore the various meanings of attachment and the way in which we, as parents, are called to fulfill them in the roles we have in the family (as husband or wife), as well as in the extended family and in our circles of friends. Together we discovered the wonderful way in which the experience of the spiritual life in Orthodoxy proves to be a fulfillment of the needs and searches for attachment, which receive a full answer in the life of the Church, in the Holy Sacraments, in the love of God, in the care of the Mother of God and finally, fully, and through all of these, in divine Providence.

Hospitality, Love, Hope and Thanks

Besides these communities, with the blessing of Patriarch Daniel and of His Eminence Nicolae, and at the invitation of His Eminence Nathaniel, I also held a series of activities in the Romanian Orthodox communities in the locations mentioned, where I was received with great warmth, care and brotherly love by Fr. Constantin Lăpuștea (Elevation of the Holy Cross Church, San Jose), Fr. Gabriel Agoston (Dormition of the Mother of God Church, Portland) and Mr. Ionuț Gusu of Seattle. Likewise, my stay and the many activities held over several days were generously looked after by Fr. Gabriel Ilieș (Austin), Fr. Valentin Ilieș (San Antonio), Dean Fr. Nicolae Lăpuște (Holy Trinity Parish, Vancouver), Fr. George Acsente (Saints Constantine and Helen Church, Atlanta) and Fr. Ioan Cătană (Holy Three Hierarchs Church, Seattle). The priests directly supported these activities, the lectures and the workshops.

The hospitality and warmth of all the Romanians are an excellent testimony to the illuminating potential that Orthodox Christian spirituality can offer in this vast part of the world. But the light, full of love and hospitality, of zeal and of virtues anchored in Christ, does not only offer an edifying witness for the North American continent, which stands at the heart of tensions and challenges decisive for the immediate future. By the mercy of the Lord, Romanian Orthodoxy can also unite the destinies of Romanians in the USA, thereby increasing the witness of a life in communion anchored in the heaven of divine love shown in the Son of God made Man and in the Holy Sacraments of His Church. With the help of the Lord and with the blessing of the hierarchs, may these works multiply!

Finally, I extend my thanks to His Beatitude Patriarch Daniel and to His Eminence Teofan for the blessings granted, to His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae for the invitation, to His Eminence Nathaniel for the invitation, and to the organizers of this tour, Fr. Gabriel Ilieș of Austin and Ionuț Gusu of Seattle. The organizers put considerable effort into scheduling the travel, securing accommodation, publicizing the events and all the other details of the activities, and they took care of me at all times.

If we judge by quantity, we could be mistaken: 14 lectures and 4 workshops, held in 7 US states and one Canadian province, after 30,000 kilometers traveled in 7 weeks, might seem a busy program. Yet it is only a tiny drop in the immense ocean of missionary needs in the Romanian Orthodox communities of North America, a small help offered to those who carry out the missionary work here every day. And so, despite all the difficulties of these long journeys, such efforts are received with great joy by our brothers and sisters across the ocean and remain welcome in the future.
