[1] To someone reading these lines whose only reference points are the cultural patterns of today’s society, this preparatory process for a journey might seem superfluous. In the environment of a confused and wounded post-postmodernity, the freedom to express everything you think and to do whatever you want, as you please, has sometimes come to be considered the only proof of courage. The idea of the freedom and autonomy of the person is stressed again and again, a kind of independence of the person, detaching one’s thinking and actions from all possible authorities and affiliations. The urge to judge anything and everything with one’s own mind, and to act however one feels, or simply as one wishes, is highly prized. Autonomy is presented as an indicator of courage, proof of personal power, a sign of maturity or normality. Being this way is the only way to remain authentic. Hidden here is a premise that is itself considered courageous, namely that all realities and all necessary meanings are already gathered in the human mind, and that the person also holds all the levers for the best decisions and for flawless actions. Christian spirituality orders everything according to another logic, anchored in the loving obedience of the Son to the Father, from which follows a heavenly and earthly, spiritual and ecclesial hierarchy, in which each becomes obedient to the one who is greater and remains full of gratitude toward those whose disciple he has been. Judged hastily, this Christian structuring of interpersonal and inter-institutional relations might be considered wholly unsuited to our present, dominated by freedom of expression and of manifestation. But it is not so. On the contrary, the perspective centered on the autonomy of the subject, who is entitled to say anything, at any time, certain that he cannot be wrong, with the right to his own point of view, is today being corrected even by some psychological and organizational explorations of intelligence. In this way it becomes evident, in a wonderful convergence with the observations of the Philokalia, that we as human beings come to know together, through a common effort and as the result of this cooperation. On the one hand, no one is anything by himself, each being indebted to many, and what we know, however much we may know, inherently has limits of validity (An excellent work here is by Steven Sloman and Philip Fernbach, Iluzia cunoașterii, Editura Publica, 2017). On the other hand, even experts, as they feel more and more sure of themselves and more self-sufficient, are more exposed to the risk of error. (Another excellent work on such matters is by Tali Sharot, Mintea influentă, Introspectiv collection, Editura Litera, 2020). Finally, the experience of personal power (nourished or strengthened by the habit of free expression or action) could erode one’s way of living over time. The repeated exercise of power, without careful watchfulness over oneself, drives away the disposition to gratitude, and one in the full exercise of power is liable to become less and less sensitive and less and less indebted to those who helped him grow. (In this regard, Dacher Keltner wrote an excellent work, Paradoxul puterii, Editura Curtea Veche, Bucharest, 2018.)

title: Press Release
intro:
November 12, 2024, Austin, Texas, United States of America

Press Release

Biserica românească - lumina viitoarelor generații
A project funded by the Department for Romanians Everywhere

The project “Biserica românească- lumina viitoarelor generații” is implemented by the Saint Mary Romanian Orthodox Church Association, the only Romanian association registered in the Austin, Texas area and its surroundings, and the only entity that unites the Romanian community of this area and seeks to preserve Romanian spirituality, traditions, language and culture. The project will conclude with the event organized for Romania’s National Day on December 1.

The funding approved for this project by the Department for Romanians Everywhere amounts to 100,000 lei.

The project is carried out along 2 main lines:

  1. The Children’s Liturgy aims, in addition to its religious component, to make the most of the Romanian cultural heritage and to stimulate the creativity of the young generation by promoting Romanian culture and the use of the Romanian language. This action is aimed at Romanian children, teenagers and young people in the Austin, Texas area and involves purchasing furniture and teaching materials for two classrooms, as well as equipping these rooms with a new audio-video system.
  2. Mica Românie din Texas aims to continue and strengthen Romanian feeling in the Austin, Texas area. Its main objective is to promote Romania’s National Day, Romanian traditions and culture through the events organized: 4 creative and cultural workshops, a Round Table to celebrate Romanian Language Day, and the celebration of December 1. These events will bring together the Romanian community of the Austin and San Antonio areas and their guests. The show organized for December 1 will include the participation of the famous Romanian choir “Tronos,” Romanian food, and the promotion of local Romanian businesses and of Romania’s tourist attractions to participants of Romanian and other nationalities.

title: Pastoral Letter of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church for the First Sunday of the Nativity Fast 2024
intro:
ON THE SIGNIFICANCE OF THE “HOMAGE YEAR  OF PASTORAL CARE AND CARE FOR THE SICK”
AND OF THE “COMMEMORATIVE YEAR OF ALL THE
HOLY UNMERCENARY HEALERS”,  IN THE ROMANIAN PATRIARCHATE

 

TO THE MOST VENERABLE MONASTIC ORDERS,
THE MOST REVEREND CLERGY
AND THE MOST BELOVED FAITHFUL
OF THE ROMANIAN PATRIARCHATE,

 

GRACE, JOY AND PEACE
FROM GOD THE FATHER, THE SON AND THE HOLY SPIRIT, AND FROM US, FATHERLY BLESSINGS!

 

Most Venerable and Most Reverend Fathers,
Beloved brothers and sisters in the Lord,

The Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church proclaimed the year 2024 in the Romanian Patriarchate as the Homage Year of Pastoral Care and Care for the Sick and the Commemorative Year of all the Holy Unmercenary Healers.

Care for the sick is a commandment of the Gospel and a condition of salvation, being one of the essential criteria by which God will judge us. Christ the Lord asks us to visit those who are sick and suffering, to help them as much as we can and to encourage them with a kind heart and with hope in the great mercy and power of God.

The Nativity Fast, which has just begun, brings the hope and joy of the coming into the world of Christ the Savior as a Child, God and Man, offering us the perfect model of purity and prayer of the Mother of God, as well as the “image of meekness” of Saint Nicholas the Hierarch, the merciful one and bringer of gifts.

Right-believing Christians,

At the beginning of creation, “God saw everything that He had made, and indeed it was very good” (Genesis 1:31); afterward, however, the disobedience of Adam and Eve to the divine commandment brought death and sickness into the world (Genesis 3:16-19). Man, who was created in Paradise in the image of God and had been adorned with every virtue, receiving from his Creator all spiritual and material gifts, came to know, as a result of sin, the pain of separation from God. Thus, the first suffering that man endured was the departure from the relationship of harmony and closeness with God and the expulsion from Paradise, where he lived in the midst of a creation filled with the divine Spirit. Saint Gregory of Nyssa highlights this truth when he says that “he who was fashioned for immortality was undone by death, and he who dwelt in the delight of Paradise was moved to this place of sicknesses and pains”[1].

Therefore, sickness, suffering and death were not created by God: “God did not make death, nor does He delight in the destruction of the living […], but through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wisdom of Solomon 1:13; 2:24). Both sickness and suffering are realities that reveal the weakness and frailty of man separated or estranged from his Creator through disobedience. For this reason, in the books of the Old Testament, when sickness, suffering and death are mentioned, people’s hope is often turned toward God and His help. The Psalmist David prays for healing from infirmities: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak; O Lord, heal me, for my bones are troubled” (Psalm 6:2), and the psalmist also confirms the help received from God: “O Lord my God, I cried out to You, and You healed me” (Psalm 29:2). In the Book of the Wisdom of Jesus, the son of Sirach, it is advised that “in your sickness do not be negligent, but pray to the Lord, and He will heal you” (Wisdom of Sirach 38:9), because “He raises up the soul and gives light to the eyes, giving healing, life and blessing” (Wisdom of Sirach 34:19). From the example of righteous Job we learn that “man brings forth his own suffering” (Job 5:7), but also that “God delivers the afflicted through his affliction, and through suffering God gives him instruction” (Job 36:15).

Therefore, God is not the creator of suffering. He does, however, bring healing to man weakened by sin, offering him His grace so that he may bear the hardships of life. That is why the psalmist recalls that “the Lord is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves such as have a contrite spirit” (Psalm 33:17).

That God is “the Physician of souls and bodies” is shown especially in the Holy Gospels. They present to us the work of the Savior Jesus Christ, Who “went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and every disease among the people” (Matthew 9:35). In the New Testament, the sick ask the Lord Jesus Christ for healing, and His disciples also heal, but with the power given them by God. The great number of healings performed confirms the Savior’s preaching and proclaims the power and compassionate presence of the God-Man among people. Christ’s teaching and His healings are always united in the deepest way, forming a single message of hope and salvation. The healings Christ the Lord performs are signs of His infinite merciful love. Through these healings He shows that the Kingdom of God is near to people and helps us understand that man’s true and deepest sickness is the absence of his communion with God, the Source of love. Only communion with God can offer us true healing and authentic life.

The central event that bears witness to God’s merciful and healing love remains the Sacrifice of the Savior Jesus Christ on the Cross. Through the Incarnation of Christ, God chose to become man and to share the sufferings of humanity, culminating in His death on the Cross. He is the One of Whom the prophet Isaiah said: “He Himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses” (Matthew 8:17; Isaiah 53:4). Through His obedience unto death, Christ the Lord healed the sin of disobedience of our forefathers Adam and Eve (cf. Philippians 2:8). The Cross of Christ is also the testimony that God entered human history to suffer with us and to save us. Through His death and Resurrection, Christ gives a new meaning to suffering, which is not seen as an end in itself, but as a reality that, though difficult and painful, can become a path of purification from the passions, of spiritual maturing and of drawing near to God. The Resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead is the proof of His victory over sin and death, and therefore also over sickness and suffering (cf. John 11:25). If death is understood as a consequence of sin, the Resurrection is the restoration of life and victory over suffering. The Resurrection of Christ is the beginning of a new creation, in which death, sickness and suffering no longer have power over the believer. Although in this material world man continues to experience sickness, suffering and death, the Resurrection of Christ bears witness to the complete healing of man at the end of the ages. That is why, in the Church, Christ Himself is medicine, and the Holy Eucharist is a remedy for the healing of soul and body, for the forgiveness of sins and life eternal (cf. John 6:54).

After the Savior’s Ascension into heaven, the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples, giving them the power to carry on His work of healing and salvation. The Holy Spirit works in the Church through the Holy Mysteries in the hearts of the faithful, healing them, strengthening them and guiding them on the path of salvation. In this context, the priestly ministry has always included the clergy’s duty to care for the sick, in fulfillment of the commandment of the Lord Jesus Christ: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons. Freely you have received, freely give” (Matthew 10:8).

Through the work of the Holy Spirit in the world, especially through the Holy Mysteries, the servants of the Church continue the mission on which they were sent by Christ, healing and relieving the sufferings of countless sick people. Besides prayer and encouragement, pastoral care for the sick is also carried out in the Church through social-philanthropic institutions. Of the 884 social and medical services run by the units of worship of the Romanian Orthodox Church, 90 are intended for the sick, with 39,439 patients benefiting from these services.

Beloved faithful,

The Christian life lived according to the rules of the Church is a means of guarding ourselves from sin and also a way of preventing illness. Prayer, fasting, temperance and almsgiving are not only moral obligations of the Christian, but also methods and remedies through which, with the help of divine grace, we cultivate a healthy physical and spiritual life.

The Church prays for the health and salvation of people. The Holy Priest and Confessor Dumitru Stăniloae shows that through the Holy Mystery of Unction “healing of the body, forgiveness of sins and cleansing of the soul from sins are asked for together. The indwelling of the Spirit has above all the purpose of cleansing from sins, healing from the passions and raising man to a life of holiness, of pure service to God”[2].

At the same time, in the Church, those who are sick and suffering receive the protection and help of the Mother of God and of all the saints. The saints are intercessors and bearers of divine grace, and through their life full of holiness and prayer they become means through which Christ pours out blessings upon people. The saints do not act by their own power, but by the power of God, Who works through them. That is why the saints are regarded as living testimonies of Christ’s love and mercy toward the world.

In particular, when it comes to sickness and suffering, the Church remembers and honors the Holy Unmercenary Healers, known for their gift of healing the sick through the power of the grace given them by God. They are called “unmercenary” because they received no material reward for their services, thus resembling the apostles, who passed on the message of the Gospel and worked miracles without asking for anything in return. These holy healers were physicians or healers who devoted their lives both to serving their neighbor and to serving God. They healed both people’s bodies and their souls, cultivating faith in God and passing on Christian love. To honor these wondrous healers, the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church proclaimed the year 2024 as the Commemorative Year of all the Holy Unmercenary Healers.

The first physician of the apostolic Church whom the Holy Apostle Paul mentions in his epistles is “Luke the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14), that is, the Holy Apostle and Evangelist Luke, the author of the third Gospel and of the book of the Acts of the Apostles. Also in the book of the Acts of the Apostles, we read about the Apostles Peter and Paul, who healed the sick in the name of Christ (Acts of the Apostles 3:6; 9:34).

In the same early period of Christianity, another healer was the Holy Great Martyr Thecla, Equal to the Apostles, a disciple of the Holy Apostle Paul.

From the first four centuries also come the twelve Holy Unmercenary Physicians commemorated liturgically at the Proskomedia: Cosmas and Damian, Cyrus and John, Panteleimon and Hermolaus, Sampson and Diomedes, Mocius and Anicetus, Thalelaeus and Tryphon, along with other holy healers of the first centuries: Saint Gregory the Wonderworker, Saint Spyridon the Hierarch, Saint Parthenius of Lampsacus the Hierarch, Saint Meletius the Hierarch, Archbishop of Antioch, or other great wonderworking saints of more recent times who are very much loved by the faithful, such as Saint Nectarios of Aegina the Hierarch, Saint Luke the Hierarch, Archbishop of Crimea, Saint Gerasimos of Kefalonia, or Saint Nikephoros the Leper the Venerable.

All these holy healers of the Church offer hope to the hopeless and grant healing where physicians cannot cure grave illnesses. The wonderworking saints, as members of the mystical Body of Christ, make known to the world the Lord Jesus Christ as the Great Physician, Who also granted them the gift of healing, as we learn from the hymnography of the Church: “What shall we call you? Physicians who heal souls and bodies, healers of incurable passions, who freely heal all, having received the gifts from Christ the Savior, Who grants us great mercy”[3]. The miracles of healing worked through the saints are testimonies of divine power, but also exhortations to faith. In most cases, the Savior healed those who came to Him with faith. In this context, the miracles worked through the saints are a call to people to strengthen their faith and draw near to God. Miraculous healings are a sign that Christ is at work in the world and that the Church is alive, animated by the power of the Holy Spirit, salvation being the most important healing.

Beloved brothers and sisters in the Lord,

Even though throughout the year 2024 the Church, through its clergy and lay faithful, has striven, more than in previous years, to bring comfort and relief to those on the bed of pain and infirmity, the coming period, that of the Nativity Fast, is a good occasion to increase Christian love and mercy.

Therefore, this year as well, we address the priests and lay faithful of our Holy Church with the fatherly exhortation to organize, in parishes, monasteries, deaneries and diocesan centers, collections of food, clothing and medicine. These will be distributed to those who are suffering and in need, to disadvantaged families with many children, to the elderly and to people who are alone, without children or relatives, especially those living in rural areas.

Trusting that this year too you will show Christian generosity and respond with love to our fatherly call in this holy work of charity and help, we thank you for the generosity shown in previous years and remind you of the words of the Lord Jesus Christ: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7).

We pray to the All-Merciful God to bless all Romanians, in Romania and abroad, granting them health and salvation, protecting them from all evil and strengthening them in every good work, to the joy of our Church and of the Romanian people everywhere. With great joy, we embrace you as a father and impart to you the apostolic blessing: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all!” (2 Corinthians 13:13).

† Daniel,
Archbishop of Bucharest,
Metropolitan of Muntenia and Dobrogea,

title: Consecration of the Church in San Antonio, Texas: Three Days Overflowing with Grace and Spiritual Joy
intro:
From November 29 to December 1, 2024, the Parish of Saint John Cassian and Saint Andrei Șaguna the Hierarch, Metropolitan of Transylvania, became the center of a celebration full of grace, spiritual  joy and spiritual strengthening, with the consecration of the church and its altar. This historic event brought together hierarchs, clergy and faithful, with guests from all corners of the world, giving the parish and the Orthodox community of Texas unforgettable moments.

Friday: Welcoming the Hierarchs, Receiving the Wonder-working Icon from Hawaii, and Great Vespers

On Friday, November 29, the parish joyfully welcomed its Primate, His Eminence Nicolae, Archbishop and  Metropolitan of the Americas, and His Grace James, Vicar Bishop of the Western American Diocese of ROCOR. The evening continued with the reception of the Wonder-working and Myrrh-streaming Iveron (Portaitissa) Icon of the Mother of God from Hawaii, brought by Fr. Octavian Mahler, to whom it had been entrusted by Fr. Nectarios Yangson.

The faithful, from all corners of America and beyond, gathered in great numbers to venerate the icon and take part in the Akathist of the Mother of God, during which divine grace was poured out upon those present through the gift of myrrh miraculously streaming from the icon. This moment filled the hearts of all present with joy, faith and hope. In his words of welcome, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae thanked Fr. Octavian for the effort of bringing this blessing to San Antonio, and Fr. Octavian spoke, offering testimonies about the miracles worked through the icon.

The evening ended with Great Vespers, at which the liturgical responses were sung by the Tronos Byzantine Choir, led by Archdeacon Mihail Bucă. The last moment of the evening was dedicated to the rite of preparing the Holy Relics and the altar for the consecration that was to take place on Saturday.

Saturday: The Consecration of the Church and the Altar

The morning of November 30 began with the reception of the Icon of the Mother of God from Hawaii and its placement for veneration, and continued with Matins. After the vesting of the hierarchs and clergy, under the guidance of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, the service continued with the Blessing of the Water, followed by the solemn procession around the church, with the reading of the Gospel, the sealing of the exterior walls with Holy Chrism and the sprinkling with holy water. After this, the hierarchs, clergy and faithful knelt before the church doors for the reading of the prayer of entrance, and after the prayer His Eminence performed the rite of the entrance itself by pronouncing verse 7 of Psalm 23: “Lift up your gates, O you princes…”, thus completing the rite of consecrating the exterior of the house of worship.

Then everyone entered the church, and Dean Fr. Iulian Aniței read the Charter of Consecration, while on the Holy Altar lay the Holy Relics of the Holy Martyrs Epictetus and Astion of Halmyris, which were to be placed in the base of the Holy Table together with the Charter of Consecration, signed by the hierarchs and priests, and the diptychs with the names of the founders and benefactors. After the reading of the psalms and the prayers of consecration, these items were placed in the base of the Holy Table, which was sealed with wax, and the Holy Table was washed with rose water and anointed with Holy Chrism. Then the Holy Evangelists were placed at the four corners of the Holy Table, and the table was covered with a new white cloth, sealed with the prayer and the seal of the hierarch. The Holy Table was then adorned with new vestments, candlesticks, a tabernacle and an oil lamp, and the Holy Antimension and the Holy Gospel were placed on it. Throughout the service of consecration, Dean Fr. Iulian Aniței described and explained every moment of the rite of consecration.

When the service of consecration ended, the Divine Liturgy was celebrated, at which the liturgical responses were sung by the Tronos Choir under the direction of Archdeacon Mihail Bucă. After the reading of the Gospel, the homily was given by Rev. Fr. Bogdan Bucur, Professor of Patristics at St. Vladimir’s Seminary in New York. Starting from the words of the Gospel, Fr. Bucur highlighted the life and spiritual work of Saint Andrew the First-Called, Protector of Romania, and of Saint Andrei Şaguna the Hierarch, Metropolitan of Transylvania, who remain spiritual models to be followed and cultivated in the life of Orthodox Christians.  The presence of the Myrrh-streaming Icon from Hawaii opened even wider the window toward the uncreated Light of God’s holiness and deepened the spiritual experience of communion between the Church Triumphant and the Church Militant.

At the end of the Divine Liturgy, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae spoke about the significance of the consecration of a church, stressing that this sacred act is not only a moment of consecrating a place of worship but also an occasion for deepening each believer’s bond with God. The consecration of a church is, in essence, a symbol of the birth of a new spiritual life, both for the house of worship and for every member of the community. His Eminence explained that through this liturgical act the church becomes a sacred space, filled with the divine presence, dedicated to prayer and communion. At the same time, the consecration is an invitation to each of us to experience a profound inner transformation by opening our hearts to the work of divine Grace. Thus, on this feast day, the faithful are called to reflect on the call God addresses to them, a call to return to Him and to a renewed spiritual life.

Metropolitan Nicolae went on to stress that our response to this call must not be passive but active, through a constant renewal of faith and spiritual life. Just as the church is consecrated to become a place of communion with God, so our life must be a space of continual encounter with divine grace. The believer is also urged to take part in the life of the church, in the liturgical services, in the sacraments of the church and in works of mercy, so as to allow Grace to penetrate deep into his heart and transform him.

In closing, His Eminence encouraged all those present to meditate on this divine call and deepen their faith, responding with joy and openness to the gifts God pours out upon every human being. Thus, through a spiritually renewed life, every believer can become a true dwelling place of God, and the church becomes a place where divine Grace is poured out unceasingly, transforming the lives of those who draw near with faith and humility.

For his work in the life of the San Antonio parish, Metropolitan Nicolae awarded the Metropolitan Cross for clergy to the parish priest, Fr. Valentin Dumitru Ilieș, and the Metropolitan Cross for laity to Preoteasa Geanina Cristina Ilieș and Mrs. Adina Pasnicu, in gratitude for their faith, sacrifice and dedication to the Church of the Savior. His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae also awarded the Metropolitan Cross for clergy, in appreciation of their devotion and dedication in the service of the Church, to Rev. Fr. Gheorghe Militaru, Eparchial Vicar of the Romanian Orthodox Diocese of Italy, and to Rev. Archdeacon Mihail Bucă, coordinator of the “Tronos” Byzantine Choir of the Patriarchal Cathedral in Bucharest. They were honored for their tireless support, active involvement and significant contribution to the spiritual growth of the “St. John Cassian and St. Andrei Șaguna” community in San Antonio. For their faith, dedication and sacrifice, all past and present members of the Parish Council were honored with the Metropolitan Certificate of Merit. The founders and benefactors received certificates of merit, commemorative plaques of gratitude, medals and icons of the parish’s patron saints, as a sign of esteem and appreciation for their material and spiritual contribution. A truly historic and moving moment was the gift brought by Rev. Fr. Gheorghe Militaru of a fragment of the relics of Saint John Cassian, a gift of inestimable spiritual value sent by His Grace Bishop Siluan of the Romanian Orthodox Diocese of Italy, which has become a priceless spiritual treasure for the whole community, strengthening the bond with the saints and bringing blessing upon the parish.

Joy Shared through a Lecture and a Carol Concert

The afternoon continued in an atmosphere of celebration and communion with a festive banquet, an occasion for drawing the members of the community closer together and an expression of gratitude for the blessings received. During this special moment, Presvytera Dr. Jeannie Constantinou, Professor Emerita of Biblical Studies and Patristics at the University of San Diego, a living example of authentic and profound spiritual life, gave a remarkable lecture on the theological meanings and spiritual implications of the consecration of a church. With vast academic experience and a deep theological understanding of the patristic tradition, Dr. Constantinou explored the consecration of a church not only as a liturgical act but as a process through which the whole community is called to spiritual transformation. She explained how this sacred act not only consecrates a place of worship but makes it a space into which divine Grace enters in a special way, renewing the souls of those who draw near with faith.

She also emphasized the close link between the consecration of a church and each believer’s personal response to God’s call. Each of us, she said, is called to become a “living church” by leading a pure life, full of love and humility, and the church, through its consecration, urges us to share in the same inner transformation. This lecture was a moment of deep reflection, in which all those present had the opportunity to meditate on the true meaning of consecration and on how this sacred act can influence and enrich the spiritual life of every believer. It was a gift of wisdom and light that inspired everyone to respond with greater faith and dedication to God’s call to live in communion with Him.

After the lecture, the Tronos Byzantine Choir, led by Rev. Archdeacon Mihai Bucă, concluded the festive gathering with a moving concert of carols and patriotic songs, paying tribute to both the Christian and the Romanian tradition.

Saturday ended with Vespers and the veneration of the Portaitissa Icon of the Mother of God from Hawaii, and His Grace James offered words of encouragement and thanks for the two days full of grace and spiritual joy spent in the Romanian church in San Antonio.

Sunday: Hierarchical Divine Liturgy, Te Deum for Romania’s National Day, and Fraternal Agape

On Sunday, December 1, the day began with the welcoming of the Wonder-working Portaitissa Icon of the Mother of God from Hawaii and continued with Matins, sung by the chanters of the Tronos Choir. At the 9th Ode of the Canon, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae and His Grace Bishop James of Sonora were welcomed. The Divine Liturgy was celebrated by the two hierarchs together with an assembly of priests and deacons that included Rev. Archdeacon Mihail Bucă and the clergy present who are members of the Tronos Choir. After the reading of the Holy Gospel, His Grace James of Sonora gave the homily. His Grace said that through the Gospel of the healing of the blind man of Jericho we are called to reflect on the spiritual light that Christ brings into our lives. This man’s physical blindness is a symbol of the spiritual blindness we often face in our lives, when we do not see God’s truth or do not understand His will. But like the blind man of Jericho, who did not hesitate to cry out for help, we too are called to open our hearts and ask for the Lord’s help. Christ not only heals the body but also enlightens the soul, driving away the darkness of sin. The response of the blind man, who believed with his whole being in the power of Christ, teaches us about living faith and about the courage to seek God even when everything seems impossible. His healing was the result of a personal encounter with Christ, and through this Gospel we are invited to have the same attitude of openness and faith. Therefore, let us pray that Christ may open the eyes of our hearts, so that we may see His truth and respond to His call, and so walk the path of salvation, following Him with faith and humility.

After the Divine Liturgy, a service of thanksgiving (Te Deum) was celebrated for Romania’s National Day, December  1, and at its end His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae spoke briefly about the historical context of this commemoration.

The hierarchs, priests and faithful had the joy of venerating the Myrrh-streaming Icon from Hawaii, and the hymns offered by the parish choir completed the festive atmosphere. The celebration ended with a fraternal agape meal, during which the faithful shared their joy and gratitude for the moments they had experienced.

A Legacy for Future Generations

The consecration of the church in San Antonio was more than a liturgical event: it was a testimony of the faith, love and unity of a blessed community. The joy of the consecration and the presence of the Wonder-working Icon of the Mother of God brought a special blessing, offering a living example of Orthodox Christian communion on American soil. This moment remains inscribed in the hearts of the Romanian faithful of San Antonio as a guiding light toward a life lived in Christ. Glory to God for all things!

Fr. Valentin Ilieș, Parish Priest

title: Celebration of the Jubilee Year and Patronal Feast of Saint Nicholas and Saint George Church in New York, December 6-8, 2024
intro:
“Unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it;
unless the Lord guards the city, the watchman stays awake in vain…” (Ps. 126:1).

Saint Nicholas and Saint George Romanian Orthodox Church in Queens, New York is celebrating a jubilee year! 50 years of faith and communion on American soil (1974 - 2024).

It is an opportunity to truly experience God’s grace and forgiveness and to renew our commitment to the faith and to the community. It is a time of reflection, prayer and reconciliation, in which the faithful are encouraged to examine their lives and strengthen their bond with God and with their neighbors. It is also an occasion to express gratitude for the blessings received and to commit ourselves to living in the light of faith in the future as well.

Together with all the faithful of the parish, we have witnessed unforgettable moments over these 50 years. Services that brought spiritual joy, radiant feasts, baptisms bringing new Christians into the Church, marriages strengthened by the presence of the Lord’s grace, and funerals consoled by the spirit of redemption have enriched our spiritual life. Each event has left a deep mark on our hearts, strengthening the bonds of community and brotherly love.

This anniversary gives us the occasion, and the duty, to remember all the efforts of those who contributed to the growth of our church. From priests to volunteers to every member who lent a hand, each one played an essential role in building a united and strong community. We deeply appreciate the work of all who have been involved in preserving and beautifying our church, including the recent work of adorning it with iconography, which has brought a new breath of life to this house of worship.

Looking back, we realize that this journey has been full of challenges but also of joys. We have learned to support one another in difficult moments and to rejoice together in the blessings received. Our community has always been an example of solidarity, and this is a testimony to the power of our faith. Nothing is done without  God’s help. He gives you health and success in all that you do. That is why the Romanian people, when beginning anything in life, first make the sign of the Cross with faith and say “God help us!” With this same thought, we too, priest and faithful, set out to have a church in Woodside, New York.

Saint Nicholas and  Saint George Parish was founded in 1974 at the initiative of a few Romanian families who had come to New York. These Romanians of good faith, having left their country, wanted to keep their connection with the motherland through the Church as well. At the meeting of April 10, 1974, His Eminence Archbishop Victorin Ursache submitted to the Diocesan Council for approval the request to establish a Romanian Orthodox parish in New York under the jurisdiction of the Romanian Orthodox Archdiocese in America and Canada. After approval, Fr. Nicolae Bârsan was transferred from Philadelphia to New York. At first, services were held in a chapel rented from the Presbyterians in Manhattan. After two years the parish became vacant, and until 1984 it was served by several priests.

On January 14, 1984,  His Eminence Archbishop Victorin appointed Mitred Archimandrite Dr. Vasile Vasilache as parish priest. With the arrival of Fr. Vasile and with the generous support of the faithful, in June 1984 the building at 45-03 48 Avenue, Woodside, NY was purchased for $85,000, a sum the faithful paid off within six years. The church was consecrated for the first time on December 9, 1984, by Archbishop Victorin Ursache of blessed memory, and its patron saints are Saint Nicholas the Hierarch and the Holy Great Martyr George.

When he took over the leadership of Saint Nicholas Parish in New York, Archimandrite Dr. Vasile Vasilache, although advanced in years, was full of energy and youthful zeal. Full of wisdom, gentleness and calm, Fr. Vasile knew people very well; he knew how to speak to and treat everyone, giving each one his heart, comfort, joy and spiritual hope. For 19 years he preached the Word of God, being instant in season and out of season, and devoted himself entirely to this Romanian community until January 6, 2003, when, at the age of 93, he passed into eternity on the very feast of the Lord’s Baptism.

After the repose of Fr. Vasile Vasilache, through the care of His Eminence Archbishop Nicolae, Protosyngellos Ioan Casian Tunaru was appointed parish priest. He shepherded the Romanian faithful with dedication and faith until July 2, 2006, when he was ordained in Chicago as Vicar Bishop of the Romanian Orthodox Archdiocese in America and Canada.  Through his monastic dedication, Fr. Ioan Casian increased the number of services even further and enriched the spiritual life of the community. At his initiative, 38 matching festal icons were painted, which gave the church a new look at the time. During this period Fr. Ioan Casian also paid special attention to involving young people in the life of the Church and to the Sunday School. Beginning in 2003, with the help of volunteers from Saint Nicholas and Saint George Church, Fr. Ioan Casian organized the first summer camps for the children of the Romanian Orthodox Archdiocese in America and Canada.

In 2006, His Eminence Archbishop Nicolae proposed Fr. Andrei Turcoane as parish priest for the church in Queens, a proposal approved by the Parish Council. Fr. Andrei continued the work of his predecessors in keeping alive among the parishioners of Saint Nicholas and Saint George “the threefold love: for God, Church and Nation”, as Mitred Archimandrite Vasile Vasilache put it in a reference work published in 1991 in New York. Catechesis of the faithful was introduced on the last Sunday of the month, with questions and answers from Holy Scripture.

After Fr. Andrei Turcoane retired in September 2011, Fr. Marius Daniel Dumitrescu was appointed parish priest of Saint Nicholas and Saint George Church. From the very beginning, Fr. Marius wanted the faithful to be involved in and share responsibility for the liturgical life of the parish, and the children and young people to be involved in social activities.

With the arrival of the new parish priest, Saint Nicholas and Saint George Church, NY experienced a revival that brought a fresh breath of life and made it an even more welcoming space, full of light. Inspired by the desire to revive the beauty of the church and to create a true place of recollection for the parishioners, the parish priest, Fr. Marius Dumitrescu, began a series of projects meant to beautify the church and strengthen the spiritual bond of the community.

On December 9, 2012, Saint Nicholas and Saint George Church was reconsecrated in a ceremony celebrated with great solemnity by His Eminence Archbishop Nicolae and His Grace Ioan Casian, Vicar Bishop, together with a large synaxis of priests. This moment marked a new stage in the life of the parish, further establishing the house of prayer as an important spiritual center for the New York community.

In 2021 the beautification of the church continued with the installation of church stalls made in Greece, replacing pews that were no longer practical. These new stalls added a note of elegance and sacredness, improving both the comfort of the faithful and the liturgical atmosphere of the church.

In 2022 another significant step was taken in beautifying the church with the addition of Byzantine-style iconography. The especially beautiful icons that now adorn the interior of the church were made in Romania, at Ponor Monastery, Alba County, by Mother Antonia, under the spiritual guidance of Abbot Irineu Curtescu. The iconography, of rare and unique beauty, has brought spiritual depth and a special atmosphere of prayer to the church. The service of blessing the iconography was celebrated with devotion and solemnity by His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae on December 11, 2022, a moment full of grace and blessing for the entire community.

All this was done with God’s help and is a solemn moment of devout gratitude and appreciation toward the founders of this Church and toward all who have preserved, restored and beautified it over time. The church, now more beautiful and welcoming, continues to be a place of prayer, communion and inspiration for all who cross its threshold.

It can be said that this year’s celebration of the patronal feast of Saint Nicholas and Saint George Church was a gift from God, an opportunity in which we lived and felt God’s presence in our midst. It was a feast that brought blessing, grace and peace to the souls of all who gathered to honor Saint Nicholas the Hierarch, a moment of special spiritual uplift, a true blessing from Christ the Savior, which strengthened the unity and faith of the entire community.

The good God blessed us this year to have at the services both hierarchs of the Metropolia, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae and His Grace Ioan Casian, Romanian Orthodox Bishop of Canada, a moment of great joy and consolation, a sign that God is near and that our prayers are heard.

The patronal feast itself opened on Thursday evening with Great Vespers with Litiya, served by His Grace Bishop Ioan Casian together with the parish priest, Fr. Marius Dumitrescu, and Fr. Ionuț Preda of Descent of the Holy Spirit Church, Ridgewood, NY. At the end of Vespers, His Grace spoke to us about the saints and holiness, recalling Saint Nicholas the Hierarch and the 16 most recent saints canonized by the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church on July 11-12, 2024. “There are saints in every generation; let us humbly open the gates of our hearts and receive their witness,” said His Grace. He then mentioned Emperor Constantine the Great and spoke of his importance and influence on Christian life. Among Emperor Constantine’s great achievements, one that profoundly changed the history of Christianity was decreeing Sunday an official day of rest, which it remains to this day.

On Friday morning the Hierarchical Divine Liturgy was celebrated by His Grace Bishop Ioan Casian, together with a synaxis of priests made up of the parish priest, Fr. Marius Dumitrescu, Fr. Ovidiu Sabău of Saint Andrew Church, Reading, PA, and Fr. Florin Spânu of Holy Apostles Church, Astoria, NY. 

His Grace began his homily on a personal note, recalling the beginnings of his pastoral work in this parish. He remembered with gratitude the moment in 2003, during Holy Week, when he took up the ministry after Archimandrite Vasile Vasilache. He then spoke about the Epistle and Gospel of the day:

 “The explanation of the Gospel of the Beatitudes, especially in the context of the feast of Saint Nicholas the Hierarch, offers us an occasion for deep reflection on our Christian life and on the essential values that Christ the Savior sets before us for a blessed life,” said His Grace Bishop Ioan Casian.

  1. “Blessed are the poor in spirit…”
    Spiritual poverty does not refer to a lack of wisdom, but to deep humility, to recognizing our need for God and emptying the heart of secondary things such as pride, the desire for power or attachment to material things. It is a call to open the soul to receive God’s will and grace.
  2. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness…”
    This hunger does not refer only to bodily needs, but to a spiritual hunger for God’s righteousness and will. During the fast, abstaining from bodily pleasures helps us focus on spiritual work, turn our hearts and thoughts toward God and live in accordance with His teachings.
  3. “Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake…”
    This beatitude reminds us of the courage and faith of the holy martyrs, who accepted suffering and even death for their faith. They are models of steadfastness in the face of trials, showing us that true joy comes from faithfulness to Christ, even in the most difficult moments.

“On the feast of Saint Nicholas, who is an example of self-giving, mercy and love, we are called to draw inspiration from these Beatitudes and to live a life of holiness, obedience and joy in the Lord,” said His Grace.

The conference on the themes “Archimandrite Vasile Vasilache: A Life Dedicated to Faith and Community” and “Romanians in America: Faith and Community Across Generations” on Saturday, December 7, 2024, was a special event dedicated to Mitred Archimandrite Vasile Vasilache, the first founder of the church, and to exploring the role Romanians in the New York area have played in preserving their faith and cultural traditions across generations.

The conference speakers:

  • Abbot Ieremia, Saint Demetrios Monastery, Middletown, NY, on the theme: “Why Did Fr. Vasile Vasilache Become Parish Priest in New York?”
  • Fr. Prof. Ioan Cozma, Saint Demetrios Church, Manhattan, on the theme: “Church Autocephaly and the Ways It Is Granted in the Light of Canonical Legislation and Church Practice”
  • Mr. Grigore Culian, New York Magazin, on the theme: “Unforgettable Memories of Fr. Vasile Vasilache”
  • Mr. Cristian Pascu, DORUL Romanian Christian Society (founded 1903), on the theme: “Us About Ourselves”.

The remembrance of Archimandrite Vasile Vasilache was a moving moment, and the speakers and participants stressed the importance of carrying on this legacy, committing themselves to keeping alive the spirit of mission and community that Fr. Vasile built with much sacrifice and love. Through his example, Fr. Vasile Vasilache remains a symbol of love for one’s neighbor and of unconditional love for the Orthodox Church.

The conference was honored by the presence of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, His Grace Bishop Ioan Casian, Vicar Fr. Daniel Ene, the parish priest Fr. Marius Dumitrescu, and Mr. Cristian Boghian, manager of Romanian TV of New York, which filmed the event, as well as a large audience eager to take part in this moment of spiritual and cultural sharing.

Great Vespers on Saturday evening was served by His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae and His Grace Bishop Ioan Casian, together with Vicar Fr. Daniel Ene and the parish priest, Fr. Marius Dumitrescu. The presence of the hierarchs at this service made the moment truly special, deepening the community’s sense of its bond with Christ. Through the Vespers service, the Orthodox Church urges us to live in prayer and communion, preparing ourselves to welcome the great feasts of our faith.

At the end of the service, Vicar Fr. Daniel Ene paid tribute to Saint Philothea, commemorated on December 7, recalling her life and virtues, a shining example of purity of soul and self-giving. The feast of Saint Philothea is a call to all of us to follow her example, to cultivate goodness and to live a life pleasing to God.

A truly moving moment of the sermon was the personal testimony of Vicar Fr. Daniel Ene about God’s help in his healing. Fr. Daniel shared with sincerity and gratitude how divine intervention had helped him through a difficult period in his life, allowing him to be present at this event. This personal experience became a living example of God’s love and care for those who trust in Him.

On Sunday morning at 9:45, a large group of faithful and a synaxis of priests in splendid liturgical vestments were already awaiting the arrival of the hierarchs, while the chanters’ stand, led by the “Saint Inochentie” Byzantine Choir of Probota, was chanting Matins. Very soon the two hierarchs arrived at the church and were welcomed with the traditional hymn of welcome for a bishop, “Our Master and Hierarch, O Lord, preserve for many years,” sung by the whole community. Vicar Fr. Daniel Ene with the Holy Gospel, Abbot Ieremia with the Holy Cross, and the parish priest, Fr. Marius Dumitrescu, received the hierarchs with great reverence and respect, as a sign of honor and esteem.

Then the Holy and Divine Liturgy began, an especially uplifting moment in which the hierarchs, priests and faithful turned the church into a true corner of heaven, a place of encounter with God. The sacred atmosphere and devout prayers allowed every soul present to feel the nearness of God and lifted every heart toward heaven. As a beautiful line from a prayer says, “Standing in the temple of Your glory, we think we stand in heaven,” the service of this Liturgy turned the sacred space of the church into a place full of light, peace and divine grace.

This Holy and Divine Liturgy, celebrated with solemnity by the two hierarchs, surrounded by priests and faithful, was an occasion of spiritual uplift in which every participant felt part of a heavenly communion, united in prayer and faith. Living such a sacred moment was a testimony to God’s love and presence in the midst of the Church, and the words of the prayers brought a deep peace of soul that filled the hearts of all present. The children of the parish Sunday School and the faithful then received Holy Communion, and at the end of the Divine Liturgy a Memorial Service was served for the founders and servants of the church who have fallen asleep in the Lord.

In his vibrant, heartfelt homily, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae began by thanking the good God for these blessed days in which we honored Saint Nicholas the Hierarch, one of the patron saints of the church, and celebrated 50 years since the founding of the Saint Nicholas and Saint George community (1974-2024).

He then spoke about the Gospel reading for the 27th Sunday after Pentecost, the healing of the bent woman: “In this bent woman we can see the consequences of man’s estrangement from God, the bending of human nature. The tragedy of her life comes to an end through the merciful word and deed of Christ.

An example of ingratitude is the reaction of the ruler of the synagogue, who refuses to acknowledge God’s saving and restoring work.

Christ teaches us all how to respond to the hypocrisy cultivated in every society: with the truth that comes from God, who defends the dignity of the human person, the right to life of the child in its mother’s womb, and the right of the elderly to health.

For 2,000 years this conflict has existed between those who have recognized the Messiah, those who seek Him, those who ask Him for salvation and those who reject Him. Christ came to raise human dignity to its full humanity, that of a son or daughter of God, a citizen of the Kingdom of God,” His Eminence said.

In the second part of the sermon, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae paid tribute to the life and example of holiness of Saint Nicholas the Hierarch, who remains a model of mercy, courage and Christian love. His Eminence highlighted the virtues of this great saint, urging the faithful to follow him on the path to salvation through a pure life, fasting and prayer, deeds of mercy and love for one’s neighbor.

After the sermon, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae presented the parish with an icon of Saint Nicholas and Saint George, as a symbol of the protection and blessing of the church’s two patron saints. This gift was a sign of deep appreciation for the parish community and a testimony to the spiritual bond between the faithful and their hierarch.

On the occasion of the 50th anniversary of the founding of the parish, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae awarded the Order of the Holy Emperors Constantine and Helen to the parish priest, Fr. Marius Dumitrescu, and the American Metropolitan Cross for laity to Preoteasa Daniela Dumitrescu, Dănuț and Ana Maria Grigoraș, Adrian and Daniela Pală, Cristinel and Roxana Sacarin, Mircea and Silvia Mone, Mrs. Felicia Badea, Mrs. Elena Fintok, Mrs. Nicoleta Furtună, Mr. Constantin Alexandru, Petrică and Florica Radu, and Ion and Fruzina Catrina. This is the highest distinction of our Metropolia, recognizing the sacrifice and dedication of those who have served the Church and supported the activities of the religious community.

Visibly moved, the parish priest, Fr. Marius Dumitrescu, in warm and especially cordial words, thanked His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae and His Grace Ioan Casian for the honor they did Saint Nicholas and Saint George Church in New York by their presence at this historic moment. As a token of appreciation, he presented the hierarchs with an engolpion and cross set and an icon of the Mother of God with the Christ Child, as a symbol of gratitude and of the deep bond between the Church and those who shepherd it with great sacrifice and dedication.

Fr. Marius Dumitrescu then thanked the concelebrating clergy, Vicar Fr. Daniel Ene and Abbot Ieremia, who served this Holy and Divine Liturgy with him, emphasizing the importance of their collaboration in divine service. Nor did he forget to thank the faithful for their presence and devotion on this day of great significance, which brought great joy and blessing to the parish community.

We noted the active and welcome presence of the members of the Parish Council throughout the service, whose constant involvement contributed to the smooth running of the event and the good organization of the entire service. The service in the Holy Altar of the young Teodor Dumitrescu, Antonie Bujoreanu and Noah Nicholas Trepca was also a sign of the continuing tradition of educating and forming new generations of servants of the Church.

Another remarkable aspect of this moment was the zeal of the “Saint Inochentie of Probota” Byzantine Choir from Romania, conducted by Fr. Constantin Magdalena, which was specially invited for this event. Their devout and beautiful chanting lifted the souls of those present, bringing an atmosphere of divine grace and communion between heaven and earth, to the glory of God.

Present at the event were the Consul General of Romania in New York, Mrs. Mihaela Simona Florea, Mr. Dorian Branea, Director of the Romanian Cultural Institute in New York, Mr. Grigore Culian, New York Romanian Magazin, Mr. Cristian Boghian, manager of Romanian TV of New York, and Mr. Cristian Pascu, DORUL Romanian Christian Society.

The faithful filled Saint Nicholas Church to overflowing for the Sunday morning service, a sign of its blessing by Christ the Savior and of the special protection of Saint Nicholas the Hierarch. This presence of the faithful at the Divine Liturgy was a testimony of love and devotion toward God and toward Saint Nicholas, known as a great protector of those in need and an example of love and mercy. The atmosphere in the church was one of deep devotion, and the prayers offered were a true source of blessing and spiritual strengthening for the entire community.

After the service, all the faithful took part in the fellowship meal, a moment of communion and closeness among the members of the community, prepared with great dedication by our church’s Ladies’ Committee. In a warm and welcoming atmosphere, the faithful enjoyed the hospitality of those who had worked lovingly to prepare this occasion for meeting and fellowship. The fellowship meal was a gift of communion and gratitude, a moment in which everyone felt the joy of belonging to a community united in Christ.

An important moment of the meal was the sweet presence of the children of the parish Sunday School and the “Saint Inochentie” Byzantine Choir of Probota, who poured the sweet myrrh of the Nativity carols into the souls of the faithful. The children’s songs, full of joy and hope, together with the harmonious voices of the choir, created a festive atmosphere of great beauty, reminding everyone of the Savior’s coming into the world. The carols, with their message of love and light, reached the hearts of those present, bringing a deep peace of soul and a priceless spiritual joy.

Also during the meal, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae presented several jubilee diplomas to those who have taken an active part in the life of Saint Nicholas and Saint George Church. These diplomas were a sign of recognition and appreciation for the dedication and sacrifice of these faithful, who through their involvement have contributed to the well-being of the community and to the beautification of the house of worship.

We thank the organizers, the donors and all the faithful of Saint Nicholas and Saint George Church in New York, who over the years have obeyed God’s own commandment to have a holy and beautifully adorned house of worship for the ages to come. Through their generous gifts and their dedication, these faithful have shown deep respect for the holiness of the place and for the traditions of the Church, thus helping to preserve and strengthen a valuable spiritual heritage for future generations. May the good God reward their love and sacrifice with boundless graces and bless them in all they do for His glory!

May the next 50 years be just as full of grace, love and unity. With the Lord’s help, let us continue to build together a community that reflects our Christian values and is an example of love and support for all around us!

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God the Father and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with us all! Amen.

Fr. Marius D. Dumitrescu, Parish Priest

title: The Feast of the Nativity of the Lord at the Metropolitan Cathedral in Chicago
intro:
The traditional carol concert of the choir of the Holy Emperors Constantine and Helen Cathedral in Chicago took place, as it does every year, on the eve of the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, Tuesday, December 24, 2024. This year the choir’s concert was preceded by carols sung by the Sunday School children under the careful direction of Miss Dora Baciu. Under the baton of the same conductor, the Cathedral choir delighted the audience with a rich program of Romanian carols, bringing great joy to the Romanian Orthodox faithful of the Chicago area, who look forward to this carol concert every year. You can watch the concert, which was streamed on YouTube, here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zi2uUvSsx9Q

Christmas Day was an occasion of prayer and joy for the Romanian Orthodox faithful of Chicago, who filled the Holy Emperors Cathedral. At the end of the Divine Liturgy, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae spoke about the meaning of God’s descent to earth, quoting from his Christmas Pastoral Letter:

“Saint Leo the Great, bishop of Rome, speaks of the humble love of God revealed in the Incarnation of His Son: ‘When the times foreordained for the salvation of mankind had come, the Son of God entered the lowest parts of this world, descending from His heavenly throne yet not leaving His Father’s glory, being born in an entirely new way… The Uncontainable willed to be contained; He Who is before all time began to exist in time; the Lord of all, veiling the splendor of His glory, took the form of a servant; the impassible God did not disdain to be a suffering man, and the Immortal One willingly submitted to the law of death.’… The revelation of this humble love of God for man is the cause of the joy of the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, sung by the angels and proclaimed to all people: ‘Let us rejoice in the Lord, dearly beloved, and be glad with spiritual delight, for the new day of salvation has dawned for us, a day long prepared, a day of eternal happiness. For the cycle of the year brings back to us the mystery of our salvation, promised from the beginning, fulfilled at the end, which will remain forever. On this day it is fitting for us to lift up our hearts and to worship the divine mystery, for what is accomplished through a great gift of God must be treasured by the Church with great joy.’

My exhortation on this glorious feast is that we lift up our hearts, that we not fear rumors of crises, unrest and wars, and that we place all our hope in God’s care and help. He sent us a Savior, and He guides our steps in this complicated and troubled world.”

Christ is born, glorify Him!

Blessed holidays to all Romanians in Romania and everywhere!

title: Christmas at Saints Joachim and Anna Parish in Seattle – A Celebration of Christian Unity and Joy
intro:
This year the feast of the Nativity of the Lord was lived with special intensity in the community of Saints Joachim and Anna Parish in Seattle. Through a series of meaningful events, the faithful came together in the joyful spirit of Christmas, weaving tradition together with the deep spirituality of this feast.

The Sunday before Christmas – A Fair of Joy

On the Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord, the churchyard was transformed into a festive space with a holiday fair. Traditional pastries, golden cozonac and beautiful flower arrangements were lovingly prepared by members of the parish. The fair not only brought support to the community but also created an occasion for fellowship, strengthening the bond among the faithful.

On the same day, Rev. Fr. Ștefan Drăgoi had the joy of welcoming the carolers. Part of the “Datina” Ethno-Folk Ensemble gave a moving performance, bringing into the hearts of those present the beauty and authenticity of the ancestral carols. With their warm voices and traditional dress, the carolers brought back into the church the atmosphere of home, of holidays spent in the Romanian village, uniting us all in the spirit of our tradition.

The Christmas Divine Liturgy – The Message of Unity and Love

Christmas Day was marked by the solemn Divine Liturgy, to which many parishioners came dressed in Romanian national costume. The parish priest, Rev. Fr. Ștefan Drăgoi, stressed the importance of our Christian and national identity, pointing out that traditional dress is a living witness to our spiritual and cultural roots. In his homily, Fr. Ștefan Drăgoi emphasized the deep meaning of the Nativity of the Savior, urging the faithful to live in unity and love. “Through the Nativity of Christ, God has given us the supreme gift: our adoption as His sons. If God is our Father, then we, as brothers and sisters, have the sacred duty to love one another. Every act of kindness, every word spoken in peace contributes to the fulfillment of the divine calling: ‘on earth peace, goodwill toward men.’ In these times, more than ever, we are called to be makers of peace and love in the world.”

Father’s words were received with emotion by the faithful, who said that the feast of Christmas had brought them closer to God and to their neighbors.

The Children’s Program and the Festive Meal

After the Liturgy, the Sunday school children, coordinated by Mrs. Doina Danu, delighted the hearts of those present with a moving program of carols and poems dedicated to the Nativity of the Lord. Their costumes, crystal-clear voices and the joy in their eyes brought a special charm to the feast.

The day ended with a festive meal, carefully and devotedly organized by the ladies of the parish. The warm atmosphere, the traditional dishes and the spirit of fellowship made this Christmas an unforgettable one.

A Christmas of Unity and Hope

This year’s Christmas feast was more than a celebration: it was a reaffirmation of our Christian identity, of our shared values and of the hope that the Nativity of the Savior brings into our lives.

May the light of the Nativity of the Lord guide us all, uniting us in love, peace and goodwill!

title: Lectures Dedicated to the Centennial of the Romanian Patriarchate
intro:
The Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas continues in 2025 the implementation of the educational program “Exploring Your Faith.” This year, the program takes place in a special context, marked by “the Centennial of the Romanian Patriarchate” and “the Commemorative Year of Romanian Orthodox Spiritual Fathers and Confessors of the 20th Century”.

Launch of the 2025 Edition

The first lecture of the program for this year took place on January 9, 2025 and addressed the theme “Introduction to the History of Romanian Orthodoxy. A Theological Look at the Past”. The lecture was given by Prof. Dragoș Ursu, a renowned historian and theologian, doctor in history of “Babeș-Bolyai” University and post-doctoral researcher of the recent history of Romania. The lecture can be watched on the Metropolia’s official Facebook page by following this link.

This series of historical lectures includes 11 lectures, one on the second Thursday of each month, except for July. All the lectures are meant to give the faithful a better understanding of the history of the Romanian Orthodox Church and of its theological, cultural and spiritual values, according to the following thematic program:

  1. “Ancient Christianity in the Danubian Area. The Christianization of the Romanian People” – An exploration of the origins of Christianity on Romanian territory.
  2. “Between the Latinity of Faith and Institutional Slavonism” – The tensions and harmonies between the cultural and institutional influences on the Church.
  3. “The First Ecumenical Council. The Birth of Christian Europe” – A defining moment for universal Christianity and its impact on Europe.
  4. “Medieval Christianity and the Byzantine Heritage (13th-16th Centuries)” – A journey into the medieval era, with emphasis on Byzantine influences and the anthropological understanding of the age.
  5. “Orthodoxy in the Pre-modern Era (17th-18th Centuries). The Peak of Cultural Flourishing” – Prominent figures such as Vasile Lupu, Matei Basarab and Saint Constantin Brâncoveanu.
  6. “Orthodoxy in Transylvania. Reformation and Counter-Reformation” – An analysis of the historical context of the religious union of 1699.
  7. “Orthodoxy in Modernity. The Church and the National Project” – The role of the Orthodox Church in the reforms under Cuza and ecclesial autocephaly.
  8. “Orthodoxy in the Interwar Period” – Prominent figures, the Church’s relationship with political power, and popular religiosity.
  9. “Romanian Monasticism in (Pre)modernity” – From Saint Paisius Velichkovsky to the 1959 decree on the partial dissolution of monasteries.
  10. “Orthodoxy and Communism” – Political recalibrations, institutional survival and spiritual resistance in the face of the totalitarian regime.
  11. “Orthodoxy in America. The Story of the Romanian Community” – The development of the Romanian Orthodox Church in the American diaspora.

An Educational Endeavor with Impact in the Romanian Diaspora

The “Exploring Your Faith!” program has become an essential pillar of the educational mission of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas. Through this project, the faithful in the diaspora are invited to explore the roots of Romanian Orthodoxy and to draw closer in spirit to the traditions and spiritual values of their country of origin.

The 2025 lecture series promises to be particularly engaging, a unique opportunity for participants to rediscover the history and spirituality of the Romanian Orthodox Church. The Metropolia thus reaffirms its commitment to supporting Romanian communities beyond the country’s borders, offering them a solid connection with their spiritual heritage.

All the faithful are invited to take part in these gatherings, helping to strengthen the ties with the cultural and religious roots of the Romanian people.

title: His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae Visits Putna Monastery
intro:
On Saturday and Sunday, February 8-9, 2025, the Holy Monastery of Putna had the joy of welcoming His Eminence Nicolae, Romanian Orthodox Metropolitan of the Americas. His Eminence had come to Romania to take part in the events marking the 100th anniversary, on February 4, of the elevation of the Romanian Orthodox Church to the rank of Patriarchate. The visit to Putna was owed to the collaboration begun in 2019 with the blessing of Archbishop Pimen Zainea, through which Putna Monastery took on the revival of monastic life at St. Dimitrios the New Monastery in Middletown, NY, United States of America.

Metropolitan Nicolae took part in the Vigil on Saturday evening, and on Sunday he served the Divine Liturgy together with the serving fathers of the monastery. During the Divine Liturgy, with the blessing of His Eminence Calinic, Archbishop of Suceava and Rădăuți, His Eminence Nicolae ordained to the priesthood Hierodeacon Chiriac Păduraru, a monk of Putna Monastery.

The period of the Triodion thus began under the word of teaching that His Eminence addressed to all present:

“Two examples of how we relate to God are placed before our eyes. First there is the example of the proud Pharisee, and then that of the repentant tax collector. The Holy Gospel of Luke tells us that both of them, the Pharisee and the tax collector, “went up to the temple to pray” (Luke 18, 10). Since we are told that they went up to the temple to pray, we must understand that their presence in the temple was not for a simple prayer, not a chance ascent; rather, just as Zacchaeus the tax collector climbed the sycamore tree to meet Christ, so the tax collector and the Pharisee went up to the temple for a significant encounter with God. Just as happened with us today at the Divine Liturgy. It is not an ordinary encounter; it is an encounter that should change our life, as it did for Zacchaeus the tax collector and for the tax collector in this parable. Only the Pharisee’s prayer does not look like a prayer. It neither gives thanks to God for His benefits, nor asks for help, nor asks for a blessing; it is self-satisfaction, boasting before God.

The Fathers of the Church speak about this very grave and very subtle sin of pride. Saint John Climacus, who wrote the book “The Ladder of Divine Ascent”, writes in Step 21 that vainglory is what gives birth to pride. Saint John makes a distinction between these two passions. Vainglory is that of the Pharisee who exalted himself, who looked at his own efforts and exalted himself before God. Saint John says that this passion is very subtle; it is like an onion: if you peel away one layer, another layer appears, then another layer and another. If I fast, I may be tempted by vainglory, because I take pride in fasting. If I do not fast, I can again be tempted by vainglory, because I thought to be moderate. If I dress in fine clothes I am tempted again, because I show myself to people in fine clothes; if I appear in modest clothes, again I am tempted, because I want to show myself in modest clothes. If I speak, I am tempted by vainglory to show what I know; if I do not speak, again I am tempted, because I am moderate and do not show myself to people. Vainglory is this subtle passion that takes occasion from every moment of our life to make us proud. Fasting, modest dress and silence should be virtues, but vainglory can turn them into pride.

And if vainglory is exalting ourselves before people, pride is an even graver sin, as Saint John says, because it is the denial of God, contempt for people, the door of hypocrisy and an occasion for anger. See how, if at first we exalt ourselves before people through vainglory, through pride we exalt ourselves before God Himself, to the point of denying God and despising people.

The parable of the tax collector and the Pharisee urges us to look into our own souls. Whether we are in the world or in a monastery, this passion is extremely subtle and can bring down all our spiritual effort in an instant. We thought we had done, that we had read, that we had prayed, and a single thought of pride tears down all our effort. What should we do then?! We turn to the second example of today, the tax collector who showed himself humble and who, according to the Savior’s word, “went down to his house justified rather than the other” (Luke 18, 14).

For the Jews, the tax collector was the perfect example of a sinful man. And yet this tax collector also went up to the temple; he did not go by chance. Like Zacchaeus the tax collector, he went up to the temple. God moved him to go up to the temple and to find there the change of his life. With this thought of changing his life he said a simple prayer: “God, be merciful to me a sinner!” (Luke 18, 13). This sinful tax collector found humility, found justification, for Christ Himself says that he returned to his house justified. Which means that his soul was converted. From a thief and a betrayer of his brothers he became a humble man who sought God, just like Zacchaeus the tax collector; otherwise we could not understand the Savior’s remark.

Again, Saint John Climacus speaks to us in another chapter of his book, “The Ladder of Divine Ascent,” about humility, which has 3 stages. The first is to accept with joy the contempt of others, the exact opposite of the Pharisee’s pride. So the first stage that we too should consider in Great Lent is to stop considering others’ dishonoring of us an insult. Then the second stage is calming our irritability, that is, finding moderation. And the third is dissatisfaction with the intellectual and spiritual goods we have accumulated and a desire for much learning. […] What if we learned not to be troubled any more by the words of others, and went on to the second stage, to discover moderation, that is, no longer to answer sharply, no longer to show that we are clever and know everything, so that these two might lead us to the desire to know more? What can a person desire more in this life than to be open to learning more? Our whole life is a pilgrimage in which we are called to learn more. […] Both in the things of the sciences and above all in the things of the spiritual life. Let us learn to pray, let us learn humility, love for God and for our neighbor.

This parable of the tax collector and the Pharisee at the beginning of the Triodion is a good occasion to learn how to spend this Triodion and especially the period of Great Lent before Holy Pascha. Let us resolve to learn humility. It is said that another translation of the tax collector’s prayer, “God, be merciful to me a sinner” is “God, be my deliverer, a sinner’s.” Which means that this prayer is addressed directly to our Savior Jesus Christ, not vaguely. The Triodion begins and then continues with the period of the Paschal Fast as a preparation for us to meet Christ who died and rose again and to recognize Him as Savior. […] Now, in the fast, is our chance to remember that God waits for us, who are created in His image, to reach likeness to His image, that is, to become saints according to God’s holiness.”

At the end of the Divine Liturgy, the Abbot, Archimandrite Melchisedec, thanked His Eminence Nicolae for his presence, for his special “patericon-like” word of teaching, for the “work of his hands”, that is, the ordination of a monk of the monastery, and also for the care he has shown St. Dimitrios the New Monastery in Middletown, New York, and its monks, while expressing his full support and encouragement for the spiritual progress of the monastery on American soil in the future.

After the Divine Liturgy, His Eminence Nicolae, together with the serving priests, went to the grave of Archbishop Victorin Ursache in the cemetery of Putna Monastery to celebrate a memorial service. Many faithful joined the group of clergy to raise a prayer for him who was archbishop of the Romanians in America for 35 years.

The visit of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae concluded with heartfelt words addressed to the community of the Holy Monastery of Putna in the monastery refectory after the evening meal. The presence of His Eminence Nicolae brought grace and blessing to the community of Putna Monastery and to the faithful present in these days at the foundation of Saint Voivode Stephen the Great.

Protosyngellos Ieremia Berbec
