title: Pastoral Letter of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church for the Sunday of Orthodoxy in the Year of the Lord 2025
intro:
To the most beloved clergy, the monastic orders and
the right-believing Christians of the Romanian Patriarchate,
Grace, mercy and peace from God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit,
and from us hierarchical blessings!

 

 Most Venerable and Most Reverend Fathers,
Beloved brothers and sisters in the Lord,

The first Sunday of Holy and Great Lent, called the Sunday of Orthodoxy, reminds us each year of the trials and joys through which the Church has passed throughout history in preserving the right faith and its dogmatic, canonical and liturgical unity. In particular, this Sunday reminds us of March 11, 843, when the veneration of the holy icons was fully and definitively restored in Constantinople, and the victory over the iconoclast heresy was understood also as the victory of the right faith over all heresies.  

The theological disputes over the veneration of the holy icons broke out in the Byzantine Empire under Emperor Leo III the Isaurian (717-741). Through two imperial decrees issued in 726 and 730, he imposed the struggle against icons as state religion. The disputes continued under Emperors Constantine V (741-775) and Leo IV (775-780), when the struggle against icons intensified and the erroneous iconoclast teachings were formulated.

The Christological disputes over the veneration of icons led the iconoclast emperors to extreme measures both against the holy icons, which were destroyed, and against those who venerated them, who were tortured, imprisoned, condemned to exile and even to death. Many clergy, monastics and faithful who venerated the holy icons thus gave their lives for the right faith.

Among the defenders of Orthodoxy in that period, Saint John of Damascus (676-749) stood out. He emphasized that veneration is addressed to the person depicted in the icon, not to the material of which the icon is made: “I do not venerate matter, but I venerate the Creator of matter, the Creator who became matter for my sake, who consented to dwell in matter and who worked my salvation through matter”[1].

The first period of persecution against the veneration of icons lasted until the reign of Emperor Constantine VI (780-797) and his mother, Empress Irene (752-802), who, with the support of Patriarch Tarasios of Constantinople (784-806), convoked the Seventh Ecumenical Council at Nicaea in 787, at which the Orthodox veneration of the holy icons was restored.

At this Council, on the basis of Holy Scripture and Holy Tradition, the Holy Fathers condemned the iconoclast heresy and formulated the truth of faith concerning the veneration of icons and holy relics, stating that the honor given to the icon passes to the prototype, and whoever venerates the icon venerates the hypostasis depicted in it. They showed with scriptural arguments that whoever looks upon the icon is placed, through it, in a personal relationship with the one represented: through the icon the archetype is known, for it is a means of raising one’s thought to Christ and of sharing or communion with Him; when we look upon the icon we call in prayer upon the one depicted on it[2].

The Fathers who took part in the Seventh Ecumenical Council at Nicaea, inspired by the Holy Spirit and in accordance with the dogmas of faith established at the earlier ecumenical councils, restored the teaching of faith concerning the veneration of the holy icons and holy relics, laying down the following in the Council’s dogmatic decision: “(We) keep unchanged all the ecclesiastical traditions, written or unwritten, entrusted to us, among which is also the making of iconic images through painting, which is in agreement with the history of the Gospel preaching, as confirmation that the becoming-man of God the Word was real and not imaginary (…). Following the God-inspired teaching of our Holy Fathers and the Tradition of the Catholic Church, for we recognize that it is of the Holy Spirit who dwells in it, we define with all exactness and care that, like the figure of the precious and life-giving Cross, so also the venerable and holy icons, whether of colors or of mosaic or of any other suitable material, be set up in the holy churches of God, on sacred vessels and vestments, on walls and on wood, in houses and by the roadsides; [namely] the icon of our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ and of our most pure Lady, the Holy Theotokos, of the honorable angels and of all the saints and holy men. For the more often they are seen through iconic representation, the more those who look upon them will be lifted up to remember and to long for the prototypes and to give them a kiss and honorable veneration. Not, however, true worship, which according to our faith befits the divine nature alone, but like that offered to the figure of the precious and life-giving Cross, to the Holy Gospels and to the other sacred objects of worship; for their honor incense will be offered and lights will be lit, according to the pious custom of the ancients. For the honor [given] to the icon passes to the prototype, and whoever venerates the icon venerates the hypostasis depicted in it”[3].

Although this decision of the Seventh Ecumenical Council was received by the Church, with the accession of Emperor Leo V the Armenian (813-820) a new iconoclast period would begin, with persecutions against those who venerated the holy icons. This period ended in 843, when Empress Theodora of Byzantium (842-846), together with Patriarch Methodios, convoked a Council in Constantinople which, on the basis of Holy Scripture and the writings of the Holy Fathers, restored the Orthodox teaching on the veneration of icons and declared valid all the decisions of the seven Ecumenical Councils. Since then, every year on the first Sunday of Great Lent, we Orthodox Christians celebrate the victory of the right faith over all heresies, which is why we call this day the Sunday of Orthodoxy.

Right-believing Christians,

The Church has understood the pedagogical role of icons, as guides toward Christ, the Source of holiness. That is why it has depicted in icons the faces of the Savior, the Mother of God, the angels, the apostles and the saints. In this way it shows that the art of the Orthodox Church is a sacred art. As Leonid Ouspensky stated, this art “must, on the one hand, transmit dogmatically formulated truths and, on the other, communicate the lived experience of these truths, the spiritual experience of the saints – that living Christianity in which dogma and life merge”[4]. For this reason, “the Church sees in the icon not one of the aspects of Orthodox teaching, but the expression of Orthodoxy as a whole, of Orthodoxy as such”[5]. The holy icons “are not added to the Orthodox faith as an appendix, but express the Orthodox faith in a complete form, as a confession of faith, through word and image, through prayer before the icon of Christ and of His saints depicted in icons”[6].

The basis for the iconographic depiction of the Lord Christ is His incarnation, as the Holy Evangelist John shows: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1, 14).

Orthodox teaching affirms that, out of love for mankind, the Son and Word of God became Man (John 3, 16), taking on a human body and form, in order to help us humans become sons of God by grace, partake of eternal life and see the image of divine glory, as He showed Himself to the disciples on Tabor. The light in the icon of Christ and in the icons of the saints directs us toward the unwaning light of eternal glory in the Kingdom of Heaven, and the holiness of the icon calls us too to the sanctification of our lives.

Our beloved spiritual children,

In the context of the anniversary events of 2025, for us Romanians the Sunday of Orthodoxy is an occasion of joy and thanksgiving to God for the blessings poured out upon our country, and also an offering of gratitude for the multitude of venerable saints and confessors who kept the rule of faith as they received it from those before them.

The Sunday of Orthodoxy is the feast of the right-believing faith, in word and deed, of those who keep and confess the teaching of faith that lies at the foundation of true Christian living and of Christ’s work in the world through the Church. It calls us to unity and communion with God and with our neighbors through works of Christian mercy.

These are the concrete expression of love of neighbor, as fruits of the right faith from which they spring unceasingly, and their purpose is to help those in trouble and suffering, as the Holy Apostle Paul teaches: “But do not forget to do good and to share, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased” (Hebrews 13, 16).

However great the challenges and crises of the world in which we live, we have the duty to remain steadfast in the right faith and in good works, putting our hope in God “who gives us richly all things to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6, 17). Let us be united in doing the good that brings comfort to those in need, relief to the sick and compassion to those in pain, helping our neighbors with generosity and a kind heart, as Christ, the Savior of the world, teaches us.

This year too, we address the priests and faithful of our Holy Church with the fatherly exhortation to organize, both on this Sunday and on the following Sundays, the collection for the Central Missionary Fund, each contributing a gift as the heart prompts, knowing well that “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9, 7). This Fund is intended to support Romanian parish or monastic communities with limited material means and social institutions in the country and abroad, for the continuation and completion of various missionary works.

We know that every good gift comes from the Father of lights; therefore, in the Divine Liturgy of Saint Basil the Great we call upon God’s mercy for those who bring offerings and do good works in the holy churches and who remember the poor, asking the Lord to “reward them with His rich and heavenly gifts (…), to remember also all His people and to pour out His rich mercy upon all, fulfilling for all their petitions unto salvation”[7].

Trusting that this year too you will show Christian generosity and respond to our call in this holy work of charity, we pray to the merciful God “that you, always having all sufficiency in all things, may have an abundance for every good work” (2 Corinthians 9, 8), and “the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all!” (2 Corinthians 13, 13).

 

President of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church

title: Pan-Orthodox Vespers on the Sunday of Orthodoxy in San Antonio
intro:
On the first Sunday of Great Lent, known as the Sunday of Orthodoxy, the Orthodox faithful of San Antonio gathered in prayer at the Saint John Cassian and Saint Andrei Șaguna Romanian Orthodox Church, where Pan-Orthodox Vespers was served. This liturgical moment of deep spiritual importance brought together priests and faithful from all the canonical Orthodox jurisdictions present in San Antonio, marking the unity of the Orthodox Church in the apostolic faith and tradition.

The service was celebrated in an atmosphere of joy, with an impressive number of faithful who came to confess together the right, catholic (universal) faith. The beauty of the liturgical hymns and the solemnity of the service reflected the spiritual richness of the Orthodox tradition, offering those present an occasion for spiritual strengthening and brotherly communion.

An important moment of Vespers was the homily delivered by Fr. Gregory Peterson, who stressed the significance of the Sunday of Orthodoxy, explaining the theological and historical context of this feast. In his sermon, Fr. Gregory highlighted the victory of the true faith over the heresies and the restoration of the veneration of the holy icons, emphasizing that this day is not merely a historical commemoration but a reaffirmation of the vocation of the practicing Christian and of our faithfulness to the apostolic faith.

Fr. Gregory also commended to those present the invitation to travel with zeal and hope the spiritual journey of Great Lent, as a time of cleansing of the soul and of strengthening in Christ. He urged the faithful to see the fast not as a mere period of restrictions but as an opportunity to grow, through humility and prayer, in love for God and neighbor.

At the end of the service, the parish priest, Fr. Valentin Ilieș, offered words of thanks to all the priests and faithful present, stressing the importance of preserving Orthodox unity and of confessing the faith in an ever-changing world. He also spoke about the context of the Homage Year of the Centenary of the Romanian Patriarchate and about honoring the confessors who suffered in the communist prisons of Romania, highlighting the power of sacrifice and of confessing the faith.

After the service, everyone present was invited to a fellowship meal lovingly prepared by the ladies of the parish. In a warm and welcoming atmosphere, the faithful had the opportunity to get to know one another better and to share the joy of communion in Christ. We thank everyone who was involved in organizing this event and whose efforts contributed to the success of this beautiful spiritual gathering.

The event was a living testimony of local Orthodox unity, giving the faithful the opportunity to pray together and to experience the joy of communion in Christ. The Pan-Orthodox Vespers in San Antonio reminded everyone of the importance of solidarity in the faith and of each Christian’s commitment to preserve and live the spiritual heritage of the Orthodox Church.

Glory to God for all things!

Fr. Valentin Ilieș

title: The Spiritual Joy of Pan-Orthodox Communion at Saint John Cassian and Saint Andrei Șaguna Parish, San Antonio, TX
intro:
On the evening of March 19, 2025, Saint John Cassian and Saint Andrei Șaguna Parish in San Antonio, TX, once again experienced the joy of pan-Orthodox communion with the celebration of the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts. This blessed tradition, begun in 2018 at the initiative of Fr. Valentin Ilieș, continues to bring together priests and faithful from all the Orthodox parishes of San Antonio in a spirit of unity and common confession of the Orthodox faith.

Present at this special service were Romanian, Russian, Greek, Antiochian and American priests and faithful, showing the beauty and diversity of Orthodoxy lived in brotherly communion on American soil.

A moment of joy and spiritual comfort was the homily delivered by Dean Fr. Iulian Aniței. In his talk, Father offered a very helpful overview of the history of the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts, stressing the importance of celebrating this service and of the faithful’s participation in it. Fr. Iulian also insisted on the need to be aware of the gift of evening Communion, emphasizing proper preparation beforehand through confession, fasting, prayer and the unceasing practice of the virtues.

During Great Lent, this rotating celebration of the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts among the Orthodox parishes of the city becomes an occasion of spiritual strengthening, offering hope and joy to all who take part, especially through partaking of the same Chalice. This common service helps priests and faithful to become more deeply aware of the Savior’s call “that they all may be one” (John 17, 21) and to bear witness through prayer and communion to unity in faith and brotherly love.

After the Divine Liturgy, all the priests and faithful shared a fellowship meal, prepared with great sacrifice by a group of ladies from the Romanian Church. This moment of brotherly agape further strengthened the spiritual bonds between priests and faithful, offering an occasion to share joy and to grow stronger in communion.

This year’s event was another living testimony that, regardless of canonical jurisdiction, all Orthodox are brothers in Christ, united in the same Holy Tradition, the same Creed and the same liturgical worship. In this spirit of prayer and working together, we hope that this beautiful tradition will continue to bear the fruit of peace, love and spiritual strengthening for the entire Orthodox community of San Antonio.

Glory to God for all things!

Fr. Valentin Ilieș

title: The Mystery of Common Holy Unction at “Saint John Cassian and Saint Andrei Șaguna” Parish in San Antonio, Texas: An Event of Communion, Mission and Hope in Christ
intro:
On Thursday, March 20, 2025, the Romanian Orthodox parish of “Saint John Cassian and Saint Andrei Șaguna” in San Antonio, Texas, hosted the service of the Mystery of common Holy Unction, celebrated with the participation of all the Romanian Orthodox priests in the State of Texas. This beautiful tradition began in 2018 as the fruit of cooperation between the priests of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas and of the Romanian Orthodox Episcopate of America – Vatra, out of a desire to bring together, during the two great fasts – Great Lent and the Nativity Fast – both the servants of the Holy Altar and the Romanian faithful in a living and comforting liturgical communion.

Every year, by rotation, this Holy Mystery is celebrated at each Romanian parish in the major cities of the State of Texas: Austin, Dallas, Houston and San Antonio. On Thursday of the third week of Great Lent, the San Antonio parish became the place of this spiritual gathering, bringing together priests, families and faithful in an atmosphere of prayer and  hope.

The service was celebrated by a group of five priests:

  • Dean Fr. Iulian Anitei, of “Protection of the Mother of God” Parish in Houston;
  • Fr. Ionuț Radu, of “Dormition of the Mother of God” Parish in Dallas;
  • Fr. Mirel Tudose, of “Saint Mary Magdalene” Parish in Houston;
  • Fr. Gabriel Ilieș, of “Nativity of the Mother of God” Parish in Austin;
  • Fr. Valentin Ilieș, parish priest of the host church, “Saint John Cassian and Saint Andrei Șaguna” in San Antonio.

This concelebration brought much joy and spiritual strength to the Romanian faithful from across the state. The meeting of priests and faithful from various cities created an atmosphere of unity and communion, strengthening the awareness of belonging to the Romanian Orthodox Church and calling to a living witness of the faith in the contemporary American context. It is a confession that starts from the soul and overflows into the life of the community, following the Savior’s commandment: “Go therefore and make disciples of all the nations…” (Matthew 28:19).

A special moment, which brought deep joy to the hearts of those present, was the reading of the seven Epistle readings by seven children from the parish school. This symbolic and liturgical gesture planted in the hearts of the little ones the deep meaning of service, giving them the opportunity to become bearers of the word of God themselves and burning torches in the Lord’s vineyard. Through their involvement, a hidden lesson about responsibility, faith and liturgical communion was passed on.

At the end of the service, Dean Fr. Iulian Anitei gave a catechesis in English, addressed with great sensitivity and clarity to all present. He explained with spiritual depth the significance of the Mystery of Holy Unction, as well as the meaning of the seven Gospel readings that make up the heart of this service of healing. After the homily, all the faithful had the joy and comfort of venerating the Holy Relics of Saint John Cassian and of Saint Andrei the Hierarch, Metropolitan of Transylvania, which are part of the patrimony of the San Antonio parish, and were anointed with the oil blessed in the Mystery of Holy Unction. 

The service was celebrated in both Romanian and English, responding to an increasingly evident pastoral and missionary need, since the participation of English-speaking faithful was significant. This reality shows the openness and dynamism of the Orthodox mission in the diaspora, where the Church, through its servants, seeks to be close to all its children, whatever language they speak.

The brotherly cooperation among the Romanian Orthodox priests of Texas is a living example of serving together, of mutual support and of a sincere desire to bring the Gospel closer to people. In a challenging missionary context, this cooperation is a light showing that where there is love, communion and prayer, there God is at work and His Body, the Church, grows.

The “Saint John Cassian and Saint Andrei Șaguna” Parish in San Antonio thus becomes not just a geographical point on the map of Romanian life in America, but a living space of encounter with God, of spiritual formation, of rootedness in the values of Orthodoxy and of openness toward a world that more and more needs light and truth.

Through the missionary work of the Romanian priests and faithful in Texas, the presence and voice of the Universal Orthodox Church in America is strengthened, and the Body of Christ grows to the glory of the All-Holy Trinity, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Fr. Valentin Ilieș

title: “The Cross, the Ark of God’s Glory, and the Call to Courage.” Theological Reflections and Testimonies of Faith at the Spiritual Retreat in San Antonio
intro:
On March 21-23, 2025, in the third week of Holy and Great Lent, the Romanian Orthodox Parish of “Saint John Cassian and Saint Andrei Șaguna” in San Antonio, Texas hosted a spiritual retreat dedicated to prayer, reflection and spiritual strengthening in preparation for the Feast of the Lord’s Resurrection. The guest of honor at the gatherings on Saturday and on the Sunday of the Holy Cross was Rev. Prof. Bogdan Bucur, Orthodox theologian and professor at St. Vladimir’s Orthodox Theological Seminary in New York. Saturday began with the Divine Liturgy, followed by a memorial service and lunch with all the participants.

After lunch came the lecture, “The Cross as the Footstool of God,” which brought to the fore an essential poetic and theological expression, frequently found in Byzantine hymnography but little explored in modern theological research. Starting from the liturgical hymns dedicated to the Holy Cross and from the royal psalms of the Old Testament, Father Professor offered participants a deep reflection on how the Orthodox Church understands and lives the mystery of the Cross.

The Cross – Hypopodion: The Footrest of the King

At the center of this liturgical and theological reflection stood the verse of Psalm 98, 5: “Exalt the Lord our God, and worship at His footstool, for He is holy” (Ps. 98,5 LXX). In Orthodox hymnography this verse is consistently applied to the Cross of the Savior: “Today the word of David, who spoke of God, is truly fulfilled: for behold, we openly worship the footstool of Your most pure feet…” (Sticheron at the Litiya, Great Vespers, September 14).

In Greek, the word footstool is rendered as ὑποπόδιον (hypopodion), a kind of step or rest at the base of the royal throne, on which the king rested his feet. The image is thus both royal and liturgical: God reigns, and His throne naturally also has a “footstool.”

Fr. Bogdan Bucur emphasized that the early Church identified this “footstool” with the Wood of the Cross, and that this identification has a particular Christological depth: the One crucified on the Cross is the Lord Himself, who sits “on the throne of His glory,” as the prophet Isaiah shows us (Isaiah 6,1) and as the Holy Apostle Paul confesses: “who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but made Himself of no reputation, taking the form of a bondservant (…), He humbled Himself and became obedient to the point of death, even the death of the cross” (Philippians 2,6-8).

The Cross – The Ark and the Place of God’s Presence

Continuing the reflection, Father Professor showed that the biblical image of the footstool is not isolated but belongs to a whole symbolic system centered on the Ark of the Covenant. In Exodus 25, the Lord commands Moses to build an ark of acacia wood overlaid with pure gold, above which there were to be two winged cherubim facing one another: “And there I will meet with you, and I will speak with you from between the two cherubim which are on the ark of the Testimony, about everything which I will give you in commandment” (Exodus 25, 22).

The Ark was therefore the place of theophany, the place where God revealed Himself to Moses, a sacred space beyond sight and touch. Above the ark was the cover called the hilasterion (the place of atonement), and before it the hypopodion, the royal footstool. Fr. Bogdan Bucur showed that, in this symbolic key, the Cross becomes the new ark, the place where God reveals Himself to the world: not in visible glory, but in humility, in suffering and in the sacrifice of love. The Cross is thus the throne of God, and also the place where Christ, the great High Priest (Hebrews 4, 14), offers His sacrifice for the life of the world.

The Mother of God – The Living Ark

Within this theological architecture of God’s presence, Fr. Bucur also recalled the title the Church gives to the Most Holy Virgin Mary: “the living ark.” Just as the ark of the Law carried the Tablets of the Word, so the Mother of God carried in her womb the Word of God.

This parallel between the Old and New Covenants, between the worship of the temple and the worship of the Church, between the Ark and the Cross, is often found in the preaching of the Fathers of the Church, especially in the works of Saint Maximus the Confessor, Blessed Augustine and Saint Gregory the Theologian.

An Invitation to Contemplate the Cross.

Rev. Prof. Bogdan Bucur’s lecture was a moment of true spiritual and intellectual uplift. Through a clear and profound presentation, the theologian offered participants a deeper understanding of the mystery of the Cross, not only as an object of veneration but as the mystery of the presence and glory of God in the world, as “His footstool,” the humble place where He reveals Himself to us and calls us to repentance, love and sacrifice. The Sunday of the Holy Cross, placed in the middle of Great Lent, thus becomes a call to contemplate the crucified love of Christ, and also to lift the soul toward that light of the Resurrection which already shines from the wood of the Cross.

The Monk Nicolae Steinhardt – A Living Model of Bearing the Cross Today

During the same spiritual retreat, held in the middle of Great Lent at the “Saint John Cassian and Saint Andrei Șaguna” Parish in San Antonio, Father Professor Bogdan Bucur also presented a second theme of particular spiritual depth: the model of bearing the cross in the life and witness of the monk Nicolae Steinhardt. Through his life, his writings and his radical conversion while a political prisoner, Steinhardt becomes, in Father Professor’s words, “a living icon of the courageous Christian, free and full of joy, even in the face of evil and suffering.”

Theophany and the Ethical Trace of God’s Presence

The starting point of the reflection was the conviction that theophanic experiences, those mystical encounters with God, always leave an “ethical trace” in a person, a visible transformation. In the case of the monk Nicolae Steinhardt, that theophany took place in prison, in the deepest darkness of a world dominated by fear, terror and degradation. In that “laboratory of dehumanization,” as he himself describes it, he received Holy Baptism at the hands of Hieromonk Mina Dobzeu, in cell 34, with contaminated water from a rusty kettle.

That sacrament was followed by an experience he describes as an outpouring of light, joy and forgiveness, a radical conversion in spirit and life, in which the experience of grace was of overwhelming intensity. Not only was his soul enlightened, but his entire perception of the world was transfigured. “I entered prison blind and came out with my eyes open,” he would later write.

Steinhardt describes this mystical light in terms reminiscent of the experiences of the great mystics of Orthodoxy, such as Saint Symeon the New Theologian or Saint Seraphim of Sarov. Not by chance, Fr. Bogdan Bucur emphasized that the experience of the light of Tabor, to which Steinhardt explicitly testifies, is deeply anchored in the hesychast tradition of the Orthodox Church, as well as in the living reality of Baptism and conversion.

The Christian Creed of the Monk of Rohia

The high point of the presentation was the reading of a text composed by Steinhardt in the 1980s, an “Orthodox Creed sui generis,” in which he confesses his faith in Christ not only as a humble and meek Lord but also as a courageous Lord who willingly ascends the Cross, who sincerely loves those who are not afraid to suffer for the truth, and who rises up against religious formalism, church bureaucracy and hypocrisy.

Steinhardt’s faith is not an “organized,” cold or bureaucratic faith. It is alive, filled with joy, humor, spiritual intelligence and a deep moral uprightness. “Orthodoxy,” he says, “does not go along with gloomy grumbling, nor with stupid seraphic giggling. It is the faith of the courageous, the lucid, the fearless.”

Fr. Bogdan Bucur stressed how much this “creed” is a living synthesis of the mystical and the ethical: theophany illumines life, but it demands a concrete, daily commitment. The joy of grace must be seen in kindness and generosity, in the ability to forgive, to see the wounded neighbor and to serve him. It is an Orthodoxy in which one cannot speak of God’s love without living responsibly and with discernment in the world.

Joy, Courage and Intelligence: Marks of Holiness According to Steinhardt

The life of the monk of Rohia is a constant call to courage in the face of compromise, to lucidity in the face of hypocrisy, to joy in the face of suffering. He calls Christianity a religion of courage, in which the cowardly are the first condemned to the lake of fire, as Revelation 21,8 also shows. At the same time, he denounces any confusion between piety and foolishness, stating plainly that “it is not fitting for the Bride of Christ to be foolish” (paraphrasing Saint Bernard of Clairvaux) and that “God, among other things, asks us to be intelligent.”

This spiritual lucidity leads Steinhardt not to be deceived by appearances or by “moral” ideologies promoted by totalitarian regimes. He condemns religious servility toward dictatorship and invokes freedom as the foundation of virtue. This is not a relativistic liberalism, but truth lived in freedom, as the Gospel requires.

A Living Model for Bearing the Cross Today

In conclusion, Father Professor Bogdan Bucur affirmed that the figure of Nicolae Steinhardt is prophetic for Orthodox Christians today. At a time when the Church faces a loss of credibility before the world, the example of a man who lived the faith in prison, in culture, in community and in humility, with joy and discernment, becomes a shining beacon.

Steinhardt is a man of the Cross, not only because he suffered, but because he knew how to see in the Cross the light of the Resurrection, to taste in suffering the mystical joy of Christ, and to urge, with realism and gentleness, that we “at least be impostors of the good,” that is, people who, though not saints, sincerely strive to live as Christians.

Presentation of the English Edition of “Jurnalul fericirii”

At the end of the gathering, participants were invited to the launch of the new English translation of Jurnalul fericirii, recently published by St. Vladimir’s Seminary Press through the efforts of a group of dedicated translators coordinated by Fr. Bogdan Bucur. The translation of this emblematic volume opens Steinhardt’s work to an international readership and was received with emotion and gratitude by those present.

The Divine Liturgy and a Word of Encouragement on the Sunday of the Holy Cross

On the Third Sunday of Great Lent, Father Professor Bogdan Bucur celebrated the Divine Liturgy in the parish church in San Antonio, bringing joy and spiritual strength to the whole community. In his homily, Father reflected on the Gospel of Mark 8, 34–38: “Whoever desires to come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow Me”. Emphasizing that taking up the cross is not a symbolic gesture but a real commitment to the sacrifice of love, Father urged the faithful to live the Cross not as a burden but as a call to suffer together with Christ, to embrace life with meaning, courage and trust in the Resurrection.

A Retreat of Encounter with Christ Crucified and Risen

The spiritual retreat in San Antonio was a true blessing for all who took part. Combining deep theological reflection with liturgical, spiritual and cultural experience, the event offered an occasion to rediscover the Cross as the place of God’s living presence, and also as a call to an authentic Christian life.

In a world often troubled and confused, such testimonies rekindle in the hearts of the faithful the light of the truth: that Christ, the Crucified Lord, becomes for all a “footstool,” so that through the Cross we may ascend to the ineffable glory of the Resurrection.

Fr. Valentin Ilieș

title: Patronal Feast and Laying of the Cornerstone for the New Church of Annunciation Cathedral, Olmsted Township, OH
intro:
Today is the beginning of our salvation and the revelation of the eternal mystery.
The Son of God becomes the Son of the Virgin, and Gabriel announces the good tidings of grace.
Therefore let us also cry out with him to the Theotokos:
Rejoice, O full of grace, the Lord is with you.

Great joy fills the soul of every worshiper of God on hearing these words, and especially the souls of the faithful of a parish who worship in a church dedicated to the Annunciation. The message of the troparion above reminds them  that this is how our salvation began: the Son of God, son of the Virgin (son of man), becomes man so that we too, from sons of men, may become sons of God; and for this we too must cry out to the Most Holy Theotokos, “Rejoice, O full of grace, the Lord is with you.”

The Lord was with us in this year 2025 as well and brought us great blessings, some more special than in other years, because this year our community took a great step toward salvation: building a new house of worship, a new cathedral, a new door to the Kingdom of God. The celebration lasted several days, since from Saturday evening, March 22, 2025, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae gave us the joy of being in our midst for 4 days.

We began our days of celebration with Hierarchical Vespers, followed by a homily on the holy confessors of the communist prisons, namely Saint Ilarion Felea, Priest and Confessor. This was followed by dinner with the Parish Council, where the project of building the new cathedral, the steps already taken and other ideas that could be implemented in the future were discussed.

On Sunday morning, March 23, 2025, the Hierarchical Divine Liturgy was celebrated, followed by a homily by His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae on the meaning of the 3rd Sunday of Great Lent:

“The Holy Apostle Paul urges the Christians of the city of Philippi to let the mind of Christ be in them as well. He tells them that He, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied Himself (Philippians 2:7). In the Divine Liturgy we celebrated today, Saint Basil takes up these words very beautifully: ‘when the fullness of time had come, You spoke to us through Your Son Himself, through Whom You also made the ages; Who, being the brightness of Your glory and the image of Your hypostasis, and upholding all things by the word of His power, thought it not robbery to be equal with You, God and Father, but, being God before all ages, appeared on earth and lived among men; and becoming incarnate of the Holy Virgin, He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming conformed to the body of our lowliness, that He might conform us to the image of His glory.’ How beautifully and clearly Saint Basil the Great urges us to follow Christ, Who, being God, did not consider it robbery to hold on to His stature, but emptied Himself, took on our form and lived together with us, not just to remain with us, but to give us the chance to attain the image of His glory. God Himself humbled Himself, emptied Himself, so that we might regain the image of God’s glory in which we were created.

If God Himself emptied Himself and took on our form, we too cannot regain the radiance of the image unless we follow Him: ‘Whoever desires to come after Me, let him deny himself.’ Christ asks nothing other than that we do what He did: deny what we think we are and let God come into our life, into our world.”

On Monday evening, the eve of the feast, Hierarchical Vespers with Litiya was celebrated, after which His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae gave another talk on the holy confessors of the communist prisons, this time on Saint Liviu Galaction Munteanu, Priest and Confessor.

The feast day of the Annunciation began with the reception of the hierarch, followed by the Hierarchical Divine Liturgy together with the Reverend Fathers: Vicar Fr. Daniel Ene, parish priest of Holy Trinity Parish in Rochester, NY; Fr. Ion Gherman, former parish priest of our parish; Fr. Andrew Lentz, parish priest of Saint Demetrios Greek Orthodox Church in Rocky River, OH; and Archimandrite Nectarije Tesanovic, serving priest of Saint George Serbian Orthodox Church in Lorain, OH. His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae gave a homily on the message of the feast of the Annunciation, after which we held a procession to the place where the cornerstone for the new house of worship was to be laid.

 The service of blessing and the laying of the cornerstone was a moment of great joy felt by all the faithful, a joy that led many to say, “Father, it feels like Pascha, just like the Feast of the Resurrection.” Surely the good God poured out grace abundantly upon us so that we might be assured that He is with us, and that the very feast of the Annunciation assures us that we may have faith in His coming down among those who love Him and wish to build Him a house on earth. Also present at this special service was Dean Fr. Călin Barbolovici, parish priest of Holy Trinity Parish in Troy, MI.

We cannot describe the joy of each one of us  who saw a long-awaited project in our parish come to pass. We give glory to God for arranging this event on the patronal feast of our church. We thank His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae for the love and courage he inspires in us to go forward with such a project, even in these times when faith grows weaker and lack of courage grows greater with each passing day.

We rejoice that we mark this event, the start of work on a new church, in 2025, the year in which the Romanian Orthodox Church celebrates 100 years since its elevation to the rank of Patriarchate. We pray that all these 100 years, and those yet to come until the end of the ages, may be to the glory of God and the salvation of the Romanian people.

We thank the Reverend Fathers present for their prayer and concelebration. At the end of the cornerstone service a fellowship meal was held, for which I heartily thank the members of our Annunciation family for all their sacrifice and faith, which bring harmony to the work of salvation of us all.

May the good God help us in all things and continue to bless all our plans  made with love and for the glory of God. Amen.

In Christ the Lord,

Fr. Petru Neaga, Parish Priest

title: Pastoral Visit to Saint Callinicus of Cernica Parish, Fredericksburg, VA
intro:
The faithful of the Romanian Orthodox community of Fredericksburg, Virginia, which is under the protection of Saint Callinicus of Cernica, celebrated the parish’s patronal feast together with their Chief Shepherd, His Eminence Nicolae, Archbishop and Metropolitan of the Americas. This year is a year of transition for the faithful of Saint Callinicus of Cernica Mission, who, with the Lord’s help and the prayers of Saint Callinicus, hope to move permanently to the new location on Poplar Rd. in Fredericksburg.

The hierarch’s pastoral visit began on the afternoon of Saturday, April 5, 2025, at the new property itself, where His Eminence Nicolae met with the members of the Parish Council to discuss the permanent move to the church’s future property. His Eminence then celebrated Great Vespers for the 5th Sunday of Great Lent, together with the parish priest of Saint Callinicus Mission, Fr. Ionel Satnoianu, and Fr. Orlando Geonea of Saint Mary Mission in Norfolk, VA.

In his homily after Vespers, His Eminence Nicolae referred to the Gospel passage from Mark 10, 32-45, emphasizing that in the Church we are called to follow the example and calling of the Savior to be servants of others and not rulers. The Lord came to sacrifice Himself for all. The clergy and members of the parish council do not hold special positions in the church but must lead by serving others.

The next day, Sunday, April 6, His Eminence Nicolae celebrated the Divine Liturgy, assisted by the parish priest of the host church, Fr. John Katsoulis, and the parish priest of Saint Callinicus Mission, Fr. Ionel Satnoianu. The responses were sung by Reader Ionuț Lupu-Pitulice together with a group of faithful.

In his homily, His Eminence Nicolae spoke first about the example of the life of Saint Mary of Egypt and invited us to reflect on her life as well, understanding that the purpose of Great Lent is to set aside everything that keeps us far from God and to return to His presence.

Metropolitan Nicolae then spoke about the life of Saint Callinicus and about the many spiritual and administrative accomplishments of the abbot of Cernica, later Bishop of Râmnic and Noul Severin. Even in broad outline, the portrait of Saint Callinicus is striking for his quality as a great spiritual father, not only for monks but also for the Christians who came to confess to him and ask his counsel for their souls. For his pure life of prayer and self-sacrifice, Saint Callinicus was blessed by God with the gifts of healing, of working miracles and of casting out demons. As a bishop, he continued his spiritual and missionary work, helping and strengthening the churches both materially and spiritually by printing religious books, which he distributed free of charge for the enlightenment of the priests and the people. He was a wonderful shepherd, attentive to the needs of his flock and much loved by the faithful. He was canonized in 1955, during the communist regime, a telling sign of divine providence, which reveals to us great examples of spiritual life for our strengthening and comfort.

His Eminence also expressed his gratitude to Fr. John Katsoulis and the Greek community for the support given to our community over the years, noting that we are close to having our own place of worship on the new property. After the Divine Liturgy, the faithful present took part in a fellowship meal lovingly prepared by the ladies of the parish.

We thank God for two days full of spiritual joy, and we also thank our Chief Shepherd for being with us and blessing us!

Fr. Ionel Satnoianu

title: Palm Sunday at the Maramureș-Style Life-Giving Spring Church in Long Valley, New Jersey
intro:
On Sunday, April 13, 2025, the day on which our holy Orthodox Church liturgically celebrates the radiant and glorious feast of the Entry of our Lord Jesus Christ into the holy city of Jerusalem, the parish priest and the parish council, together with the parishioners of the Life-Giving Spring Parish in Long Valley, New Jersey, welcomed with great spiritual joy His Eminence Nicolae, Metropolitan of the Americas, who made a pastoral visit and celebrated the Holy and Divine Liturgy.

Palm Sunday holds a special place in the Orthodox Church. It is the triumphal Entry of our Lord Jesus Christ into Jerusalem, shortly before His Passion. As He drew near to Bethany, the Lord sent two of His disciples to bring Him the colt of a donkey, on which He humbly sat to enter the city. The people ran to meet Him, holding palm branches and crying out in faith: “Hosanna! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord”.

The holy events of this day show in a unique way the divine and human nature of Jesus: the humility of the Messiah, who does not enter as an earthly king with horses and armies, but “riding on the foal of a donkey”, bringing peace and salvation. The joy of the people, however, is fleeting. In just a few days, some of them will move from “Hosanna” to “Crucify Him!”

Our Church calls us to live these events not merely as a historical memory, but as a personal participation in the Passion and Resurrection of the Lord. Palm Sunday, with its fragrant branches and the bright sadness that pervades it, opens the door to Holy and Great Week. Christ, knowing the road to Golgotha, calls us to follow Him with repentance, love and faith in the Resurrection.

In his sermon, His Eminence spoke about the Lord’s triumphal Entry into Jerusalem:

“The Jews who had come out to meet Him with their children, just as at the Feast of Tabernacles, began to wave palm branches and cry out: Hosanna! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord! The King of Israel! These are a few words from Psalm 117 used at the Feast of Tabernacles, but now with a unique meaning. Hosanna means save, as does the name Jesus (Yeshua in Hebrew), the Savior. Those who met Christ with palm branches now recognize Him as the long-awaited Messiah, the Savior of the Jewish people. That this is so, and that there is no misunderstanding, we discover in the Holy Gospel of Luke, chapter 19: hearing these words of welcome, the scribes and Pharisees cautioned the Savior: Teacher, rebuke Your disciples. And the Savior answers them: if these should keep silent, the stones would cry out (Luke 19:39-40).

The scribes and Pharisees knew that those verses of Psalm 117 are addressed to the Messiah. Hearing them now, they do not want to acknowledge that He is the Messiah, but the Savior tells them very directly, as He will also do in the following days, that those verses are rightly attributed to Him, for He is the Messiah. In these days we too can wave palm or willow branches, but we can also listen to the words of Saint John Chrysostom, who urges us to bring as ‘a gift to Christ kindness, virtue, fasting, tears, prayers, vigils.’

In this Week of the Holy Passion, it is fitting that we follow spiritually the Lord’s steps toward the crucifixion, that we desire to defend Him before the judges, that we show our steadfastness in faith and do not deny Him. Let us also suffer together with Jesus the Man, Who suffered for us and offered His life on the Cross as a ransom! With the assurance that He passed through death and conquered it as God, with the joy that the powers of hell have been shattered, with the faith that we too partake of the light of the Resurrection at every Divine Liturgy, and with the hope that if Christ is risen, we too shall rise!”

At the end of the Divine Liturgy, His Eminence Nicolae blessed the palm branches and offered the faithful small icons of the Synaxis of the Romanian Saints prepared for the Commemorative Year of the Romanian Orthodox spiritual fathers and confessors of the 20th century. The fellowship meal prepared by the ladies of the parish concluded this festive day.

Fr. Roman Galben, Parish Priest

title: Palm Sunday at Saint Luke the Evangelist Mission, Columbia, SC
intro:
“Palm Sunday comes with sunshine
And the sunshine comes with Palm Sunday”

“Let the little children come to Me, and do not forbid them; for of such is the kingdom of God” (Luke 18. 16).

The Savior’s words remain across time a living and open invitation addressed to every Christian family: to remember the high mission of guiding children to Him through faith. Faith is the most beautiful way of life. All the more so for a child. And learning it begins in the mystery of the parental home.

The true School and the true Church begin in the family and are perfected through education. Family - School - Church. An equilateral triangle. A child learns by doing. Not only by being told about God, but by seeing, hearing, doing, kneeling and creating a living dialogue with Him.

Such an example was created through yesterday’s procession when, on the Entry of the Lord into Jerusalem, the children of Saint Luke the Evangelist Mission welcomed our Lord Jesus Christ with branches while the adults sang the Palm Sunday Carol to Jesus.

In moments of deep spiritual peace, after a calm and quiet Divine Liturgy, the Very Reverend Hieromonk Fr. Andrei knelt before the Holy Altar and blessed the traditional willow branches, which every Christian received at the end of the Divine Liturgy as a living reminder that:

“Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!”

Reported by

Mihaela Livingston

title: Pastoral Visit of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae for the Feast of Saint George the Great Martyr at the Romanian Orthodox Church in Las Vegas
intro:
Christ is risen! Truly He is risen!

Three decades of existence and the patronal feast of the Romanian Orthodox Church in Las Vegas were the two memorable occasions that ennobled Sunday, April 27, 2025, through the pastoral visit of His Eminence Nicolae, Metropolitan of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas, who came specially from Chicago to bless this historic anniversary, and through the presence of His Excellency Andrei Muraru, Ambassador of Romania in Washington.

On Saturday, April 26, 2025, the parishioners welcomed His Eminence Nicolae with bread and salt, a gesture of honor and welcome, and then Vespers was celebrated. This was followed by a Parish Council meeting chaired by His Eminence Nicolae, so that on the following day the event would carry, besides its spiritual weight, a solemn sense of appreciation and gratitude, along with good cheer.

Thus, on the 2nd Sunday after the Resurrection of the Lord, the Sunday of Saint Thomas the Apostle, the Romanian Orthodox community of Las Vegas lived a moment of high celebration, marking both the 30 years of existence of the Romanian Orthodox Church in Las Vegas, the only Romanian Orthodox church in the state of Nevada, and the patronal feast of Saint George the Great Martyr and Trophy-bearer.

In his homily at Vespers, His Eminence Nicolae took the faithful through Bright Week, noting that Friday, April 25, 2025, brought together several important feasts and commemorations:

The Life-Giving Spring, an Orthodox Christian feast dedicated to the Mother of God, a special day for the blessing of waters, with services for the blessing of springs.

The Syrian Icon of the Mother of God at Ghighiu Monastery.

Saint Mark, the evangelist, author of the Gospel according to Mark.

Saint Basil of Poiana Mărului, a great Romanian spiritual father and hesychast of the 18th century.

140 Years of Autocephaly: 2025 marks 140 years since the Romanian Orthodox Church was recognized as autocephalous (in 1885).

In his homily at the Sunday Divine Liturgy, His Eminence Nicolae spoke about the experience of Saint Thomas the Apostle:

Saint Thomas the Apostle also wanted to have the experience of the Apostles; he could not believe that Christ had risen from the tomb. We today believe precisely on the basis of the testimony of these Apostles and of the others who met the Risen Christ. But Thomas’s faith did not come from touching the body of Christ with his hand, with his senses, but from his encounter with the Risen Christ. Our faith is not about touching, about having material proof, about convincing all our senses that Christ has risen from the tomb; our faith is grounded in their testimony, the testimony of those who met Christ, and in the words of the Savior Himself: “Because you have seen Me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed”, all of us who did not meet the Risen Christ 2000 years ago. In faith in the Risen Christ the words of the Holy Apostle Peter are fulfilled: “Jesus Christ, whom having not seen you love. Though now you do not see Him, yet believing, you rejoice with joy inexpressible and full of glory, receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls” (I Peter 1, 8-9).

As a sign of appreciation and blessing, at the end of the service His Eminence Nicolae presented the parish with an icon depicting the two patron saints of our church: Saint George the Great Martyr and Saint Demetrios the New. The gesture highlighted both gratitude for the pastoral work of the parish priest, Fr. Mihai Bălan, and the importance of the saints’ protection in the life of the community.

After the Divine Liturgy, the festive atmosphere was completed by the feast-day meal sponsored by Mrs. Lia Roberts, Honorary Consul General of Romania in Las Vegas and president of the church’s Parish Council, whom we thank on this occasion for her generosity and tireless philanthropic involvement. A moving ceremony was held to present certificates of gratitude and distinctions, which will remain testimonies to the road traveled together, from modest beginnings to a beloved house of worship that continues to shelter whole generations. Among the special guests, respected leaders and prominent figures of the Las Vegas metropolitan area, were:

Mr. Stavros Anthony - Lieutenant Governor of the State of Nevada.

Mr. Brian Knudsen - Council Member and Mayor Pro Tem of the City of Las Vegas.

Judge Shannon Nordstrom.

Mrs. Sonia Joya - Regional Representative of the Governor of the State of Nevada, Joe Lombardo.

Mrs. Angelica Hernandez - Representative of Congresswoman Susie Lee.

Mrs. Geri Schroeder - Chief of Staff to the Mayor of the City of Las Vegas, Shelley Berkeley.

His Excellency Joe Campos - Honorary Consul of the Republic of Korea and Dean of the Consular Corps of Nevada.

Her Excellency Kathleen Blakely - Honorary Consul of Japan.

His Excellency Andy Armenian - Honorary Consul of the Republic of Armenia.

Joe Cortez, world-renowned referee, inducted into the Hall of Fame.

We were also honored by the presence of the distinguished physicians Dr. Jacobs, Dr. Shaffak, Dr. Brookman, Dr. Fleming and Dr. Brescan.

The festive event continued with a high-quality artistic program featuring Valeria, professor at UNLV (piano), Mike Leonetti (entertainer), Shelly & Wesley (professional entertainers and songwriters) and the CIULEANDRA folk dance group. The Sunday School children also prepared a short program of poetry recitations:

Alex and Andreas - the poem “De Paști” by George Coșbuc

Gabi and Madeleine - “Vine, vine primăvara” - song

Luke and Sophia - the poem “Somnoroase păsărele” by Mihai Eminescu

Annabelle - piano

As we celebrated through prayer, music and fellowship, we were reminded that the true strength of a church is reflected in the love and unity of its people, and that, with the support of such special friends and allies from the American community as well, the future shines brighter than ever. The parish priest, Fr. Mihai, conveyed a message of thanks to all the members of the Parish Council and to all who, with pure hearts and self-sacrifice, contributed to organizing this special anniversary: 30 years of our parish’s existence.

And above all, in these holy days, let us strengthen our faith like Saint Thomas, let us drink from the Spring of Life, and let us be grateful that we could witness a memorable day and receive once again the blessing of the Primate of the Romanian Orthodox Church of the Americas, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae.

Reported by Mihaela Gliga

title: Pastoral Visit of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae to St. Mary Mission in Norfolk, VA
intro:
On the 4th Sunday after Holy Pascha, His Eminence Nicolae, Romanian Orthodox Metropolitan of the Americas, was in the midst of the faithful of the Nativity of the Mother of God Mission in Norfolk, VA. In keeping with church tradition, the Hierarch was welcomed in the morning with bread and salt, and then celebrated the Divine Liturgy together with the parish priest, Fr. Orlando Geonea.

In his homily to the faithful, His Eminence interpreted the Gospel of the Sunday:

“In this Paschal season we too try to receive the proclamation of Christ’s Resurrection, to be filled with it and to show ourselves worthy of passing it on… The Fathers of the Church see in the situation of this man, sick for 38 years, humanity itself, which after the sin of Adam was sick, paralyzed, far from God and awaiting salvation. The whole history of humanity from Adam to Christ is the history of man’s attempt to regain God, whom he had lost. The sacrifices of the Jews and the gods of the pagans were somehow trying to bring God back into the world of humanity, into the world in which we live. From Adam to Christ it is a history of man’s failure to find God again. Since man did not succeed in finding God again by his own powers, God Himself came. God Himself came down to earth, God Himself took on human flesh to heal sick human nature, to reconcile man with God, then to bring him through death and to conquer death itself.

We should see that this sick man had great patience, that his illness, this state of helplessness joined with patience, turned into repentance. Repentance for what? Repentance for his sins, for after healing him, when they met again in the temple, the Savior warns him: Sin no more, lest a worse thing come upon you (John 5, 14), a clear sign that his 38-year illness was the consequence of sin. Patience together with prayer turned into repentance for sin, and this repentance showed him ready to receive God Himself, who would heal him. In the fullness of time the Messiah came, when humanity was ready to receive its Savior. From Adam to Christ, God sent prophets, established the Law among the Jewish people, and when humanity was ready to receive its Savior, He sent Christ. Here again is the history of fallen humanity in the story of this sick man. When his repentance was complete, he met the God-man, who healed him completely.

We too must pay attention to our relationship with God, to our desire to receive correction and salvation, to our prayer, our patience, our repentance, so that we may be prepared to be made worthy of the healing and salvation that come from Christ…”

His Eminence also recalled that this year is dedicated to the Centennial of the Romanian Orthodox Patriarchate and is the Commemorative Year of Romanian Orthodox spiritual fathers and confessors of the 20th century, inviting the faithful to pay attention to the Metropolia’s activities and conferences held in person or on the Zoom platform. In conclusion, the Hierarch extended his good wishes to all mothers on the occasion of “Mother’s Day” and distributed small icons of the 2025 Homage Year.

The event ended with the customary fellowship meal, followed by a meeting of His Eminence with the Parish Council. We thank God for these special moments and give Him glory for everything!

Fr. Orlando Stelian Geonea

title: Patronal Feast of Holy Trinity Parish in Troy, MI, June 2025
intro:
Each year the feast of the Descent of the Holy Spirit brings the joy of celebrating the patronal feast of Holy Trinity Parish in Troy. This year, as is his custom, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae blessed our church community with his presence!

On Saturday evening, Vespers was served by His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, assisted by Fr. Ion Gherman of Cleveland. At the end of the service, the Metropolitan spoke about this year as being dedicated to the 100th anniversary of the elevation of the Romanian Orthodox Church to the rank of Patriarchate (February 4, 1925), an event commemorated on February 4 with the Divine Liturgy at the Patriarchal Cathedral and a solemn session of the members of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church. The second theme is dedicated to the spiritual fathers of the 20th century, with reference to the fathers who suffered martyrdom under the communist regime in Romania. In our Metropolia, the Centenary of the Patriarchate was marked by symposia held first in Chicago on the Sunday of Orthodoxy (March 9, 2025), on the occasion of the blessing of the iconography of the Metropolitan Cathedral there, and then in New York on June 2, in collaboration with the Consulate General of Romania and the Romanian Cultural Institute in New York. His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae then spoke about the life and martyrdom of two of the 16 holy confessors canonized by the Romanian Orthodox Church last year: Saint Liviu Galaction Munteanu and Saint Ilarion Felea.

On Sunday, the feast of the Descent of the Holy Spirit, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae celebrated the Hierarchical Divine Liturgy, assisted by Fr. Ion Gherman and Fr. Călin Barbolovici, the parish priest. In his homily, His Eminence Nicolae spoke about  the fact that Pentecost is the feast of the sending of the Holy Spirit into the world to enlighten, renew and sanctify us. The Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles at Pentecost and enlightened them so that they might begin the work of mission. At the beginning of his speech, Saint Peter says that the prophecy of Joel has been fulfilled: “And it shall come to pass in the last days, says God, that I will pour out of My Spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your young men shall see visions, your old men shall dream dreams” (Acts 2:17-18):

“Through this speech Saint Peter reveals to them the mystery that has been fulfilled: the descent of the Spirit and the beginning of the work of our salvation. This is seen at once, for those present were cut to the heart by Saint Peter’s words and asked what they could do to enter into this plan of salvation as well: ‘Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ; and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit’ (Acts  2:38) is Saint Peter’s answer.

This is the miracle that happened at Pentecost: these unlettered, untaught, fearful men, who had abandoned Christ in the most terrible moments of His life, at His trial, Passion and death on the cross, now receive strength from the Holy Spirit to become Apostles. Now they are enlightened and receive power from on high to confess Christ as Lord and Messiah; now they become the Apostles of Christ who will go out into all the world to proclaim the Gospel of the Resurrection to each in his own language, as happened at Pentecost. Now the Church comes into being through the descent of the Spirit, through our calling to enter into this mystery, which is revealed to us in several stages…

Each of us, too, enters the Church through these steps. Whether we were children or received baptism as adults, we confess, ourselves or through our godparents, that we wish to draw near to God, to repent, and we confess our faith. Baptism is followed by the Mystery of Chrismation, when we receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. When the child or adult is anointed on the forehead, hands, feet and back with the Holy and Great Chrism, these very words are said: The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit. We all receive the gift of the Holy Spirit and are anointed, we are sealed just as Christ was anointed (Messiah means the Lord’s Anointed One); we all become christs, we all receive the chance to dwell in the Church together with Christ and to journey toward salvation. We all receive the gift of eternity, because we already live together with Christ in the Church, the Kingdom of God on earth.”

At the end, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae congratulated the community on completing the project of beautifying the church with the iconostasis and new furnishings, and encouraged them to continue this effort further by painting the church.

The celebration ended with the customary fellowship meal, attended by all present.

Fr. Călin Barbolovici

title: The Feast of the Dormition of the Mother of God at the SS. Constantine and Helen Metropolitan Cathedral, Chicago
intro:
SS. Constantine and Helen Cathedral in Chicago celebrated the Feast of the Dormition of the Mother of God in a special way this year as well. The feast began on Thursday evening, August 14, 2025, with the Lamentations of the Mother of God, celebrated by His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae and the priests of the Cathedral, together with the Cathedral’s group of chanters and the faithful. Together they sang the Lamentations and marveled at the laying in the tomb of the Mother of Life.

After the procession around the Cathedral, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae explained the meaning of the event:

“Let us try to look at the icon of the Feast of the Dormition of the Mother of God and understand what it teaches us. First of all, we discover the assembly of those who were present at the Dormition: Apostles, disciples, heavenly hosts. They are all bending over the now lifeless body of the Mother of God. But at the center of the image is Christ the Savior, the Son of the Virgin, who receives her soul. The fact that the gathering is bent over the body of the Mother of God and all eyes are turned toward the Holy Virgin suggests the unperceived presence of the Savior. They all knew that the Mother of Life was passing over to Life, but they did not know that at that very moment Life was present to receive the soul of the one who had given Him human life. Christ the Lord receives in His arms the soul of the one who carried Him in her arms. This reality is captured in the despotic icon of the Mother of God found on the iconostasis of every church. The Mother of God carries the Infant Jesus in her arms, presenting Him to the world. The Mother shows her love for the Child in response to God’s love for mankind…

But if we look once more at the icon of the Dormition of the Mother of God, we also discover depicted there a reality that we all know, though without having fully perceived its meaning. The icon of the Dormition of the Mother of God is the icon of our own falling asleep. All of us are accompanied on our last journey by family and acquaintances. The faithful know, however, that the road to the grave is only the last earthly road, for our life continues in another life, together with Christ. Our sorrow, as we bury a brother or a relative, is pierced by hope, for our brother has fallen asleep in the Lord. Which means that we express our faith that his soul is received into His arms by Christ the Lord Himself, as in the case of the Mother of God.”

The feast continued on Friday, August 15, with the hierarchical Divine Liturgy served by His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae and the priests of the Cathedral. At the conclusion of the Divine Liturgy, His Eminence Nicolae delivered to the faithful present a rich homily on the mystery of the Virgin Mary:

“On the Feast of the Dormition of the Mother of God it is profitable to discover what the Fathers of the Church teach us about the veneration of the Theotokos. For all who have dared to write about the Mother of God have used words of praise for the one who gave the incarnate God to the world.

Saint Gregory Palamas even asks whether words are able to contain the mystery of the Theotokos: “What word could describe, O Mother of God, O Virgin, your divinely radiant beauty? For it is not possible to comprehend all that is yours in thought or word, since all is beyond mind and word. But it is possible for us to praise you, who in your love for mankind receive us to yourself. You are the dwelling place of all gifts and the fullness of all beauty and all goodness…” It is not possible to comprehend with the mind and to express the mystery of the Virgin Mary, but it is possible to praise her…

We discover in the words of the Fathers the purpose of hymnody and its benefit. The mysteries of God are impenetrable to the mind and hard to express in words. But in hymnody the veil of mystery is lifted and we become partakers of God’s revelation. What cannot be comprehended by the mind and expressed in words is received directly by the spirit through hymnody. The human spirit receives “heavenly delight and joy beyond this world.”

The feast concluded with a fraternal agape meal prepared by the ladies of the Cathedral.

We pray to the Mother of God to protect us all with her prayers!
