title: Pastoral Letter of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church for the First Sunday of the Nativity Fast 2025
intro:
Most Venerable and Most Reverend Fathers,
Beloved brothers and sisters in the Lord,

Keeping unbroken the practice established in 2008 regarding homage and commemorative years, the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church proclaimed 2025, in the Romanian Patriarchate, as the Homage Year of the Centennial of the Romanian Patriarchate and the Commemorative Year of Romanian Orthodox Spiritual Fathers and Confessors of the 20th Century.

Throughout its 100 years of activity and institutional organization, the Romanian Patriarchate has preached the Gospel and led the faithful, through the work of the Holy Spirit, to Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, being at the same time a factor of national unity, social stability and cultural flourishing, while the Romanian Orthodox spiritual fathers and confessors of the 20th century lived and defended the Orthodox faith in the hostile times of the atheist communist regime.

The Romanian Patriarchate Became the Symbol of the Spiritual Unity of All Romanian Orthodox

Both the recognition of the autocephaly of the Romanian Orthodox Church in 1885 and its elevation to the rank of Patriarchate on February 4, 1925, are two historic events of capital importance for the church life of the Romanian people, because they had a particular influence on the dynamic institutional and administrative development of the Romanian Orthodox Church, and were also the natural expression of the spiritual and national unity achieved through the Great Union of December 1, 1918.

The canonization of Romanian saints, the establishment of new dioceses, the organization of the Romanian Orthodox diaspora, and the substantial contribution of the Romanian Orthodox Church in the field of inter-Orthodox, inter-Christian and interreligious relations could not have been achieved without these providential moments of its history and development.

Founded in the historical context of Greater Romania, the Romanian Patriarchate became the symbol of the spiritual unity of all Romanian Orthodox, reunited within the same national borders after centuries of administrative and ecclesiastical separation.

The Great Union brought important changes in the life of our Church as well, establishing the principle of a unified organization of church life in all the provinces of the kingdom of Greater Romania. On December 31, 1919, Bishop Miron Cristea of Caransebeș was elected Metropolitan Primate. He had taken part in the historic act of December 1, 1918, being one of the hierarchs who officiated the Te Deum service for the assembly of the delegates who voted the Resolution of Union of Alba Iulia, and was a member of the Transylvanian delegation that handed the Act of Union to King Ferdinand on December 14, 1918, in Bucharest.

In this context, several church, political and cultural figures supported and argued for the idea of establishing the Patriarchate as an act of prestige for an autocephalous Church and for Greater Romania, which, after the Bolshevik Revolution (Nov. 6-7, 1917), “was the largest Orthodox state in Europe,” as Professor Alexandru Lapedatu, Minister of Religious Affairs, noted (Archim. Tit Simedrea, Patriarhia Românească. Acte și documente, Bucharest, Tipografia Cărților Bisericești, 1926, p. 11), and “the only Orthodox people with a mere metropolitan primate at the head of an autonomous Church” (Archim. T. Simedrea, Patriarhia Românească…, p. 7), as the scholar Nicolae Iorga observed.

On February 4, 1925, at the proposal of Metropolitan Pimen Georgescu of Moldavia, the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church decided to establish the Romanian Patriarchate, a proposal voted unanimously. At the same session, Bishop Vartolomeu Stănescu of Râmnic-Noul Severin read the Act of Establishment of the Romanian Patriarchate and the decision was communicated to the government for enactment into law.

After the bill was adopted by the legislative bodies (Feb. 12 and 17, 1925), the law was promulgated by King Ferdinand I on February 23, 1925, and published in the Official Gazette of February 25, 1925. Thus, after the Great Union, the diversity of church organization in Bessarabia, Bukovina and Transylvania made evident the need for unification under a single church authority, with its seat in Bucharest.

The Ecumenical Patriarchate, represented by Patriarch Basil III (1925-1929), considered “welcome and justified […] the elevation of the sister Church of Romania to patriarchal dignity” (“Tomos of the Holy Ecumenical Patriarchate, no. 1579,” in: Archim. T. Simedrea, Patriarhia Românească…, p. 133). The Tomos of the Ecumenical Patriarch issued on July 30, 1925, canonically confirmed the patriarchal dignity of the Romanian Orthodox Church, and the enthronement of the first Patriarch, Miron Cristea, on November 1, 1925, marked the beginning of a new era of Romanian Orthodoxy.

In its 100 years of activity, the Romanian Patriarchate has asserted itself as a fundamental institution for preserving the national and spiritual identity of the Romanian people. It has also passed through very difficult historical periods, such as the royal dictatorship, the Antonescu regime, and above all the atheist communist regime, uniting suffering with hope and surviving with vigor, to flourish after 1989 in a period of spiritual and missionary rebirth on a large scale.

The Patriarchs who have shepherded the Romanian Orthodox Church in this century (1925-2025) have been wise and worthy hierarchs who contributed, each in his own way, to the continuity and development of church life among the Romanian people.

The desire of the Romanian Orthodox faithful to have a new Patriarchal Cathedral, as gratitude offered to God for the achievement of Greater Romania, was fulfilled through the building of the National Cathedral.

Thus, in the Centennial Year of Greater Romania 2018, the Altar of the National Cathedral was consecrated on November 25, with the patronal feasts of the Ascension of the Lord (Heroes’ Day) and Saint Andrew the Apostle, the First-Called, Protector of Romania, and on October 26, 2025, on the feast of Saint Demetrius the Great Martyr, the Myrrh-Streamer, the exterior and the iconography of the National Cathedral were consecrated, the cathedral being a gift of the right-believing Romanian people springing from faith in God and from honoring the Romanian heroes.

Through all its component elements, the National Cathedral can be considered today an open book of Orthodox theology, written in stone, color and light, calling to prayer and holy communion. Through its consecration, it becomes a foretaste of eternal communion with the Holy Trinity in the Kingdom of Heaven, a truth very strongly emphasized in the service of the consecration of the church, when the troparion is sung: “This house the Father has built, this house the Son has strengthened, this house the Holy Spirit has renewed, has illumined, has sanctified, and has sanctified our souls”.

Therefore, the church has been consecrated by the grace of the Most Holy Trinity, to be for people an ark of salvation, a cruciform space of the communion of the faithful with Christ crucified, risen and ascended in glory into heaven, and at the same time the house of the Most Holy Trinity.

With the help of God, the generosity of the Government of Romania and the contribution of the Romanian clergy and faithful in Romania and abroad, the Romanian Orthodox Church now has in Bucharest a cathedral representative of the faith and piety of the majority of the Romanian people. The new Cathedral in Bucharest is called the National Cathedral because it is located in the capital of Romania and ceremonies of national symbolic value take place here, and it is dedicated to all Romanian heroes of all times.

The building and consecration of the National Cathedral mean the fulfillment of an ideal which His Beatitude Patriarch Daniel received as a mandate, together with the Holy Synod, the clergy and the faithful, from our worthy forebears, and the realization of this ideal took concrete form especially through the cooperation of all the hierarchs of the Holy Synod in supporting this project, both by adopting the necessary synodal decisions and by continuing the National Church Collection in the dioceses.

On this occasion, we thank all the donors and benefactors for their support in fulfilling this Romanian ideal, in the light-filled year of the Centennial of the Romanian Patriarchate.

These Saints Are the Most Precious Fruit Our Church Has Brought Forth in This Century

On the anniversary of the Centennial of the Romanian Patriarchate (1925-2025), it is fitting that we honor in a special way the great shepherds of souls, confessor priests, martyrs and great spiritual fathers who shone through their praiseworthy deeds in this span of 100 years, as holy fruits of the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ on Romanian soil.

Thus, on February 4, 2025, the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church proclaimed the canonization of 16 Romanian saints who confessed faith in Christ during the difficult period of the communist regime in Romania. These saints are the most precious fruit our Church has brought forth in this century, because through them the mysterious work of the grace of the Holy Spirit in the Romanian Orthodox Church is concretely shown.

They were canonized because the signs of holiness were shown in their lives: Orthodoxy of faith, a holy life of repentance and prayer, humble and merciful love for their neighbor, sacrificial confession of the faith and the working of miracles, as well as the piety of the people toward them. The Church honors them above all because they resisted persecution with courage and dignity and confessed the truth of Christ even under torture and in the face of death, thus offering a living example of full Christian life.

Among the newly canonized saints who adorn the calendar of our Church are the martyrs who confessed faith in Christ at the cost of their lives. We mention Saint Constantin Sârbu the Priest-Martyr, who received a martyr’s death because he refused to betray the Mystery of Holy Confession; Saint Liviu Galaction of Cluj the Priest-Martyr, who was arrested for his catechetical activity, defending religion classes in schools, and died in terrible torment in Aiud prison; Saint Gherasim of Tismana the Venerable Martyr, a great hesychast ascetic, who confessed faith in Christ and died as a martyr in Târgu-Ocna prison; Saint Visarion of Lainici the Venerable Martyr, who, after terrible beatings, died confessing Christ at Lainici Monastery in the Jiu Valley; Saint Ilarion Felea the Priest-Martyr, a parish priest and professor of theology, who passed to the Lord after severe suffering in Aiud prison; and Saint Alexander of Bessarabia the Priest-Martyr, who at the age of 80 was deported, stripped, beaten, pulled by the beard, starved and humiliated, and committed his soul to God in the Church of the Most Holy Theotokos in the Russian city of Kazan in the Soviet Union.

At the same time, we recall the company of confessor priests in the communist prisons, who sanctified their lives through patience, love and humility, forgiving those who beat, tortured and mocked them, and thus departed in peace to the heavenly mansions. Among these God-pleasers we should mention Saint Sofian of Antim the Venerable Confessor, a hesychast man of prayer and church painter, who confessed faith in Christ in the prisons of Bucharest, Jilava, Aiud, Galați and Balta Brăilei, and after his release became one of the most beloved spiritual fathers of the Capital, being called by Father Cleopa Ilie of Sihăstria “the Apostle of Bucharest”; Saint Dumitru Stăniloae the Priest-Confessor, the greatest Orthodox theologian of the 20th century, who survived years of imprisonment at Jilava and Aiud and is esteemed as translator and interpreter of the Romanian Philokalia and other patristic texts, as well as a wise teacher of Romanian spirituality; Saint Arsenie of Prislop the Venerable Confessor, who went through four detentions and after his release was forced to live in the world, yet secretly kept the rule of monastic life, and after his repose in the Lord has worked many miracles; Saint Ilie Lăcătușu the Priest-Confessor, who suffered in labor camps and prisons, a great man of prayer, whose body was found incorrupt and fragrant after his repose in the Lord, working a multitude of miracles; and Saint Iraclie of Bessarabia the Venerable Confessor, one of the greatest Romanian missionaries of the interwar period in the territory between the Prut and the Dniester, who confessed faith in Christ for eight years in the labor camps of the Soviet Union, and whose holy relics, after his repose in the Lord, have shown themselves to be myrrh-streaming.

Also among the saints proclaimed this year is the assembly of venerable fathers, recognized by the right-believing people as men of prayer, spiritual fathers and wise guides of souls on the path of salvation. Among these great hesychast men of prayer and spiritual fathers are: Saint Paisie of Sihăstria the Venerable, who led a life of harsh hermitic struggle, full of humility and love toward those who visited him, and who after his repose in the Lord has worked many miracles; Saint Cleopa of Sihăstria the Venerable, one of the most beloved Romanian spiritual fathers of the 20th century, a great preacher and Orthodox apologist, a wise guide of clergy and faithful, who also received from God the gift of working miracles; Saint Dometie the Merciful of Râmeț the Venerable, a humble spiritual father and man of prayer, who throughout his life stood out for the charisma of non-acquisitiveness, being a merciful father and giving everything he had to help those in need, and who after his repose in the Lord was called by the people “the Apostle of the Moți”; Saint Serafim the Patient of Sâmbăta de Sus the Venerable, who was a guide of many souls on the path of salvation and for his holy life received from God the gift of foresight and of working miracles; and Saint Calistrat of Timișeni and Vasiova the Venerable, a humble missionary and spiritual father in Banat, who kept the rule of monastic life with great zeal and for his humility and ascetic struggles received from God the gift of healing and of casting out unclean spirits.

In the face of the many material and spiritual problems of today’s world, the celebration of the Centennial of the Romanian Patriarchate calls us to a profound reflection on our mission and responsibility to preserve and pass on the light of the Orthodox faith and of national unity, in the spirit of our forebears.

The Centennial of the Romanian Patriarchate is therefore a moment of holy joy and gratitude for all of Romanian Orthodoxy. Looking back, we see not only a rich history but also a luminous spiritual heritage left by our forebears – patriarchs, hierarchs, priests, monastics and lay faithful, who defended and passed on the Orthodox faith over time.

The ecclesial unity and the dignity of the Romanian Orthodox Church as a Patriarchate call us to a profound spiritual communion in faith, in prayer and in service, contributing to the strengthening and promotion of church and national unity, following the example of our forebears who saw the Romanian Patriarchate as a symbol of service to the spiritual unity of the Romanian people.

With the help of the Merciful God, we are at the beginning of the Nativity Fast, also called the Christmas Fast. This period is first of all a preparation for the sanctification of our souls and bodies through Confession and Holy Communion, but also an occasion for mutual help and almsgiving. Deeds of Christian almsgiving, seen as fruits of the right faith, are the concrete form of humble love for God and for people.

In the current context, marked by economic crisis and uncertainty of life, there is a continued need for increased prayer for the end of wars and for the spiritual strengthening of those who suffer because of them. Today, when loneliness and depression, poverty and uncertainty about tomorrow are multiplying around us, let us pray to the Lord Jesus Christ to strengthen us in our Christian work of helping the sick, the elderly, orphans, the poor and those who mourn and are sorrowful.

That is why we address the priests and lay faithful of our Holy Church with the fatherly exhortation to organize, as every year, in parishes, monasteries, deaneries and diocesan centers, collections of food, clothing and money. These will be distributed to those in suffering and need, to disadvantaged families or families with many children, to the elderly and to persons living alone, without children or relatives, especially those living in rural areas.

Confident that this year as well you will show Christian generosity and respond with love to our fatherly call to this holy work of charity and help, we thank you for your constant generosity and remind you of the words of the Lord Jesus Christ: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5, 7).

We pray to the All-Merciful God to bless all Romanians in Romania and abroad, granting them health and salvation, protecting them from all evil and strengthening them in every good work, for the joy of our Church and of the Romanian people everywhere.

With great joy and appreciation, we embrace you in a fatherly way and share with you the apostolic blessing: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all!” (2 Corinthians 13, 13).

The text is signed by Patriarch Daniel together with all the members of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church

title: Pastoral Letter of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church for the Sunday of Orthodoxy in the Year of Our Lord 2026
intro:
Most Venerable and Most Reverend Fathers,
Beloved brothers and sisters in the Lord,

In the spiritual light of the beginning of Holy and Great Lent, the Church sets before us, as the first stop on our ascent toward the Resurrection, the Sunday of Orthodoxy – the celebration of the victory of the right faith over all heresies and errors and, in a special way, the Sunday of the solemn restoration of the veneration of the holy icons in Constantinople in the year 843.

To understand this victory fully, it is fitting to recall, even briefly, the arduous path traveled by the Church in the 8th and 9th centuries.

At that time, emperors such as Leo III the Isaurian and Constantine V Copronymus, faced with political and military pressure from neighboring peoples and wishing to cooperate with non-Christian peoples of the East, waged a fierce struggle against the veneration of icons. This attempt at a political and religious compromise inflicted a deep wound on the life of the faithful and the monks of Constantinople.

Under the care of two empresses of holy life, Irene and Theodora, God arranged the formulation of the Orthodox faith concerning the veneration of icons.

Thus, at Nicaea in 787, the Holy Fathers of the Seventh Ecumenical Council established the dogma of the veneration of icons, and in 843, through the synod convened in Constantinople and the proclamation made by Patriarch Methodios, Orthodoxy triumphed completely. From that moment, the first Sunday of Great Lent became the feast of the triumph of the right faith.

Two great empresses, two women of holy life – Irene and Theodora – succeeded in fulfilling the will of God in a wondrous way, in a period of history when, sadly, some male emperors had become persecutors of the holy icons.

Saint John of Damascus – “the trumpet of the Holy Spirit against the iconoclasts” – said in the 8th century: “I do not worship matter, but I worship the Creator of matter, who became matter for my sake”1. And Saint Theodore the Studite, in the 9th century, confirms the same truth of faith, according to which “the Invisible One became visible so that we, seeing His imprint, might desire likeness to Him”2.

Thus, the icon becomes a window onto the Kingdom of God, a place of the presence of grace, a call to holiness and a confession of the truth that Christ is “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1, 15).

In the light of these teachings, the Sunday of Orthodoxy is an occasion of deep gratitude toward the confessors of the right faith – hierarchs, monastics, theologians and a multitude of faithful of pure life – who defended the truth even at the cost of their lives. They are “so great a cloud of witnesses” (cf. Hebrews 12, 1) that accompanies us still today on the path of fasting and repentance.

Man Is the Living Icon of God

The Sunday of Orthodoxy shows us that man is the living icon of God, created in His image (cf. Genesis 1, 26), called to reflect in this world the love, purity and glory of the One who made him. Saint Gregory the Theologian urges us: “Honor God through yourself, for you are His image”3.

The icon of the saints is not merely a remembrance but a living testimony of the fulfillment of man, a proof that grace can transfigure an ordinary life and raise it to likeness with God. Saint Basil the Great says: “The honor given to the icon passes to the prototype”4, and the honor given to the saints passes to God. The icon thus reveals to us two great truths:

  • who God is for man: the One who became visible and near, that is, the God-Man;
  • who man can become in relationship with God: like God through grace, light and holiness.

Looking at the icon, we understand that every human face is called to eternal life. In a world that often humiliates, manipulates or blurs the value of the person, the Church defends and affirms the unique and eternal value of every human being: child, elderly, sick, refugee, lonely, marginalized, because each is an icon of God, and in the humblest the face of Christ truly shines (cf. Matthew 25, 40).

In 2026, declared by the Holy Synod as the “Homage Year of the pastoral care of the Christian family” and the “Commemorative Year of the holy women in the calendar (myrrh-bearers, martyrs, nuns, wives and mothers)”, we are called to look more attentively at the dignity of the human face illumined by grace: in the family, in the quiet sacrifice of mothers, in the devotion of wives and in the steadfastness of faithful women who keep the flame of love burning in their homes.

In this commemorative year, the Church has also added to the liturgical calendar 16 holy women, canonized in the previous year (2025) by the Holy Synod, who, through their luminous lives of witness, have entered the assembly of the saints in heaven.

At the same time, we also commemorate with piety those holy women who sanctified the history of the Church and defended the truth of the faith with their whole being over time, among them the empresses Irene and Theodora, through whom God worked the victory of the Church over the heresy of iconoclasm. They bore the weight of their times with courageous hearts and unshakable love for Christ, becoming luminous images of the confession of faith and models of life for all the faithful.

Through them and through all the contemporary saints – spiritual fathers, confessors and tireless servants – we understand that true holiness is born in the heart, where love, forgiveness and reconciliation restore the image of the merciful God in each of us.

Today we celebrate the triumph of Orthodoxy, which means the victory of the living right faith, for faith must also be lived, not only confessed. Orthodoxy means right faith, but also right understanding; right thinking, but also right glorification; right depiction (iconography), but also right singing (hymnography); right ascetic struggle (asceticism), but also right judgment or measure (discernment, the virtue of all virtues, as the fathers of the Church saw it).

Seeing these and taking them to heart, we understand that Orthodoxy is also the right vision of God, which corrects our own thinking and vision as beings created in His holy image. It corrects our own spiritual growth and our glorification of the One who gave us life; it corrects our own piety and repentance, as well as our asceticism and prayer, our faith and true living.

Orthodoxy is nothing other than sanctified human nature, as it has been made known to us through the God-Man, Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God.

We Commemorate with Piety Those Holy Women Who Sanctified the History of the Church

If the icons in churches show us the glory of the Kingdom of God, the icon of a brother or sister who is suffering shows us the concrete way in which we can attain this glory.

Love for one’s neighbor is the light of Orthodoxy in everyday life. The Holy Apostle John asks us: “But whoever has this world’s goods, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his heart from him, how does the love of God abide in him?” (1 John 3, 17). And Saint John Chrysostom urges: “Do you wish to honor the body of Christ? Do not despise Him when you see Him hungry or naked”5.

Philanthropy is, therefore, the living icon of our faith. It is not merely a social gesture, but a work of the Spirit, an extension of God’s love in the world. Thus, the Sunday of Orthodoxy becomes the day on which the whole Church reaches out its hand to those who are tried: people burdened by many needs and sufferings, communities in difficulty, missions carrying their cross in hard places, and parishes that live with few resources but with great hope.

As every year, on this blessed Sunday a collection is organized for the Central Missionary Fund, established by the Holy Synod as a form of solidarity in the life of the Church. This fund supports the social-philanthropic and missionary work of our Church, helping:

  • dioceses, parishes and monasteries in difficulty;
  • vulnerable families, children without support and persons who are suffering;
  • educational, social-philanthropic and social-missionary programs;
  • communities in disadvantaged areas, which need strengthening and hope.

Through this blessed work, each Christian shares in the life and needs of the Church, “that there should be no schism in the body, but that the members should have the same care for one another” (1 Corinthians 12, 25). In the gift of every Orthodox Christian, whether small or great, lies the power to restore a living icon: the face of a sorrowful person, a child in need, a lonely elderly person, a parish in great trial.

The Icons in Churches Show Us the Glory of the Kingdom of God

On this Sunday of Orthodoxy let us approach the holy icons with a pure heart, discovering in them the beauty of the calling that God has planted in each of us. Let us look with the same piety upon the face of our neighbor in need and support him as we are able, as a living testimony of the love of Christ.

At this first spiritual stop of Great Lent, let us strive to become ever more like the Lord Jesus Christ, the Image of the Father and the source of our holiness. In these blessed days, each of us is called to show the light of faith through our deeds, “that (people – ed. note) may see our good works and glorify our Father in heaven” (Matthew 5, 16).

Thanking you for the generosity you have shown through all the years toward the Central Missionary Fund, with fatherly love we address to you all the apostolic blessing: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all!” (2 Corinthians 13, 13).

The text is signed by Patriarch Daniel together with all the members of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church.

Notes

1 St. John of Damascus, Contra iconoclaștilor 1, 16, in the volume Cele trei tratate contra iconoclaștilor, translation, introduction and notes by Fr. Dumitru Fecioru, Ed. Institutului Biblic și de Misiune Ortodoxă, Bucharest, 2016, p. 65.

2 Cf. St. Theodore the Studite, Scrieri împotriva iconoclaștilor, translation and introduction by Policarp Pîrvuloiu, Ed. Institutului Biblic și de Misiune Ortodoxă, Bucharest, 2017.

3 Cf. St. Gregory the Theologian, Oratio I, 4, in PG 35, col. 397.

4 St. Basil the Great, Despre Sfântul Duh 18, in St. Basil the Great, Scrieri. Partea a treia, translation, introduction and notes by Fr. Teodor Bodogae, coll. Părinți și Scriitori Bisericești, vol. XII, Ed. Institutului Biblic și de Misiune al Bisericii Ortodoxe Române, Bucharest, 1988, p. 60.

5 Cf. St. John Chrysostom, Omilia 50, 3, in St. John Chrysostom, Scrieri. Partea a treia, translation, introduction and notes by Fr. Dumitru Fecioru, coll. Părinți și Scriitori Bisericești, vol. XXIII, Ed. Institutului Biblic și de Misiune al Bisericii Ortodoxe Române, Bucharest, 1994, p. 584.

title: A Day of Celebration in San Antonio, TX
intro:
A day of great joy and blessing was lived today at Saint John Cassian Romanian Orthodox Parish in San Antonio, Texas, where the faithful gathered with hearts full of gratitude to take part in the Holy and Divine Liturgy. Young and old, the members of the community came to welcome Christ and to receive Him into the chamber of their souls, in an atmosphere of prayer, peace and holy communion. 

After the Divine Liturgy, the community’s joy continued with a very special and moving moment: the celebration of five of the parish’s young people, who had reached an important milestone in their lives, completing the first great test of adulthood. Four of them graduated from high school, and one completed the first part of university studies, thus marking the beginning of a new road of responsibility and personal fulfillment. Dressed for the occasion, radiant and moved, the young people were at the center of attention for the whole community, which surrounded them with love and prayer. 

A special moment was the heartfelt address prepared by Preoteasa Cristina, a profound and warm message to each of them. In her words, she recalled the years in which she had watched them grow up in the bosom of the parish, children who never missed the Divine Liturgy, who stayed close to the Holy Chalice and to prayer, carrying forward with dignity the Orthodox faith and Romanian identity in foreign lands. The community rejoiced to see the fruits of the work and upbringing they received in their families and in the Church. The academic results of these young people were truly remarkable: they received high academic honors such as Summa Cum Laude, Magna Cum Laude, White Cord Recognition and other distinctions of merit, which opened the way for them to continue their university studies through grants and scholarships offered by prestigious universities in the United States. These achievements are the fruit of their persistent work, of their families’ support and of their formation in an environment where faith, education and Christian values went hand in hand.

In particular, those who have chosen the path of medicine were urged never to forget that it is God who heals and saves, and that man becomes only an instrument of His work in the world. As a sign of love and blessing, each young person received heartfelt gifts from Father and Preoteasa: icons of Saints Paisie and Cleopa and of the Venerable Arsenie of Prislop, as an encouragement to call upon them in prayer at every moment of life, and above all in times of trial. Along with these, other gifts, the applause of the whole community and the embraces of those present made this a memorable day for the entire parish. 
This celebration was followed by another moment full of emotion and great joy: the awarding of the prizes for the 2026 Religion Olympiad, organized by the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas. This year too, the children of our parish took part in the competition with great seriousness and dedication, prepared and guided with much love by Preoteasa Cristina Ilieș, Mrs. Adina Pașnicu and Mrs. Maria Zamfir, the coordinators of the parish Sunday School. The competition took place in two stages: the parish round and the Metropolia round, held on April 26, 2026, bringing together children and young people between the ages of 8 and 18. The results brought great joy to the whole community, the fruit of sustained work, of steady preparation every Sunday, of online lessons and tests, and above all of love for the faith and for the Church.

The results achieved by the children of our parish were truly remarkable. First Place was won in both the 8–12 and the 13–18 age categories, by Ana Maria Aron and Harry Andres Ortiz-Pasnicu. Second Place was won by Andreea Aron and Alexandru Chira, and Third Place in the 8–12 category went to Lazlo Alexander Bartos. Several honorable mentions were also awarded, to Sofia Chira, Cristian Nectarie Huszar, Sofia Maria Mihai, Gabriel Scull and Iarina Stoian, rewarding the effort and commitment of all the participants. In appreciation of their work and results, each child received a diploma from His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, as a blessing and recognition of their efforts. The parish priest and Preoteasa also prepared heartfelt gifts for each participant, bringing much joy to the children and their families.             

In a special way, the First Place winners were crowned with wreaths of roses, as a sign of the beauty of the fruits borne through work, faith and perseverance. The parents’ support played an essential role in this fine achievement, as they constantly encouraged and supported the children in their preparation. The results showed once again the seriousness and love with which these children approached their participation in the Religion Olympiad. 

The day ended in an atmosphere of deep gratitude and communion, with the whole community gathering around a festive meal lovingly prepared for the children and young people. On this blessed Sunday of the Blind Man, the Gospel set before us the miracle of the healing of the one deprived of sight, showing us that true light comes through the encounter with Christ. And looking at the children and young people of our parish, at their faith, purity and desire to stay close to the Church, we felt that God continues to enlighten souls and to give birth to hope in the midst of our community.

Just as the blind man in the Gospel opened his eyes to the light and to the knowledge of God, so this day was for us a living testimony that when children grow up close to the Holy Chalice, to prayer and to the love of their parents and of the Church, they become a light for the world and
a blessing for the future. With hearts full of thanksgiving, we raised prayers to the good
God for all the gifts poured out upon our parish and for the joy of seeing a young generation that carries forward with dignity the Orthodox faith and Romanian values in these blessed lands.    

Preoteasa Cristina

title: Message of His Beatitude Patriarch Daniel on the Day of Romanians Everywhere
intro:
His Beatitude Patriarch Daniel issued a message on Thursday for the Day of Romanians Everywhere, observed on the last Sunday of May, which this year coincides with the feast of the Descent of the Holy Spirit.

“Romanians who left the country for various reasons have carried the faith of their forefathers with them throughout the world, have carried in their souls the church back home, and have lived Orthodox spirituality and the holy Orthodox faith far from their homeland.”

His Beatitude highlighted the role of the family in Romanian communities abroad, emphasizing that “Romanians wish to preserve the unity of the Christian family, made up of man, woman and children, because the family blessed by God is the most precious intimate space in which conjugal love is expressed, as well as parental, filial and fraternal love.”

“Thus, the Church has the duty to support and strengthen the Christian family, offering pastoral guidance and spiritual support for all stages of family life,” the Patriarch of Romania also said.

The full message:

The Day of Romanians Everywhere: An Occasion of Joy and Blessing

On the last Sunday of May we celebrate the Day of Romanians Everywhere, an event of strong spiritual and national-identity significance and a good occasion to reaffirm the common values that underlie our unity: the Romanian language, Romanian culture and the Christian traditions of the Romanian people.

The year 2026 was proclaimed by the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church as the Homage Year of the Pastoral Care of the Christian Family and the Commemorative Year of the Holy Women of the Calendar (Myrrh-bearers, Martyrs, Monastics, Wives and Mothers), and the last Sunday of May (May 31) this year, when we celebrate the Day of Romanians Everywhere, coincides with the Great Feast of the Descent of the Holy Spirit.

Romanians who left the country for various reasons have carried the faith of their forefathers with them throughout the world, have carried in their souls the church back home, and have lived Orthodox spirituality and the holy Orthodox faith far from their homeland. That is why the Mother Church, caring for her spiritual children, has established numerous parishes and eparchies in the diaspora to meet the spiritual needs of the Romanian Orthodox faithful.

We live at a time when the institution of the family, both in the homeland and in the diaspora, faces multiple challenges. In this context, the role of the family and of women in the Church and in society requires deeper understanding and appreciation.

Thus, the Church has the duty to support and strengthen the Christian family, offering pastoral guidance and spiritual support for all stages of family life: the Christian education of children, the preparation of young people for marriage, overcoming difficulties, and strengthening the bonds of love among family members.

Saint John Chrysostom tells us that the Christian family is not merely a social unit, but a little church (for the home too is a little church), in which the Orthodox faith is lived and handed on in a living and natural way. Holy Scripture describes God’s bond with the world as a relationship of intimacy, as a marriage and a family (cf. Ephesians 5, 21-33).

The Church is the place where, through the cleansing work of the Holy Spirit upon the soul of the humble person, we live brotherly love in God the Son made Man and the fatherly love of God the Father, Whom our Lord Jesus Christ taught us to call upon thus: “Our Father in heaven”. The Church is, therefore, the Family of the love for mankind of the Most Holy Trinity, and the Christian family was rightly called by Blessed Augustine “the church at home” (“Ecclesia domestica”).

In the current context of the worldwide phenomenon of migration, the Romanian Orthodox Church is developing and intensifying its pastoral and social mission and responsibility toward Romanian Orthodox people outside Romania, whom it considers its faithful children and an integral part of the Romanian Orthodox communion everywhere.  

The beneficial work of the Church is received, lived and passed on to children above all through families formed of Orthodox men and women. The family is the primary setting in which faith is embraced, practiced, cherished and passed on to descendants. Communion with God through prayer, familiarity with His saints and the beauty of the feasts are discovered through the work of spiritual shepherds and of devout people who show their faith in life with joy and kindness.

In this sense, Romanians wish to preserve the unity of the Christian family, made up of man, woman and children, because the family blessed by God is the most precious intimate space in which conjugal love is expressed, as well as parental, filial and fraternal love.

It is also very necessary to educate the young generation in the spirit of love for God, for the Church and for the nation, and to cultivate essential virtues in the souls of children and young people, such as love and compassion, solidarity with people in difficulty, friendship, courage and hope.

The pastoral, liturgical, philanthropic and cultural work of the Romanian Orthodox Church in the diaspora promotes the unity of the family, the Romanian language, the Christian faith and Romanian culture in dialogue with the spiritual values of the countries where Romanians live.

Therefore, we wish that the families of Romanians in the diaspora may give birth to and raise people who are faithful, hardworking and generous, lovers of Romanian spirituality and promoters of friendship among peoples.

We wish all Romanians everywhere health and salvation, peace and joy, hope and happiness for many good years!

With fatherly blessing,

† Daniel
Patriarch of the Romanian Orthodox Church

title: 2017 Religion Olympiad
intro:
With the blessing of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas, the final stage of the eighth edition of the Religion Olympiad, 2017, took place on Sunday, May 14, 2017, in six metropolitan centers in the United States and Canada and in two special centers. A total of 189 children took part in the written test at the parish level, and 87 candidates competed in the parishes hosting the metropolitan center stage: 58 in the 8-12 age group and 29 young people in the 13-18 age group.

The tests were based on the new curriculum of the Parish Schools for 2016-2017. Thanks are due to the Education Commission of our Holy Archdiocese, which organized and prepared the tests, especially to Mr. Stelian Ghinea of Rochester, NY, and to Mrs. Ileana Gavriș and Mrs. Veronica Ciocan of Edmonton, AB, to the teachers at the two grading centers, and to all the teachers on the committees, both in the parishes and in the metropolitan centers, who took part in this edition. A word of appreciation is also due to the eight parishes that hosted the eighth edition of the Religion Olympiad with great joy.

Every candidate received a certificate of participation, and the first-place winners in each category received a free voucher to attend the Metropolia’s summer camp in Allegan, MI.

The results are available at this address.

title: Trinitas TV - Service and Mission on American Soil
Meeting of the Deanery for the Eastern United States
intro:
The priests and parish delegates of the Deanery for the Eastern United States of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas gathered on September 15-16 at Life-Giving Spring Parish in Long Valley, New Jersey, for the deanery meeting. The meeting was presided over by His Eminence Nicolae, Romanian Orthodox Metropolitan of the Americas.

The first session of the meeting was dedicated to the Homage Year of the holy icons, iconographers and church painters and to the Commemorative Year of Patriarch Justinian and the defenders of Orthodoxy during communism in the Romanian Patriarchate. During this session, Fr. Ionuț Voicu, parish priest of Life-Giving Spring Church, gave a presentation entitled “Patriarch Justinian: Defender of the Church during Communism”, and Mrs. Ileana Dascălu, president of the Metropolia’s Ladies’ Auxiliary, gave a presentation entitled “Saint Pavnutie Pârvul the Iconographer, 1657-1735”. At the close of the first session, the priests took part in a pastoral conference moderated by His Eminence Nicolae.

The deanery meeting continued on the morning of the second day, when His Eminence Nicolae served the Akathist of the Holy Cross together with the priests present, after which he elevated Rev. Fr. Daniel Ene to the office of Dean of the Deanery for the Eastern United States of America.

During the second session, Rev. Fr. Nicolae Clempuș of St. Mary’s Parish in Atlanta, Georgia, gave a presentation entitled “Defenders of Orthodoxy during Communism: Cele șapte cuvinte către tineri. Fr. Calciu’s Forbidden Sermons”, and Rev. Fr. Dean Daniel Ene delivered a lecture entitled “Liturgical Innovations in the Holy Sacraments: Their Liturgical, Canonical-Disciplinary and Pastoral Implications.” This was followed by a Trinitas TV report on the wonder-working icon of the Mother of God at Nicula Monastery.

In the context of the events to take place in 2018, which the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church has declared the Homage Year of the unity of faith and nation and the Commemorative Year of the makers of the Great Union of 1918, the participants watched a Trinitas TV documentary on the significance of the People’s Salvation Cathedral, which will be consecrated on November 30, 2018.

The second part of the session was dedicated to the financial reports and to the activity reports of the Education Commission, the Ladies’ Auxiliary and the youth association of the Metropolia, followed by the election of the members of the deanery council.

In closing, His Eminence Nicolae thanked those present for taking part, and the community of Life-Giving Spring Parish for hosting.

The meeting ended with Great Vespers, served by His Eminence together with Protosyngellos Vincențiu Temirov of Saint Dimitrie Monastery in Middletown, NY, parish priest Fr. Ionuț Voicu, and Fr. Ovidiu Sabău of St. Andrew Church in Reading, Pennsylvania. The next deanery meeting will take place at St. Mary’s Parish in Atlanta, Georgia.

title: Pastoral Letter of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church for the First Sunday of the 2017 Nativity Fast
intro:
On the first Sunday of the Nativity Fast, the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church addresses a pastoral word to all the faithful within the Romanian Patriarchate.

In the context of the 2017 Homage and Commemorative Year, the hierarchs of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church refer in their pastoral letter to the icons and the painting of the church, which they describe as the visual vesture of the liturgical space and part of the liturgical life.

Every holy icon, whatever its subject, makes visible the mystery of the humble and most glorified love of Christ, “the One Holy,” the One crucified, risen and ascended in glory, a love present in Him and in His Saints. That is why painters of icons and frescoes must be people able to convey, through their spiritual and artistic work, this mystery of the light, peace and Paschal joy of Christ given to the saints, the text of the pastoral letter states.

The Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church reminds the faithful that this year we commemorate the defenders of Orthodoxy during the communist period. This commemoration is, first of all, as the pastoral letter states, a moral duty toward our forebears who, in times hostile to the Church and to religion in general, confessed their faith in Christ crucified and risen, even at the cost of their freedom and their lives.

Of the Nativity Fast, the hierarchs of the Holy Synod say that it is a time of spiritual renewal, of more frequent communion with the Holy Eucharist and of increasing the works of merciful love.

During this period of the Nativity Fast we are called to unite humble prayer and sincere repentance with merciful love, showing spiritual and material charity toward people in need, urges the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church.

Download the pastoral letter in PDF format here.

title: Christmas Traditions and Customs at SS. Constantine and Helen Cathedral in Chicago
intro:
At birth, a person has one people, one homeland, one language and one faith. We find this oneness in the Romanian soul, which has not changed over the centuries, as witnessed by the ancient traditions and carols that our ancestors sang, that we sing too, and that we hope our descendants will also sing.

We can draw borders across waters and lands, but never across the spirit, and our spirit is Romanian wherever in the world we may be. Having the joy of being part of the community of SS. Constantine and Helen Cathedral, on January 7, 2018 we gathered for the Christmas traditions and customs event, now organized for the fifth consecutive year. Just as it happened long ago, when the children of the village set out with the star from the house of the priest, where they received his blessing, and then went caroling to all the householders of the village, so too the lovers of Romanian traditions, under the guidance of Fr. Vasile Mureșan, gathered together and began the greetings and carols. The hosts of the event, the Baciu and Obreja families, together with the families of Fr. Vasile Mureșan and Fr. Nicolae Cărbune, dressed up for the feast in national costumes, all in the setting of a peasant house, itself decorated for the holiday. And because the beauty of the Christmas holidays lies in going caroling and proclaiming the Nativity of Christ, we welcomed carolers and guests from the other Orthodox churches in Chicago, Mr. Gavriș Rus, from the Nativity of the Lord Church, completing the atmosphere with his good cheer.

The traditions, customs and carols that gladdened our hearts came from Transylvania, Bessarabia, Moldavia and Wallachia, and the national costumes came from all over the country. The youngest carolers were also present, in national costumes, and they greeted us with the sorcova and wished us all the best in the New Year. The warm atmosphere conveyed that our national identity is a well-defined one and that, even far from home, we have not forgotten that we are Romanians. In fact, as we have closed this event for the past 5 years, all those present sang: “Nu uita că ești român/Că sus în deal la tine-n sat, Popa Ioan te-a botezat.”

For the two hours the event lasted, our thoughts went to the Romanian village of old, “there” becoming “here”: “Here every thought is slower and your heart beats more rarely, as if it beat not in your chest but somewhere deep in the earth,” as Blaga writes, in the village where eternity was born.

title: Online Romanian Language and Culture Course for Teenagers in the Diaspora
intro: Designed as a journey through the literary, historical and geographical treasury of Romania, this course aims to offer teenagers in the diaspora both an introduction to Romanian culture and a concise presentation of some of the lexical and grammatical elements needed for better oral and written communication in the Romanian language. The teaching materials will include texts and audiovisual elements, and the teaching method will be communicative, which will require the active participation of the students, who will connect in real time and communicate orally and in writing. The final project will be the design and brief presentation of a virtual tourist itinerary. The course will be offered online every Tuesday, from April 17 to June 19, 2018, from 6:30 to 8:30 PM (Eastern Standard Time - Canada and U.S.). Each session will be recorded so that it can be viewed later by students who are unable to connect in real time. For more information, please visit the website www.LenguaViva.ca or send an e-mail to ioanadimitriu@icloud.com

title: Pastoral Letter of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church for the Sunday of Orthodoxy 2018
intro:
To the most venerable monastic orders, the most reverend clergy and
the most beloved faithful throughout the Romanian Patriarchate,

Grace, joy and peace from God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit,
and from us, fatherly blessings!

Most Venerable and Most Reverend Fathers,
Beloved faithful, 

 

The first Sunday of Great Lent is dedicated to the victory of the Orthodox faith over the heresies. The Holy Fathers who gathered in the Ecumenical Councils of the fourth to eighth centuries established the right teaching about the divinity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, as well as about the true veneration due to the holy icons. Instituted by the Synod of Constantinople of March 11, 843, this feast was dedicated to the victory of the right faith over those who fought against the veneration of icons, of the Holy Cross and of the holy relics, and it is at the same time a feast of the victory of the right faith over all heresies or false teachings in general. The Sunday of Orthodoxy recalls the victory of the Orthodox over the heretics, which culminated in the restoration of the veneration of the holy icons. Thus, the decision to name the first Sunday of Great Lent the Sunday of Orthodoxy was taken in the year 843, at the Synod of Constantinople, but it had been prepared by the Seventh Ecumenical Council of Nicaea in 787, when the Holy Fathers proclaimed the veneration of the holy icons as a manifestation of the Orthodox faith.

Less well known is the fact that this feast of the Sunday of Orthodoxy was superimposed on the older commemoration of the prophets Moses, Aaron and Samuel, attested a century earlier, in the time of Patriarch Germanus of Constantinople († 740). Great Lent was once full of biblical commemorations: in the 2nd week the Righteous Noah was commemorated, in the 4th week the sacrifice of Isaac, and in the 5th week the Patriarch Isaac himself. The feast of the prophets suited the first week of Great Lent and the Old Testament atmosphere of the readings at the holy services. This feast dedicated to the prophets was not abolished; it remained linked to the feast of the Sunday of Orthodoxy, the reason being that the prophets anticipated and announced the Incarnation of the Word, to which the holy icons bear witness.

In this regard, the Vespers service of the Sunday of Orthodoxy says: The grace of truth has shone forth: the things once foreshadowed now have been openly fulfilled. For behold, the Church is clothed with the image of Christ in the flesh as with an adornment beyond this world, foreshadowed of old by the image of the tabernacle of witness, and honoring the right faith[1]. Saint John of Damascus († 749) already pointed out, in his Treatises on the icons, the analogy between the holy icons and the visions of the prophets. The prophets did not behold the holy visions with bodily eyes but with the spiritual eyes of the soul, just as the apostles beheld the glory of Christ on Mount Tabor, and the visions of the prophets were manifestations of God’s work, not of His essence. These visions were anticipatory “images” of what was to be fully revealed through the Incarnation of the eternal Word of God. For this reason, in the New Law, the visions of the Old Testament prophets were replaced by the holy icons, whose theological foundation is the event of the Incarnation of the Son of God, since Christ is the image (icon) of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15). Because the visions of the prophets prefigured the Incarnation of Christ, Who is “the natural Icon of the Father”[2], the prophets can be celebrated together with the veneration of the holy icons on the First Sunday of Great Lent, says Makarios of Simonopetra in his beautiful work on the Triodion[3].

Through this twofold celebration of the prophets and of the holy icons, the Sunday of Orthodoxy reveals to us a wondrous work of God in the history of salvation. For although no one had seen the face of God until the Incarnation of the Son, until He assumed human nature, the prophets nevertheless announced Him, seeing spiritually, in advance and across time, the face of God Incarnate, Jesus Christ. The eternal Word, the Son of God, awaited “the fullness of the time” (Galatians 4:4) to appear as the Savior of the world, and His chosen ones, the prophets, received this revelation as a pledge, in order to keep awake among the people the faith in the coming of the Messiah – Christ.

The icon is a window to the Absolute[4], which reveals to us the transfigured world, that is, the world of those who partake of the glory of divine grace, and at the same time discloses to us the content of this transfiguration, namely holiness. The depiction of the saints in icons confirms the Church’s faith in the Incarnation of the Word of God, as the Holy Evangelist John testifies when he writes: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14). And in his first catholic Epistle, the same Holy Apostle testifies: That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life – the life was manifested, and we have seen, and bear witness, and declare to you that eternal life which was with the Father and was manifested to us – that which we have seen and heard we declare to you, that you also may have fellowship with us; and truly our fellowship is with the Father and with His Son Jesus Christ (1 John 1:1-3). Likewise, Saint John of Damascus strengthens us in the truth of the legitimacy of depicting God in icons, saying: I depict the invisible God, not as invisible, but as One Who became visible for our sake by partaking of flesh and blood. I do not depict the invisible divinity, but I depict the visible flesh of God[5].

Of course, the icon is founded not only on the Incarnation of the Son of God but also on His Resurrection. Without the Resurrection of Christ, the icon would not be a depiction of the transfigured heavenly life, but merely a commemorative painting. The icon presents to us the Son of God, Who took on a human body and passed with it through death and Resurrection. In the holy icons we find the face of Christ with a halo, that is, illumined by the glory of the Resurrection, the face of the Mother of God and the faces of the saints, all illumined by the same uncreated glory of the Kingdom of Heaven, expressed in the nimbus of light around the head. In the holy icons we discover the human face restored, renewed and sanctified, illumined by the glory of the Kingdom of God, as a call to attain likeness to God, through the radiance of the image of God’s glory on the faces of the saints.

In this sense, we read in Holy Scripture that man was created by God in His own image (cf. Genesis 1:27). Unlike the Son of God, Who is of one essence with the Father, Adam could attain likeness to God by grace, in constant obedience to God and fulfillment of His will. But wishing to become like God, yet without God, Adam lost the image of light, falling into disobedience and estrangement from God, the Source of life, and thus fell all the way to death, both spiritual and bodily (cf. Romans 6:23). That is why the divine light given to Adam by God when He created him no longer shone on the face of Adam, who had disobeyed God.

Looking at the face of Christ in the icon, that is, at the New Adam, Who humbled Himself and became obedient to God to the point of death (cf. Philippians 2:8), every person feels the call to renew his or her own image, that is, to reflect the love and light of Christ through life and good deeds. Looking at the face of Christ and at the faces of the saints in the icons, we discover the possibility of receiving the sanctifying grace of Christ ourselves and of making it active through prayer and merciful love, through communion with God and with His saints lived in the Church.

Beloved spiritual sons and daughters,

Such an understanding of the holy icons helps us look with hope and joy upon the mystery of our own life and of our neighbor’s life. The holy icons assure us of the value of the human person, of our own person and also of our fellow human being. Christ and the saints look at us from the icons and urge us to have a pure, sincere and kindly gaze. We ought to direct this pure gaze toward our neighbor as well, who bears on his face the seal of the image of God, for every human being is a unique and unrepeatable person, full of mystery, a being called to live eternally in the love of the eternal God. This image of God in man can be darkened by sins, by selfish passions, by the lack of humble and merciful love. But this image can regain its radiance through prayer and repentance, through participation in the liturgical life of the Church, through receiving the Holy Mysteries, and through cultivating brotherly love together with all who confess Christ as Savior and Healer.

Every Christian can take part in fulfilling this spiritual work of restoring and sanctifying his own image and that of his neighbor, after the luminous image of Christ and of His saints. Each of us can become the merciful Samaritan who helps the one fallen into suffering to rise and leads him on the path of spiritual and bodily healing. Let us not forget that the Fathers of the Church see in the merciful Samaritan of the parable (Luke 10:25-37) the Savior Jesus Christ Himself, Who came to raise us up from sickness, from sin and from death.

Therefore, each of us can follow Christ and become a neighbor to the one who is suffering. This work is fulfilled starting with a good word that strengthens in faith and hope, continuing with helping our fellow human being and offering the material gift needed for the philanthropic or social-charitable work of the Church. The liturgical work of the Church in which we take part should be continued through social assistance and philanthropic programs, through building places of worship and Church institutions such as soup kitchens for the poor, children’s homes, homes for the elderly, medical facilities for the sick and the like.

Beloved brothers and sisters in the Lord,

As you know, the Romanian Orthodox Church has initiated and expanded many such projects in recent years. There are already many social assistance institutions established and supported by the Church, with large sums of money allocated and with significant maintenance costs. In order to continue these programs and to start others, it has become a tradition that on the Sunday of Orthodoxy a collection is taken in all the churches of the Romanian Patriarchate in support of the Central Missionary Fund of our Church. Therefore, we urge you to offer, according to your means, the help needed for the Church’s work in society. Christ Himself urges us: Therefore be merciful, just as your Father also is merciful (Luke 6:36). Mercy toward those in need makes us like God Himself and helps us give a good answer before God (cf. Matthew 25).

And the Holy Apostle Paul counts among the fruits of the Holy Spirit also goodness, through which faith is made manifest (Galatians 5:22-23). Through this enumeration, Saint Paul wishes to assure us that the presence of the Holy Spirit in our life has visible signs for those around us. The virtues that our fellow human beings can see directly are: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness. Doing good to those who suffer and need our help is therefore not just an ordinary act of human solidarity. It is the sign of the presence of the Spirit in our life, the proof that we are Christians who make the work of the Spirit visible in the world. Through doing good we offer others not only material help, but the very witness of the work of the Spirit, Who makes the humble and merciful love of God fruitful in the world, in people’s lives.

With the hope that our fatherly exhortation will be a strengthening in faith and a call to good deeds for the benefit of our neighbor, we pray to God to bless you with His rich gifts and to help you in the spiritual ascent of Great Lent. At the same time, the Centenary Year of the Great Union (1918-2018) is a welcome occasion to bear witness in the world to our unity of faith and nation, that is, it can be an occasion to strengthen the brotherly communion of all Romanians in carrying out this philanthropic work for the poor and the suffering, the sorrowful and the estranged.

The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all! (2 Corinthians 13:13).

 

President of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church,

title: Pastoral Itinerary in South America
intro:
This year, the year of the Centenary of Greater Romania, we celebrate 100 years since the union of the Romanian Principalities of Wallachia, Moldavia and Transylvania into a single state. To mark this Centenary, the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church has named this year “the Homage Year of the Unity of Faith and Nation and the Commemorative Year of the Founders of the Great Union of 1918”.

Together with the Romanians at home, Romanians all over the world are celebrating this Homage Year for Romania. Our Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas wished to mark this celebration of the Romanian people through several events, in our parishes in the USA and Canada as well as in Latin America.

To organize events that share the rich history and culture of our nation, we are already working closely with the Embassies of Romania in the USA, Canada, Mexico and on the South American continent, and in partnership with the General and Honorary Consulates of Romania in these countries.

To this end, with the blessing of His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan NICOLAE of the Americas, Fr. Daniel Ene, Eparchial Secretary and Dean of New York, New England and the Eastern USA, has visited and will visit several cities in Latin America to meet with Romanians, to pray and rejoice together with them in this celebration, taking part in the events dedicated to the Centenary of Greater Romania.

The schedule of the visit is as follows:

  • February 15-19 - MEXICO (Mexico City)
  • February 19-26 - PERU (Lima)
  • February 26 – March 2 - CHILE (Santiago)
  • March 2 - 8 - ARGENTINA (Buenos Aires)
  • March 8 - 15 - BRAZIL (São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Brasilia)

The Visit to MEXICO

The first stop on this journey was the United Mexican States, in the capital, Mexico City, from February 15 to 19, 2018. Fr. Daniel’s visit took place at the invitation of the Embassy of Romania in Mexico and enjoyed the support of His Excellency Mr. Ion Vîlcu, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Romania to the United Mexican States. On Friday, February 16, 2018, Fr. Daniel Ene met with Ambassador Ion Vîlcu and the embassy staff at the Embassy of Romania. They discussed matters concerning the presence of Romanians in Mexico, as well as the particular circumstances and difficulties Romanians face in adapting. The ambassador informed us that there are small Romanian communities in Mexico and in the countries of Central America. About 630 Romanian citizens live in Mexico, around 180 of them in the capital, Ciudad de Mexico, with the rest scattered across the other 31 states of the Mexican Republic, while in the Central American countries, such as the Republic of Nicaragua, the Republic of El Salvador, the Republic of Costa Rica, the Republic of Guatemala and the Republic of Honduras, which fall under the care of the Embassy of Romania in Mexico, there are very small communities numbering a few dozen citizens.

On Saturday, February 17, with the blessing of His Eminence Metropolitan Ignatius (Samaán) of the Antiochian Orthodox Church of Mexico, Central America and Venezuela, the Divine Liturgy was celebrated for the Romanian community at Saint George Cathedral, the city’s old Antiochian cathedral. It was organized with the support of the Association of Romanians in Mexico, and our thanks for preparing this holy service go to Mrs. Tamara Ariton and the members of the Association’s board. More than 50 Romanians were present. In addition to the Divine Liturgy, a memorial service was held for the departed members of the Romanian community, and the flag of Romania that will be flown at the Romanian Association was blessed. A meeting with the Romanian community followed in the social hall of the Antiochian cathedral.

Saturday afternoon was an occasion for pastoral duties such as confessions and the blessing of homes, as several Romanian families had asked Fr. Daniel to do. An important moment of this visit was the visit to the Antiochian Cathedral of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul in Mexico City, which is also the seat of the Metropolis of Mexico and Central America of the Antiochian Orthodox Church. The Antiochian Church, as well as the Greek Church in Mexico, are a great support to our Metropolia, providing pastoral care for the Romanians who are widely scattered across the Mexican metropolis. Fr. Daniel Ene met with Archimandrite Andres Marcos, the vicar of the Antiochian Metropolis. They discussed the life of the Orthodox in Mexico, especially in the capital, Mexico City, as well as details of the cooperation between our Metropolia and the Antiochian Metropolis in the pastoral care of Romanian Orthodox faithful in Mexico. The care and love that the Antiochian Church has shown for Romanians for many years, and the active participation of Romanians in the life of the Antiochian Church, deserve to be emphasized. Through the kindness of His Eminence Metropolitan Ignatius, the classes of the Romanian school in Mexico City are held on the premises of Saint George Cathedral. The Romanian Association organizes these Romanian language lessons for a large number of Mexicans who wish to learn Romanian. Fr. Daniel expressed his support by providing teaching materials and Romanian primers for the Romanian language classes and encouraged the Association to also start religion classes for the children of Romanian families in Mexico, promising all the teaching support needed.

On Sunday, February 18, 2018, the Divine Liturgy was again celebrated in the midst of the Romanian community of Mexico City, this time at the Greek Cathedral of Saint Sophia, with the blessing of His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan ATHENAGORAS of the Greek Orthodox Metropolis of Mexico, Central America, Colombia, Venezuela and the Caribbean Islands, which is under the jurisdiction of the Ecumenical Patriarchate. Besides a large number of Romanian faithful, the Divine Liturgy was attended by the Ambassador of Romania to Mexico, Mr. Ion Vîlcu, together with Minister Counselor Ionuț Marian Vâlcu. Also present was Dr. Magdalena Ionescu, the best-known and most respected Romanian woman in Mexico. With a distinguished professional career, Dr. Ionescu was the physician and closest collaborator of Ana Aslan. After the Divine Liturgy, a moving gathering took place in the garden of the Greek cathedral, where the Romanian faithful received Orthodox calendars and small icons of the Mother of God from His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae. The Romanians repeatedly expressed the wish that a representative of our Metropolia be with the Romanian community in Mexico City at least once a year. Thanks and appreciation are due to Archimandrite Damian, Hieromonk Melitos and Archdeacon Filareto, who opened the doors of the Cathedral and made it a home for the Romanian community in Mexico for a long time. At the end of the Divine Liturgy, Fr. Damian also delivered words of welcome to Fr. Daniel Ene on behalf of His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan Athenagoras.

Words would be too few and too poor to express the love and spirit of brotherhood between the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas and the Orthodox Metropolis of Mexico and Central America.

The visit to Mexico ended with Fr. Daniel Ene’s visit to the church of the Holy Virgin Mary of Guadalupe, the holiest place of the Mexican people.

Fr. Daniel Ene

title: First Divine Liturgy in Romanian in Lima, Peru
intro:
Once again, it was the celebration of the Centennial of Greater Romania that occasioned the first Romanian Orthodox presence in the former land of the Incas, the third-largest country in South America, PERU. From February 19 to 26, with the blessing of His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan Nicolae and at the invitation of the Embassy of Romania in the Republic of Peru, Fr. Daniel Ene was among the Romanian community in Lima.

Fr. Daniel Ene’s first meeting, right after arriving at Jorge Chávez Airport in Lima, was with His Excellency Mr. Gabriel GAFIŢA, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Romania to the Republic of Peru, and the diplomatic staff of the Embassy of Romania in Peru. From the very first moments one could feel the love and joy of the ambassador and Mrs. Ileana Gafița, together with Consul George Andrei Ștefan and the family of Diana Florentina and Mihai Ionuț Matei, who serve at Romania’s mission in Peru, at having in their midst the representative of the Romanian Orthodox Church and of our Metropolia.

The conversation focused on the characteristics of the Romanian community in Peru and how it differs from those in other South American countries. The estimated number of Romanians is 120 in Peru, 30 in the Plurinational State of Bolivia and 70-80 in the Republic of Ecuador. In Peru there is also an honorary consulate in Arequipa; Ecuador has two, one in Quito (where the consul is Mr. Radu Mihail) and one in Guayaquil; and Bolivia has one in Santa Cruz de la Sierra.

On Tuesday, February 20, Fr. Daniel Ene met with Fr. Sergio Benavides, parish priest of the Holy Trinity Greek Orthodox Church in Lima, the only Orthodox church in Peru. The church community brings together Greeks, Romanians, Serbs, Antiochians, Russians, Ukrainians and Peruvian converts. Fr. Daniel thanked Fr. Sergio for the pastoral care he gives to the Romanian faithful and assured him of the full support of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas in continuing this bond of brotherhood and support for the good care of the Romanian Orthodox faithful in Peru, and especially in Lima. Fr. Sergio spoke with great love about the support the church receives from the Romanian Orthodox and about how active they are in Orthodox life in Lima. The meeting between Fr. Daniel and Fr. Sergio, held at the Greek church, was also attended by Ambassador Gabriel Gafița and Consul George Andrei Ștefan, showing their interest in being actively and genuinely involved in the life of the Romanians in Peru.

The following days gave Fr. Daniel the opportunity to understand the devoted work of a small but highly professional diplomatic staff, for whom, even here so far away, respect and care for the Romanian community, as well as love for their nation and ancestral traditions, are a true priority. At Romania’s mission in Lima, the experience and professionalism of the ambassador and of the secretary blend perfectly with the youth and early-career enthusiasm of the consul, who is on his first posting.

These days were also an occasion for Fr. Daniel to get to know a country with a remarkable history and special people. The riches of the Inca world and its monuments, and above all the best-known site in the whole world, Machu Picchu, were among the places Fr. Daniel visited. Until 1911 the site was unknown to the civilizations of the other continents. The Incas built it in 1450 but abandoned it a century later, during the Spanish invasion. Hiram Bingham is the American historian who made this forgotten corner of the world known, and it has since been included in the UNESCO World Heritage list. Almost all the buildings have been restored to show visitors what the original structures looked like.

On Friday, Saturday and Sunday Fr. Daniel had countless meetings with members of the Romanian community, who shared with him their experience of life in Peru. There are Romanian families in Peru who came more than 40 years ago and who, with tears in their eyes, spoke about their country, Romania, and remembered their childhood, Romanian traditions, the village church and the holy feasts.

The consular records and conversations with the Romanians point to two groups within the Romanian community: 1. Romanians who came, for the most part, many years ago and no longer have very close ties with Romania. This group, however, also includes a few Romanians who came in recent years, brought by their “hearts”, as they so beautifully put it: married to Peruvian citizens they met as students in Romania, they are extremely active both at the Greek church and on social media (there is already an active WhatsApp group called “Fetele din Peru”). 2. People of Romanian descent, children of former Romanian citizens of Jewish origin who emigrated mostly from Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina in the 1940s, in the context of the Second World War. Most were born in Peru and hold Romanian citizenship, but they do not speak Romanian; nevertheless, they have a special respect for the country and for their Romanian identity.

On the afternoon of Saturday, February 24, at the Embassy of Romania, in its exceptionally beautiful garden tended by the distinguished Mrs. Ileana Gafița, a Te Deum service was held, followed by a meeting with the Romanian community attended by more than 70 people, not counting the lively and wonderful children of our Romanians. At the end of the service the national flag of Romania was blessed and handed to the ambassador, to be displayed from now on in the protocol and reception hall of our Embassy in Peru. In his homily, Fr. Daniel Ene stressed the importance of the year 2018 and the opportunity we have in these days of the Centennial to share with Peruvians, too, the beauty of the culture, faith and tradition of our people. As it was the first week of Lent, Fr. Daniel urged the Romanian Orthodox faithful to care for their souls as well in their spiritual ascent toward the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection. Gifts, small icons and calendars were handed out on behalf of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, and everyone present then enjoyed the agape meal specially prepared for them by the Embassy of Romania in Peru.

The Sunday of Orthodoxy, February 25, 2018, found the Orthodox community of Lima at its most beautiful: Greeks, Romanians, Serbs, Russians, Ukrainians, Arabs and Peruvian Orthodox praying together at the Divine Liturgy. Fr. Daniel Ene was the first celebrant, serving the Divine Liturgy according to the Romanian Orthodox tradition and order and delivering the homily. The Divine Liturgy, concelebrated by Fr. Daniel Ene and Fr. Sergio Benavides, was attended by His Excellency Mr. Gabriel Gafița, Ambassador of Romania to Peru, and also by His Excellency Mr. Yerassimos Davaris, Ambassador of Greece to Peru. The responses at the Divine Liturgy were sung in several languages, gladdening the souls of those present. The words of welcome and thanks were offered by Fr. Sergio, who emphasized the close bond and brotherly love between the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas, led by His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan Nicolae, and the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Buenos Aires and South America and His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan Tarasios, who gave his blessing for the Divine Liturgy to be served in Romanian for the first time in the Greek church in Lima. After the Divine Liturgy, Fr. Daniel Ene met with members of the Orthodox community of Lima, and especially with Peruvian Orthodox faithful, who shared with him what Orthodoxy means to them and how they found their way to it.

Fr. Daniel also encouraged the Romanian community in Peru to step up its educational activities, and at his request Fr. Sergio of the Greek church  agreed that a Romanian language and religion school may begin in the church’s premises, coordinated by Mrs. Sanda Veliciu. Educational resources and coordination will be the responsibility of our Metropolia.

The first visit of a Romanian Orthodox priest to Peru ended on Monday, February 26, leaving a flawless impression of the “City of Kings” (Lima), with happy, good and extremely welcoming people, and with united Romanians who enjoy the support not only of the diplomatic staff but also of Fr. Sergio.

Peru, a country everyone should see at least once in a lifetime, was a gracious host for the Romanians’ first celebration in a year as special as the Centennial.

Fr. Daniel Ene
