title: Pastoral Visit of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae to Holy Trinity Parish in Philadelphia, PA
intro:
On November 23 and 24, 2019, the parishioners of Holy Trinity Romanian Orthodox Parish in Philadelphia had the joy and honor of having in their midst His Eminence Nicolae, Archbishop of the Romanian Orthodox Archdiocese of the United States of America and Metropolitan of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas. His Eminence’s annual visit was a comfort the parishioners of Philadelphia rejoiced in all the more because, owing to his extremely busy schedule and the great distances, His Eminence comes to Philadelphia less often.

On Saturday evening, November 23, the Hierarch presided over the pan-Orthodox assembly of priests who served Great Vespers. Besides the two priests of the church, parish priest Fr. Nicolai Buga and Fr. Timotei Avram, two other priests also served: Fr. Emmanuel Pratsinakis, an old friend of our community, and Archimandrite Hristofor Grecu. After the dismissal, His Eminence gave the church a beautiful icon of Saint Irodion of Lainici, recently canonized and included in the Church’s calendar of saints by decision of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church. The faithful present had the opportunity to venerate the relics of Saint Irodion and to receive a small icon of the Saint as a gift. The evening ended with a fraternal agape meal prepared by the two priests’ wives of our parish, Mrs. Rodica Buga and Mrs. Simona Avram. At dinner, the discussions His Eminence had held with the members of the Parish Council before Vespers continued, this time in a less formal atmosphere.

The next day, Sunday, November 24, His Eminence celebrated the Holy and Divine Hierarchical Liturgy together with the two priests of the church. At the end of the Divine Liturgy, in his homily, His Eminence explained the Gospel reading of the day (Luke 18, 18-27) about the Savior’s conversation with the rich ruler who had come to ask Him what he must do to inherit eternal life. His Eminence stressed the importance of keeping the commandments as a condition for inheriting eternal life, showing that Saint Irodion is among those who, wishing to be perfect, detached themselves from concern for material goods and, fulfilling the Savior’s word “come, follow Me” (Lk. 18, 22), entered the monastery, taking the vow of poverty along with those of chastity and obedience, and thus became the disciple of Saint Kalinik of Cernica and later even his confessor. In the context of the approaching national holiday, the brief presentation of the life and miracles of this holy monk had a special effect on the listeners, whom the skilled preacher reminded—with remarkable oratorical mastery and great delicacy—that we Romanians are called more than ever to confess our faith not so much in words as above all by keeping the commandments and through good deeds. His Eminence urged us to remember the Savior’s call to follow Him, never forgetting that all earthly goods are passing, and that only faith and good deeds become spiritual joys that give us the hope of inheriting eternal life.

The day ended with a festive meal offered by Holy Trinity Parish in honor of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae. It was a good opportunity for our faithful to receive His Eminence’s blessing, and for the members of the Parish Council to converse with the distinguished guest, in an atmosphere of rare joy and Christian love.

This time, too, we parted from His Eminence with regret that the two days of celebration had passed too quickly. We hope, however, that if the Good God so wills, next year he will also visit us for our main patronal feast, Holy Trinity. We always await him with great love!

Reported by

Fr. Nicolai Buga, Parish Priest

title: Pastoral Visit of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae to Saint Andrew Parish in Reading, PA
intro:
On Sunday, December 1, 2019, the parishioners of Saint Andrew Parish in Reading, PA had the joy of having His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae in their midst for the celebration of the parish’s patronal feast and of Romania’s National Day. Serving the Divine Liturgy together with His Eminence Nicolae were the parish priest, Fr. Ovidiu Sabău, Protosyngellos Vincențiu and Hierodeacon Serafim of the Monastery of Saint Demetrios the New in Middletown, NY, and Fr. Mircea Airinei. His Eminence Nicolae offered special prayers for the victims of the earthquake in Albania and prayed for the repose of all the founders of Greater Romania.

After the Divine Liturgy, a Te Deum service was held for Romania’s National Day, invoking God’s help and blessing upon all the sons and daughters of the Romanian people everywhere.

In his sermon, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae spoke about the Gospel of the day, the parable of the talents, recalling Saint John Chrysostom’s interpretation of the multiplying of the talents through good deeds toward one’s neighbor: “God’s gift ought to be multiplied, likewise with God’s help. In offering and multiplying our gifts we too shall have the joy of God Himself, who as a father rejoices to give us gifts and to bless us. God, who is rich, wants us to be like Him, rich and generous.”

His Eminence Nicolae continued his sermon by speaking about Saint Andrew and the mission he fulfilled in the region of Scythia Minor, in Dobrudja. From there the hierarch went on to recall the meaning of celebrating Romania’s National Day for us, the Romanians in America, the heirs of Saint Andrew and his disciples. His Eminence Nicolae then briefly recounted the life of Saint Irodion of Lainici, whose holy relics and icon had been brought for veneration. In closing, Metropolitan Nicolae presented the parish with a new holy antimension and explained its significance.

The celebration in the church of Saint Andrew Parish in Reading concluded with the marking of ROYA Sunday through the reading of a short report on the activities of the young people of the Metropolia and an invitation to the winter camp in Allegan, MI. At the festive meal that followed, the children and young people of the parish presented a lovely program of carols and verses dedicated to the parish’s patron saint, to Romania’s National Day and to the feast of Christmas.

The celebration in Reading was also attended by Mr. Cătălin Dancu, Consul General of Romania in New York, and Mr. Radu Ancuța, Minister Plenipotentiary.

title: Celebration of the Romanian Village and the Patronal Feast of Saint Nicholas Church in Queens, New York
intro:
The Holy Fathers of the Orthodox Church, by the power of the Holy Spirit and by the mercy of God, established the fasts throughout the year as true sources of awakening of the Orthodox conscience, of purification of the soul, and of lifting up the soul through humility and prayer. The Nativity Fast, or the fast of joy, as the people call it, is an added occasion of spiritual joy for the community of Romanian Orthodox Christians in New York as well, which on Sunday, December 8, 2019,  celebrated Saint Nicholas, its patron.

It can be said that this year’s patronal feast of Saint Nicholas Church was a true blessing from God, through the liturgical services from Thursday evening to Sunday, but also through the love and joy of the faithful who, to the glory of God, were able to venerate the relics of Saint Nicholas the Hierarch and of the other saints with which the church has been adorned. The crown of the feast, blessed by the great and merciful Nicholas, was the Divine Liturgy on Sunday morning, celebrated by the parish priest, Fr. Marius Dumitrescu, Protosyngellos Vincenţiu Temirov and Hierodeacon Serafim of Saint Dimitrie Monastery in Middletown, New York, followed by a memorial service for the founders and servants of the church who have fallen asleep in the Lord.

At the end of the service, Fr. Vincențiu offered an edifying word on the meanings drawn from the Gospel reading and urged the faithful to works of mercy and love toward God and neighbor. The parish priest conveyed the blessing of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae to the faithful on this great feast. The faithful filled Saint Nicholas Church to overflowing at the Sunday morning service, a sign that it is blessed by our Savior and by Saint Nicholas the Hierarch.

After the service, all the faithful took part in the fraternal agape meal prepared by a group of families from our church. An important moment during the agape was the celebration of the Romanian Village. The Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church proclaimed 2019 the Homage Year of the Romanian village (of priests, teachers and diligent mayors). Thus, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, the Holy Synod confirms the inspiration of the poet Lucian Blaga, “Eternity was born in the village”, where… “the thirst for salvation is healed”… and the statement of the great Romanian poet Mihai Eminescu that “the Orthodox Church is the mother of the Romanian people”.

The celebration was opened and led by Fr. Marius Dumitrescu. A short film about the Romanian village produced by TRINITAS TV was shown. The festivities continued with a sweet appearance by the children of Saint Nicholas parish in a touching skit. This was followed by a concert of patriotic songs that touched the souls of those present through the fine performance and through the spontaneous innocence of the performers. Then the choir of Saint Nicholas Church poured the sweet myrrh of Nativity carols into the souls of the faithful. The festivities ended with a concert of patriotic and folk songs by the artists Brândușa Covalciuc Ciobanu and Lăcrămioara Dumitrescu.

Also attending the event were Mr. Catălin Dancu, Consul General of Romania in New York, and Mr. Dorian Branea, Director of the Romanian Cultural Institute in New York.

We thank the organizers, the donors and all the faithful of Saint Nicholas Church. May the Good God reward their love and sacrifice!

Fr. Marius Dumitrescu, Parish Priest

title: Divine Liturgy in Romanian and Meeting with the Romanian Community in Mexico City
intro:
With the blessing of His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan Nicolae, and at the invitation of the Embassy of Romania in Mexico, through Mr. Ionuț Marian Vâlcu, Minister Counselor and Chargé d’Affaires of Romania in the United Mexican States, Fr. Daniel Ene, diocesan secretary and Dean of New York, New England and the Eastern USA, visited the Romanian community in Mexico City, the capital of the Mexican Federation, from December 6 to 10, 2019.

On Friday afternoon, at the headquarters of the Embassy of Romania, Fr. Daniel Ene met with Minister Counselor Ionuț Vâlcu, Chargé d’Affaires of Romania in Mexico and interim ambassador (Romania currently has no ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary in Mexico), and with the Embassy staff. They discussed matters related to the presence of Romanians in Mexico, as well as the particular circumstances and difficulties Romanians face in adapting. In this regard, the Minister informed us that there are small Romanian communities in Mexico and in the countries of Central America. Thus, more than 800 Romanian citizens live in Mexico, over 200 of them in the capital, Ciudad de México, with the rest scattered across the other 31 states of the Mexican Republic, while in the Central American countries such as the Republic of Nicaragua, the Republic of El Salvador, the Republic of Costa Rica, the Republic of Guatemala and the Republic of Honduras, which are under the care of the Embassy of Romania in Mexico, there are very small communities of a few dozen citizens.

On Saturday, December 7, with the blessing of His Eminence Metropolitan Ignatius (Samaán) of the Antiochian Orthodox Church of Mexico, Central America and Venezuela, the Divine Liturgy was celebrated for the Romanian community at Saint George Cathedral, the old Antiochian cathedral of the city. It was organized with the support of the Association of Romanians in Mexico, and our thanks for preparing this holy service go to Mrs. Tamara Ariton and the members of the Association’s board. In addition to the Divine Liturgy, a memorial service was held  for the Romanian heroes of the 1989 Revolution and for the departed of the Romanian community. At the end of the Divine Liturgy, Fr. Daniel conveyed the blessing of His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan Nicolae to those present and gave Mrs. Ariton, President of the Association of Romanians in Mexico, an icon of the Mother of God to be the protector of the Association from now on, along with a complete set of textbooks for teaching the Romanian language and a textbook of the History and Geography of Romania. In this regard, Fr. Daniel expressed his support for the Romanian language classes with teaching materials and Romanian primers, urging the Association to also start religion classes for the children of Romanian families in Mexico and assuring them of all the teaching support needed. A meeting with the Romanian community followed in the social hall of the Antiochian Cathedral.

Saturday afternoon was an occasion to tend to pastoral needs, such as confessions, which several Romanian families greatly desired, as well as memorial services at the city cemeteries where Romanians have been laid to rest.

Sunday, December 8, 2019, brought another celebration of the Divine Liturgy among the Romanian community of Mexico City, this time at the Greek Cathedral of Saint Sophia, with the blessing of His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan Athenagoras of the Greek Orthodox Metropolis of Mexico, Central America, Colombia, Venezuela and the Caribbean Islands, which is under the jurisdiction of the Ecumenical Patriarchate. Besides the Romanian faithful, the Divine Liturgy was attended, as on the previous day, by Minister Counselor Ionuț Marian Vâlcu and members of the Embassy, together with Dr. Magdalena Ionescu, the best-known and most esteemed Romanian woman in Mexico. With a brilliant professional career, Dr. Ionescu was the physician and closest collaborator of Ana Aslan. At the end of the Divine Liturgy a Te Deum service was also held in honor of the National Day of Romania. A moving gathering followed the Divine Liturgy in the garden of the Greek cathedral, where the Romanian faithful received Orthodox calendars and small icons of the Holy Martyr Filofteia of Curtea de Argeș from His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae. The wish the Romanians expressed again and again was that at least once a year a representative of our Metropolia be among the Romanian community of Mexico City. At the end of the Divine Liturgy, Fr. Daniel gave His Eminence Archbishop Athenagoras an icon of the Mother of God in the Nicula depiction.

Another important moment of this visit was the visit to the Antiochian Cathedral of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul in Mexico City, which is also the seat of the Antiochian Orthodox Metropolis of Mexico and Central America. The Antiochian Church, as well as the Greek Church in Mexico, are a great support to our Metropolia, providing pastoral care to the Romanians who are widely scattered across the Mexican metropolis. Fr. Daniel Ene met with Archimandrite Andres Marcos, the vicar of the Antiochian Metropolis. They discussed matters related to the life of the Orthodox in Mexico, especially in the capital, Mexico City, as well as details of the cooperation between our Metropolia and the Antiochian Metropolis in the pastoral care of the Orthodox Romanians in Mexico. Special mention should be made of the care and love the Antiochian Church has shown Romanians for many years and of the active participation of Romanians in the life of the Antiochian Church. As a sign of gratitude, Fr. Daniel offered Fr. Andres, for His Eminence Metropolitan Ignatius, an icon of the Mother of God in the same unique Nicula depiction. Through the kindness of His Eminence Metropolitan Ignatius, the classes of the Romanian school in Mexico City are held on the premises of Saint George Cathedral. The Romanian association organizes these Romanian language classes for a large number of Mexicans who wish to learn Romanian.

The visit to Mexico ended with Fr. Daniel Ene’s presence at the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, the holiest place for Mexicans.

Fr. Daniel Ene

title: The Good News of the Incarnation Proclaimed through Carols at SS. Constantine and Helen Cathedral in Chicago
intro:
The joy of the Birth of the Savior of the world is proclaimed to each of us at this time through the carol, through the old song that reminds us of the sacred story of the event and its significance for us. The carol is the folk versification of what Holy Scripture reveals to us about the birth of the Child. Children and young people go caroling on Christmas Eve, bringing each of us the good news of the Incarnation of the Word, the news of God’s coming down to earth to save mankind. The carol therefore brings joy because it carries this good news. Each of us receives the carol, repeats it and passes it on to our loved ones, just like any caroler. We could say that together with the carol we too travel and are witnesses, together with those present, of the great event.

The carol is by no means a tender song that entered tradition because it passes on the memory of a historical event; rather, its value and authority rest on the message it conveys, a message identical to that of Scripture. And if the theology of the Incarnation of the Son is at times complicated and hard to understand, the carol tells us in simple words set to a melody that God came down to the human creature “to save it from evil”.

The carol urges each of us to prepare our homes and our souls to receive God. In the days of Christmas Eve, although we are fasting, we prepare our homes and fill our tables, as one carol says. But this is not for the carolers; it is for God Himself, who comes down into every home and brings blessing. This is the joy we share with the carolers. We are the hosts, and God is the heavenly guest who dwells among us. And He brings with Him the peace and happiness of the world beyond.

The choir of SS. Constantine and Helen Cathedral in Chicago presented its long-awaited program of Christmas carols on the Eve of the great feast. The caroling continued during the days of Christmas at the Divine Liturgy, and also in the homes of the lonely in nursing homes in the Chicago area. His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, the Cathedral clergy and the faithful went to proclaim to them as well the Birth of the Savior, the Good News of the Incarnation of the Son of God. The carol bore fruit and brought joy to the souls of those who were caroled, along with the hope of salvation!

title: Christmas Traditions and Customs at SS. Constantine and Helen Cathedral in Chicago, December 29, 2019
intro:
For the seventh year in a row, the program of Christmas traditions and customs took place at SS. Constantine and Helen Cathedral in Chicago on December 29, 2019. Just as it was in days gone by, when the children of the village set out with the star from the house of the priest, where they received his blessing, and then went caroling to all the households of the village, so too the lovers of Romanian traditions gathered at the Cathedral in Chicago and began the greetings and carols. The hosts of the event, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae and the priests and faithful of the Cathedral, prepared for the celebration with a setting depicting the story of the Lord’s Nativity in the manger at Bethlehem.

The traditions, customs and carols that gladdened our hearts came from Transylvania, Bessarabia, Moldavia, Muntenia and Banat, as did the folk costumes. The youngest carolers, the children of the Cathedral, were also present and greeted us with the sorcova, wishing us all the best in the New Year. They were joined by the children of the Nativity of the Lord Church in Chicago, the Hora group from the same church, Bessarabian carolers and those from the Romanian Cultural Center of Chicago. The Țurca was performed by a group of faithful of the Cathedral. The warm atmosphere conveyed that our national identity is well defined and that, even far from home, we have not forgotten that we are Romanians. In fact, as we have ended this event for the past 6 years, everyone present sang: “Nu uita că ești român/Că sus în deal la tine-n sat, Popa Ioan te-a botezat.”

For the two hours the event lasted, our thoughts went back to the Romanian village of old, with “there” becoming “here”: “Here every thought is slower and your heart beats more rarely, as if it beat not in your chest but somewhere deep in the earth,” as Blaga writes, in the village where eternity was born. This beautiful program concluded the activities dedicated to the Romanian Village in 2019 at SS. Constantine and Helen Cathedral in Chicago.

title: The 27th “Mihai Eminescu” Symposium: January 11-12, 2020, New York
intro:
For nearly three decades, the most important cultural event of the Romanian-American diaspora has been held every year in New York: the “Mihai Eminescu” Symposium, dedicated to the life and many-sided work of our national poet. The Symposium has reached its 27th edition, and the topics discussed continue to capture many aspects of the great Eminescu’s poetic and journalistic work.

This year, the symposium took place on Saturday, January 11, and Sunday, January 12, under the auspices of several distinguished institutions: the Academy of Romanian Scientists (USA branch), the Union of Professional Journalists of Romania, the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas, the Romanian Institute of Orthodox Theology and Spirituality in New York, the “Dorul” Romanian Christian Society, and “Saint Andrew” Romanian Orthodox Church in Jamaica, New York. The 2020 Symposium has a special significance, since January 15 of this year marks 170 years since the poet’s birth and, as is well known, January 15 was declared National Culture Day in 2010, as a sign of deep homage to our great poet and thinker.

The first part of the proceedings took place in the social hall of “Saint Andrew” Church in Jamaica, New York, under the motto of the historian Al. Paleologu: “Eminescu: The Guarantee of Our Identity”.  The President of the Romanian Institute of Orthodox Theology and Spirituality, Fr. Prof. Theodor Damian, as organizer, opened the symposium, welcoming the participants and guests. The whole audience sang the student song “Gaudeamus igitur”, followed by the patriotic song “Când era să moară Ștefan”. Fr. Theodor Damian read the messages of congratulations received from His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, from Doru Dinu Glăvan, President of the UZPR, and from M.N. Rusu, editor-in-chief of the journal “Lumină Lină”.

The guest of honor at the symposium, Dr. Dorian Branea, Director of the Romanian Cultural Institute in New York, presented Fr. Theodor Damian with the book “Constantin Brâncoveanu, puterea viziunii; Constantin Brâncoveanu, the power of vision” (in Romanian and English), an edition with evocative articles and photographs created by Elena Murariu. Mr. Branea congratulated the organizers for their continuing and noble work of speaking about Eminescu and honoring him through the annual symposium and the bimonthly sessions of the literary circle. The President of the “Dorul” Romanian Christian Society (founded in 1903), engineer Cristian F. Pascu,  co-organizer of the symposium, highlighted the achievements of the venerable society and spoke about important community projects. The scholarly papers brought to light little-known aspects of the life and work of Mihai Eminescu.

Marian Nencescu, PhD in philosophy, writer, journalist, editor and researcher at the Institute of Philosophy of the Romanian Academy in Bucharest, was the guest of honor at the symposium. We quote selectively from Mr. Nencescu’s CV: graduate of the Faculty of Letters of the University of Bucharest, postgraduate course in journalism, doctorate on a topic from Romanian folklore, reporter, editor-in-chief, scientific researcher, with monthly/quarterly columns of literary criticism, literary history and philosophy in numerous prestigious journals in Romania, a major contributor to the volume “Însemnări din zilele Revoluției”, award winner at the Civic, Legal and Police Book Fair of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, member of the Union of Professional Journalists of Romania and of the Writers’ Union.  Mr. Marian Nencescu presented the paper “Eminescu’s Archaeus, from Tale to Being”.

Known and appreciated by the Romanians of New York, guest of honor and participant in many editions of the “Eminescu” Symposium, Professor Ștefan Stoenescu is a renowned scholar of English and Romanian, a comparatist and editor, and a prominent figure in Romanian, English and American culture alike. He presented the paper “Historical Consciousness in Mihai Eminescu’s Vision”.

Writer and university professor Valentina Ciaprazi is a presence Romanians look forward to with interest, since her words add meaning and color to the text under discussion. With remarkable gifts as a literary critic, she is a brilliant personality who contributes to a better understanding of the creative act. Valentina Ciaprazi’s paper was entitled “Eminescu, the Spiritual Architect of Romania Yesterday and Today”.

Fr. Prof. Dr. Theodor Damian is a writer, professor of philosophy and ethics at Metropolitan College of NY, president of the American Branch of the Academy of Romanian Scientists and of the Romanian Institute of Orthodox Theology and Spirituality, but above all he is the friend and counselor of the people of the Romanian-American community, our cultural mentor and, at the same time, an awaited and valued messenger in Romania, where he presents the literary and philosophical works of Romanians in the diaspora and speaks with affection about our achievements. No one else, no other Romanian, carries on so many important activities at once: priest, college professor, organizer and leader of symposia, literary circles and literary evenings, editor of cultural journals, author of books of fiction and philosophy. A wonderful man, a 21st-century Heliade Rădulescu, here, far from the homeland, but with a Romanian Renaissance soul who has left his cultural mark on the consciousness of the present generation and of those to come. Fr. Theodor Damian presented the paper “The Unity between Church and Nation in Eminescu’s Conviction”.

Prof. Dr. Doru Tsaganea teaches mathematics at Metropolitan College of New York, but we are sure that he also teaches his students civic standards of life, for Mr. Doru Tsaganea is a refined intellectual, a luminous personality of the Romanian-American community. His statements are always supported by relevant, convincing quotations. Present at many of our major activities, and an amateur photographer with great artistic intuition, he is appreciated by all who listen to him and admire his photographs. Prof. Doru Tsaganea’s paper was “The Significance of Eminescu’s Conception of the Nation for Safeguarding National Identity in Europe”. The symposium was moderated by Professor Mariana Terra.

The second part of the anniversary event took place on Sunday, January 12, at “Holy Apostles Peter and Paul” Church in Astoria, Queens, NY, on the theme “Homage to Eminescu: Culture and Creation”. The guests of honor at the event were Dr. Marian Nencescu and his wife Camelia, Consul Călin Radu Ancuța and his wife, and Economic Consul Gabriel Duțu with members of the Consulate General of Romania in New York. A moving memorial service was held in the church for Mihai Eminescu, Grigore Vieru, Metropolitan Antonie Plămădeală and George Alexe.

The second part of the symposium continued in the church’s social hall.  The guest of honor at the symposium was Prof. Dr. Marian Nencescu who, appreciating the fruitful activity of the Romanian-Americans of New York and of the community around Fr. Theodor Damian, warmly congratulated the organizers and participants. From Eminescu’s work, Alexandra Țurcanu performed songs set to the verses of “Pe lângă plopii fără soț”, “Sara pe deal”, “Mai am un singur dor”, “De ce nu vii”, “Ce-ți doresc eu ție, dulce Românie”. Poems by Eminescu were also recited by Valentina Ciaprazi, Elena Mitru, Cristian Pascu, Paul Murariu, Cătălin Condurache and Stephan Benedict.

Dr. Napoleon Săvescu, President of the Parish Council of “Holy Apostles Peter&Paul” Church, highlighted Eminescu’s invaluable contribution, through articles and historically inspired poems, to a deeper knowledge of the ancient history of our Geto-Dacian people. The song “Eminescu e cu noi” was played. Alex Marmara, photojournalist of the newspaper “Romanian Journal” and of the journal “Lumină lină”, captured special moments of the two days of the symposium. Engineer Cristian Pascu closed the cultural session of the 2020 “Mihai Eminescu” Symposium, praising the remarkable quality of the act of homage and the joy of being together again, for a few hours, in the company of fond thoughts of Eminescu.

The symposium bearing the name of our national poet proved once  again that we Romanians, wherever we may be on this earth, know how to honor the geniuses of Romanian culture and to take pride in those who hold high the red, yellow and blue tricolor flag, to eternity and back.

Prof. Mariana Terra

title: Hierarchical Visit and Service at the Patronal Feast of the Romanian Orthodox Church in Tarragona, Spain
intro:
Ever since the founding of the “Holy Hierarchs Callinicus of Cernica and Fructuosus of Tarragona” Parish in 2004, a beautiful custom has taken shape: every January a hierarch  of the Romanian Orthodox Church comes to Tarragona for the second patronal feast of this community, Saint Fructuosus of Tarragona, the first bishop of the city and also the first known saint of the Iberian land, who was martyred on January 21, 259, burned at the stake together with his two deacons, Saints Augurius and Eulogius. 
 
This year, with the blessing of His Grace Bishop Timotei of the Romanian Orthodox Diocese of Spain and Portugal, His Eminence Nicolae, Romanian Orthodox Archbishop of the United States of America and Romanian Orthodox Metropolitan of the Americas, came among us, becoming the 10th hierarch to visit our community. 
 
On Sunday, January 19, 2020, the Divine Liturgy was served in the parish church in Tarragona, presided over by His Eminence Nicolae together with Fr. Vasile Băltărețu, the parish priest of the community, and Deacon Lucian Crasovan. 
 
In his homily, His Eminence Nicolae spoke to the faithful about the importance of gratitude, giving as an example the leper healed by the Savior who returned to Him to give thanks. His Eminence Nicolae also gave a presentation on the Romanian Orthodox communities in the United States and Canada, some of them more than 100 years old and now in their 4th or 5th generation of faithful, and on their efforts to keep their ancestral faith after so long a time. 
 
As a sign of gratitude and appreciation, Fr. Vasile Băltărețu and the community presented His Eminence Nicolae with a blessing cross and two silver-plated icons, and the two shared memories from the time when both of them, natives of Constanța, were young students at the Faculty of Theology in Sibiu. 
 
At the end, the faithful present each received  a small icon from His Eminence Nicolae and venerated the relics of Saint Fructuosus and of Saint Callinicus of Cernica, received as gifts from the Cardinal of Genoa (Italy) through our ruling hierarch, His Grace Timotei, and from His Beatitude Patriarch Daniel of the Romanian Orthodox Church, respectively. 
 
In the evening, at the church in the city of Reus, the Mystery of Holy Unction was served, led by His Eminence Nicolae and surrounded by a synaxis of priests: Fr. Vasile Băltărețu of the host parish, Fr. Ionuț Ilie of the Tortosa Parish, Fr. Gheorghe Crăciun of the Vielha Parish, Fr. Alexandru Poșteanu of the Manzanares Parish, and Deacon Lucian Crasovan. 
 
At the close of this holy service, His Eminence Nicolae spoke to the faithful about health of body and of soul. 
 
The hierarch from across the ocean also visited the parish school room, set up in 2005 in the church’s choir loft and coordinated by Preoteasa Prof. Elena Băltărețu, where several generations of Romanian children have learned about the Romanian language, culture and spirituality. 
 
Holy Hierarch Fructuosus, pray to God for us!
 
Preoteasa Elena Băltărețu

title: The Union of the Romanian Principalities Celebrated in Mexico
intro:
The 161st anniversary of the Union of the Romanian Principalities and the 170th anniversary of the birth of the national poet Mihai Eminescu were also an occasion for celebration for the Romanians in Mexico. On Friday, January 24, 2020, the Embassy of Romania in the Federal Republic of Mexico hosted the traditional annual gathering with the Romanian community in Mexico to celebrate the Day of the Union of the Romanian Principalities (January 24) and National Culture Day (January 15).

At the invitation of Mr. Ionuț Marian Vâlcu, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim of the Embassy of Romania in Mexico, Fr. Daniel Adrian Ene, diocesan secretary and Dean of New York, New England and the Eastern USA, attended on behalf of the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas. Many Romanians from the Mexico City area and from other cities of the federation took part, spending a few hours speaking and feeling Romanian.

The gathering began with words of welcome from Mr. Ionuț Vâlcu, who stressed the historical importance of the Union of the Principalities and also outlined some of the main activities the Embassy will carry out during 2020.

In his address, Fr. Daniel Ene warmly thanked them for the invitation, which made possible the meeting with the Romanian community and the joy of bringing the blessing of His Eminence Archbishop and Metropolitan Nicolae, and urged those present to unity: “Speaking about the Union of the Romanian Principalities, we feel bound to bring to the fore the need for unity among ourselves, the Romanians whose steps have been guided to these beautiful and sunny lands. We do not have a church here, but the church does not consist of walls, but of our unity, as Christ says in Holy Scripture, Where two or three are gathered together in My name, I am there in the midst of them. This unity brings God’s blessing and the spiritual progress of the community. But in order to form a community, a church of Christ, we must be much more active and more responsible; we must become part of the church, and the church must also become an active part of our lives.”

An important moment of the gathering was the report presented by the Association of Romanians in Mexico through Mrs. Tamara Ariton, who invited everyone to the Association’s General Assembly to be held on Saturday, February 8, 2020.

The most moving and beautiful moment, however, came in the second part of the gathering, when Mexican students from the Romanian language class of UNAM (Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México - the largest and best-known Mexican university) recited Scrisoarea a III-a and Luceafărul by Mihai Eminescu. The Romanian language course at UNAM (Department of French, Catalan and Romanian) is coordinated by Professor Mihaela Liana Mihăilescu. The evening ended with the Hora Unirii.

Orthodox calendars, small icons and the journal “Lumină lină” of the Institute of Orthodox Spirituality in New York were some of the gifts Fr. Daniel Ene brought to those present. His visit to Mexico ended on Sunday, January 26, 2020, with the Holy and Divine Liturgy and a memorial service in Romanian, held with the blessing of His Eminence Metropolitan Ignatius (Samaán) of the Antiochian Orthodox Church of Mexico, Central America and Venezuela at Saint George Cathedral, the old Antiochian cathedral of the city.

The agape meal that followed in the church’s social hall gave Fr. Daniel the opportunity to discuss various topics with the community. The first part was catechetical in nature, and the second administrative. The Romanian community asked to have a Romanian Orthodox priest and the Holy Services in Romanian for the Feast of Holy Pascha.

Reported by
Fr. Daniel Ene

title: Patronal Feast for the Romanians of Syracuse, New York
intro:
January 30 and the feast of the Three Holy Hierarchs are each year an occasion of great celebration for the Romanian community of Syracuse, a city in the center of New York State, which has the only church under their patronage in the Romanian Orthodox Archdiocese of the United States of America.

This year an encouraging number of faithful took part in the Divine Liturgy celebrated by Dean Fr. Daniel Ene (the administrator of the mission) at St. Sophia Greek Church in Syracuse, which has long been host to the mission. Fr. David Smith, the parish priest of the Greek church, served together with the dean.

Immediately after the Divine Liturgy, the ladies of the parish prepared the patronal feast meal in the social hall. During the meal there were two presentations. The first was about the Metropolia’s youth organization, ROYA, and consisted of a short film about the “Rădăcini” summer camp. The film was accompanied by some comments and impressions from young Elena Coman, who took part in the ROYA congress and the winter camp on behalf of the Syracuse mission.

The second presentation was about the “Calea” catechetical plan, which is under way in all the parishes of the Archdiocese of the United States. The first topic was the Call to Faith.

The Three Holy Hierarchs Romanian Orthodox Mission in Syracuse, NY (The Three Holy Hierarchs: Basil, Gregory, and John Romanian Orthodox Church) was founded out of a desire to serve the spiritual and faith needs of the Romanian community in this city. The preparation for this founding came through the visit of His Eminence Nicolae, Archbishop of the Romanian Orthodox Church in America and Canada, and the idea took shape through his grace-filled encouragement, addressed to us at the meeting that followed the Divine Liturgy in February 2004. The founding meeting of the Mission took place on March 21 under the pastoral care of Fr. Daniel Adrian Ene, of Holy Trinity Church in Rochester. At this meeting a Parish Council was elected by open vote, the name of the mission (the Three Holy Hierarchs) and its patronal feast, celebrated on January 30, were decided, also by open vote, and the date of the first religious service was set. The President of the Mission then drew up the Mission’s Articles of Incorporation, which were signed before a notary on March 26, 2004. This document was filed with Onondaga County in May 2004. The first Divine Liturgy was celebrated by Fr. Daniel Ene on May 15, 2004. It was attended by all the founding members and a small number of other faithful contacted directly by the Mission’s council members or who came to the service on their own initiative. Only two months later, the Act of Recognition dated July 2, 2004, was received from the Romanian Orthodox Archdiocese in America and Canada.

The first patronal feast of the Three Holy Hierarchs Romanian Orthodox Mission took place on January 29, 2005, at St. Sophia Greek Church in Syracuse. The Divine Liturgy, celebrated by His Eminence Nicolae, Archbishop of the Romanian Orthodox Church in America and Canada, the parish priest of St. Sophia Church, and the parish priest of Holy Trinity Church in Victor, was followed by a festive meal attended by guests from Rochester and Ithaca and by parishioners of other Orthodox churches in Syracuse and nearby towns. There was also a viewing of a Romanian cultural and folk exhibition prepared by the parishioners of the Mission.

The period that followed was one of shaping our identity, not only as Orthodox Christians but also as Romanians. Services are still held once a month in the beautiful chapel of St. Sophia Church in Syracuse, NY. The holy mysteries of Baptism, Marriage and Holy Unction are also special moments in the life of our mission. In 2009-2010 there were several attempts to purchase a former Roman Catholic church, which unfortunately ended without any result. The mission is growing slowly, and we hope soon to begin again the process of acquiring our own place of worship. All the activities of our mission are under the blessing of our Fr. Daniel Adrian Ene of Rochester, NY, who has always tried to bring a ray of spiritual fulfillment to the Romanians of Syracuse as well. We have also enjoyed several pastoral visits from our hierarchs, His Eminence Nicolae and His Grace Vicar Bishop Ioan Casian of Vicina, on the occasion of the mission’s patronal feast.

Even though they are a small community, we hope, with the help of the Good God, that they will remain strong in the true and right faith of Christ. Always in everyone’s mind has been the word of the Holy Gospel of Luke, which says: “Do not fear, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12, 32)

title: Hierarchal Visit and Blessed Ministry at Putna Monastery
intro:
On February 15–16, His Eminence Nicolae, Romanian Orthodox Metropolitan of the Americas, was present at Putna Monastery, taking part in several church services held on those days.

On Saturday, His Eminence Nicolae, together with the Abbot of the monastery, Archimandrite Melchisedec Velnic, and other clergy of the monastery, served the 40-day memorial service for Colonel Gheorghe Butnaru (March 28, 1949 – January 9, 2019), founder of Saint George Church within the Border Guard Regiment in Rădăuți.

Mr. Gheorghe Butnaru, a career officer, commanded the 74th Border Guard Regiment in Rădăuți. The colonel was a man of deep faith who, out of love for God, shared the faith with others like a lay missionary. An exceptional husband and father in his own family, he was also a true father to his subordinates. In the mind of the monastic community, which knew him very well over the past 30 years, he is an example of seriousness in faith, in love for his nation and in responsibility toward his fellow men.

In his word after the memorial service, His Eminence Nicolae spoke about the awareness of eternal life and the preparation for it, things that were essential for Colonel Butnaru and that all of us, monastics and laity, are called to fulfill.

In the afternoon, His Eminence Nicolae, together with the Abbot and clergy of the monastery, celebrated a service of thanksgiving for the 30th wedding anniversary of Adrian and Carolina Alui Gheorghe. The writer and teacher Adrian Alui Gheorghe has taken part in many cultural and youth activities organized at the monastery in recent years.

His Eminence Nicolae congratulated the couple and spoke about the importance of the family and the need for role models for young people, to show them the beauty and blessing of the family.

“Romania will not survive if families do not bring children into the world. Counsel and example are expected from you and from priests. Only in this way will Romania be saved. In the history of humankind we see that peoples have been saved through sacrifice and through understanding this: that the blessing of God poured out upon a family must be multiplied through the birth of children and through example.”

On the Sunday of the Prodigal Son, His Eminence celebrated the Divine Liturgy in the voivodal church.

In his homily, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae first spoke about the parable of the prodigal son.

“It is one of the most beautiful pages of Holy Scripture, in which each of us finds the way of return to the heavenly Father. God’s love is so great, it is beyond our power of understanding.

The younger son thought himself a mature man who could manage his life on his own. But he ended up spending his money on prodigal living and discovered that he was not mature enough. How much separation from the heavenly Father can cost us! Each of us has this temptation, to do what we want and forget the father’s love.

In his search for independence, the prodigal son was no longer himself; he was not in his right mind. But he understood his estrangement, and these are the steps of his repentance: he came to himself, he resolved to ask forgiveness, and then he carried out this resolve.

The father was waiting for him. His fatherly love had not died out. The father did not wait for an explanation of how he had spent his inheritance.

The son plans to say: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants.”

But he did not say all he had planned; he said only: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight, and am no longer worthy to be called your son.” For he saw on his father’s face a fatherly love, a love that would not have allowed him to become a hired servant, but only a son.

The prodigal son understood that he was immature and wished at least to become a hired servant again. He was received back as a son. He is an example of repentance for all of us, a repentance that must find its hope in God’s fatherly love. He shows us what it means to be sons of the heavenly Father.”

In the second part of his homily, His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae spoke about the Romanians in America and the role of the church for them.

“We are all parents and we must build a spiritual home for our children. Let us bring them to church and give them a Christian education. What would have happened to the son if he had not had a home and had not remembered his father’s love? He would have kept wandering in the world, because he would have had no home to return to. If we do not build a spiritual home for our children, then when our children find themselves in the situation of the prodigal son, they will not know where to return and will go astray.

Over there we are trying to build a spiritual home to which the Romanians who have gone to America can return. We are trying to take care of their children, so that they do not lose their way after leaving Romania for foreign countries and remain astray. Many Romanians are looking for both spiritual and material settlement. If they do not also find the spiritual one, they are not content with the material one alone.

We went as shepherds after the flock. We went to build churches and communities for these Romanians who left Romania, and especially for their children. Young people in particular are subjected to many pressures.

The call to all parents, both to you who are in Romania and to those who have left Romania, is to build a spiritual home for parents and for their children.

We must take care of children and young people. We must pass on to them a fundamental truth: that the church in which they pray now, at their age, is their church, not just their parents’ church, to be abandoned when they leave for school or start families of their own. It is their church and they must be responsible for it. They must be the ones who will continue to pray in it.

We have parishes that are 80 years old, 100 years old. Some have continued to exist, others have not. Living the Christian faith is not a game; it is a very serious matter, and this way of life is tested over time, across generations. If we have not raised our children and grandchildren in the church, that church will disappear. Which means that we have not lived our Christian life authentically. We have not understood what it means to be a Christian, to set an example for our children and grandchildren, what it means to be part of a community, responsible for its well-being and its future. In 60 years, in 100 years, it will be seen how Christian we were. There, in America, we already see it.

That is why we must understand how to raise our children, how to build them a spiritual home, how to care for their future, so that they do not lose their way in this world.”

We continue to be one family, you who are in the homeland and we who have left. We have the responsibility to pray for one another, to remain one family.”

The Abbot thanked His Eminence Nicolae for his words and said he hopes that the bond with the Romanian brothers and sisters in America will continue in the future.

title: Pastoral Letter of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church for the Sunday of Orthodoxy in the Year of Our Lord 2020
intro:
To the most venerable monastic orders, the most reverend clergy and the most beloved faithful of the Romanian Patriarchate,
Grace, joy and peace from God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and from us fatherly blessings!

Most Venerable and Most Reverend Fathers, servants of the Holy Altars,
Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ the Lord,

 

We are in a period of particular spiritual richness, with a distinctive spiritual beauty, expressed in a unique way through the liturgical order we have gone through in the first week of Great Lent. The call of the liturgical texts to recognize our state of sin and to strive, through repentance, toward “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4, 13) has enlightened the soul in the first days of this season of the Fast of Holy Pascha.

This spiritual journey toward the feast of the Resurrection will continue alongside Christ the Lord, the Great Pilgrim, Who accompanies us through the Sacraments of the Church, especially through frequent Confession and Communion, with more careful and more intense preparation.

The first Sunday of Great Lent is called the Sunday of Orthodoxy and is a real call to cultivate our spiritual identity and to answer the call of the Lord Jesus Christ: “Follow Me” (John 1, 43), as today’s Gospel text shows us. In today’s confused society, the orthodoxy of life means uniting the confession of the right faith with right daily living. In this way we too can address to our fellow human beings the invitation of the Holy Apostle Philip: “Come and see!” (John 1, 46).

Sharing or communicating the true faith is accomplished through the word, but also through the light of a person’s life in communion with Christ. In this sense, Fr. Dumitru Stăniloae stated: “The words of Christ have an exceptional unifying power through the evidence of the truth they express and through the love they communicate… In fact, the word is a person, or the person is a word. One cannot exist without the other. The word is a person for a person, and the person is a word for a person. Even when silent, the person speaks to me… because it is life that pulses for me, that is attentive to me and tells me this through words or through its mere presence.”[1] In a crowded world that is nevertheless so lonely in spirit, Orthodoxy offers us a way out of this crisis through the communion of persons in the love of God, a communion that is “deeper when (people) think together and communicate their thinking through words referring to God, as their Origin, and to the world as the common environment necessary to their persons.”[2]

Right-believing Christians,

This living and luminous expression of our right faith through liturgical communion is celebrated especially on the Sunday of Orthodoxy. The origin of this feast lies in an extremely troubled period, between the years 726 and 843, when those who venerated the holy icons suffered the contempt of those who disregarded the icons, called iconoclasts. The pride and hostility of Emperor Leo III the Isaurian (717-741) led to iconoclasm becoming the official religious policy of the empire. Overcome by arrogance and lacking credible arguments, Emperor Leo the Isaurian justified the decisions he took against the veneration of icons by an absolutist and radical principle: “I am emperor and priest at the same time”[3]. This arrogant and abusive attitude was brilliantly and firmly opposed by Saint John of Damascus, of the Monastery of Saint Sabbas near Jerusalem. He protested both against the emperor’s taking upon himself rights that had no foundation in Christian teaching and against the new imperial policy that rejected the icons.

In his effort to define the icon, arguing that it is not a graven image or an idol, Saint John of Damascus offers a logical explanation of the icon as a likeness that depicts the original. In this sense, he says: “The icon, then, is not identical with the original but differs from it in something and by something. The icon is a likeness, a model, an impression of someone, which shows in itself the one depicted in the icon.”[4] In other words, the icon shows us the Person depicted on it, Whom we cannot have physically before us, for if the Person were physically beside us, we would not need the icon. Thus, the icon aims to direct the soul toward the Person represented on it, because “man, being circumscribed in time and space, cannot have direct knowledge of things invisible, nor of things past or future, nor of things distant in space.”[5] Christ the Lord became man substantially and really, dwelt on earth, lived among people, worked miracles, suffered, was crucified, rose again and ascended into heaven, all of this taking place really, in the sight of people. Therefore, “when these things happened, His image was depicted in the icon to remind us of Him and so that we, who were not present then, might receive teaching, so that, without having seen, but hearing and believing, we may share in the Lord’s blessedness.”[6] The tradition of venerating icons is unwritten, just as bowing toward the east or making the sign of the holy cross is unwritten, and by bowing before the holy icons we honor the Person depicted in the icon, not the material from which the icon is made. That is why Saint John of Damascus said: “I do not worship matter, but I worship the One Who for my sake became matter”, that is, Christ Who became incarnate and became man.

The Seventh Ecumenical Council, held in Constantinople from September 24 to October 13, 787, debated the problem of iconoclasm. By the consensus of the participating Holy Fathers, the church tradition concerning the veneration of the holy icons was reaffirmed, and in the final session the Orthodox teaching on the holy icons was formulated. However, the reception of the decisions of the Seventh Ecumenical Council was difficult, especially after the crowning of the iconoclast Emperor Leo the Armenian (813-820), who, shortly after the teaching on the veneration of icons had been defined, opened another period of rejection of icons and persecution of those who venerated the holy icons. For this reason, the final victory of Orthodoxy over the iconoclasts was proclaimed only in the year 843, on the first Sunday of Great Lent. This victory was due in great measure to the right-believing Empress Theodora, and also to Patriarch Methodios of Constantinople (843-847), who, together with the Orthodox people, definitively and officially proclaimed the veneration of the Holy Icons through a triumphal procession in the capital of the Byzantine Empire. In remembrance of this victory, to this day, on the feast of the Sunday of Orthodoxy, processions are held in which the Orthodox faithful confess their faith carrying holy icons in their hands.

Orthodox Christians,

Through the veneration of the holy icons, this Sunday of Orthodoxy calls us to discover the image of the eternal God imprinted in man (cf. Genesis 1, 26-27), and also the immortality of the human soul that results from this quality. Saint Athanasius the Great, in the “Treatise on the Incarnation of the Word,” states that God gave man not only existence, but also the capacity to know God and to live eternally in communion with Him[7].

Overwhelmed by many problems and temptations which he can no longer cope with, man today no longer finds time to cultivate the image of God within him, in order to attain likeness to the Holy God, that is, holiness. By neglecting communion with God and the cultivation of the image of God within him, and also by overvaluing the body as the interface of dialogue, man becomes a stranger to himself and to his vocation to attain eternal life. And in the void of his sadness he aggressively proclaims that God has abandoned him or that God does not exist, and that human life ends with the death of the body. Yet, “only by loving God and only by being conscious that he is loved by God does man advance in a life of which he never tires. Even whoever truly loves a person and is loved by that person would wish that neither he nor that person should die,” says Fr. Dumitru Stăniloae[8].

In this regard, God’s saints in heaven, painted in icons, are our teachers and intercessors for us, at all times and in every place, because in them works the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, Who is “the same yesterday, today, and forever” (Hebrews 13, 8). Coming to this knowledge of man’s vocation to attain holiness through communion with God, the One Who alone is Holy, we will understand man’s need for healing from sin as selfish existence, in order to discover the joy of communion with God and with our fellow human beings, in time and in eternity. That is why the Holy Apostle Paul urges us, saying: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see the Lord” (Hebrews 12, 14).

Beloved spiritual sons and daughters,

In order to highlight the generous contribution of church communities to helping those in need, as a concrete response to the merciful love of Christ celebrated in the Eucharistic Liturgy, the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church dedicated the year 2020 as the “Commemorative Year of Romanian Orthodox Philanthropists”. The Church’s organization of philanthropy over time is a model that our Church embraces today as well. The more than 800 social and philanthropic institutions, projects and programs organized and supported by the Romanian Orthodox Church are a living witness to the value placed on the image of the human person in poverty and suffering. Thus, the vocation of merciful love of the generous believer can be expressed in Christian philanthropy, in concrete deeds of help for people in difficulty.

That is why, especially during the Fast of Holy Pascha, we have the opportunity to show our merciful and humble love toward people who are suffering. Whenever they have been called to support their fellow human beings in need and suffering, our faithful have shown brotherly love and generosity. Our Church makes such an appeal on the first Sunday of Great Lent as well, by organizing a collection for the Central Missionary Fund, to support the pastoral, missionary and social-philanthropic projects of the Romanian Orthodox Church.

We therefore urge you, with all fatherly love, to help the missionary work of the isolated and aging parishes, ever more numerous in our country, where diligent and self-sacrificing priests serve God and people. Through everyone’s contribution, the philanthropic work of the Church in society, in support of our neighbors in difficulty, will be broader and more effective, because “He who has pity on the poor lends to the Lord, and He will pay back what he has given” (Proverbs 19, 17). Responding to this call through our common support, the Romanian parish communities in the diaspora will also feel closer to home, strengthening their identity of faith and nation.

Giving thanks to the Lord for pouring out upon us His good giving and His perfect gift, we wish you all a beneficial spiritual ascent during the Fast of Holy Pascha, at the end of which may we meet Christ Jesus, Crucified and Risen, “that our joy may be full” (2 John 1, 12). We bless you in a fatherly way with the words of the Holy Apostle Paul: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13, 13).

President of the Holy Synod of the Romanian Orthodox Church,

title: A Whole World “Met” in New York on the Sunday of the Lord’s Resurrection!
intro:
In the Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas, at Holy Trinity Parish in Rochester, in New York State, so sorely tried by this pandemic, the Vespers service of Pascha Sunday, popularly called the “Second Resurrection,” was truly memorable. With the blessing of His Eminence Metropolitan Nicolae, the Holy Gospel, which is read in several languages to symbolize that the joy of Christ’s Resurrection is proclaimed everywhere, was read by priests from various countries of the world or who serve in the very countries where each language is spoken.

In the context of the fight against the spread of this new plague that has befallen us, services are now broadcast online in most parishes of our Metropolia, without the participation of the lay faithful. This process of adapting to the modern means of live streaming is difficult both for the serving priests and for the faithful, especially those who are not yet familiar with electronic devices.

New York State quickly became the world epicenter of this pandemic, and the Romanian community living both in NYC and in the other metropolitan areas of the state is equally tried. Of the total of 830,789 people infected and 45,638 people deceased in the USA, 258,589 are in New York State alone, and of the total number of deceased, 19,118. The number of Romanians, however, is still very small: consultation with the parishes of the Metropolia in New York State shows that there are around 20 Romanians who have tested positive for COVID 19, most of them recovering, with only one person in a more serious condition and only 2 people deceased.

Knowing these things, Fr. Daniel Ene, Dean of New York, New England and the Eastern USA, organized this special Paschal service, in which priests and deacons from several countries of the world took part, to strengthen and comfort all those who are being tried.

Thus the Holy Gospel could be broadcast live in ROMANIAN, read by the parish priest and Dean of New York, Fr. Daniel Ene; in ENGLISH by Fr. Timothy SAS (Duluth, MINNESOTA USA, who celebrated the first Divine Liturgy in the community in this area of New York 18 years ago and is a founder of the church); SPANISH – Fr. Antonio GARCIA (Caracas, VENEZUELA – parish priest of the Romanian Church of SS. Constantine and Helen); LATIN – Fr. Asst. Prof. Dr. Alexandru BARNA (Bucharest, ROMANIA – “Justinian Patriarhul” Faculty of Orthodox Theology); GREEK – Fr. Iustinian DEAC (Los Angeles, CALIFORNIA USA – Elevation of the Holy Cross Church – formerly a co-serving priest in NY with the Dean); FRENCH – Deacon Dr. Florin Ciprian PETRE (doctor of theology of the Catholic University of Strasbourg, FRANCE, and coordinating editor of Religious Programs at Radio TRINITAS, producer of the program EVANGHELIE ȘI VIAȚĂ – formerly a cantor at Holy Trinity Church in Rochester more than 10 years ago); PORTUGUESE – psychiatrist and priest Fr. Benedict BOTH (Lisbon, PORTUGAL/ CLUJ ROMANIA, a spiritual son of the church in New York); ITALIAN – Fr. Dr. Paul Octavian PORCESCU (Settimo Torinese, ITALY – formerly serving in our Metropolia and now serving in the sorely tried Diocese of Italy); GERMAN – Fr. Cosmin STAN (MonchengladBach-Viersen, GERMANY – parish priest of the Romanian Church there); ARABIC – Fr. Gheorghe COSTEA, priest of the Romanian Orthodox in SYRIA and LEBANON; UKRAINIAN – Fr. Ioan ARDELEAN (Seattle WASHINGTON USA – formerly a member of the church in NY, now parish priest of SS. Joachim and Anna Church in Seattle); and in RUSSIAN by Fr. Ioan Bidașcă (Izvorul Mureșului, HARGHITA ROMANIA – priest of the sister parish in Romania under the twinning agreement begun in the Centennial year of Greater Romania).

At the end of the service, Dean Fr. Daniel Ene spoke to the faithful both about the symbolism of this reading of the Holy Gospel in several languages and about the fact that, although we are isolated at home and cannot embrace one another, as the doxastikon at the Praises of the Resurrection Matins says, and cannot meet as we would wish, we must nevertheless remain in brotherly communion. And just as borders and such great distance did not keep us from serving together, even virtually, so too our love for one another and for the whole world must grow, together with prayer. Thanking all the priests for their presence and for the love they showed to the Romanian community in New York, the Dean gave each of them the opportunity to say a few words over the internet. Fr. Antonio Garcia of Caracas, Venezuela also gave a short message in Spanish for all the Romanians who live or find themselves in these times in the countries of Latin America. Fr. Daniel Ene then offered, at the end, words of encouragement and strength for the Romanians in New York, as well as for the diplomatic corps and the Romanians in Mexico and South America.

In a few words, we can say that a whole world “met” in NEW YORK on the Sunday of the Lord’s Resurrection!

The service can be watched on the parish’s Facebook page

https://www.facebook.com/112628190142937/videos/232559771350313/

Dean Fr. Daniel Ene

title: Virtual Camp, July 2020
intro:
Dear teachers, parents and children,

The Romanian Orthodox Metropolia of the Americas invites you to take part in the virtual camp organized for children ages 7 to 14 on the following dates:

  • Friday, July 10 (7.00 pm – 8.00 pm CST)
  • Saturday, July 11 (11.00 am – 2.00 pm CST)
  • Friday, July 24 (7.00 pm – 8.00 pm)
  • Saturday, July 25 (11.00 am – 2.00 pm)

The camp will take place online, using the Zoom platform.

The organizers’ wish for this camp is to familiarize the children with the Orthodox Christian faith and Romanian traditions. The program includes common prayer, Orthodox education, interactive games, puppet theater, group discussions, drawing, cooking lessons, etc.

To register, please fill out the online form at this address: 

https://forms.gle/R2vjSfHJVdBTis1UA

For more information, please contact us by email:

Violeta Vancea: violetavancea@yahoo.com

Mirela Manga: mirela_manga@yahoo.com

Mariana Somogyi: mariana.somogyi@gmail.com

We look forward to seeing you!
